# GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO
# LORD OF MIRANDOLA AND
# Count of Concordia,
## AN EXAMINATION OF THE VANITY OF THE DOCTRINE
## of the gentiles, and of the truth of Christian Discipline.
### DIVIDED INTO SIX BOOKS,
Of which three attack every sect of Philosophers in general, and the remaining
attack the Aristotelian sect and Aristotle's own weapons in particular,
WHILE EVERYWHERE THE CHRISTIAN
Discipline is both asserted and celebrated.

Reader, enjoy this golden work,
recently brought into the light.

--- Page 5 ---
Pope Leo X

<margin>d</margin> Beloved son, greetings and apostolic blessing. It has always been our particular custom (which our house also observed previously) to freely embrace and cherish those men who excel in any condition of learning and virtue. Among all others, however, we have pursued your family with every zeal of benevolence and duty of affection—both for its own splendor and nobility, and for the excellence of your uncle, Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note>. He was a man unique in his age and conspicuous for his mastery of manifold types of knowledge, and he lived in the closest and most familiar friendship with Lorenzo de' Medici, our father according to the flesh, of grateful memory. To this is also added that you, endowed with the highest intellect and the greatest erudition, never degenerate from your ancestors, but by following their footsteps in an outstanding manner, you show yourself worthy and fit. Thus, you are able not only to maintain the bond of ancient friendship between us, but also to excite and daily increase our love and paternal charity toward you and yours in a greater measure. Indeed, you have applied perfection and refinement to all the works composed by your uncle—which, overtaken by death, he had left behind partly incomplete and partly uncorrected—as well as to the many excellent works which you yourself have published. As our beloved son Hercules, Cardinal of Aragon and Deacon of Saint Agatha, has reported to us in your name, you have decided to publish these works for the common use of scholars (whom we favor above all) in a more corrected form than before, and to gift them to the public. To ensure they come out more amended and polished, you have hired a printer in your town of Mirandola at your own expense and under your own supervision.

But because you fear that if these volumes were to go out without protection, they might immediately be reprinted by others to the prejudice of your honor and your financial loss, you have taken care to have us humbly petitioned through the aforementioned Cardinal, that we might deign to kindly provide you with a suitable remedy. We, therefore, inclined by such petitions and desiring (as far as we can with God's help) to grant your honorable wishes and likewise to provide for your indemnity—so that you may undertake the completion of such a laudable work more promptly and securely—do hereby command and expressly forbid, by these presents, all and singular persons professing the Christian faith anywhere. Under penalty of excommunication <note>original: "excommunicationis latae sententiae," a formal ecclesiastical censure that happens automatically upon committing the forbidden act.</note>, from which no one can be absolved except by the Roman Pontiff (save at the point of death and after prior satisfaction), and for our subjects also under penalty of two hundred gold coins and the loss of the volumes themselves—half to be applied to the accusers and the rest to whomever you please—to be incurred immediately and in fact by anyone of whatever condition or rank who acts to the contrary, and which penalties are to be irrevocably exacted: that no one, under any pretext or sought-after color, dare or presume to print, or hire others to print, these works and books of yours and your uncle's to be published by you as stated above, for as long as you live, without your express consent and grant.

We command all and singular our legates and legates of the Apostolic See, vice-legates, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, ordinaries, and their vicars, and all others whom it concerns or may concern in the future: that they must assist and stand by you in the premises as often as necessary, and when requested by you or your mandated agents appointed for this purpose, by virtue of holy obedience and with all opportune favor and help, out of reverence for us and this Holy See. And lest ignorance of this our inhibition and mandate should occur, we will that a copy of these presents be printed and placed word-for-word on the first leaf of each of the said books, and that indubitable faith be held by everyone in it, as if these presents were signed under the Ring of the Fisherman, notwithstanding any apostolic constitutions and ordinances or anything else to the contrary.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman, on the 10th day of April, 1519, in the seventh year of our Pontificate.

On the back:                                                                                                Jacopo Sadoleto <note>A famous humanist scholar and secretary to Pope Leo X.</note>.

To our beloved son Giovanni Francesco Pico, Lord of Mirandola and Count of Concordia.
                                                                                                                ii

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of the work to Pope Leo X. It establishes the author's relationship with the papacy and the long-term nature of this intellectual project.</meta>

-># TO POPE LEO X, SUPREME PONTIFF,<-
-># GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO<-
-># WISHES HAPPINESS.<-

Since I owe all my scholarly labors to you, Leo, Supreme Pontiff, for many reasons, I did not wish to allow this *Examination* <note>The full title of the work is *Examen vanitatis doctrinae gentium* (Examination of the Vanity of Pagan Learning)</note> to be published without your name. Even though several of my other volumes have preceded this one—also dedicated to you—in which I frequently cited this very work, it has only recently been issued. Indeed, so great and laborious a task could not have been completed any sooner. However, unless I am very much mistaken, I believe I shall compensate for the loss of time with the utility of the work, which I trust you will approve of, if your busy schedule or moments of relaxation allow you to read what I have written.

Farewell and be happy. From Mirandola, on the third day before the Ides of July <note>July 13th</note>, 1520.

<summary>A formal dedication by Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to Pope Leo X, introducing his long-awaited scholarly critique of pagan philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, Pope Leo X, dedication, Mirandola, 1520, Renaissance philosophy, papacy</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the Table of Contents for the work. It establishes the author's intent to contrast the "vanity" of pagan philosophy with the "truth" of Christian doctrine, following the intellectual tradition of the Pico della Mirandola family.</meta>

->TABLE<-

->TABLE OF THE PRINCIPAL CHAPTERS OF GIOVANNI FRANCESCO<-
->PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, LORD AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA,<-
->IN THE EXAMINATION OF THE VANITY OF THE DOCTRINE<-
->OF THE GENTILES AND THE TRUTH OF THE<-
->CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE.<-

**S**ummarily contained in the first book are the beginnings and progress of the doctrine of the Gentiles <note>original: "gentium"; referring to non-Christian, primarily Greek and Roman, pagan thinkers</note>. Likewise, the variety of sects and the discord of opinions upon every single matter, both of the greater and the lesser world <note>The "greater world" refers to the Macrocosm (the universe) and the "lesser world" to the Microcosm (man)</note>. From which its manifold vanity can be detected; and afterwards the truth of the Sacred Scriptures is celebrated, both from principles given by divinity and received by the unanimous consent of the faithful, and from supernatural proofs corresponding to those very principles. There it is shown that, if they are weighed in the examination, even one of its dogmas outweighs all human doctrines.

Preface of the entire work. <margin>page 1</margin>
On the origin of the doctrine of the Gentiles: that is, of their theology, wisdom, and philosophy. Chapter 1. <margin>chapter 3</margin>
How varied the kind of philosophizing is among the Gentiles, how varied the sects of those philosophizing from the first centuries to our times, and why the author philosophizes in this work by a different path than his uncle Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher known for his "900 Theses"</note> was accustomed to do. Chapter 2. <margin>chapter 4</margin>
That the philosophers of the Gentiles agree neither in dividing their philosophy nor in inhabiting it <note>i.e., practicing or specializing in its branches</note>. Chapter 3. <margin>chapter 8</margin>
Whether there be any truth? And if there be, whether it can be possessed or not at all? That the philosophers of the Gentiles have not agreed. Their most diverse opinions are reported, and there it is also shown that Plato, concerning this matter, was pulled apart and torn into pieces, parts, and fragments by his followers in most combative discord. Chapter 4. <margin>chapter 9</margin>
That concerning the truth of rational, natural, supernatural, mathematical, and moral philosophy, the philosophers of the Gentiles have brought forth nothing certain and constant. Chapter 5. <margin>chapter 11</margin>
How variously the philosophers of the Gentiles have thought concerning the arts of grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic, which are usually held to be the instruments for capturing truth. Chapter 6. <margin>chapter 11</margin>
That concerning the mathematical arts of arithmetic and geometry, and concerning the intermediate arts of Astrology and music, the philosophers of the Gentiles do not agree. Chapter 7. <margin>chapter 12</margin>
How variously and even combatively the philosophers of the Gentiles have thought and decreed concerning the parts of supernatural, natural, and moral philosophy, especially the general and principal ones. Chapter 8. <margin>chapter 12</margin>
That the philosophers of the Gentiles, differing about the principle of all things, do not agree. Chapter 9. <margin>chapter 13</margin>
That concerning the causes of things, and concerning the determination of nature and its principles, there is much dissension among the philosophers of the Gentiles. Chapter 10. <margin>chapter 13</margin>
On the constitution and end of the world, and on its unity, magnitude, and figure, and on matter and form: what varied and even clashing things are produced by the philosophers. Chapter 11. <margin>chapter 16</margin>
That the philosophers of the Gentiles have discussed—discordantly and combatively—both the highest parts of the world (the sky, the stars, and all things generated on high) and the lowest and even subterranean parts, and their motions. Chapter 12. <margin>chapter 18</margin>
How varied the opinions of the philosophers are found to be universally concerning man—that is, the lesser world—what he is, whence he came, and where he goes? Chapter 13. <margin>chapter 22</margin>
How great and how many are the dissensions and brawls among the philosophers of the Gentiles concerning the human soul? Where it is shown how great thanks for the things divinely shown through Christ even in this matter...

¶ In the second book are contained, in summary, many opinions and numerous, combative reasons of the philosophers of the nations regarding the judgment of truth. From this, much vanity is uncovered, and finally it is shown that truth is given to men by divine providence, and has been both revealed and explained by Truth itself, which is Christ; where it can be perceived that the Christian discipline outweighs all others by a very great margin.
Preface. page 37.
That the "criterion" <note>original: "κριτήριον" (kriterion), a standard for judging truth</note>—called the *judicatorium* by the Greeks—is understood in many ways; what must be done regarding it, what is to be treated in this very book, and in what manner? Chapter 1. page 37.
Whether there is any criterion of truth, and whether any truth is found in common or not at all? How many reasons are brought forward on both sides. And also therein, what is true and what is truth, with many opinions of the Stoics, the Peripatetics, and our own theologians. Chapter 2. page 38.
Concerning the opinion and reasoning of Xenophanes of Colophon in doing away with the criterion of truth. Chapter 3. page 40.
Concerning the opinion and reasons of Xeniades of Corinth and Anacharsis the Scythian, who abolished the criterion of truth. Chapter 4. page 40.
Concerning the opinion and reasons of Protagoras, by which he wished the criterion of truth to be removed only in a universal sense; and therein something against Aristotle; and concerning the opinion of Dionysiodorus, Euthydemus, and Nausiphanes. Chapter 5. page 41.
By what arguments Gorgias used in overturning the criterion of truth, and therein several things against Gorgias; and concerning the opinion of Metrodorus and Anaxarchus, by which they wished that very criterion to be removed. Chapter 6. page 42.
Concerning the opinion of the natural philosophers who followed Thales, and the opinion and reasoning of Anaxagoras, by which it pleased them that the judgment of the senses be removed, but that of the mind remain; and how falsely Aristotle insulted them. Chapter 7. page 43.
Concerning the opinion and reasoning of Parmenides, and how falsely Aristotle both reported and rejected it in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Chapter 8. page 44.
Concerning the opinion of the Pythagoreans, and the reasoning of both Philolaus and Posidonius in asserting the criterion of truth. Chapter 9. page 48.
Concerning the opinion and reasoning of Empedocles regarding the judgment of truth; and how falsely Aristotle recites and attacks his opinion in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Chapter 10. page 48.

On the opinion and reasoning of Heraclitus regarding the determination of the criterion of truth; likewise on the opinion of Democritus, and how Aristotle in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and Cicero in the *Academics* reported them incorrectly. Chapter XI. Page 44.

On the opinion and reasoning of Plato regarding the determination of the criterion of truth, and how various authors interpret him differently. Chapter XII. Page 45.

On the opinion and reasoning of Speusippus and Xenocrates the Platonists <note>Speusippus and Xenocrates were the immediate successors of Plato in the Academy</note> in establishing the criterion of truth. Chapter XIII. Page 46.

On the opinion and reasonings of Arcesilaus the Platonist <note>Arcesilaus was the founder of the "Middle Academy" and introduced a more skeptical approach to Plato's teachings</note> concerning the criterion of truth, drawn from many authors. Chapter XIV. Page 46.

On the opinion of Carneades, differing from others, in determining a threefold criterion; and how various authors have disagreed about him. Chapter XV. Page 47.

On the sentiment and reasonings of the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy that emphasized subjective feelings and pleasure as the only certainties</note> for establishing a criterion of truth, including several points against Cicero, and on the opinion of Asclepiades. Chapter XVI. Page 48.

On the opinion and reasonings of the Stoics in measuring truth and falsehood. Chapter XVII. Page 48.

On the opinion of Aristotle, Theophrastus, and their followers in determining the criterion of truth. Chapter XVIII. Page 49.

On the opinion of Epicurus in judging the truth. Chapter XIX. Page 50.

How the Skeptical philosophers sharply contradict all others who would establish any criterion of truth, using a threefold path and method; wherein certain matters are found more deeply explored, and the excellence of the Christian faith is discussed. Chapter XX. Page 50.

On the "modes" <term>locis: literally "places," but used here as the technical term for the Skeptical "Modes" or "Tropes"—logical tools used to suspend judgment</term> which the Skeptics maintained both for withholding assent and for opposition. Chapter XXI. Page 51.

On the first mode for withholding assent, which is prepared from the diversity of living creatures; wherein certain points are raised against Aristotle, demonstrating that his arguments in the fourth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note> concerning the truth of the senses are easily refuted. Chapter XXII. Page 51.

On the second mode for withholding assent, established because of human diversity, also including several points against Aristotle. Chapter XXIII. Page 54.

On the third mode raised for withholding assent, founded upon the diversity of the senses; wherein there is also something against Aristotle. Chapter XXIV. Page 55.

On the fourth mode for restraining assent, which is derived from circumstances or dispositions. Chapter XXV. Page 56.

On the fifth mode prepared for the convenience of retaining assent, based on the location of things, their position, and their distance. Chapter XXVI. Page 58.

On the sixth and seventh modes prepared for leading men away from judgment, one of which is established from mixture, the other from quantity and composition. Chapter XXVII. Page 58.

On the eighth mode, which concerns relativity; in which matter something is said against the Skeptics, but much in their favor. Chapter XXVIII. Page 59.

On the ninth and tenth modes established by the ancient Skeptics for suspending assent; the former of which is composed of things seen rarely or frequently, while the latter is gathered from choices of life, customs, laws, mythical beliefs, and the opinions of philosophers. Chapter XXIX. Page 59.

On the five modes for withholding assent which are credited to the younger Skeptics. Chapter XXX. Page 60.

On two other modes for withholding assent. Likewise on the eight modes which Aenesidemus—

What and how manifold is the disapproval of the highest part of philosophy—which many call **metaphysics**, others **first philosophy**, and others the **theology of the gentiles** <note>original: "gentium theologiam"; referring to pagan religious philosophy</note>—devised by the skeptics. And therein also something against them. Chapter 11. page 99.

How the **Skeptics** <note>original: "ephectici"; those who practice 'epoche' or suspension of judgment</note> differed against the physicists; where also there are several points against them. Chapter 12. page 100.

What the Skeptic philosophers disputed against the moral dogmas of the remaining philosophers. And therein how weakly the human race would be led to conduct life based solely on the teachings and morals of the philosophers, and how salutary the **Christian discipline** was. Chapter 13. page 104.

The epilogue of the examination of the third book. In which it is shown that all the sects of the philosophers have hitherto attained some shadow of truth, insofar as they themselves have emulated from afar the divine dogmas of the **Sacred Scriptures**: in which can be seen, collected eminently and sincerely, whatever is found impurely and thinly interspersed in those profane books of theirs. Chapter 14 and the last of the third book. page 108.

¶ In the **fourth book**, it is discussed that the doctrine of **Aristotle** has not been held, nor ought to be held, of such great importance as it is usually estimated by many: and by ten ways it is shown to be generally neither entirely true nor certain; and this very point is shown especially by the authorities of writers of great name. Thence it is proved that the doctrine of the Sacred Scriptures, if it be taken up for examination, surpasses the doctrines of all others by the consensus of the world, by reason, and by miracles. Preface. sheet 110.

That the doctrine of Aristotle, when weighed in the examination, displays more of empty weight than of truth, and that it fails by a triple vanity. And therein the order of the three following books is also explained in detail. Chapter 1. page 111.

From whence has such great authority been attributed to Aristotle in our times? # PREFACE

->**To the Reader**<-

Since the study of ancient languages and the wisdom of the past <note>original: "sapientia veterum"</note> serves as the foundation for all higher learning, it is necessary that we approach these texts with both diligence and a clear mind. Many have attempted to interpret the sacred and secular authors without first mastering the grammatical structures that support them.

Therefore, in this work, I have endeavored to:
1. Clarify the obscure passages of the Greek poets.
2. Reconcile the differences between the Hebrew idioms and our own Latin tongue.
3. Provide a systematic method for the student of eloquence.

<margin>Note on the Greek text: The author refers here to the Homeric dialect.</margin>

It is not enough to merely translate words; one must capture the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"</note> of the original author. As the ancients said, <note>original: "Verba volant, scripta manent"</note> *Spoken words fly away, but written words remain.* Thus, we commit these observations to paper so they may serve future generations.

<column-break/>

The following table outlines the progression of study required for the mastery of the three primary languages:

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Latin** | Rhetoric and Law | Cicero |
| **Greek** | Philosophy and Epic | Plato or Homer |
| **Hebrew** | Sacred Scripture | The Prophets |

Let the reader proceed with patience, for the root of learning is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.

<meta>This page begins the Prooemium (Preface) of the work, establishing the author's intent to challenge the long-standing dominance of Aristotelian philosophy.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

I have hoped for this from the start, being plainly content with only my own conscience as witness and the judgment of a few men. For I am not unaware of what strength is needed to abolish an opinion deeply rooted in the minds of men, even if it has been weakened by its own falsehood. Who does not claim that all Aristotelian teachings are certain, all are true, and nothing can be said against them? I, however, shall show that they are not certain but merely probable, since many reasons from those same foundations, and many authorities as well, can very easily be brought against them. I shall show that not all are true, but that most are equally false. But more on this matter when we undertake this very task in Book IV. At this point, I would only wish for my readers to be asked not to despise these things before they have understood them. Nor should they condemn them before they have read them, nor judge that I have wished to hunt for empty, fleeting glory by disparaging another’s teaching. Such popularity might perhaps have followed me with the public breeze if I had published commentaries on all or most of Aristotle's works, as I have done for some of his dogmas.

->BOOK ONE<- [right] III [right]

...others have written much, and we ourselves have written some things elsewhere, especially in our theorems on faith. We have done so both in the course of our work during disputes, frequently at the beginnings of books, and always at the ends, so that we might not be accused of merely casting aside false things without having adopted the true. We shall soon have a few words to say on this. Presently, we must discuss in a dedicated work that love which faith brings forth. But now, by divine aid, we shall set out to explode the vanity of the doctrine of the nations <note>original: "doctrinae gentium," referring to non-Christian/pagan philosophy</note>—that is, to weigh the wisdom of the world in a balance—so that when compared with the weight of our own discipline, their vanity and our truth may be most clearly discerned.

->THE FIRST BOOK OF GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, LORD AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA, ON THE EXAMINATION OF THE VANITY OF THE DOCTRINE OF THE NATIONS AND THE TRUTH OF THE CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE.<-

On the origin of the doctrine of the nations: that is, of their theology, wisdom, and philosophy. Chapter One.

**F**ELICITY, which ingenious men affected to pursue through the study of truth, cannot be attained by the efforts of mortals themselves, since it surpasses their own powers. Hence, I believe it has happened that regarding this matter, nothing true or consistent has been committed to writing, but rather things false and dissonant. In this regard, it should seem marvelous that only a few have recovered their senses <note>original: "resipuerint," to come to one's senses or return to a right mind</note> upon observing that for so many centuries, among those whose footsteps posterity ought to have followed, strife and wars have always flourished. All these men, however (as I suppose), were deceived by the ostentation of a false name. For even if those ancients were by no means in possession of the thing they sought, they assumed a name for themselves from it as if it had been both understood and possessed. Thus it happened that among those who pursued these doctrines, the names of "Theologian," "Wise Man," and "Philosopher" arose. For some boasted that they had found God, and were gifted with the surname of Theologians; others, rashly asserting that they knew both divine and human things at once, claimed for themselves the name of Wisdom; others, somewhat more modestly, were content with the nomenclature of Philosophy. There was only one people <note>The Hebrews/Israelites</note> whose leaders those who followed were granted the ability to avoid the darkness of errors, and a path was made toward that path of felicity which had been the highest of their prayers to obtain. And certainly, men both ought to have and were able to follow them, since the fame of that people’s name was great among all nations, as was the dignity of their antiquity. For to them all those who were held to excel in the glory of letters were accustomed to flock, and from a certain most ancient whirlpool of wisdom, they were accustomed to quench their thirst for knowing. For by many centuries of years, the doctrine of the Hebrews was both older than that of the nations and was held to be so by famous authors. Lucretius sings that the reason of the nature of things was discovered recently; and Seneca writes <margin>Lucretius, Seneca</margin> from the beginnings...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola introduces his critique of pagan philosophy, arguing that true happiness and truth cannot be found in human reason alone but are found in the ancient Hebrew tradition and Christian faith.</summary>

those things alone, when they even offered divine worship to irrational animals and the fruits of the earth. Others preferred to bestow divine honors upon statues moved and agitated by a malignant demon. Heraclitus and Empedocles established that God was an "intelligible fire" <note>original: *ignem intelligibilem*. A philosophical concept where God is a rational, creative heat.</note>. Others held other views, as we have reported elsewhere; and on this matter, one or two places in this very work have been set aside by me. For a little later, I shall report the various opinions of the nations concerning divine matters; indeed, in later books, I will refute those very ideas when we dispute against the supernatural philosophy of the nations. Let it suffice to have brought forward a few points regarding the origin of the doctrine of the nations, so that their most ancient zeal in seeking and honoring gods may be understood.

->**Theologians of the nations.**<-
<margin>Theologians of the nations.</margin>
Those, therefore, who were engaged in this investigation and worship attained the name of "theologians." By that name, the most ancient among them, Orpheus, was deemed worthy; likewise Hesiod, Homer, and others who were also poets. For Orpheus taught of many gods and their worship in song; Hesiod also sang of their generations in verse; Homer even composed hymns to the gods—to say nothing of the others, all of whom nevertheless handed down various, dissonant, and controversial things, as will become manifest when the battle against them is undertaken. Indeed, everything is full of ambiguities, full of the deceits of demons, by which that unrefined age was deluded, the mention of the one true God having been neglected. If they had preferred to cling to the footsteps of Abraham and Job of Uz, worshippers of the one God, they could have been drawn from the darkness of superstitions to the true religion—especially that Egypt, the most superstitious of all regions, which the grandsons of Abraham inhabited. Regarding this matter, it was well handled and consulted by Orpheus, who, after he visited Egypt, despised the worship of many gods and was gifted with the knowledge of the One; this, Justin the philosopher and martyr shows in that book which we have translated from Greek into Latin.

->**The Sages of the nations.**<-
<margin>Justin Martyr. Sages of the nations.</margin>
After Orpheus and the others for whom the surname of "theologians" was made, the title of "Sage" <note>original: *sapientis*. Often translated as "Wise Man."</note> emerged. For if Lycurgus was once held as a sage, and likewise Ulysses and Nestor, skilled in wars, nevertheless that name was afterwards accustomed to signify all among the nations who placed their studies in the contemplation of things; by which name those who discoursed on nature were also especially called. For they were not only called physicists and physiologists, but "Sages." Whence also that famous Thales, who is said to have been the first to hand down the precepts of natural philosophy, was honored by that nomenclature beyond controversy; and among those seven who were preeminently dignified with the name of Sage, he held the first place among many. Eusebius and others have recorded that they flourished in the times of Cyrus. Those theologians of the nations were much more ancient than them, yet if they are compared in age to those first Hebrews, they will be found to be much younger, as we have indicated; a matter which Porphyry also mentions, to say nothing of Africanus, Eusebius, and many of our own.

Whether those who obtained the surname of wisdom were more or fewer than seven is a great question; likewise, whether those seven were truly sages or not is no small controversy. Cicero seems to deny this on the authority of the ancestors who discoursed more subtly on this matter, rather than affirming that Lucilius, Acilius, Cato, Scipio, and Socrates were "Sages." But that wisdom which the Stoics interpreted, Laelius (in the same Cicero) says was possessed by no one. The same appellation was also shared with others, so pleasing to the human race that it was usurped by many craftsmen of ignoble arts; this may be seen in Homer, an imitator in many things of the Mosaic discipline, in which one can see smiths dignified by the title of "Sage." From this, perhaps, it happened that whoever was able to invent or produce something worthy of human memory, the name of Sage was extended to them, as if they were held worthy to have honor imparted to them. For good authors of the Greek language derive the name *sophos* <note>Greek: σοφοῦ</note> from *seuomai* <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ σέυομαι, meaning to move quickly or revere</note>, so that a *sophos* is, as it were, a *sobos* <note>Greek: σοβὸς</note> who is worshipped by all. It pleased Aristotle that he especially excelled in the name of wisdom who directed and ordered things toward an end, and contemplated the highest causes of things; a mention of which matter was made both at the beginning of the books of First Philosophy <note>The *Metaphysics*</note> and in the sixth volume of the *Ethics*. But a certain distinction of a Sage could also be held: when we could deservedly impart that name to someone, both by the consideration of the whole universe and by the inclination of a particular business prudently and gravely transacted.

<margin>Bernard</margin>
But it pleased many of our theologians, especially Bernard and certain younger ones, to so separate "knowledge" from "wisdom" that the former pertained to the intellect and the latter to the affection <note>In medieval thought, "affection" refers to the will, heart, or emotional disposition toward God.</note>.

...concerning wisdom, they defined it differently than the philosophers do now; but at that time—that is, in the age of those who were called "The Wise"—they used that name indiscriminately for the sake of both honor and glory. Therefore, when a name of such excellent dignity had begun to be shared even with the common people, someone emerged who wished for it to be changed. For this reason, Pythagoras took another title for himself, and instead of a "Wise Man" <note>original: "sapiente"</note>, he called himself a "Philosopher" <note>literally "a lover of wisdom"</note>. I speak of Pythagoras, who is considered by many to be a Samian and the son of Mnesarchus, even if I sometimes find his father named Mnemarchus in the writings of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras</note>. <margin>The Philosophy of the Gentiles.</margin> Although there were those who did not consider him a Milesian, as Iamblichus and many others do, there were also those who wished him to be a Tyrian or a Tyrrhenian, and even some a Syrian; <margin>Disagreements concerning the fatherland of Pythagoras.</margin> regarding this matter, besides Laertius, both Eusebius and Theodoret have discussed it. But while there is disagreement about his homeland, there is none at all regarding his invention of the name "Philosophers," which many attribute to the modesty of the man, etc.

<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion on the definitions and origins of philosophy, likely following a preface or a general opening statement.</meta>

# BOOK

<note>original: "LIBER"</note>

The guide adapted for the instruction of men. Nor does Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the soul's ascent to the divine.</note> seem to disagree with Cicero, who in another work—that is, in the second book of *On Duties*—affirms that philosophy is the study of wisdom, and that wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these things are contained. From this, many definitions of philosophy have emerged, concerning which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of thought.</note>, especially the Greeks who interpreted the works of Aristotle, have discussed, gathering them chiefly from the Pythagoreans and the Platonists. Epicurus, however, defined it through discourses and disputations which might establish a happy life. The Stoics called it prudence, the knowledge of things good, evil, and neutral; and they held it to be the art of conducting one's life, which only those who grasped it would be truly good and truly wise. All of them, nevertheless, looked toward this goal: to signify that happiness proceeds from philosophy. Thus, some called it the leader of life and the expeller of vices; others called it the likeness of God, insofar as that is humanly possible.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Italian school of philosophy, specifically focusing on the internal divisions and sects within the Pythagorean tradition.</meta>

->BOOK ONE<-                                                                                                                            V

Nor was that famous harmony in Italian philosophy—that agreement of morals and doctrines so wonderfully praised by Pythagoras—preserved intact for long. For it was not only divided, as some have thought, into *esoteric* and *exoteric* <note>original: "ἐσωτερικους & ἐξωτερικους" — referring to "inner" teachings for initiates and "outer" teachings for the public</note>, that is, internal and external members. I have found many sects among them, and those same groups were in discord. Indeed, there was not only a disagreement between the "Pythagoreans" and the "Pythagorists"—which was not merely a matter of names, as between the Attics and Atticists, as Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the life of Pythagoras</note> relates—but there was much dissension in the matter itself, according to the same author. <margin>Division of the sect of Pythagoras and the distinction between Pythagoreans.</margin> The former lived in a communal monastery, while the latter remained in their own private homes; the former were clothed in linen and were admitted to the sight of Pythagoras and to the inner chambers of the mind and senses. Furthermore, they sold all their possessions before they were admitted and placed their coined money before Pythagoras. Finally, some things were known and approved by the one group, and other things by the other. Indeed, even those who were called "Hearers" <note>Latin: *auditores*</note> disagreed with the "Mathematicians," as we shall explain shortly; it was not as Taurus the Philosopher <note>A Platonic philosopher mentioned by Aulus Gellius</note> thought in Gellius, that within the period of silence there were first Hearers, then Mathematicians, and soon after Physicists. <margin>Against Taurus in Gellius.</margin> For they were diverse and for the most part so opposed that the Mathematicians themselves were judged unworthy of the name of Pythagoreans by the Hearers, inasmuch as the doctrine they used was said not to be that of Pythagoras, but of a certain Hippasus—whom some say was from Croton, others from Metapontum. On the other hand, the Mathematicians boasted that they were more truly Pythagoreans and ought to be regarded as such, because they possessed the demonstrations of the things being said, whereas those called Hearers had only simple narrations, with which Pythagoras was accustomed to address the elderly and those unskilled in discipline, as people who, by reason of age, were not permitted to attain difficult things through study and the fatigue of speculation. And they said the beginning of their sect was when Pythagoras, fleeing the growing tyranny of Polycrates in Samos, sought Croton. Others resisted, contending that those secrets were the true things of Pythagoras which they themselves had drawn, divided into three parts: for one signifies *what a thing is*, another *what it is most*, and the third *what must be done or not done*. But there was also that distinction among the Pythagoreans: that some thought it a divine sin <note>Latin: *nephas*</note> to give precepts commonly and to the public, a rule said to have been kept by Eurytus, Philolaus, Charondas, and Zaleucus, who as young men were accustomed to assist the elderly Pythagoras; and besides these, Bryson, the elder Archytas, Empedocles, Aristeus, Lysis, Zamolxis, and others. However, Hipparchus thought otherwise, to whom there exists a letter from Lysis, who was indignant that the secret dogmas of Pythagoras were being profaned; he claimed it was no less a sin not to keep them secret than if the Eleusinian mysteries were revealed to the uninitiated. <margin>Iamblichus. Bessarion. Giovanni Pico.</margin> Iamblichus records this letter in the first book of the Pythagorean sect; Cardinal Bessarion <note>A 15th-century scholar-cardinal who defended Plato</note> brings it forth among his defenses of Plato; and my uncle Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance philosopher</note> also cites it in the *Heptaplus*. There was also that disagreement regarding a certain knowledge through numbers which the Pythagoreans kept against others, which rumor said Pythagoras had communicated to Abaris the Hyperborean. Nor was there agreement on doctrines, as some judged certain symbols to be legitimate and others to be supposititious and spurious, and they varied wonderfully in their interpretations of them. While some rested nakedly and simply on the sound of the words, others sought an allegory of deeper understanding. Thus, many maintained that Pythagoras commanded abstinence from eating beans and meat, and that he himself was not accustomed to eat them; on the contrary, others maintained that he avoided beans and piglets, but did not affirm an interdict against Pythagoreans eating beans. They wished something else to be signified by "beans," and another reason for not eating meat was suggested, as Aristoxenus in his book on Pythagoras, and also Plutarch (relying on Aristotle) in his *Life of Homer*, have indicated; Aulus Gellius also mentions this matter in his *Attic Nights*. And indeed, Iamblichus refers the so-called "Pythagorean Sacrificial Rites" <note>original: "θυολολογίας" (thyolologias)</note> to certain sophists. So too, the consensus of the learned has held that the so-called "Golden Verses" of Pythagoras should be attributed not to him, but to Philolaus. They also differed in their opinion of numbers, a matter which will be mentioned when we speak of the Mathematicians in the third book of this work. They even differed in their estimation of Pythagoras, whom some called the Pythian...

Some believed him to be the Hyperborean Apollo <note>A mythical sun-god from the far north</note>; others thought he was one of the spirits who inhabit the moon; others held different views. They did not agree with the other, older Pythagoreans concerning the first principles of things. They descended from the study of numbers to the study of the earth, as will become clear shortly when we discuss those principles. Nor did Diophantes of Syracuse agree with either of these groups; for although he was considered a Pythagorean, he followed Democritus of Abdera, establishing for himself indivisible bodies <note>original: "indiviſibilia corpuſcula"</note>. # BOOK ONE [space] VI

The origins of medicine were agitated by no fewer controversies than the very philosophy of which we treat. For its most illustrious authors believed the knowledge of nature <note>natural science or physics</note> was necessary for themselves, and they called themselves the "Rationalists." Galen, in his *Introduction* <note>original: "Isagogico"</note>, names Hippocrates as the leader of this sect which is called Rational. Opposed to them were Serapion and those who followed him—Glaucias, Heraclides of Tarentum, the two Apollonii, and Sextus the African—who, placing medicine in practice and experiments, assumed the name "Empiricists" from their very profession. This is according to the author Cornelius <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, the Roman encyclopedist</note>, although Galen teaches in his introductory book for doctors that the faculty of the Empiricists should be credited to Philinus of Cos, who was the first to separate it from the Logical or Rational sect. Nevertheless, some have made Acron of Agrigentum its author; Pliny the Second followed these in the twenty-ninth book of his *Natural History*, assigning it to Acron just as he assigned Clinical medicine to Hippocrates. He claims Hippocrates established it from the records in the Temple of Asclepius after it was burned, as Varro believed. He also made Paedicüs of Selymbria the author of the "Iatraleptic" <note>The "ointment-doctor" or massage-based sect</note> method. However it may have been, Serapion and many others joined Acron (or Creon, as it is written by others), according to Galen. Relying on experience itself, they did so not because they lacked logic and learning—as some in our own time believe, and as Pliny also seems to have felt—but because they believed that medicine does not consist of "reason" (that is, it cannot be acquired by theory), but only by use and experiments. They argued most sharply against those who professed to be Rationalists. This can be clearly gathered both from the first book of Cornelius Celsus *On Medicine*, and from the sixth book of Pyrrho <note>likely referring to Sextus Empiricus's Outlines of Pyrrhonism</note>, who also wrote on the Empiric sect. Later, there were those who called themselves "Methodists," founded by Thessalus <note>The text says Themison, his predecessor</note>, differing from both previous groups. Although Cornelius seems to deny this in his first book and strives to bring forth reasons to show how they agree with the others, Galen confesses—both in his book *On Sects* and especially in the *Introduction*—that they are clearly different. Sextus himself writes aptly on this, teaching that they agree most with the Sceptics, from whom not only the Rationalists and Dogmatists, but even the Empiricists themselves, aptly dissent.

But I return to the philosophers, among whom Socrates introduced another kind of teaching. For while most were seeking divine and natural things—and believed they should spend great effort on the "Logical" faculty (of which the Pythagorean Zeno is said to be the inventor) so these things could be discerned—Socrates himself held those things in lower regard. He did not consider it worthy (if we believe Xenophon) for a philosopher to occupy himself with them. Instead, he gave his labor solely to the composing of morals and the calming of the disturbances of the soul. For this reason, it is said that he called Philosophy down from Heaven and placed her in cities and homes. It was also written by Aristotle in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals* that the use of "definition" increased in the times of Socrates, but the investigation of natural things ceased, and the entire study of philosophizing was transferred to useful virtue and civil practice. Truly, Origen <note>The text likely refers to the "origins" of the sect, though the margin notes "Origenes"</note> makes Socrates the prince of Ethical philosophy, just as he makes Aristotle the prince of Dialectic. From him, however, as if from a fountain, different rivers of doctrine flowed. He had two disciples especially famous for their eloquence by the consensus of all: Xenophon and Plato. As far as the knowledge of things is concerned, the former took up the care of morals, while the latter took up the investigation of all nature and mixed philosophy itself. For in Natural philosophy, as most hold, he followed Heraclitus; in Divine matters, Pythagoras; in Moral and Rational matters, Socrates; and in Mathematics, Theodorus of Cyrene. Apuleius and others record that Plato traveled to Cyrene to hear him, and even went as far as Egypt to become skilled in astrology. However, Xenophon clearly recorded in his literary monuments that Dialectic was not handed down to Plato by Socrates. Indeed, Plato varied from Xenophon in his style of writing; for while the most ancient thinkers handed down their dogmas in verse, and later in prose (though obscurely, and even the Pythagoreans were accustomed to riddles), Xenophon commended his thoughts to letters most clearly and limpidly. Plato, celebrated for great elegance and rich eloquence, under the guise of mathematics...

...or adorned it: although I am not unaware that it was once written differently, and I know that authors have not at all agreed on who should be included in this Platonic succession. For Diogenes Laertius uses one method, Numenius and Eusebius another, Lactantius another, Augustine another, and others differently still. Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus</note> uses one way, and Cicero another—who, even though Aristotle actually disagreed, does not separate him from the Old Academy. To this, Cicero also joins the New Academy which Arcesilaus founded, and he says that Carneades remained in that same school of thought. However, others aptly deny this, as will become clear in the progress of this work. But enough of these matters for now; for the manner in which the Academies differ among themselves will become known briefly in the fourth chapter of this book, and more fully in the following book, when I shall reveal what each or most of them prescribed regarding the notion of truth.

<margin>How many sects there are in Peripatetic philosophy.</margin>
Furthermore, there were also many families of Peripatetics; for almost every philosopher of the Peripatetic sect after Theophrastus and Neleus busied himself with founding his own, to such an extent that the Lyceum <note>The school founded by Aristotle</note> was distracted and, as it were, torn into many parts, until it began to be reintegrated under Alexander of Aphrodisias. He was of such great celebrity while he lived that almost all Peripatetics were not believed to be such unless they were also thought to be "Alexandrians." This was so even if he was later harassed by many as time went on—to say nothing of Themistius who flourished later, and not to repeat from Simplicius, who measured the dogmas of those contemporaries who had preceded them by his own small plumb-line.

Thereafter, Greece having been plundered and Italy devastated by frequent incursions of barbarian nations, philosophy reached the Moors and the Arabs. By them, Aristotle was cultivated in a wonderful manner, Plato but little, and others not at all. The cause of this, as far as we have been able to reach by conjecture, we shall relate in the fourth book of this work. But whatever that cause was, the Arabs and Moors themselves never disputed while walking in the Portico or the open spaces, nor did they wish to sit in the many chambers within it. Likewise, the name of the Sceptics is nowhere found among them, although many of them existed both before and after Aristotle and most sharply harassed his writings; many also lived at the same time as Aristotle.

<margin>Concerning the Sceptics and Sextus the Pyrrhonist.</margin>
For the Sceptic Pyrrho flourished in the time of Alexander the Macedonian. Moreover, there was the philosopher Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus</note> under the Emperor Marcus the Philosopher <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, a kinsman of Plutarch, who wrote Sceptic works, as is found in the collections of Suidas and others. And he, I think, is the Sextus whom Apuleius mentions; for Apuleius recorded that he drew the foundations of his maternal origin from both the philosopher Sextus and from Plutarch. And in the *Life of the Emperor Marcus the Philosopher*, Julius Capitolinus writes that Sextus of Chaeronea, the grandson of Plutarch, was a teacher of Marcus himself. There is also mention in Suidas of a Sextus the Sceptic, a Libyan and not a Chaeronean. I myself have read ten books by Sextus the Sceptic, who also wrote the *Empiric Memorials*; he was likewise called "the Empiric," but whether he was someone other than those two, or one of them, I have not yet sufficiently ascertained. Certainly Galen, in his book *On Sects*, mentions Sextus the Empiric the African; and in his *Introduction* there is also mention of Sextus the Empiric.

<margin>Against certain correctors of Quintilian.</margin>
And from this, perhaps, those can be refuted who think that the passage of Quintilian in his tenth book pertains to this, when he says that Cornelius Celsus wrote a great many things following the "Sextii." For the fact that others read "Sceptics" instead of "Sextii" does not satisfy me, since mention of the Sextii is found in Seneca, and in Cicero's books—especially the letters to Atticus—the name of Sextius is often cited. Horace also writes to Sextius. Indeed, there could have been Sextii who were not Sceptics, even if someone called Sextus might be placed among the Sceptics.

<margin>What kind of philosophers were the Sceptics?</margin>
Seneca himself, in the last volume of his *Natural Questions*, says: "The sect of the Sextii, new and of Roman vigor, having begun with great impetus among its beginnings, was extinguished." But the Sceptic faculty was not new but ancient; not Roman but Greek; and not extinguished when it began, but long-lasting. It was the custom of all Sceptics to "stretch their sails to the wind" (as they say) by neither affirming nor denying anything on either side, but to consider all things most diligently and to contradict all those who asserted any dogmas whatsoever.

<margin>The Eclectic philosophers</margin>
There was also no mention of those who called themselves "Electors" <note>Eclectics</note>, whose role was to choose what was pleasing from individual schools in the manner of bees, and finally, by their own labor and work, to offer the collected and compacted honey for others to taste...

# On the Discord of Philosophers

...among their followers; and they flourished even among themselves. Soon, I shall direct my pen against all of them. <margin>In what manner the philosophers fought amongst themselves.</margin>

->**Giovanni Pico and his praises.**<- <margin>Giovanni Pico and his praises.</margin>

But first, I must mention that most celebrated man, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance nobleman and philosopher (1463–1494) known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note>, who was endowed with such sharpness of mind and such a variety of learning that he seemed to be a miracle of nature. He attempted to reconcile the sects of the philosophers, especially the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> and the Platonists. However, while he sought peace, he could not escape the weapons of his detractors. For even he, though he excelled in eloquence and doctrine, was seen to be unequal to so great a task. <margin>What the author cares about.</margin>

Therefore, I do not care for the empty praises of the world, nor do I fear the bites of the envious. My purpose is to show how far the truth of the Christian religion surpasses the vanity of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians, specifically the ancient Greeks and Romans</note>. For if one considers the teachings of the philosophers, they do not agree even on the most basic principles of their own wisdom.

### That the philosophers of the Gentiles agree neither in dividing their philosophy nor in cultivating it. Chapter Three.

<note>original: "Quod philosophi gẽtiũ: nec ĩ partiẽda sua phia nec ĩcolẽda cõueniũt. Caput tertiũ."</note>

B ii

<summary>The author critiques the internal contradictions of ancient philosophical schools and mentions Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's failed attempt to reconcile them, introducing a chapter on the fundamental disagreements among Gentile philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Peripatetics, Platonists, Gentile philosophy, religious truth vs. philosophy, philosophical discord</keywords>

--- Page 30 ---
BOOK [I]

We have seen how the philosophy of the nations, torn apart by various sects, does not agree with itself. Now we must consider whether the philosophers themselves can agree on how to divide or cultivate it, so that they might be consistent with one another; we shall take our beginning from the very division of the subject. Of philosophy, therefore, some have made no division at all; others established a two-fold division; others divided the whole into three parts. Even among those who wished there to be only a single kind, there is still great discord. For some wished that one part to be **Physics** <note>Natural philosophy or the study of nature</note>; others **Logic**; others **Ethics** <note>original: "morale"</note>. Of the first opinion were Thales, Anaximenes, and Anaximander of the Ionic race; and from the Italian race, Empedocles and Parmenides, with whom Heraclitus agreed. Yet even in this, there is no single consensus among them all, since those Ionics thought that [nature] was entirely constant and unmixed, whereas Empedocles and Parmenides did not think so. For the latter, on the authority of Aristotle, taught concerning rhetoric; and Parmenides was not unskilled in dialectic, of which Zeno of Elea—known to Parmenides—is considered the founder, according to the same Aristotle. Regarding Heraclitus, it is also doubted whether he was a natural philosopher or a moral philosopher. Those who were content with a single kind, but preferred it to be Logic rather than Physics, are recorded as Panthoides, Alexinus, Eubulides, Bryson, Dionysiodorus, and Euthydemus. Xenophon, who was his constant companion and joined to him in closest friendship, recorded that Socrates also established a single but moral kind; and Timon asserted the same. Both of them attacked Plato because he ascribed both the faculty of Logic and Physics to Socrates. There are also those who affirm that the Cyrenaics were content with that single moral kind of philosophy, although this is not sufficiently certain, since they also considered causes and proofs. Ariston of Chios clung to the moral side to such an extent that he even circumscribed most things that others freely admitted, such as admonitions and instructions, thinking that the mere attainment of virtue and the expulsion of vice were sufficient for living happily.

Furthermore, many made philosophy two-fold, but they did not use the same method of dissection. For Xenophanes of Colophon divided that universal and supreme kind of philosophy into Physics and Logic, omitting Ethics; whereas Archelaus the Athenian embraced Ethics and distinguished it directly from Physics, making no mention of Logic. Some think Epicurus should be numbered with him, as he rejected logical speculation; others feel to the contrary, contending that he did not entirely bypass the rational faculty, but only blamed the way it was handed down by the Stoics; wherefore they think philosophy was considered three-fold by him, not two-fold. Nor were there lacking those who asserted the Cyrenaics divided philosophy into two species, Ethics and Logic, excluding Natural philosophy.

But Plato was the leader in establishing philosophy as three-fold, so that one kind was Logic, another Physics, and the third Ethics. Xenocrates, Aristotle, and the Stoics followed him. Although some called these parts "topics" <note>original: "locos"</note>, Apollodorus named them "species," and Chrysippus and Eudromis called them "genera." But there was not even total agreement among the Stoics in this matter: for Cleanthes established six parts of philosophy on the authority of Diogenes: Dialectic, Rhetoric, Politics, Physics, Theology, and Ethics. Cleanthes himself and Zeno treated Ethics quite simply, but those who came after them pulled it apart into smaller pieces. Indeed, Chrysippus, Archedemus, Zeno of Tarsus, Apollodorus, Diogenes, Antipater, and Posidonius divided it into the following topics: on appetite, on goods and evils, on perturbations <note>passions or emotions</note>, on virtue, on the end <note>the "summum bonum" or ultimate goal</note>, on primary value, on actions, on duties, and on exhortations and warnings.

Truly, even though three kinds of philosophy were established, there is no common agreement found in the order of the parts, nor any consensus of doctrines. For some thought one should begin from the faculty of Logic, such as the Stoics and others; some from the moral kind, following Socrates; and many from the physical kind, like the followers of Antigonus. Furthermore, in the dissection of the specific parts, no less a dissension arose than in the main parts: since some wished the logical kind to encompass Grammar and Rhetoric along with Dialectic. Others excluded one, and some even excluded the other. In Ethics also, both Plato and Aristotle established three small parts, while the Cyrenaics preferred five.

<summary>This page catalogs the historical disagreements among ancient Greek and Roman philosophers regarding the fundamental divisions of philosophy into Physics, Logic, and Ethics. It traces the evolution from single-subject schools to the tripartite system established by Plato and later expanded by the Stoics.</summary>

<keywords>divisions of philosophy, Physics, Logic, Ethics, Stoics, Plato, Aristotle, Socrates, Hellenistic sects, history of logic</keywords>

# On the Certainty of Human Knowledge

<margin>
<unclear>Artis / obnog... / ap. 25...</unclear> <note>Possibly a citation to a classical work on the arts, though the ink is heavily faded.</note>
</margin>

-> **The First Part** <-

Truly, it is necessary for us to first consider whether any certain knowledge can be grasped by the human mind, or if all things are instead shrouded in the darkness of uncertainty. For if we cannot be sure of anything, then the pursuit of wisdom itself would seem to be a vain labor.

<margin>
Dogmatic philosophy.
Academic philosophy.
Skeptic philosophy.
</margin>

We recognize that there have been many who doubted the very possibility of truth. The Academics and the Skeptics argued that the senses are deceptive and the intellect is prone to error. They claim that we can only ever reach the level of probability, never the firm ground of absolute truth.

<margin>
There are three supreme and most general parts of philosophy according to Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a proponent of Pyrrhonism</note>, but four according to Galen.
</margin>

However, we must ask: can the mind truly be satisfied with mere opinion? To be able to know <note>original: "posse"</note> is a natural desire of the soul. If this power <note>original: "posse"</note> were entirely absent, our nature would be frustrated in its highest aim. We must therefore examine the foundations of our understanding to see if we can find a rock upon which to build.

<margin>
Nicholas of Cusa <note>A 15th-century philosopher known for his work on "learned ignorance."</note>
</margin>

Even if we admit that our knowledge is limited compared to the infinite wisdom of the Creator, we still possess a certain capacity <note>original: "posse"</note> for truth within our own sphere. We should not yield to total doubt, for even the act of doubting proves that there is a mind present which seeks the truth.

<summary>This page explores the fundamental question of whether human beings can achieve certain knowledge, contrasting the views of Dogmatists, Academics, and Skeptics. It argues that the innate human desire to know suggests that some level of certainty must be possible.</summary>

<keywords>epistemology, skepticism, certainty, Academic philosophy, Nicholas of Cusa, Sextus Empiricus, Galen, human understanding</keywords>

BOOK I

### Concerning the question of Democritus
For there were those who said that the Sceptic philosophy had a commonality with that of Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) was a pre-Socratic philosopher famous for his atomic theory of the universe.</note>. This is resisted by the Sceptics, if only for the reason that Democritus asserted that both Atoms and the Void exist; the Pyrrhonists <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis, the founder of Scepticism, who advocated for the suspension of judgment.</note>, however, withheld their assent from these things. They would speak both against Democritus and in favor of Democritus, should anyone think he had decreed falsely. Indeed, this dispute does not properly tend toward the dividing of sects, but toward this very point: whether truth could be grasped by any instrument of truth.

Furthermore, some who followed the Pyrrhonist Aenesidemus <note>Aenesidemus was a 1st-century BCE Sceptic philosopher who revived Pyrrhonism.</note> thought the Sceptic sect was a path to the Heraclitean philosophy <note>The philosophy of Heraclitus, who famously believed in universal change and the unity of opposites.</note>. This was because Heraclitus had perceived that contraries both exist within and appear to the same subject; and this latter point—that they appear so—is also admitted by the Sceptics. Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE), whose writings are the primary source for Greek Scepticism.</note>, himself a Pyrrhonist, stood against this, asserting that the fact that contraries appear to exist regarding the same thing is not a specific dogma of the Sceptics, but rather a matter common not only to them but to almost all philosophers. And indeed, it is common to any ordinary person; for no one is found who does not see that honey is sweet to the healthy, but bitter to those with jaundice <note>original: "ictericis"</note>. Whether it truly is so or not, however, is its own...

In Plato there is such variety that even the Dialogues themselves are still a matter of debate as to their intended purpose. Regarding the *Parmenides* <note>A notoriously difficult dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of "The One" and the "Many."</note>—whether it concerns the single principle of all things or the Ideas—Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous Renaissance translator of Plato.</note> and others have written. My uncle, Giovanni Pico <margin>Giovanni Pico</margin> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the celebrated humanist philosopher.</note>, in his book *On Being and the One*, judges that this Dialogue should by no means be placed among the dogmatic works, as it is more truly suited for logical exercise. And if anyone considers the dogmas of Marinus the Platonist <margin>Marinus</margin>, who heard Proclus <note>original: "pelū" likely referring to Proclus, the Neoplatonist.</note>, he will easily understand that he sided with my uncle in this dispute. Atticus the Platonist <margin>Atticus</margin> <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who defended Plato against Aristotelian influence.</note> also agrees with him in that work he wrote against those who, after professing Aristotle, failed to follow Plato. For he affirms that Zeno, Parmenides, and those who were professors of the Eleatic school studied only the faculty of logic; but who could doubt that in Plato, in that Dialogue, the opinion and doctrine of Parmenides are treated?

Archelaus, the leader of the Second Academy <margin>On the Second Academy: Arcesilaus, Numenius</margin> (which is also called the Middle Academy), dissented from the leaders of the First and clung to the views of Pyrrho <note>The founder of Pyrrhonian Skepticism, who advocated for the suspension of judgment.</note> to such an extent that he was considered almost one of their followers. Numenius, in his book on the disagreement of the Academies, affirms that he was a Pyrrhonian in reality, but an Academic in name, out of respect for Crantor, whom he loved, and who was of great name in the Academy. Even if Arcesilaus affirmed that nothing can be known—not even this very fact of knowing nothing, which Socrates used to leave for himself—Marcus Varro is the authority in Cicero's writings that he did not differ from the First Academy. However, others who think they have more sharply discussed his meanings want Arcesilaus to be considered "multiform." They suggest that he took up the business of a Skeptic to test his listeners—to see if they were strong enough to untie the knots of Platonic dogmas—but once they were approved and legitimate, he would instill the Platonic dogmas that were to be held. For this reason, the saying of Ariston <margin>Ariston</margin> is often cited: that Arcesilaus was "Plato in the front, Pyrrho in the back, and Diodorus the Dialectician in the middle," <note>A famous ancient joke describing Arcesilaus as a hybrid of different philosophical styles.</note> referring to the one whose precepts he used. Sextus confirms that he should clearly and manifestly be judged a Platonist, but Numenius denies it. But more on him in the following book.

Carneades followed this same Arcesilaus and is said by many to have established the New Academy with him. <margin>Carneades</margin> For neither Cicero, in the books he published on the Academics, makes mention of any but the Old and the New; nor likewise does Lactantius in his third book *Against the Pagans*. Augustine, however, in those books he wrote *Against the Academics*, accepts Carneades as the leader of the Third Academy; he makes no mention of a fourth or fifth, although he speaks of Philo, Antiochus, and Plotinus. The leaders of the New Academy (which was also given the name of the Third) <margin>On the Third Academy</margin> persevered in this, dissenting from others: that all things are incomprehensible, whereas others judged some things certain and others doubtful. Some attribute the invention of this opinion to Xenophanes; others trace it back to Homer; Origen seems to attribute it to Ecphantus of Syracuse. <margin>Origen</margin> However it may be, if Carneades did not invent it, he certainly expanded it greatly. Yet his followers confessed they did not approach matters vainly or by chance; for just as others spoke of "certain" and "uncertain," so they used the terms "probable" and "improbable." Cicero mentions this distinction elsewhere and in the second book of *On Duties*. They did not want to say things were "certain" or "uncertain," and thus not "comprehensible," and in this they differed from the Skeptics: because the things they turned over in dispute they denied could be grasped, except for this one thing (and not even this expressly): that they grasped that those things could not be grasped with certainty.

Cicero himself, in the first book of the *Academics*, following the opinion of Varro, does not distinguish much between the opinion of Carneades and that of Arcesilaus, inasmuch as he says his Academy is the "New" one; and he says the same in the first book of *On Laws* and elsewhere. However, as we have said, it is usually attributed to Carneades as the "Third" and Arcesilaus as the "Middle." In the second book, he teaches that it was decreed by both that nothing can be perceived, although he seems to attribute *epoche* <note>original: "epochen" — the suspension of judgment.</note> (that is, the retention of assent) more willingly to Arcesilaus than to Carneades. Yet they both differed from the dogmatists in that, for the dogmatists, the comprehension of many and great things was decreed without controversy. In the judgment of good and evil, the followers of Carneades also differed so significantly from the Pyrrhonians that they placed those things in "persuasion," judging that to be "good" which was more probable and persuasive...

<meta>The translator is working from a Latin manuscript discussing the origins and etymology of the term 'Philosophy'. The OCR notes indicate standard scribal abbreviations (e.g., 'phiæ' for 'philosophiae', 'p̃tagoras' for 'Pythagoras') which have been expanded in this translation.</meta>

# On Philosophy

All those who devoted their efforts to the study of wisdom were formerly called "Wise Men." This continued until the time of Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician, c. 570–495 BC</note>. He was the first to answer those who asked what he professed by calling himself a "Philosopher"—that is, a lover of wisdom. He did this because it seemed to him exceedingly arrogant for a man to proclaim himself "Wise."

Furthermore, after his time, the name "Philosopher" grew so much in prestige that whoever appeared to excel in the knowledge of divine or human affairs was considered to be, and was called, a Philosopher. Philosophy is also defined by some as the knowledge of divine and human things, joined with the pursuit of living well.

## On the Parts of Philosophy

Philosophy is divided into three parts:
1. **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: "Physica"</note>, which treats the hidden causes of nature.
2. **Moral Philosophy** <note>original: "Ethica"</note>, which concerns itself with the regulation of conduct.
3. **Rational Philosophy** <note>original: "Logica"</note>, which deals with the method of discerning truth from falsehood.

Pythagoras first proposed the term "Philosopher," but it was later scholars who divided the discipline into these specific parts. They preferred to distinguish the various branches of study so that the different types of knowledge could be recognized more clearly. Through these parts, a perfect understanding of the world and of human life is sought.

And **Democritus** seems to agree with the Skeptics <margin>**Democritus**</margin> when, in his work called the *Canons*, <margin>*Canons*</margin> he sharply contradicted the logical and demonstrative faculty. That the philosophers of the nations, differing on the principle of all things, do not agree. Chapter nine.

<margin>From where the author may have gathered the disagreements of the philosophers.</margin>

But perhaps those who were unable to grasp the truth for themselves because of their disagreements did not think that philosophy itself relied upon truth; they judged its instruments to be not entirely true, and they cast aside the universal and most principal parts of natural, supernatural, and moral doctrine as if they were not supported by truth at all. Nevertheless, it might seem that they thought the particular dogmas of philosophy did not shrink from the likeness of truth; for that reason, they were led into them by common consent, and decided upon them peacefully and amiably. But it will be clearly seen that this is not the case. However, so that we may arrive at a discovery of the discordant errors of the philosophers from the highest to the lowest by relying on some order: let us collect their disagreements—not all of them, certainly, but the most numerous and distinguished—not only from Aristotle, Plato, Plutarch, Seneca, Firmianus <note>Lactantius</note>, Laertius, Augustine, Ambrose, and Eusebius. I do not use the version of Eusebius translated into our language by George of Trebizond, for it is so diminished and maimed that not even a third part seems to have been translated. Rather, I draw from the Greek text of Eusebius itself, which is primarily great and copious, but also from Galen, Iamblichus, Sextus the Pyrrhonist, and likewise from Athenagoras and Justin, the Christian philosophers, and Theodoret and others—authors who are neither entirely worn out by use nor known to the common crowd.

First, however, the disagreement concerning the first principle of things offers itself to us. And indeed, there were those who established a principle of things, those who did away with it, and those who remained ambiguous in both doing away with and establishing it. For those who professed that they would hand down dogmas asserted that there is some principle of things, but what might that be? Is it God, separate from all things? Or the soul of the world, or rather not one thing but many? Furthermore, there is much disagreement among them as to whether it is a body or a spirit. Those who affirm that nothing can be perceived say that even that first principle does not fall under the knowledge of truth; those who truly hesitate about all things even call into doubt whether there is a principle or not. But in this matter, a distinction is also found: for the Sceptics felt about the principle as they did about religion and laws, which they acquiesced to without formal teaching and, as they themselves said, <term>un-dogmatically</term> <note>original: "ἀδοξάστως" (adoxastos) - meaning without holding a firm opinion or belief</note>. The Sceptic philosophers, however, did so in no way, but disputed on either side with equal arguments, as they themselves claimed. But many hesitated in this one matter, although they remained least doubtful in other things; and they, rather than the Academics, thought that the weights of contrary reasons were equal.

Certainly, there were also those who denied that there are gods—not only among the philosophers who utterly rejected everything else, but even among those who built up many things. Such were Diagoras of Melos (or more correctly as some say), and Theodorus of Cyrene, and Euhemerus. Plutarch, Sextus the philosopher, and Bishop Theodoret held him to be from Tegea, but Lactantius brings forth Euhemerus from the city of Messana, whose work was translated into our language by Ennius. But those who confessed that there was some principle of things agreed neither in number, nor in essence or nature, nor in seat. For it pleased Anaximander that the stars were celestial gods, an argument perhaps drawn from the decrees of the Egyptians, whom Diodorus claims were the first to think the sun and moon were gods, giving the name of Isis to the latter and Osiris to the former. The Greeks perhaps imitated these; indeed, Plato writes in the *Cratylus* that it seems to him the first men who inhabited Greece thought only those were gods whom many of the barbarians also worshiped in their time: namely, the sun.
