**Chapter Ten. That there is great disagreement among the philosophers of the nations in determining the causes of things and concerning nature and its principles.**

And so, that crowd of philosophers, who disagreed when discussing the beginning of things, was found to be in no way harmonious when teaching about natural causes and principles. For here one man devised divine causes, another natural and material ones, and another mathematical ones; for Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, and Plato decreed diversely. Nor were there lacking those who introduced only one cause, those who brought in two, and those who summoned three. It is also not laborious to find those who, content with three, rejected the rest, as well as those for whom four were not enough and who adopted "co-causes" <note>Secondary or contributing factors</note> besides those. Truly, the discord is not over number alone. In the things themselves—what they are and by what names they should appropriately be called—there is still great contention. For some contend they are corporeal <note>Physical/material</note>, while others say they are incorporeal. The Stoics bring three into the midst, one of which they call "preceding" <note>original: προηλαγμένην (proēlagmenēn)</note>, another "principal" <note>original: προηγουμένην (proēgoumenēn)</note>, and the third "containing" <note>original: συνεκτικήν (synektikēn)</note>. There are also those who indeed admit the "containing" cause but wish it to be a "co-cause," and others too, which if anyone called "cooperative"—from the Greek word *synerga* <note>original: συνεργά</note>—he would not be mistaken. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> accept two intrinsic causes, form and matter, and two extrinsic ones, the agent (or transmuter) and the end <note>The purpose or final cause</note>; for that which transmutes informs the matter for the sake of some thing, and as soon as that which acts has shown itself, the matter is immediately surrendered, the form arises, and the end is revealed. The Platonists added co-causes, since they say that both "Ideas"—by which the mind of the craftsman is stirred to action—are required, as well as the instruments by whose help he finishes what he conceived in his mind. But there is controversy on this matter too: since Plato separates the Ideas from matter, which Aristotle resists; on this point, others explain Aristotle in different ways, and they decide that the opinions of Xenocrates go against those of Plato. Zeno the Stoic seems to have recognized only our own Ideas or species of things which we carry in the mind. Nor is there harmony on this matter, since many wish them to be innate to the soul, while most affirm they are implanted from things. Furthermore, the Sceptics admit no acting cause and rail against the rest of the philosophers, whose arguments will be explained in the third book of this work. But in natural principles, what strifes, what battles of disagreeing philosophers are there, openly warring even over what nature itself is? Some call it an "artful fire," others God, others the power of the whole universe, others the principle of motion and rest, and Anaxagoras calls it composition and division. Others say it is nothing at all—not because they are followers of Carneades or Sceptics, but because nature itself seems to be nothing on its own except the measure and mixture of elements, as Heraclitus thought. Some judged that no principle at all should be admitted; others held the opposite; others, positioned between either opinion, remained silent as far as their own judgment was concerned. Otherwise, they are most vocal in refuting the opinions of others. Moreover, of those who admitted principles, some mixed together the corporeal and incorporeal, the spiritual and the material: namely God, Ideas, and matter...

matter; Plutarch attributes this opinion to Socrates and Plato among the pagans, while among our own writers, <margin>Plutarch</margin> Ambrose attributes it entirely to Plato. Justin Martyr writes that Plato’s <margin>Justin Martyr.</margin> opinion on principles, as in most other matters, was inconsistent: for he sometimes posited three principles—God, matter, and form <note>original: "speciem"</note>—and sometimes four, since he added the soul of the world to those three. The opinion of Aristotle is now known to almost everyone: he established matter, form, and privation <note>The absence or lack of a specific form</note> as the principles of natural things. Hence, I wonder why I have read in some authors, and even in Ambrose himself in the first book of the *Hexaemeron*, that Aristotle posited two principles—matter and form or appearance—and with them a third <margin>Explanation of the passage in Ambrose.</margin> which is called the "operative" principle, which would have the power to effectively carry out what he had intended to undertake. Perhaps he did not wish to mention "privation," and instead adopted an efficient cause that works by itself. Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoicism</note> generally agreed, but he mentioned neither privation nor the "fifth body" <note>The quintessence or ether</note>, to which Aristotle attributed a unique nature and motion entirely different from composite natural things. Although many, both among the pagans and our own people, have contradicted Aristotle in this matter, as will become clear as the work proceeds. However, when we speak of principles at present, we primarily understand material ones—at least composite ones, not those first and simple ones to which most philosophers attributed everything that is made. But since these are frequently confused, we have not so strictly or distinctly separated composite elements from simple principles and causes. Thus, regarding those who spoke of composite principles: some entirely excluded corporeal and natural things; others admitted only natural things and not corporeal ones; others admitted corporeal but not natural; and others established both corporeal and natural principles. Pythagoras, having cast aside natural bodies subject to motion and change, introduced mathematics—namely numbers and proportions which he calls Harmonies—and from these he composed geometric elements; for even before this, he had established Unity and the "Indefinite Dyad." Some mathematicians also posited the boundaries and extremities of bodies. Straton the physicist was content with natural qualities alone. Democritus, however, posited indivisible bodies, and Epicurus posited atoms, which they intended to be bodies perceptible by reason: uncreated, infinite, perpetual, and incorruptible, which could neither be broken nor changed as far as their substance is concerned, yet they would move through an infinite vacuum. They varied, however, in that Democritus thought only two things happened to bodies—magnitude and shape—to which Epicurus added weight. Heraclides of Pontus and Asclepiades of Bithynia posited "irregular masses" <note>original: "ἄνομοι ὄγκοι" (anomoi ogkoi)</note>. Those who introduced both corporeal and natural principles at the same time, and did not do away with the motion, generation, and corruption of things, were also wonderfully varied. Some were content with one principle, but not with a harmonious opinion: for "finite" and "infinite" gave birth to another controversy. Another arose from the qualities of the elements. Furthermore, there were those who preferred two principles, among whom Zareta the Chaldean <note>Zoroaster</note> established light and darkness under the names of father and mother; the former being hot, dry, light, and swift, while the latter is cold, moist, heavy, and slow. Another joined a third to the two. To others, the number four was pleasing in this matter. Nor were there lacking those to whom five principles were more agreeable. There are even those who added a sixth. But truly, the crowd of philosophers is no more settled or peaceful regarding the nature and quality of the thing than they were in agreement regarding the number. Indeed, of those who introduced only one principle, one wanted it to be earth, another...

BOOK ONE <column-break/> XVI

...and that all things come to an end. <note>original: "καὶ τὸ τὴν πάντα τελευτᾶ"</note> Anaximander, a student of Thales, also devised a single principle, but he preferred it to be infinite rather than finite. However, Hippus of Rhegium mixed water and fire. Oenopides of Chios chose fire and air. Parmenides chose fire and earth. Onomacritus, in the Orphic writings, connected three: fire, water, and earth. To these three, Empedocles added air, and he was followed by both the Stoics and the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note>. Truly, it is handed down that he believed certain very minute filings or tiny bodies preceded the four elements; these "filings" and particles are also said to have been accepted by Heraclitus. Nevertheless, Empedocles placed two incorporeal forces over the four corporeal principles: Love and Strife, to which action and generation are attributed. Aristotle, however, placed a fifth body <note>The "quintessence" or ether.</note> over the elements, so that their power might depend on it and be governed by it. Furthermore, Anaxagoras introduced an innumerable crowd of material principles, which he himself named *homeomeries* <note>original: "ὁμοιομερῶν"</note>, that is, "similar particles." And Diodorus, nicknamed Cronus, devised minimal and indivisible bodies. Let these diverse and clashing opinions on principles suffice, lest I seek older opinions further back from Moschus the Phoenician <margin>Moschus the Phoenician</margin>, since Posidonius wished to claim that these ideas originated from him. I believe this is the same man mentioned by Iamblichus in the first book on the Pythagorean sect. However, he mentions "Mochus," not "Moschus," when he writes that Pythagoras spent time in Phoenicia with the Hierophants <note>High priests of sacred mysteries.</note>, the sons of the prophets, and Mochus the natural philosopher. But Origen, on the testimony of Diodorus of Eretria and Aristoxenus the musician, writes that Pythagoras went to Zaretas the Chaldean and drew much from him. But enough of these matters for now; we must hasten to other controversies.

**On the constitution of the world and its end; on its unity, size, and shape; and on matter and form, and the various conflicting things published by the philosophers. Chapter Eleven.**

This entire machine by which we are surrounded, which the ancients called the "world" <note>Latin: *mundus*</note> from its adornment and a "globe" from its shape, and to which (as Plutarch says when discussing the opinions of philosophers) Pythagoras was the first to give the name *Cosmos* <note>From the Greek *kosmos*, implying order and beauty.</note> because of its order: will the philosophers perhaps teach us about this with unanimous consent, peace having now been established among them? Not in the least. For there are always greater battles among them—no peace, no agreement. For some wish it to have been established by the providence of God, such as the Pythagoreans and the Platonists, although there are those who think that Plato, following the Pythagoreans, did not think exactly so. Others believe it was neither this nor that, but a mixture, as if you were to say something made of both providence and chance. Indeed, both Atticus and Plutarch the Platonists think the order of the world had a beginning, but that it was preceded by a disordered motion driven by a depraved and formless soul. So great is the controversy stirred up regarding what Plato felt on almost every question <margin>The difficulty of understanding Plato's meaning.</margin>, as we have said and will say more extensively. Certainly, whoever has learned and followed the Mosaic accounts judges that it was established by the providence of God, and they believe that by His will it shall never cease to exist, even though by its own nature it could perish and be destroyed. Plutarch is the authority that Pythagoras thought so previously, and the dialogue of Plato titled *Timaeus* makes it clear enough that he intended the same. Moreover, Timaeus of Locri himself <margin>The work of Timaeus the Pythagorean</margin>, whom Plato follows with great zeal in that work, was a Pythagorean. A book of his concerning the world survives to this day, written in the Doric dialect; and although I have observed this in only one author I know, Tertullian in his *Apology*...

Pythagoras considered the body of the world to be unborn (to use his own words) and uncreated. However, others have reported differently concerning him, and have said that his opinion was explained by Plato. <margin>Ambrose</margin> Ambrose, in the first book of the *Hexaemeron* <note>A commentary on the six days of Creation</note>, writes that Plato thought matter was uncreated and without beginning, from which God established the world not as a creator, but as a craftsman. <margin>Varro</margin> Varro, certainly, among the beginnings of the second book of *On Agriculture* while discussing the origin of livestock, affirms that Pythagoras and Aristotle thought there was no beginning for animals. On the contrary, Thales of Miletus and Zeno of Citium held the opposite. But many certainly thought the world was created. Nor were there lacking among them those who thought that very thing would be destroyed by a lack of nourishment—an opinion I cannot say is more worthy of laughter, hissing, or rather silence. For there were those who reported that the stars and the Heaven are nourished by vapors. <margin>Concerning fate and providence, how they vary.</margin> The Stoics accept that there will be a conflagration and a purification of this world. But they do not speak in harmony, since some say it will be of the whole, others of a part; and thus it is purified and renewed by parts and, as it were, rises again. These same people also contend that there is fate, and they explained it by the example of a dog tied to a chariot: if he is willing, he follows; if he is unwilling, he is compelled. Others denied fate itself, admitting only providence. It also seemed to some that both ought to be granted, but among these there is a fight, since they did not sufficiently agree on how they related to each other and to which more should be given and attributed. I return to the world, which <margin>Against Aristotle.</margin> others think was made by a concourse of atoms and by chance, and that the same will perish. Others, following Aristotle, maintain that the heaven and the elements had no beginning and will have no end, and they think they have confirmed this with the most certain demonstrations, leaning on this foundation: that otherwise motion would be discovered to have existed before any motion existed. O you who are destitute of things and lacking in reason! As if God created the heaven and those things enclosed within it through motion, and as if they did not flow from His will, as our Christian religion believes, and most excellently believes. <margin>The author's book on providence.</margin> Regarding this matter, a place has been set aside for discussion in the last book of this work, when we shall dispute against the dogmas of Aristotle. But those philosophers who think the world was created by the providence of God, and think it is ruled by the same, do not agree entirely, since some attribute this to the Supreme Being, others to a nearby Mind, and differently according to their differing opinions on the Ideas. Regarding this matter, I myself have discussed many things in the second part of our work, which is titled *On the Providence of God against the Pseudo-Philosophers*. Those who want the world to have been established and not eternal also contend: from where, indeed, did its beginning start? What first beginning, what first origin did it receive? And those who wanted Chaos to have preceded the world draw one thing after another from it in the first stages. <margin>Zareta the Chaldean</margin> Empedocles first separated the ether, then fire, then earth, and finally he wanted water to have gushed forth, from which the air arose; and the heaven was established from the ether, but the sun proceeded from fire. But lower and earthly things were fused from other elements. Zareta the Chaldean, he whom Pythagoras heard <note>Zareta is likely a reference to Zoroaster</note>, generated the world from light and darkness as if from a woman and a man; he wanted this to be the same as nature and musical Harmony. Some think the beginning was taken from the earth as if from a center. Plato established the visible world according to the example of the intelligible world; he first drew out the soul of that which is seen, and soon after the corporeal mass, constituted from fire and earth, and from water and air. Pythagoras starts from the first bodies, but—submerging his own bodies in a mathematical sea—he fabricates the world from five figures of <term>solids</term> <note>original: "στερεῶν" (stereōn)</note>. From the pyramid he extracts fire, from the eight-sided figure <note>octahedron</note> air, from the twenty-sided figure <note>icosahedron</note> (if I may say so) water, he makes earth emerge from the cube, and from the twelve-sided figure <note>dodecahedron</note> he devises the sphere of the universe. BOOK ONE XVII

Both Timaeus the Pythagorean and Plato delighted in this union, and they navigated this same Sea in their own vessel. But regarding its unity and magnitude, how great a dispute flourished among the nations! Thales, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Parmenides, Melissus, Heraclitus, and Zeno of Citium—the disciple of Crates and leader of the Stoic sect—and others, decreed that there is but one world. This was held most strongly by Aristotle and Plato, although many attempt to dismantle the arguments by which they tried to prove it, as will become clear in the course of this work. Anaximander, however, as well as Anaximenes and Archelaus and others, being by no means content with a single world, built many. So too did Diogenes and Leucippus; Democritus and Epicurus likewise fabricated innumerable worlds. Indeed, Democritus claimed they were infinite and differed so much in size from one another that in some of them he said there was neither sun nor moon, while in others, larger ones were found than those seen among us, and in certain others, there were even multiple suns. He ordained that these worlds of his were spaced unequally apart, some of which (as Origen reports) were increasing, while others were diminishing and being destroyed. <note>The author is discussing the ancient philosophical debate between "Monism" (one universe) and "Pluralism" (multiple or infinite worlds).</note>

From this indeed, they truly judge that both the heavens and all the superior bodies, driven in a perpetual circle, are exempt from matter <note>original: "immunia materiae"</note>, and are in every way free from its fluctuations. There are those who think that one single matter should be placed in all bodies, yet even on this point they do not speak harmoniously or amiably, for literary battles are undertaken. They dispute whether the matter found in the superior bodies and that in the lowest bodies is of the same nature and reason, or diverse. Furthermore, there is a struggle over the dimensions of matter: whether they are infinite or have received some limit; nor does the fight end there. For they contend whether matter possesses any actual existence <term>actum: the state of being "actual" or "realized" as opposed to just "potential"</term> of itself, or whether it is mere potentiality, capable of receiving anything and fit to be clothed in all forms, but as far as its naked essence is concerned, entirely void and lacking any actuality.

<margin>Objection</margin> You will say that these wars have already been fought in an orderly fashion between Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher influential in Western thought</note> and our own theologians regarding the matter of the heaven and its dimensions; and that on the same cause, dissensions flourished between Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, and Giles <note>Giles of Rome</note>, and the lawsuits are still before the judge, since the followers of Thomas and Scotus do not agree upon the actuality of matter itself, nor could the distinction of a "double act" succeed in removing the controversy.

<margin>Solution</margin> I confess that is true, but from where did these discords flow? Certainly not from Moses or the twelve prophets, as far as I remember, nor to my knowledge from the Gospel. Rather, they proceeded from the philosophers of the nations <note>i.e., the Pagans</note>, and especially flowed from the doctrine of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, who spoke so ambiguously that each man has busied himself confirming his own opinion from their sayings. I would not entirely deny that the ancient theologians dealt with this matter somewhat, but more sparingly; for they were occupied with other things pertaining to human salvation and, above all, to attaining the friendship of God Himself. So much so, that the great Ambrose, when in the work he titled the *Hexahemeron* <note>Ambrose’s commentary on the six days of Creation</note> the discourse fell upon the place and seat of the elements—a question certainly well-worn and discussed by the ancients as much as any—he nevertheless rejected it on purpose, intending to devote his time to more useful things.

<margin>Ambrose</margin> But I shall perhaps seem to attack the men of our own time who are occupied in venting these matters; therefore, I return to the ancient philosophers of the nations who battled variously and diversely concerning matter. For Thales, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, and the crowd of Stoics thought it to be changeable and transmutable. But Democritus, Metrodorus, and Epicurus would not even allow it to be acted upon, because atoms and the void are (so to speak) impassible. Some held that matter was made along with the world, others that it is eternal, as did the Peripatetics and the Platonist Xenocrates.

Even in discerning "form," the philosophers are found not to be unarmed—I mean form, not the "figure" by which the world is thought to be built externally, whether into a sphere, a cone, or the likeness of an egg or an apple. For that form which is more truly called "figure" is adventitious <note>External or added on</note>, since it happens to an essence already constituted; for that is properly called "form" by which a thing acquires the very thing that it is. This form some have said is the "soul." Others have removed the soul and utterly denied it is in the world. Others have spoken with such a two-headed sense that to this day there is a struggle over the words of certain philosophers who committed their thoughts to literary monuments two thousand years ago. Nor are there lacking disputes moved among theologians on this matter, because they have read the philosophers of the nations decreeing various things. For it is believed by many that Plato thought the world was a living animal. Others think Aristotle was of the same opinion. Against this stand many who in no way agree that a soul was attributed to the world by Aristotle. Among the theologians called "Parisians," Thomas Aquinas, a man of excellent judgment, denies the world is an animal. Aureolus asserts it with many reasons, which are resisted by those who stand with Thomas. Among the ancient theologians, Jerome, in his commentary on Solomon’s *Ecclesiastes*, seems to have wanted the orb of the sun to be animated.

<margin>Concerning the form and soul of the world, how varied.</margin>

But—

BOOK ONE                                                                                              XVIII

But let us not discuss our own people for the present, but rather bring forth the opinions of the pagans, just as there is a discordant consensus among those who thought the world was a living being <note>original: "animatum"</note> as to what that soul might be, which some think is God. Others believe it to be a preeminent and intellectual substance, but hanging many degrees below the First Mind, in which—namely—the ideas of things to be created are stored. Others place a First Mind over the world, created by the one and supreme God, by whose providence they also believe it is administered. Thus, between Plotinus, Proclus, and the other Platonists, there is discord concerning the form of the world, just as it is already established that among the most famous philosophers there was a vigorous debate concerning the whole universe—its constitution, end, magnitude, figure, and matter. Setting aside that contemplation, it now occurs to us to see whether, in determining and deciding upon the parts and effects of the world, philosophers can be found to be as discordant as we have found them to be contentious and combative regarding the universe itself.

### Chapter Twelve.
### That the philosophers of the pagans differed discordantly and combatively both concerning the highest parts of the world—the Heaven, the stars, and all things generated on high—as well as the lowest and subterranean parts and their movements.

And first, they tear the Heaven—the most noble and supreme part of the world—into many pieces, and by no means harmoniously. For some established eight spheres, others nine, others more than thirty, and even forty. Aristotle, dealing with metaphysics, agrees with these latter numbers, referring himself to Callippus and Eudoxus, rather than undertaking the care of investigating the matter, let alone comprehending it. I pass over those epicycles <note>small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones, used to explain planetary motion</note>, or "little globes" inserted into larger globes as some think, while others do not; this is touched upon so variously and combatively that Averroes, having trusted as a young man that he could settle such controversies, despaired of it as an old man. 

<margin>Concerning the heaven and the order of these celestial spheres.</margin>

Furthermore, in sanctioning their order, there is no order among the philosophers. Plato, after the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "non errantem," the stars that do not wander</note>, placed the globes of the wandering stars: first Saturn, then Jupiter, then Mars, after that Venus, then Mercury, next the Sun, and finally the Moon. On the contrary, Anaximander, Metrodorus of Chios, and Crates made the Sun the highest and outermost of all; next, Metrodorus, Crates, and Anaximander placed the Moon in order, and only after that the sphere of the immobile stars and the remaining planets. Aristarchus, however, placed the Sun after the sphere of the fixed stars, making it the first and highest of the planets. 

The ancient mathematicians were also various and diverse in this matter; for some established the Sun in the middle of the planets, which Ptolemy himself approved, while they preferred the Moon to hold the last seat among them. Others, following the Egyptians and imitating Plato and Aristotle, made the Moon the nearest, but placed the Sun above it with nothing in between. This opinion has been embraced by some of the younger mathematicians, who have refuted Ptolemy. 

<margin>Alpetragius</margin>

Yet Alpetragius (although he was not from the pagans, but professed himself to be a Christian) approved neither this nor that; for he did not place the Sun in the middle of the planets, nor did he want it to be the first above the Moon, but placed it immediately above Mercury, so that Venus would be higher than the Sun and judged to be in the middle among the planets. Nor were there lacking those who pronounced the order of the three superior planets to be entirely uncertain. 

<margin>Giovanni Pico, the Author's book on the Pre-knowledge of things, and the question of Astrology.</margin>

I remember this matter was mentioned both by my uncle Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), famous Renaissance philosopher</note> in his new work against the astrologers, and by myself in the fifth book of *On the Pre-knowledge of Things*, and in the *Question on the Falsity of Astrology*; and as this work proceeds, a place has been set aside for us to dispute against astrology. Now let our discourse return to the ancient philosophers. Democritus and Leucippus clothed the world as if with a garment and covered it with a membrane. Parmenides previously fashioned certain entwined "little crowns" <note>original: "coronulas"</note> out of the dense and the rare, tempered them with light and darkness, and placed them upon the orb. Thus...

<meta>This page continues a survey of classical and pre-Socratic cosmological theories, specifically focusing on the motion and physical composition of the heavens and celestial bodies.</meta>

# BOOK

...nevertheless, so that which surrounds the rest might be as firm and solid as a wall. Epicurus limited some of his worlds with a thin boundary and others with a thick one, bestowing motion upon some and rest upon others. Regarding this motion, although almost everyone agrees that it occurs in a circuit <note>original: "in gyrum"; referring to circular orbits</note>, they do not agree on the manner and the cause. For Diogenes and Anaxagoras maintained that they turned toward the south; some younger mathematicians—relying either on that same opinion or moved by reasons and observations—agree with them, introducing a motion of latitude. 

However, Alcmaeon was the first, as far as I know, to say that the planets also move in a contrary direction and that the highest Heaven <note>The "Caelum," or the sphere of fixed stars</note> does the same; afterwards, a great crowd of both philosophers and mathematicians followed him. These same men held that the spheres move of their own accord. Others wished for the motion to be received from minds separated from matter <note>referring to "Intelligences" or divine movers</note>. 

Regarding the right and left of the world, they are by no means in agreement: for Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle decreed that the region of the east both is and ought to be considered the right, while the west is the left. But Empedocles assigned the right parts to the summer tropic and the left to the winter. Nor were there lacking those who preferred the motion to occur from top to bottom. 

Now, no greater consensus appears in the very nature and essence of the matter than in its number and order. Some thought the heavens were fiery; others, crystalline; others, participating in no way in the essence of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, but belonging to a certain fifth nature <term>Quintessence: the "aether," a celestial substance believed to be incorruptible</term> of its own and entirely separated from lower things. Aristotle is held to be the first author of this opinion, suggesting that the heaven does not contain heat within itself or its own form, but imparts heat to lower bodies by its own power. Democritus, however, affirmed that the sun has by no means a hot nature, according to Plutarch in his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "istromatis," likely referring to the *Stromateis*</note>. 

<margin>
On the sun and
moon and their
diverse
natures.
</margin>

But you might perhaps think they were in agreement regarding the stars and planets: Xenophanes thought the sun and moon were fiery clouds, fashioning the sun out of small sparks, and he did not deny that it is created anew each day. Thales, however, judged them to be earthy, and Anaximenes also fabricated them from earth. 

Even in shape, opinion is not in agreement: Aristotle wanted them to be spherical and to have the nature of the "fifth body." Heraclitus preferred the sun and moon to be formed in the likeness of a boat <note>original: "scaphae"; a bowl-shaped vessel</note>, and there were those who made them similar to the wheels of a chariot. Anaximenes affirmed that the sun is flat and spread out like a curtain. Others established that the moon was created in the form of a cylinder. Diogenes preferred it to be in the appearance of an ivy leaf. And Philolaus the Pythagorean thought it was crystalline, yet assumed its splendor from the fire which is in the universe. It was estimated by Plato that the sun and moon have a great deal of fire, yet are not devoid of other elements. 

Certainly, Anaximenes, Parmenides, and others composed the moon from fire alone; Pythagoras judged it to be a stony body; Heraclitus, earth enveloped in gloom. Anaxagoras and Democritus, besides wanting it to be a fiery firmament, even established fields, mountains, and valleys within it, so that they now seem to differ almost nothing or very little from the fictional tales of Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, author of "A True Story," an early satire involving a trip to the moon</note>. Certainly Xenophanes (as found in Cicero and others) said that the moon is inhabited and that it is a land of many cities and mountains; and some Pythagoreans also thought the moon was inhabited just like this earth we tread upon—since it appears earthy and dense—but by animals and trees fifty times larger than those seen among us. 

Thales of Miletus judged the multitude of stars to be earthy and ignited. But it pleased Anaxagoras that the stars were indeed earthy, but had previously been rocks which were snatched up into the heights by the rotation of the universe, became inflamed, and, being fixed to the sky, obtained the name of stars. Democritus confirmed this opinion, and it did not displease Metrodorus, who also fashioned the sun from an ignited rock. Anaximander fashioned them out of air and drove them in a circuit like a wheel and filled them with fire, so that they emitted flames as if through certain bellows. Diogenes also wanted them to be breathing holes and gave them the shape of ivy, adding that some occasionally fall down to the earth...

I shall relate this in English <note>original: "latine" (Latin); the author is writing in Latin to ensure his warning reaches those who might otherwise ignore it due to a lack of Greek</note> lest some, through ignorance of the language, fail to be warned of a bold error: "Is it really necessary," he asks, "to bring up those fables they tell regarding figures, eclipses, and distances?" For they do not only disagree about the space between the stars, but even define how much space lies between them and the earth, counting four hundred thousand <term>myriads</term> <note>A myriad is ten thousand; here referring to a vast, specific calculation of distance</note> of <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note> or more from the earth to the moon, and as many again from there to the sun. Nor do they blush, though ignorant of the depth of the sea—which a fisherman can at least measure by dropping a line—to burn with the desire to measure the air and the ether. They are neither mindful of the uselessness of the task they have assumed, nor do they recall that Aeschylean warning: *Do not seek in vain for things that do not help.* For even if every one of these things could be discovered, it would nonetheless be useless.

And lest we seem to have forgotten the nations, Xenophon, in his memoirs concerning Socrates, writes as follows: <margin>Xenophon on Socrates</margin> "He altogether forbade being curious about the celestial things which God has engineered; for he did not think they could be discovered by man, nor did he think it pleasing to the Gods for one to seek what they did not wish to declare. Indeed, he thought that one who meditated on such things ran a risk and was insane, and that Anaxagoras was no less foolish for attempting to reveal the works of the Gods by his 'high wisdom.'" And again on the same matter: "No one ever saw Socrates doing, or heard him saying, anything impious or unjust. For he did not dispute about the nature of the universe or other things as most do, considering how that which the sophists call 'the world' <note>original: "mundus" (the cosmos)</note> holds together, or by what necessity the celestial bodies move. Rather, he demonstrated that those who cared for such things were insane." He proceeds further to produce many notable points to restrain the bold insolence of such researchers, which would be long to relate.

But let us return to where we diverged, so that it may be understood that those who could not agree on the whole of the stars, nor on the more notable ones, have least of all agreed upon those tiny stars collected together to form that circle which is called <margin>On the Galaxy</margin> the **Milky Way**. You will find that this circle was thought by certain Pythagoreans to be the scorched path of a star that fell from its proper seat; by others, it was once the orbit of the sun's course. There were even those who thought it was created by a certain refraction of the sun's rays, appearing as it does—just as happens with rainbows and clouds—though it seemed to one thinker to be a refraction not of the sun's light, but of the light of stars not encompassed by the sun. Metrodorus was pleased to call it the sun's path, inasmuch as it is and ought to be considered the sun's own circle. Anaxagoras attributed it to the shadow of the earth. Parmenides thought it should be referred to a mixture of the rare and the dense, from which the milky color burst forth. Democritus judged it to be the splendor of many tiny stars positioned together, illuminating one another due to their density and frequency. 

<margin>Diverse opinions on the Galaxy attributed to Aristotle. Albertus, Plutarch, Proclus</margin> This opinion Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval scholar</note> noted was later accepted by Aristotle and placed in his *Meteorology* as his own. However, Plutarch assigned another view to Aristotle: that he thought it came from a dry evaporation, and indeed some of his words in the *Meteorology* seem to imply this, and several have suspected it based on his mind. This opinion Proclus the Platonist seems to have embraced in his *Sphere* when he writes that the milky circle consists of a thin, nebulous substance; yet others have decided otherwise, as we have sufficiently indicated. But more on this in the Sixth Book. Posidonius thought it a certain constitution of fire, a sort of condensation more splendid than a star and denser than light. This controversy concludes the entire part regarding the superior corporeal world. For since some attribute it to stars fixed in the sphere, and others to vapors and such things generated on high, it becomes the boundary of both subjects. Now, concerning meteorological matters...

We must now treat **meteorological matters**, so that having completed our disputes concerning the greater world <note>The "macrocosm" or the universe at large</note>, our discourse may turn toward explaining the conflicting and clashing opinions regarding the lower world. First, we encounter **comets**, which some of the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras</note> maintained were stars, but that they only appear at certain intervals and do not shine constantly. <margin>On comets</margin> **Diogenes** likewise called them stars. However, **Anaxagoras** and **Democritus** claimed they were a gathering of brilliance emitted by two or more stars. Nor were there lacking those who thought comets were reflections toward the sun, occurring almost in the same way as happens with the magnification of lenses. **Aristotle** viewed them as a certain ignited substance bursting forth from dry evaporation. Indeed, **Straton** was pleased to think a comet was the light of a star caught in a dense cloud. **Heraclides of Pontus** thought it a high cloud illuminated by light. **Epigenides** called it a downward flow of ignited spirit <note>pneuma or gas</note> mixed with something earthy. **Boethus** preferred it to be an appearance of rarefied air. **Xenophanes** called it a collection and commotion of inflamed clouds. **Metrodorus** called it a violent casting of the sun into the clouds.

Philosophers agree no more closely regarding **thunder, lightning-flashes, and thunderbolts**. <margin>On thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts</margin> **Anaximander** believed these took their origin from the spirit; for whenever it is caught in a thick cloud and violently shaken out due to its thinness and lightness, then the eruption creates the noise, while the contrast against the blackness of the cloud creates the brilliance—to say nothing of what **Seneca** reported in the second book of his *Natural Questions*. **Metrodorus’s** opinion is that when the spirit falls into a cloud thick with density, the breaking of it produces the noise, while it shines by the striking and splitting; through the speed of its descent, it takes heat from the sun, and a thunderbolt is emitted, the weakness of which fades into a mere lightning-flash. **Anaxagoras’s** opinion is that when heat falls into cold—that is, when an ethereal part falls into the air—thunder is produced by the sound, while lightning-flashes are caused by the appearance of the cloudy blackness. By the magnitude and multitude of the light, the thunderbolt arises, just as a whirlwind <note>original: "typhonem"</note> arises from a more corporeal fire, and a lightning-flash from a cloudy one. But the **Stoics** were pleased to define thunder as the collision of clouds; lightning as the ignition from that collision; and the thunderbolt as the flashing of a more violent collision. **Aristotle**, however, thought all these things should be attributed to dry evaporation, which, when it encounters moisture, prepares an exit by force; by collision and dragging, it makes the sound of thunder, but by the burning and inflammation of the heat, it makes lightning. Lightning-flashes and whirlwinds result from an excess of matter, which draws each of them—the former being hotter, the latter thicker. I am silent regarding "leaping goats," "beams," "globes," the "halo" or "crown," and other things about which both **Aristotle** in his books on *Meteorology* and **Seneca** in his books of *Natural Questions* dispute; <margin>Aristotle, Seneca</margin> though these are full of various disagreements, they are nevertheless available to even the moderately learned.

Furthermore, **Anaximenes** thought that **mists** were generated from air that was far thicker; <margin>On mists and rain</margin> when this is more collected and condensed, **rains** are squeezed out. Moreover, **snow** is formed after water has fallen, but **hail** whenever it is caught by a moist spirit. **Metrodorus** asserted that clouds are formed from a watery descent, which **Epicurus** composed of exhalations. He maintained that both hail and rain are rounded or made smooth by their long fall. Truly, it is well established that these things generated on high do indeed exist. But there are things which do not exist as physical substances, yet they appear, and are so conspicuous that they were a source of no small wonder to the men of old. Hence the **Iris** <note>The Rainbow</note> itself, the celestial arch, was called the daughter of **Thaumas** <note>The Greek god of wonder</note> because of this admiration, as **Plato** judged. <margin>On the rainbow</margin> They dispute how it is made, whether by straight, curved, or refracted lines. Indeed, it happens in the air that we see conspicuous lines from shining stones and horns, but we perceive bent and curved lines in water, when vision is deflected because of the denser matter of the water; hence oars also seem curved even if they are straight, when seen from a distance...

We observe those things tied to ships and submerged in the sea. And in mirrors, we see many things refracted and leaping apart. There are those who believe that moist evaporation, when it falls into the clouds, is immediately separated into small fragments: and so, as the sun turns toward the west, every rainbow is seen from the opposite side, at the moment when the vision, meeting the scattering of the stars <note>The author likely refers to "stellae" here as droplets or points of light</note>, is refracted: they think these scatterings are forms not of shape but of color, because first something reddish-purple, second purple, and third blackish and green present themselves to the gaze. Metrodorus, however, maintained that the Rainbow occurs when the sun shines through the clouds, specifically because the cloud turns black and the brightness itself glows reddish underneath. Anaximenes attributed the cause of the Rainbow to the brightness of the sun meeting a dense, thick, and black cloud, when the rays are unable to penetrate and pass through the cloud. It pleased Anaxagora that refraction happens from a thick cloud which resists the solar flash. It pleased Seneca that the rainbow is an image of the sun, both dewy and conceived in a hollow cloud.

<margin>On the winds, which are varied.</margin> In the nature of the winds, there is also a disparate consensus. It pleased Anaximander that wind was a flow of air, fused from the most subtle and moist parts in it, either moved or liquefied by the sun. Aristotle believes wind to be a dry evaporation. The Stoics simply call it a flow of air, having received different names from the different regions from which it is accustomed to blow. Metrodorus thought wind was made from watery evaporation due to the scorching of the sun, by the impulse of divine spirits. <margin>Author of the commentary on the hymns.</margin> But concerning the winds and why they are carried obliquely, we have said more in the commentaries on the hymns.

Concerning its number, its nature, its shape, its position, its inclination, its motion, and concerning the sea by which it is surrounded and washed. Thales thought there was only one earth: Aristotle and the Stoics thought the same. But Icetes the Pythagorean thought there were two: this one which we inhabit, and an opposite one <note>original: "adversam" — referring to the 'Antichthon' or Counter-Earth theory</note>: so also Philolaus, whose opinion Aristotle also mentions in the second book of *On the Heavens*, and attributes it to the Pythagoreans in general. Moreover, of those who said there was one, some thought it finite, such as Aristotle and the Stoics. Xenophanes, however, thought it sent roots into infinite depth from its lower part, which Aristotle also reports, and that it was fused from air and fire: and perhaps Cicero wished to note this in the *Academics* when he says, "so that we may see whether the earth is fixed deep within and clings as if by its own roots, or hangs in the middle." ->placed and brought to it; and for that reason it happens that those who are in one part are unable to see those who are situated in the other. Leucippus <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher, often credited as the founder of atomism.</note> thinks that this earth of ours inclines toward the southern region, and he attributes the cause to the thinness <note>original: "raritati"</note> which abounds in the south, while the parts lying toward the north are thickened and frozen by the cold. Democritus held the same opinion: but he believed that because the southern part is weaker, the earth, having increased in weight, sinks there. Anaximenes, however, thought that the whole earth was gradually increasing and infinite, and was not enclosed by air on every side, if what Plutarch taught in the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "stromatis"</note> is true. There were some who believed that this very earth does not move. But Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher who first suggested the Earth moves around a central fire.</note> thought it moved in a circle around a fire, in an oblique circle like the sun and the moon. Heraclides of Pontus and the Pythagorean Ecphantus do not move it from its place, as if it were fixed like a wheel, but nevertheless they move it from west to east around its own center. Therefore, this earth—which most think is immobile, others say is struck, Philolaus says is moved in a circle like the sun and moon, and Heraclides and Ecphantus say is agitated from west to east—Nicetas of Syracuse (according to the reports of Theophrastus and Cicero) thought that it alone moved, and that nothing else in the world moved besides it, inasmuch as it turned itself around its axis with the greatest speed. He believed the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and finally all things above stood still. Some have even judged this to have been the opinion of Plato in the *Timaeus*, though expressed somewhat more obscurely. Socrates and Ariston of Chios thought that none of these things could be known; yet Democritus seemed to himself to have known it in some way, for walking a middle path between them, he thought that from the beginning the earth was indeed moved and wandering, on account of its smallness and lightness; but after it became thickened, and in the course of time was made heavy, it stood immobile. Thus it seems less strange to me if Nicholas of Cusa, in the second book of *On Learned Ignorance*, <margin>Nicholas of Cusa</margin> asserted that the earth is neither spherical in shape nor immobile. But that it is moved and trembles from within and by accident, besides the natural motion of the whole mass—by which motion and trembling buildings are seen to change and collapse—is so clear that those who do not believe it often experience it at their own peril. But why this happens, different men say different things. Thales and Democritus refer the cause to water. <margin>Various opinions on the trembling of the earth</margin> Anaximenes thought the cause of earthquakes themselves was the dryness and thinness of the earth, and that they were caused by the increase and overflow of waters, as reported by some; although Seneca reports that opinion differently in the sixth book of *Natural Questions*, as he does many other things. It pleased Anaxagoras to seek the reason why the earth trembles in the air. Others preferred to refer the cause of its motion to fire, which Seneca mentions: who, not as it seemed to the Greeks (he says), but to a man of divine and sweet eloquence, and polished without effort <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or a similar authority</note>, does not seem to shrink entirely from Aristotle and Theophrastus in estimating the cause of the earth's motion. If indeed you ask the Stoics whence comes the trembling in the earth, they will certainly answer that the shaking occurs because the moisture which is in the earth is divided and departs into the air and falls away. But if you ask the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> what is the cause for the earth to both move and shake? They will answer that it is due to the gathering of cold from everywhere: for the hot vapor, which is in perpetual battle with the cold, hastens to strive for the higher places, being light; but the opposing exhalation stands in its way with barriers and excites the commotion. Metrodorus, proceeding by an opposite path, does not think the earth is moved naturally, since he thinks no body is moved in its own place unless someone either pushes or pulls it: but that some of its parts are impelled by others. Parmenides and Democritus wish it to remain still because it is equidistant from all parts.<-

The earth is moved very little, or rather, it is only shaken. Anaximenes <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> believed it rests upon the air because of its breadth. Others prefer the idea that it moves upon the water, not unlike those things which prevail by their width, and like a plank that is tossed by the waves. Plato denied the motion of the earth across every difference of position, since it is driven neither upward, nor downward, nor forward, nor backward, nor to the right, nor to the left, because it is the lowest of all things; however, he allowed that some of its parts are moved due to their rarity. Epicurus also mixes in a bit of air and water to excite motion.

->**On the Sea and its various motions.**<-
<margin>On the Sea and its various motions.</margin>

Furthermore, concerning the sea which flows around the earth, what is the inquiry? It concerns its flavor, its ebb, and its flow. For Anaximander thought the Seas were the remains of the first moisture, a great part of which fire had scorched away, and the heat of the burning had transformed the remainder. It seemed to Anaxagoras that while the moisture was stagnant from the beginning, a part of it was consumed by the frequency of the sun's path; and once the fatty part had evaporated, the remainder yielded to saltiness and bitterness. Antipho did not entirely shrink from this opinion of "sweat," thinking the cause to be the sweat of the earth burned by the sun's heat. Metrodorus, however, thought differently, as did the Platonists, who hold that the part of the elemental water which has the most air becomes sweet due to cooling, but the part which has undergone exhalation through heating and inflammation has contracted saltiness. Xenophanes attributed this to the mixing of the earth, by the conjecture that shells are found in the middle of the land and in the bowels of mountains; and once in the stone quarries of Syracuse, a certain shape of fish and seals was found, and on the island of Pharos, the shape of a laurel in the depths of the rock.

Others have attributed the true flow of the sea to the sun, which raises the winds that drive the waves; when these winds subside, the sea settles and flows back. Neither Heraclitus nor Aristotle shrank from this opinion. Plato seems to have attributed this matter to other causes. Pytheas of Massalia <note>An ancient Greek geographer and explorer</note> assigned the increase of the sea to the waxing of the moon, and its decrease to the waning. Timaeus the Pythagorean attributed the cause of the increased and diminished surge of the sea to rivers discharging into the Atlantic Ocean. Seleucus the mathematician mixed the earth and the moon together to explain the cause of the flooding and drying of the shore. Others have said other things, as did my uncle Pico <note>referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> in the fourth book *Against the Astrologers*,

<margin>Jo. Pico</margin>

and as we also have reported elsewhere. But indeed, regarding motion—not only of the flowing and ebbing

<margin>On the various motions of all bodies.</margin>

water, but concerning every motion of bodies—is there not a great and eternal dispute? I speak of motion that is not violent and impetuous, but natural: some say it comes from the generator and the remover of obstacles, others from an internal form, and all of these claim they do not depart from Aristotle. The former cite his own words, but the opinion of Ecphantus of Syracuse opposes them all, asserting that bodies are moved not by weight or impulse, but by a divine power which he calls Mind and Soul.

But perhaps enough and more than enough has been told concerning this matter and the whole "greater world" <term>Macrocosm: the universe as a whole</term>. Now we must report how great the disagreements and quarrels of the philosophers are found to be in the "lesser world" <term>Microcosm: man as a miniature reflection of the universe</term>; first concerning man in general, then concerning the soul, and likewise concerning those things which the soul is said to have in common with the body, and then we shall treat the body itself: so that afterwards we may perceive what conflicting things they have brought forth concerning morals and the end <note>The "telos" or ultimate purpose</note> of men.

...that the earth has always been filled with a full abundance of men, and they maintain it shall always be full. There are those who prefer to believe it had a beginning and a birth in time: and among these, too, there is no small dispute. Some think men were first born in Attica <note>A region of Greece, including Athens</note>. Others say in Arcadia, others in Egypt: and it is decided differently by yet others, as is found in Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian</note> among the origins of the "Birthday." I have read in Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*, something which I have not yet fully decided whether it is more worthy of laughter or of refutation: that the first generation of men and quadrupeds, if it had a beginning, emerged either from an egg or rather from a worm. But indeed, there were those who would bring forth both male and female from the same region at once: nor were there lacking those who believe that males first sprouted from the earth toward the east and the south, and females toward the north. Empedocles, dealing with this opinion on the generation of male and female, gave his assent. However, Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> opposed this, thinking instead that males arose toward the north wind <note>original: "boream"</note> and females toward the south wind <note>original: "austrum"</note>. And by chance...

among philosophers, controversy flourished. But now the very place into which we have fallen seems to warn us that we must deal with the controversies regarding the soul itself.

How great and how many were the disagreements and quarrels among the philosophers of the nations concerning the human soul; wherein it is shown how great the thanks are we ought to give to Christ for the things divinely revealed to us on this matter. [space] Chapter Fourteen.

Having completed the narrative of the manifold disagreement of the philosophers concerning the greater world <note>The macrocosm or universe</note> and its parts, as far as seemed expedient for the proposed work, and having already declared in general the many disagreements concerning the lesser world <note>The microcosm</note> which is man: it remains for us to discuss his parts. And since there are two parts held to be the greatest and principal ones—the soul and the body—it seems we must begin with the soul, as it is certainly the more worthy part. Some have made this soul single in man, others multiple. But of this, more later. Let us first deal (if it pleases) with the more celebrated disagreement, that is, concerning its immortality. And to repeat from the beginning, many of the philosophers investigated whether it was mortal or not—that is, whether it perished with the body? Or whether it remained a survivor? Pherecydes the Syrian <margin>Pherecydes</margin> is recorded as the first to have disputed concerning its immortality. There were those, however, who did not believe the soul departed from the body, but that the mind and body died together. Those who thought the mind was not extinguished thought differently: some that it remained forever, others for a long time, others that it was dissolved immediately. Pythagoras, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> the pupil of Pherecydes, asserted that it was indeed immortal, but wandering and, as it were, leaping from place to place, as one which would pass into diverse bodies, both human and even those of beasts, and would return at various turns of time. These things are well-worn, not only among the philosophers and those who wrote his life in Greek and those who discussed his dogmas, but they are even chanted among the poets. For which reason, that poet <note>Ovid, in the Metamorphoses</note> says in the persona of Pythagoras himself: "Souls are free from death, and having always left their former seat, they live and dwell received into new homes." <note>original: "morte carent animæ semperque priore relicta sede nouis domibus uiuunt habitantque receptæ"</note> Moreover, the reason why Pythagoras was moved to bring forth these ravings is added: "For I myself remember that in the time of the Trojan war, I was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose opposing breast once stuck the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus <note>Menelaus</note>. I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand, recently in the temple of Juno in the fields of Argos." <note>original: "ipse ego nam memini troiani tempore belli panthoides Euphorbus eram..."</note> But he used to say that he had not been Euphorbus alone, but many others whom Adamantius cites. Likewise others and diverse ones whom both Clearchus and Dicaearchus, and after them Gellius, have named—even adding Alce, a beautiful woman but a prostitute. Many followed him in defending this vain opinion, among whom was Empedocles, who sang in his own poems that he had once been both a fish and a shrub. And he even wanted it to be believed that he had been a boy and a girl before; whence those words of his...

Democritus and later Epicurus held a path contrary to this one, being enslaved to the senses of the body. They wrongly judged that souls die entirely with the body. A vast crowd followed them, not only of Greeks but of Latins whose monuments have perished, <margin>Against Lucretius.</margin> except for the six books of Lucretius. These were preserved to the great ruin of young men; for once imbued from their earliest years with these beast-like opinions, they easily neglect religion. So much does habit in one's tender years matter. For Lucretius himself, believing neither in a providence over affairs nor that the soul would survive the body, loosened the reins for voluptuous men toward every shameful crime. He is said to have written that Epicurean work during intervals of insanity; but to me, he seems to have been more insane when he was writing and thought to be sane. For it is the height of insanity to have believed the "sane" opinion of Epicurus concerning many things, and most especially concerning the soul.

The Stoics stand roughly in the middle between those whose opinions we have explained. For they believe the soul survives the body, but not forever. They hold that the souls of the unlearned are weakened and perish gradually, but those of the wise persevere until the universal conflagration <note>The Stoic concept of *ekpyrosis*, where the universe is periodically consumed by fire and reborn.</note>. Indeed, they have not deviated at all from Zeno of Citium, who judged that souls are transfused into offspring through the human seed of the parents; for which reason it followed that they would be liable to corruption—even if he is said at times to have thought the human soul is not corrupted. However, we read that Panaetius, although a Stoic, disagreed with other Stoics; and this is no wonder, since even that sect conflicted within itself. For some held virtue to be the only good, while others, like Ariston and Antiochus and others who disagreed with the rest, held other things to be good besides virtue, and distinguished a "most blessed" life from a merely "blessed" one. But I return to Panaetius: Cicero is the authority that although Panaetius was a wonderful admirer of Plato in other matters, he nevertheless did not approve of Plato's opinion on the immortality of the soul. Yet it seems Panaetius wished to distinguish the soul from the mind.

Certainly, both the Pythagorean Numenius <margin>Numentius</margin> and the Platonist Longinus attacked that common, vain, and impious opinion of the Stoics. Numenius says they claim the soul is both generated and corruptible, yet it is not corrupted immediately upon being released from the body, but lingers around it; however, these durations differ, since the souls of the foolish endure for certain spaces of time, but those of men endowed with virtue <margin>Longinus</margin> endure until the resolution of all things into fire. Longinus adds that one might rightly be angry with Zeno and Cleanthes for disputing so insultingly about the soul; for both called it an "exhalation" <note>original: "ἀναθυμίασιν" (anathymiasin) - a vapor or breath rising from the body.</note> from a solid body. He said these things both Platonically and piously.

But among the Platonists there is no small dispute, for we showed above that Proclus, Porphyry, and his other followers did not agree. <margin>How varied the opinions are on what Plato felt about the soul.</margin> Furthermore, it must be known that other controversies also flourished: some asserted that Plato affirmed the soul to be unbegotten and incorruptible, with this reason supporting it: since it is always in motion and not only moves itself, but is the source and principle of all motion. Others contradicted this, contending it seemed to Plato that the soul was indeed incorruptible but "generated" <note>Created at a specific point in time by the Creator.</note>, attaining immortality itself by the will of God. Nor were there lacking those who thought Plato judged the soul to be both generated and liable to corruption, and decreed the same to be a composite. They bring up that "mixing bowl" <note>The *Crater* mentioned in Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> which Plato mentioned, in which the soul is forged; and they bind and couple a body to it—not an earthy and heavy one, but thin and bright and, as they themselves say, "luminous" <note>original: "ἀυγοειδές" (augoeides) - meaning "shining like the sun" or "spirit-like."</note>. Many stand against this, teaching that Plato could by no means have thought this, since he established judgments after death, and punishments and rewards. <margin>Opinion of the author.</margin> These things certainly seem to me to speak more in the Platonic manner. For in his *Gorgias*, Socrates says that a man who is truly a man should not wish to live here for any length of time at all, nor is this life to be loved; and in the same dialogue, Socrates...

->**BOOK ONE**<- [right] **24**

Socrates <note>The author begins by citing Socrates' view on the fear of death</note>—for indeed, no one fears dying unless they are devoid of reason and cowardly; rather, one fears acting unjustly. For a soul filled with many sins to descend to the underworld is the ultimate of all evils. Also in the books of the *Republic* <note>original: "τῆς πολιτ'ας" (tēs politeias), the Greek title for Plato's Republic</note>—which the Latins call the books *On the Commonwealth*—he is seen to write most clearly concerning the immortality of the soul, and the punishments that await wicked men after death. For in the first part of that work, he mentions the fear by which those who have treated other men unjustly are tormented before death; and in the tenth book of the same, he reports the punishments of the tyrant Aridaeus and others whose souls were tortured in infernal and subterranean places. There is no doubt that the better crowd of Platonists believed that Plato held the soul to be immortal. But among these, some think he proposed transmigration <note>The migration of the soul into a new body</note> and the Pythagorean *Palingenesis* <note>original: "Παλιγγενεσία," meaning rebirth or reincarnation</note> at certain fixed and decreed times. Others resist this, asserting that Plato taught that souls receive fixed places according to their merits, and they use his own words as the firmest testimony: in which he explains that some will be with Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, others with other Gods, while others will remain in everlasting punishments.

There is also another and no small dispute among the Platonists as to where the soul comes from. The most ancient thought it proceeded as an incorporeal thing from the Supreme God. Others that it is a portion of Him. Others that it is created by the Supreme God. Others by the Soul of the World. And of those who thought it created, some wished it to be created before the body so that it existed by itself, and soon after entered the body—either to expiate the crimes of a former life (as those who adhered to the decrees of Pythagoras held) or to undergo punishments which it could not undergo while incorporeal. These believed the soul to be a substance existing by itself, separate from the body and not needing the body.

<margin>How obscurely Aristotle wrote concerning the soul</margin> Aristotle spoke so obscurely about the rational soul that there is still great debate as to what he felt regarding the immortality of the soul. The ancient writers of our religion <note>Early Christian Church Fathers</note>, and some from the pagans, judge that Aristotle thought the rational soul was mortal. The younger scholars think it immortal. Although there are those who defend the opinion of the ancients, a matter we shall deal with when we dispute the uncertainty of Aristotle’s doctrine itself, especially in the fourth and sixth books of this work. However, what we ourselves think of Aristotle’s opinion, we have indicated in our commentaries on his third book *On the Soul*. <margin>The author's commentary on the third book of Aristotle's *On the Soul*</margin> There we revealed how differently he is to be understood from Alexander and Averroes <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias and the Islamic philosopher Averroes, famous Aristotelian commentators</note>, since the former contends the soul is mortal, and the latter that a single [universal] intellect is taught by him: both in vain, both impiously. Nor are there lacking in our time those who babble that their opinion is at least true according to philosophy—as if the school of Averroes and Alexander were the whole of philosophy, and as if a truth could be contrary to the Truth. <margin>Against some, Pope Leo X</margin> Their error was also recently condemned by Pope Leo X in the Lateran Council, in the year of Christian salvation one thousand five hundred and thirteen, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 19, 1513</note>, in the eighth session, in which I myself sat and saw the decree itself pronounced.

But concerning this matter, more elsewhere. Now let us return to the diverse opinions, discordant not only on immortality itself, but in the declaration of what the soul actually is. <margin>What the soul is: various and conflicting views. Thales, Alcmaeon</margin> Thales first called the soul an immobile nature. Alcmaeon a self-moving nature (though Plutarch is the authority that Thales also thought this). Pythagoras called it a self-moving number, with which Xenocrates agreed; but Pythagoras is said to have taken "number" to mean "mind." Plato called it an intelligible substance, self-moving, and moved according to Harmonic number. Aristotle called it the "first Entelechy" <note>A Greek term for "actualization" or "perfection"</note> of a natural body having the potential for life. <margin>Concerning Aristotle's *entelechia*</margin> By the term *Entelechy* (or *Endelechy*), originally coined by the author himself, a certain act and perfection is signified; and as it pleased Cicero, it was expressed under a new word as if it were a "continued and perennial motion," even if speaking of it elsewhere...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical survey of classical opinions regarding the nature and substance of the soul, likely following a discussion of the "fifth essence" or quintessence mentioned in the opening line.</meta>

# BOOK

The fifth, he says, is that nature which is not so much named as it is not understood <note>original: "non nominata magis q̃ nō intellecta naturā." This refers to the Aristotelian 'quintessence' or aether, which was often considered a fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire.</note>. Dicaearchus taught that the soul was nothing at all: although someone might think he set forth that opinion under the judgment of Pherecrates of Phthiotis, being moved by the words of Cicero in the first *Tusculan Disputation*. But Cicero himself posits that he felt this way, and as the work proceeds, making mention of those books of his which were called the *Lesbiacs*, he affirms that he argued most sharply against immortality. And in the second *Academic*, as we were saying above, he reports the opinion of Dicaearchus, to whom it seemed there was no soul. Galen, in his book on *Philosophical History*, and some Greek authors report Dicaearchus's sentiment on the soul as being either exactly the same or certainly not dissimilar. And without any doubt, Sextus the Pyrrhonist writes that it was the opinion of Dicaearchus that there is no soul; wherefore he did not wish to take upon himself the labor of naming and defining it for free.

But Plutarch writes that it pleased Dicaearchus to call the soul a "Harmony" of the four elements, an opinion which Theodoret ascribes not to Dicaearchus but to Clearchus. Nor did the physician Asclepiades shrink from this definition, opining that the soul was the mutual exercise of the senses. Philoxenus pleased to call it a harmony. Others called the Heart the soul. Empedocles said it was the blood poured around the body, as Cicero reports of him. Others said it was a part of the Brain. But some placed it in the heart, others in the brain. Zeno called it fire; others preferred "spirit" <note>original: "spiritum," meaning breath or wind</note>, whence come the words *anima* and *animus*: from the Greek *zoe* [life] and *spiro* [I breathe], whence also *anemos* [wind]. Almost all of these, however discordant they may be, seemed to agree on this one thing: that the soul was either entirely incorporeal—as those who called it a "number" and the "act of the body" and an "intellectual substance"—or at least not a solid body, as those who used the names of "harmony" and "spirit."

But there were those who thought it corporeal, such as Archelaus, and before them Anaximander, Anaximenes, and Anaxagoras: all of whom pleased to define it as being of an airy nature. Varro perhaps followed them, who (as Firmianus reports) wrote: "the soul is air conceived in the mouth, heated in the lungs, warmed in the heart, and diffused into the body." Parmenides and Hippasus, however, thought the soul was Fiery. Democritus preferred it to be a fiery mixture of those things which can be grasped by reason, which indeed had "spherical Ideas" <note>referring to the spherical atoms of fire in Democritus's atomic theory</note>, and a fiery power, so that he finally thought it was a body. Others wish for Heraclitus to have differed in no way from Parmenides and Hippasus. There are those who prefer to think he believed the soul of the world was an evaporation of the humors within it, and thus derived the soul of all living things from external and internal exhalation. Many of the Stoics called it "spiritual," participating in much heat. But Heraclides betook himself to Light in weighing it. Others wanted it to be derived from a certain "starry breath." Epicurus composed the soul from four certain qualities—fiery, airy, spiritual, and another which he did not know how to name—making a mixture like a pottage. Others say Empedocles did not make the soul as Cicero says, but from a simpler mixture, and fashioned it from that ethereal and airy substance. Critias preferred it to be composed of blood and humor, whom perhaps Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> imitated when he sang: "he vomits forth his purple soul." Although, as poets are wont to do, he took now this opinion and now that, varying and adorning his poem as was fitting; wherefore he frequently felt concerning the soul in both the Pythagorean and Platonic manner.

<margin>On the great discord regarding the number of souls.</margin> In the number of the soul there is also much discord, for some wanted one, and several wanted many: it pleased many that there were three—one which rendered the body vigorous by taking in nourishment, growing, and generating; another which rendered it sensitive; and a third by which man became intelligent. This last is proper to man, the second is common with the beasts, and the other with plants (which Empedocles and Plato wanted to be called "animals" or "living things," if we stand with Plutarch, though Aristotle did not). But the soul nevertheless...
