<meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of the soul, moving from its definition to its internal divisions and physical location within the body according to various ancient schools of thought.</meta>

->**BOOK ONE**<- [right] **25**

nevertheless, he did not deny that they possessed it and called them "animated" <note>original: "animata"; meaning things endowed with a soul or life-force</note>. And yet three <note>referring to the Platonic division of the soul</note> created them, separated them by location, and gave them their own places in the head, the midriff, and the liver. There were those who thought that only one soul was placed in man, which nonetheless performed the duties of the other souls and enclosed them within itself. Among these, too, there was great discord: would it carry those lower virtues with it when separated from the body? Or would these rather be destroyed along with the body, as we said above was debated among the Platonists? That controversy later flowed down to their successors, not yet sufficiently resolved. Furthermore, even those who spoke of one soul fight over its division no differently than soldiers dividing loot. There are those who want it for themselves whole; there are those who wish it to be cut in two; nor are there those lacking who think a triple dissection should be used. There are also those who, protesting against everyone else, prefer it to be torn into eight parts. The older philosophers, content to have one soul for themselves, sent notice of dismissal to the rest. Plato summoned three. Aristotle held one which contained the others by a certain power and virtue, so that it performed the functions of sensing and nourishing the body; but as far as intelligence is concerned, there is much dissent among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, and also regarding what happens to the lower powers when it is separated from the body. But indeed, those ancients who spoke of one soul, preferring to have it whole for themselves, did not divide it in any way. Pythagoras and Plato thought there were two parts of the soul: that which is called **rational**, and that which is **irrational**; and they thought this latter part should be split in two, naming one part by the term **wrath** <note>original: "irascentia"; the spirited or emotional part</note> and marking the other with the name **concupiscence** <note>original: "concupiscentia"; the part of desire or appetite</note>. Democritus and Epicurus, while embracing the rational, also judged that the part lacking reason should not be cast off. Xenocrates separated the soul into a **sensory** and a **rational** part. Aristotle numbered five parts or powers: the **appetitive** (if one may say so), the **nutritive**, the **sensitive**, the **motive** (according to place), and the **intellective**. The successors of Pythagoras also assigned five parts, though not the same ones. For just as they constituted human bodies from five things—namely the four elements and the ethereal body—so they assigned to each of them its own little portion of the soul, the names of which were: **prudence, intellect, knowledge, opinion, and sense**. The Stoics, thinking the soul should be divided into eight parts, handed over to each of the senses its own portion: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch; and besides these, a sixth portion for the voice, a seventh for the seminal power, and an eighth for the **governing part** <note>original: "principi parti"; the *hegemonikon* or ruling faculty</note>, which is **reason**, by which the others are moved, no differently than those multiple tentacles are moved by a polyp fish.

<margin>How great the discord is concerning the principal seat of reason.</margin>

But where the principal part of the soul resides, as if in a palace, philosophers have brought forth views as diverse as can be. Democritus, Hippocrates, and Plato placed it in the **brain**. Erasistratus placed it around the membrane of the brain's ventricle. Herophilus in the cavity of the brain, which is also the base. Straton in the interior part of the forehead. Parmenides and Epicurus thought it was situated in the **whole chest**. Empedocles and Aristotle placed it in the **heart**. The Stoics likewise in the heart, or in the spirit <note>original: "spiritu"; often meaning pneuma or breath</note> around the heart. It pleased Diogenes that it remain in the hollow artery of the heart, which is spiritual. I have also found those who said Empedocles placed it in the **constitution of the blood**. Others preferred it situated around the small membrane of the heart. Others judged it to stay around the neck of the heart. Others preferred it in the **whole body**, so that there was no specific place for the mind, but it ran scattered through the whole body; Firmianus is the authority that this pleased Xenocrates. Nor were there lacking those who placed it in the partition which is called the **Diaphragm** by the Greeks. Pythagoras preferred the vital part to be placed around the heart, and the rational part around the brain. Others among the younger men whom Plutarch records wanted it to be extended from the head all the way to the diaphragm. Whence it is no wonder if, in later times also, there is disagreement with Aristotle regarding the primacy of the brain and the heart.

BOOK I

<margin>Averroes acting like a rustic judge.</margin> Galen, the physician of Pergamon, and Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> at the end of his book *On the Soul*, discussed many things regarding the primacy of the heart, even descending to the point of performing dissections on living creatures. Averroes, striving to settle their discords, seems to have behaved like a "rustic judge" <note>A proverbial expression for an arbitrator who splits the difference between two parties without deep legal nuance.</note>, granting one part to this man and another part to that one. He settled the controversy in such a way that he did not stand entirely with either, nor did he grant the suit according to one or the other; namely, he bestowed the **beginnings** of operations upon the heart, but their **ends** upon the brain.

<margin>Where the soul is; how many disagreements.</margin> Furthermore, do not think that everyone has agreed that the soul itself is incorporeal. For some held it to be a body; others placed the body within the soul itself. Indeed, there were those who said the intellect was joined to the soul just as a part is joined to the whole, and that the "inseparable affections" <note>The essential properties or emotions that cannot be removed from a being.</note> belong to the very essence of the thing to which they are attributed. There were others who thought it entirely different. Yet not even all of these were in agreement on this matter: for some wished that which we call the intellect to be the intellect of the soul itself, whence the soul would be called "intellectual" or "intellective." Many of our theologians ascribed this opinion to Aristotle—those who have obtained the surname "Parisians" because they frequent the schools of Paris and write in their manner; I speak of Thomas Aquinas, a man of great learning and distinguished by the title of sanctity, as well as John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note> and many others.

However, Averroes trod the opposite path, believing the intellect to be of another nature, a certain substance separated from the soul. But there was no consensus even in this, since he thought one single intellect was present for all human beings. Others preferred the view that individual intellects were given to individual men. It is well known even among the moderately learned—so much so that it hardly needs proof—how many battles were stirred up by our scholars against Averroes. Many, in dedicated works, refuted his opinion of the "unique intellect," especially Thomas Aquinas and Aegidius Romanus, both excellent men, the former even enrolled among the number of the saints. 

Nevertheless, among many theologians—not insofar as they are theologians, but insofar as they are interpreters of Aristotle—there is no agreement on that sentence of Aristotle: "this is separated from that, as the perpetual from the corruptible." Indeed, some wish that the intellective soul, when it departs from the body, carries with it (as we have already warned) all the powers of the sensitive soul as if in a root; others wish these to be destroyed. But this is not the place to deal with this matter, as we are only discussing the dissensions of the nations. 

Therefore, let us return to the ancient philosophers, among whom Pythagoras and Plato wished that which we call the intellect or mind—the Greeks call it *nous* <note>original: "νουν"</note>—to be a certain divine particle, which Aristotle by no means wished to be destroyed. And yet, even among those who granted primacy to the intellect, there was no agreement on how it related to the lower powers: for some established it as a prince of absolute power, so that it might rule all affections at its will. Others preferred it to be a servant of necessity, subjecting it to the Fates and destiny, and did not exempt it from the celestial rotation <note>The influence of the stars and planets.</note>. Plato resisted these most sharply, wishing the soul to be endowed with all liberty, the prince and mistress of all affections and disturbances; he held it to be within its power to turn wherever it wishes, whether it prefers to conquer or be conquered. He declared this most clearly in the *Laws*, writing that the first and best of all victories is to conquer oneself, while to be conquered by oneself is both most shameful and most wretched. 

Thus the philosophers bicker and fight among themselves concerning their own souls. From this, as from many other—if not innumerable—instances, we ought to be moved to give the greatest thanks to Christ, God and man. For He has taught us the immortality of the soul, and the dogma of His Church has declared that human souls are created by God and simultaneously infused into the bodies of which they are the "forms" <note>The organizing principle that gives a body life and identity.</note>, and that they will receive eternal rewards for good deeds and everlasting punishments for crimes.

->BOOK ONE<-                                                                                                                             XXVI

### That the philosophers of the nations most openly disagree concerning the functions of the soul and the duties shared with the body. Chapter Fifteen.

It must certainly not be thought that those who were discordant regarding the soul itself would agree on its affections and the functions handed over to the body. Regarding sensation—which some have called "sensory perception" and others "conception"—there were those who thought it belonged to the soul alone, while others thought it belonged to both the soul and the body; the philosophers distinguished and named this in many different ways. <margin>Disagreement concerning sensation.</margin> For among the **Stoics**, "sensation" is said to encompass the state, the power, the act, and the *phantasia* <note>original: "phantasia"; here meaning the mental image or impression</note> through the sensory organ. Again, the "sensory organs" are also called "intelligible spirits" extending from the principal part of the soul to the physical instruments. **Epicurus** was pleased to hold that sensation is a power, but that which is "sensitive" is what he calls an *energeia* <note>original: "ἐνέργημα"; an activity or operation</note>. **Plato** thought that sensation was a communion of the body and the soul regarding external things; he gave the power and virtue to the soul, but the instrument to the body, so that both, through the mediation of *phantasia*, might become captors of those things which are outside. **Leucippus** and **Democritus** thought that sensation and intellection occur by the falling in of "specters" or "images" of things that lie outside. 

But let them be in agreement on this matter if you like; will they later agree whether true sensation and true *phantasia* actually exist and are held? The **Stoics** think that sensations are indeed true, but they do not believe that "visions"—whether you prefer to call them imaginations or *phantasias*—are all true; rather, they judge many to be false. On the contrary, **Epicurus** ordained that every *phantasia* as well as every sensation prevails in truth. However, of opinions, he thought some were true and others slipped into falsehood. But if sensation were deceived only regarding intellectual matters, it was thought that *phantasia* could be deceived both regarding these and regarding sensation. **Empedocles** and **Heraclides** wanted particular sensations to arise from the "commensuration of pores"—that is, only when each thing is fitted to its own proper sense. **Aristotle** thought the sense is deceived if it concerns a "common object" <note>Attributes like motion or size that are perceived by more than one sense</note> or something opposed by accident, but not if it is a "proper object" <note>Attributes like color for sight or sound for hearing</note>, or if it is separated by a gap greater than necessary. <margin>Against Aristotle.</margin> But concerning this matter, words will be made especially in the fifth volume of this work, when it will be shown that the sense is deceived in other ways than those numbered by Aristotle, and that his judgment ought not to be held as solid and constant as he had claimed; therefore, we shall deal with these in their proper place; now let us do what is at hand. 

Discussing the "common sense," Aristotle—a man of great genius and, as I think, of even greater judgment and attainment—noticed that in the eye, for example, no questioning or judgment occurs regarding the greatness or smallness of a visible thing, but only the diversity of color is received. <margin>Controversy concerning the internal senses.</margin> He thought this belonged to another sense, not one of the number of the other four—namely taste, smell, hearing, and touch—but to one more common, whose parts were the "distinguishers" of composite things. Therefore, he did not add a sixth sense, but established a common and superior one over them. Many after Aristotle have sweated over dividing this; for they have partitioned the "internal senses" so that there are now five among many writers, more so that they might correspond in number to the senses positioned externally than because any necessity compels it. For both *phantasia* and "estimation" and internal senses of this kind were introduced by later thinkers—so much so that they even attribute to **Avicenna** a disagreement between "imagination" and "*phantasia*," even though he did not judge them to differ in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*. All these are placed under one "common sense" by the ancient Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, as may be observed in the monuments of **Themistius** and **Alexander**, who distinguished the common sense by different names and offices, but not in reality. There is much dissension regarding the seat or "royal palace" of this internally placed sense: for there were those who located it in the heart, and those who located it in the brain; and of those who made several internal senses, some placed them in different parts of the brain...

did not think there were so many senses in man. Instead, he affirmed there were more than what is commonly thought, and that these were given to irrational animals, to the Gods, and to the wise. <margin>The author's commentary on the third book of *On the Soul*.</margin>
by us in our commentary on Aristotle’s third book of *On the Soul*. Truly, there is also much disagreement concerning each individual sense placed on the outside. Democritus and Epicurus thought that vision happens by the falling of "idols,"
<margin>Debate concerning sight.</margin>
specters, or images of things, or by the opposition of certain rays: which, when they have fallen upon an opposing object, are reflected back again to the sight. Empedocles mixed rays with the specters and images of the seen thing. Hipparchus wanted rays to be emitted from both eyes and to be extended all the way to the boundaries of those objects. I know that a controversy still thrives between the Platonists and Peripatetics as to whether vision happens by sending something out <note>extramission theory</note> or by receiving something within <note>intromission theory</note>; the latter is ascribed to Aristotle, the former to Plato, whose view is also commonly circulated: that a certain kind of fire, as Gellius says, and light goes out from the eyes, and this, being joined and continued either with the light of the sun or with the light of another fire, by its own and external force, brings it about that we perceive whatever it strikes and illuminates. The Stoics also brought forward the emission of rays from the eyes, but simultaneously the tension of the air in the middle. The controversy is even further multiplied regarding visions in a mirror, which Empedocles thought happened according to a deflection. Democritus and Epicurus, however, thought that mirror appearances happen from the substances of the images which are carried from us, but are fixed in the mirror because of reverberation. The Pythagoreans preferred it to be according to the refractions of sight. For they held that vision is carried out in an extended way until it reaches the object, but then, falling upon a dense and polished body, it steps back. Seneca, in the first book of *Natural Questions*, reports that there are two opinions concerning mirrors. For some, he says, think that there are "idols" in them,
<margin>Two opinions concerning mirrors.</margin>
that is, the figures of our bodies, sent forth and separated from our bodies. Others say the images are not in the mirror, but that the bodies themselves are seen as the sharp gaze of the eyes is twisted back and deflected into itself. Later, in the course of the same book, he says: "For we judge nothing in mirrors to be anything but a deception, nothing other than a lie to those measuring a foreign body. For that which is shown is not in the mirror, otherwise it would not go out, nor would it be immediately covered by another image, nor would innumerable forms now perish and now be received. What then? Those are images and an imitation of true bodies." These are the words of Seneca. A doubt also arose whether darkness could be seen; the Stoics
<margin>Whether darkness may be seen.</margin>
affirm it, inasmuch as it is seen by them because a certain splendor is extended from the sight into the darkness, and the vision is not deceived, since it truly sees that there is darkness. But others would not admit this through itself, but by accident, that is, as a lack of light.
<margin>Disagreements concerning hearing.</margin>
In hearing also, what diverse dogmas of the philosophers have we heard? Empedocles said it happens by the spirit <note>pneuma or air</note> being received in the passages of the ear, which he says, once received, is then raised up into the ear. Alcmaeon holds that hearing is received by the vacuum which is implanted in the ears, and that this is what resonates when the spirit is received: since all empty things emit a sound. Diogenes preferred that the air be the cause, inasmuch as since it is in the head, it is struck and moved by the voice. Plato and those who followed him thought the air which remains in the head is struck, and once struck, it is refracted and leaps apart, and thus the sensation of hearing happens. But whether the air which is outside is moved, being beaten by a sound or voice, various men have put forward various things regarding the sensory organ of hearing; for there are those who want the hearing to be moved and stirred only spiritually: they think that Aristotle decided no differently. There are those who, relying on the same author and also supported by reasons, judge it necessary
<margin>Disagreements concerning the voice.</margin>
that the air be admitted into the inner chambers and the furthest windings of the ears. Concerning the voice itself, how diversely voices are reported is known to anyone even slightly more learned than the common folk, since even the grammarians dispute its definition, and the logicians say quite a bit, though they borrow it from the natural philosophers. There is also much debate concerning dreams: some believe that all humans dream, while others think not everyone does, excepting many individuals, as can be seen in Aristotle’s fourth book *On the Nature of Animals* and in Plutarch’s book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. That which is drawn out from the body, he proves to be body; but many have thought that the seed is something incorporeal. Others have said it is incorporeal in terms of its power, but clearly a body in terms of its matter. Aristotle strongly presses those who said that the seed is secreted from every part of the body <note>This refers to the theory of pangenesis, where every organ contributes to the seed.</note>, and he sharply attacks their reasons for proving this in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*. These reasons were based chiefly on the intensity of pleasure, on maimed infants born to parents who were themselves maimed <note>original: "mancis... parentes"</note>, on the resemblance of children to their parents, and on the proportion of the whole to the part. However, there is a wonderful disagreement as to whether it is the role of the man alone to cast it forth, and the role of the woman alone to receive it. <margin>Whether the woman also casts forth seed, which is debated.</margin> Pythagoras, Democritus, Hippocrates, and Epicurus decreed that the woman also casts forth seed. Aristotle decided otherwise, although there are those who wish to believe he felt the same, among whom is Lactantius. After Aristotle, Galen set him aside and joined the ancients. Averroes later followed Aristotle, by no means approving of this, and almost the entire later crowd of physicians has fought over this matter in the past and clearly fights to this day. But let us return to the ancients. Aristotle and Zeno used a certain new explanation so that they would not seem to deny what is sometimes perceived by the senses. For they were mistaken that a certain moisture—by no means seminal, however—flows from the female like sweat shaken out by exercise; even if Aristotle does not entirely deny that some seed comes from the female, for in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals* he calls it "female seed," and in the preceding work, he says the menses are unconcocted seed. Hippon, however, claimed that seed flows no less from the female than from the male, and that the bones are formed from the men, but the flesh from the women. Aristotle, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, judges that the matter and the body are supplied by the female, but the power and the sensitive soul are provided by the male. Furthermore, regarding the cause of males being generated in the womb, others have traced it to the seed itself, in which there is a contrariety of sex: <margin>On the cause of the diversity of sex, of what sort it is.</margin> among these was Anaxagoras, who also wanted the location of the womb—the right and left sides—to be the cause in some way, since they said females come from one side and males from the other. Others preferred to trace the cause to the womb itself: for they derived males from a warm womb and females from a cold one, as did Empedocles. Why there should be such heat or coldness in the wombs, they traced to the nature of the menses. Democritus rejects the cause in the womb, but not because of heat or cold. Rather, it depends on which seed prevails: that which comes from the part where the male and female differ from each other. Aristotle also reports this in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals* and refutes it at length; and in a long discourse, he himself traces the cause to the superiority and power of the principle—that is, the male seed—and its "concoction" <note>A biological term for the "cooking" or ripening of fluids by body heat.</note>. When this process declines into the opposite, he believes a female, the opposite of the male, is generated. He thought the male seed might not prevail due to youth, old age, or other causes; and from this, he also derived the various similarities and dissimilarities to parents and ancestors, both in whole and in part, attributing everything to the motion of the "agent" <note>The active force in reproduction.</note>. For the act and the potential are not the same, but vary—being degenerate, or next, or near, or loosed. These things he explained very extensively in that book with quite many and often repeated words. There were also those who thought that heat and cold had great momentum in the distinction of sex, and it has been recorded that some thought the first earth-born males were generated toward the east and south, but females toward the north. On the contrary, Parmenides decreed otherwise, tracing the male to the cold of the north, and he brought forward this reason: that a man has more density in himself, while the temperature of the body is more "rare" <note>Thin or porous.</note> in a woman; therefore, she arose toward the south rather than the north. But the opinion of Hipponax was that the cause of diversity should be traced to the seed, whether it be well-compacted and robust, or more fluid and weak. To this <unclear>... </unclear>

that males are received and that it is both owed and possible for them to be returned <note>The author is discussing the balance of male and female births</note>; this indeed seems to me to have been the opinion of **Hippocrates**, clearly set down at the end of his book *On the Fetus*, when he discusses twins, whether they be males, females, or a male and a female. For then he attributes the male sex to a thicker and stronger seed, but the female to a more humid and weaker one. For he judges it impossible for the seed to always be the same, both that which is ejected first and that which follows even in a single act of intercourse; wherefore it is held to be sometimes weaker and sometimes stronger, from which both Male and Female are generated. **Anaxagoras** and **Parmenides** maintained that the seed from the right side ought to be cast into the right part of the womb, and that from the left into the left; but when a change of this order occurs, then females are generated. **Leucippus** taught that this happens through the exchange of small particles. There are also other disagreements on this matter. **Aristotle**, in the sixth book of *The History of Animals*, while discussing the mating and offspring of sheep and goats, attributed their sex to the diversity of waters, and furthermore ascribed males to the blowing of the north winds and females to the south winds. Regarding humans, however, in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*, he felt as we reported above—although even there he asserted that males are produced more by northern winds than southern ones, and he also said that waters were a cause, since they are used so much; hence if they were raw or cold, he thought they contributed to female birth. He also maintained that lands, because of nourishment and the disposition of the body resulting from the temperament of the surrounding air, are a cause of why a diversity of sex is produced. 

But let us imagine that they had agreed upon the manner in which the conception and generation of a human occurs; what disagreement follows? From what source is the beginning of forming and establishing this human in the womb? **Aristotle** thought the heart was made first, although **Plutarch** thinks otherwise and writes that it pleased Aristotle that not the heart be formed first, but the <term>navel</term> <note>original Greek: ὀμφαλός (omphalos)</note>. Just as in the construction of a Ship, the keel is built first. Certainly, Aristotle placed the heart first, both elsewhere and where he discusses Youth and Old Age, Life and Death, and also frequently in his books on the *History of Animals*, and especially in the second book of their *Generation*, where he says that very thing is discovered both by sense and reason; and he writes that the veins arise from there, and he judges this to be evident from those things he published concerning the histories and dissection of animals. **Physicians** <note>The term "Medici" refers to the medical authorities of antiquity</note> also gave primacy to the heart in the generation of man, although **Hippocrates** preferred it to be given to the umbilical cord; and in his book *On the Fetus* which we cited above, he claims to have read and seen seed that had remained in the woman's womb for six days: and having examined it immediately after it was ejected by leaping, he beheld a certain subtle thing which seemed to him to be the umbilical cord, and that it breathed with it, and from it the whole thin membrane, by which the seed was enclosed, was extended. **Plutarch** sanctioned that in which there are both veins and arteries. But Aristotle also maintained that the veins arise from the Heart, as we have said. And concerning their order and path, he disagrees with **Synesius the Cypriot**, **Diogenes of Apollonia**, and **Polybius**, in the third book of *The History of Animals*. **Alcmaeon** maintained that the head is formed before all other members: and **Lactantius** also seems to have been of this opinion in his book *On the Formation of Man*, taking an argument from birds, because in their eggs he often detected the eyes being fashioned first in the fetuses. 

<margin>Disagreement concerning the beginning of the formed human in the womb.</margin>

On the contrary, **Aristotle** thought otherwise in the sixth book of *The History of Animals*, when he wrote that in the egg the heart exists like a bloody point in the white liquid, which even now leaps and moves like an animal. Nor should you believe there were lacking those who judged that the big toe of the foot is formed before all other members; if **Ovid** had known all these opinions, I would think he had sung those lines of his with a laugh: *That day existed when we dwelt in the womb of our first mother only as seeds and the hope of men.* <note>A reference to Ovid's Metamorphoses, suggesting the poet's simplicity compared to the complex debates of philosophers</note> So that, for example, he might have said "seed" because the philosophers had harmoniously decreed that nothing else was formed earlier or later in the maternal womb. But let us perhaps (if you please) imagine that something was established by common consent concerning the first and the remaining fashioned parts.

**BOOK ONE** [space] **TWENTY-NINE**

<margin>On the many things about which there are many disagreements.</margin> Will the quarrels over the origin of this animal <note>The human being</note> ever cease? Will they not also battle over the time, not only of the gestation, but of the formation within the womb? Will there not remain many things concerning the already formed infant that are always discussed but not yet settled? Namely, in what manner is it nourished and increased? Does it dream or wake in the mother's belly? Furthermore, since we see that the seed of certain men is not at all fertile, and women also are known to be entirely barren: will they even agree on the cause of sterility? Not at all. And when we also see at other times not just one, but twins and even more brought forth in a single birth; likewise, when we behold those who are wrongly fertile and those who give birth to monsters <note>In this period, "monsters" (monstra) referred to any birth with physical abnormalities or congenital disabilities.</note>, will they perhaps inquire into and find the causes of these things in a friendly manner? But even if all women were fertile and all males possessed potent seed, and one healthy infant—or more, if we prefer—were conceived, and we were free from the fear of sterility: let them be brought into the light, and they may even be judged unlike their parents. I ask, is this similarity or dissimilarity going to produce differing opinions among the philosophers? Let the boy grow, reach adolescence, and flourish in youth: and let him reach old age, which is desirable to most: yet when that age, full of evils, brings forth death, will they at least agree upon those things closest to death, or will they rather close their final day oppressed and disgusted by altercations? They even leave undiscussed what death itself is, of which sleep is so similar—that long sleep of which it is a healthy reminder. Therefore, let us examine each point, reporting the diverse decrees.

<margin>On which day the seed rises into a fetus; how great the dissension.</margin> Regarding the future human already conceived in the womb through the received seed, Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher</note> wanted the formation to begin from the thirty-sixth day, but to be completed in all its parts by the forty-ninth. Others say the fortieth: an opinion usually attributed to Aristotle and Varro. Certainly, Aulus Gellius rightly inspected those views situated in the *Hebdomades* <note>A lost work by Varro titled "On Portraits" or "Hebdomades" concerning the number seven.</note> of Varro (for they are lost to us): the genital seed is gathered into a mass in the first seven days, and is curdled and made fit to take a shape; in the fourth week, the head and the spine of the future male are formed; in about the seventh week, the whole human is completed in the womb. Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> extends the formation of the female up to the thirty-fifth day, and the male up to the forty-fifth. Indeed, Aristotle in the seventh book of *The History of Animals* reported that a male who was expelled by miscarriage on the fortieth day had distinct limbs; and that the fetus itself appeared the size of a large ant; but a female who broke out by miscarriage before the third month was not yet clearly distinguished. Asclepiades preferred males, on account of their heat, to begin from the twenty-sixth day and be finished in their parts on the fiftieth; but for females, the beginning of formation is perceived from the second month and the end from the fourth. Hippocrates felt more correctly, as it seems to me, and decreed more prudently in his book *On the Fetus*: for although he assigned the fortieth day for the female to be formed and the thirtieth for the male, he allowed a little less and a little more time, and he was most pleased with the forty-second for females and the thirtieth for the male.

<margin>On the delay of carrying in the womb; how great the disputes.</margin> However, some wanted the stay in the womb to be seven months, most all said nine, not a few said ten, and some even wanted eleven. Aristotle, in the seventh book of *The History of Animals*, affirms that one time for giving birth is given to other animals, but for humans it is manifold: for he left it written that some women touch the seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and even the eleventh month. Others even wanted the infant to be carried for fourteen months, a matter which we have dealt with sufficiently in the commentaries on our hymn <margin>The Author's Hymns and their commentaries</margin> which is addressed to the Virgin, while we were explaining those verses; he <note>The poet/author</note> wanted her to be carried in the belly for nine full months. Hippocrates assigned the tenth month for a mature human birth, and indeed by a long progression, nor does he want a longer time for birth to be given, [lest women] be deceived...

He considers women who assert this to be mistaken: namely, those who swell with wind in their wombs and believe they are swelling with a false seed. Nor does he think the time given is shorter, unless some force intervenes or nourishment is lacking. In the book on *Nourishment* <note>original: "de alimento"</note>, he assigned both the ninth and tenth month; he wished for birth to happen both sooner and later, though neither much sooner nor much later. Varro, in his *On the Weeks* <note>original: "hebdomadibus"</note>, wished for the infant to be born in the fortieth week after conception. But in the fourteenth book of *Divine Matters*, as Gellius reports, he wished it possible to be born even in the eleventh month, and affirmed that they are sometimes born in the eighth. Furthermore, I have found those who say the eighth month is not only sometimes viable, as Aristotle and Avicenna thought, but even useful for birth; Hippocrates, however, denied this in his dedicated book. For so felt Polybus and Diocles, the first of whom judged that a viable infant could be born even at six months; but it happens that it is called a seventh-month birth because of the days transferred from the sixth to the seventh. On the contrary, Aristotle, in the place we cited above, decrees that a fetus which comes forth earlier than the seventh month is by no means viable. But there are those who wished the infant to be able to enjoy life if it comes forth from the mother's womb provided it remained in it for one hundred and eighty-two days and a fraction of a day.

<margin>Many disagreements on how the infant is nourished in the womb; likewise whether it sleeps or wakes.</margin>

But even if all infants remain in the womb for an equal time (if it pleases the philosophers and physicians), will it please them thereafter that they take nourishment equally? Or will Democritus and Epicurus provide it to them through the mouth; Alcmaeon through the whole body; the Stoics and almost everyone else through a specific part and the umbilical cord? Some have reported this to have been the opinion of Anaxagoras as well. Certainly, it was also the opinion of Aristotle, who reported in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* that the fetus increases through the attached umbilical cord; he asserts that by the very power of nourishing which is in animals, the umbilical cord is immediately driven into the womb like a root. Hippocrates certainly wished for growth to occur through the umbilical cord and for the fetus to breathe through it, though he also affirmed in the same book *On the Fetus* that it breathes through the mouth and nostrils alike.

<margin>The author against many.</margin>

But I would think that if infants, while they were in the womb, had been able to use reason and philosophy, they could indeed have established something more true than the weak conjectures these men use. For Democritus and Epicurus thought the unborn infant is nourished through the mouth because, immediately after birth, it is drawn to grasp the breasts with its mouth, because it was accustomed to suckle certain "little breasts" <note>original: "mamillas"</note> in the matrix. Others imagine a "little piece of flesh" <note>term: caruncula - a small fleshy growth or structure</note>, which Aristotle both reports and rejects along with Democritus in that same second book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Another, imagining the infant to be like a sponge, thought it attracts the surrounding nourishment to itself from everywhere; others say other things, so that they do not even agree on whether it is an animal when it first begins to be nourished and grow, any more than they agreed on the rest. Regarding sleep and wakefulness while they are carried in the womb, Aristotle discusses many words on this matter near the beginning of the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*. And from here, he inquires whether wakefulness or sleep comes first? Or should that first disposition more truly be thought of not as sleep, but as something similar to sleep? Since animals live the life of a plant during that time, he both inquires and is tormented by a long investigation.

<margin>How many battles there are concerning the causes of sterility.</margin>

But indeed, the seed from which these human bodies are made can be of such a kind that it is never rightly conceived. And since this can happen from either one, or from both who come together as one, being void of offspring, it is marvelous how pugnaciously those practicing philosophy disagree on this matter as well. Aristotle clearly discusses why men and women do not procreate fetuses in his books *On the Generation of Animals*, and not just once. For in the fourth book, he says the cause is a lack of moderation, either of heat or of cold. For if the heat greatly exceeds, it dries out the moisture; if it is much lacking, it does not "cook" <note>term: concoquit - the physiological process of "ripening" or digesting fluids through heat</note> it. Thus it happens that spouses joined together do not generate, but when separated, they can. In the second book of the same work, regarding humans...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of reproductive biology and the causes of infertility, moving from general principles to specific ancient authorities.</meta>

He believed that infertility occurs not only in humans, but also among other types of animals such as horses and sheep. He thought that males and females may fail to produce offspring if the areas suited for mating are damaged, whether from birth <note>original: "ab ortu naturae"</note>—which is why some men do not grow beards and some women do not reach puberty—or as age progresses, due to an over-abundance of bodily nourishment. In such cases, the seed in heavier men and the menstrual flow in women are lacking, as these substances are instead consumed by the body itself. He also teaches that disease can cause a man’s seed to be emitted too watery and cold, while in women, the monthly purgings may be corrupted and rendered unhealthy. Furthermore, in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he traced sterility to an immoderate genital organ, because the seed is carried too great a distance and therefore becomes cold and unfruitful.

<margin>Diocles</margin>
Diocles <note>A 4th-century BC Greek physician</note> believed the cause for people who lack offspring and are frustrated in their hopes was either that they do not cast their seed alone, or that less is discharged than is necessary, or that it is tainted and thus not at all generative. He also considered that the organs might be weakened and deprived of their proper function, or that it could happen because of a crookedness of the male member, which prevents the seed from being emitted straight, or because the genital parts of the male and female cannot be properly fitted together. 

The Stoics also held this view. I would be ashamed to write these things were it not for the fact that similar matters are set forth much more openly in the most approved books of our Catholic Church—specifically in the Decretal Letters <note>Papal decrees forming part of Canon Law</note> when dealing with those who are "cold" <note>impotent</note> or bewitched. 

<margin>Decretal Letters. Theologians.</margin>
Likewise, our theologians dispute matters of morality pertaining to salvation and the intercourse of spouses so that the sins which men must confess to a priest according to Christian rite may be distinguished. 

<margin>Stoics</margin>
Thus was the opinion of Diocles. The Stoics further blame the hostile forces and qualities of those who labor for children; for this reason, they think it happens that a woman who was barren with one man might conceive and give birth with another. Conversely, a man who has taken a new wife might succeed in conceiving what he could not with his previous one. 

<margin>Erasistratus.</margin>
Many physicians, and especially Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician</note>, lay the blame on the womb: either because its temperament is too thick, too thin, or too hard; or because the passages are blocked, or too fleshy, or too weak and feeble, or of a bad habit; or because the seed, once conceived, is scattered or torn away. 

Diocles also attributed the cause of infertility to the womb as far as the woman is concerned—and not only to the womb, but also to the seed, just as he had determined for the man. But while discussing the womb, he testifies that he observed in "anatomies"—or as I should say in Latin, "dissections"—of mules, that they have the same causes of sterility as women. 

<margin>Empedocles</margin>
He subscribes to the view of Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher</note>, who asserts that the failure to conceive and carry offspring occurs for no other reason than the smallness, the low position, or the narrowness of the womb, which may be attached to the belly in a distorted way so that the seed cannot be cast rightly into it, nor could the womb receive it even if it were cast. However, Aristotle, in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, ascribes a different opinion to Empedocles than the one Diocles attributes to him here. I do not think it can be seen which is truer except from the poem of Empedocles itself. For Aristotle says that Empedocles thought (as Democritus had also thought) that all creatures that mate outside of their own kind are sterile. 

Yet Aristotle had previously taught that mating is mixed among dogs, foxes, and wolves, and that Indian dogs are generated from a certain wild beast and a dog. This has also been observed in birds, such as partridges, hens, and different kinds of hawks. He adds that it is believed to happen even in sea creatures; for example, the "rhinobatos" <note>a guitarfish</note> is born from a shark and a ray. 

<margin>Aristotle's opinion on the sterility of mules.</margin>
He notes this also happens in Africa, which gave rise to the proverb: "Africa always brings forth something new." He himself refers the sterility of the mule rather to the nature and temperament of the horse and the donkey—and this through a long and subtle progression, though I do not know if his assessment of both animals is true.

Democritus reports that there are two seeds, one of which enters before the other, and then <margin>Democritus</margin> they are mingled; Aristotle both recounts and refutes this opinion. Empedocles, however, refers all similarity to parents to the power of the seeds, but thought dissimilarities happen because the heat of the seed has exhaled. Lactantius, in his book *On the Formation of Man*, refers the similarity of the newborn to the seed of one parent which has evidently overcome the seed of the other while both mixed seeds were coalescing; that seed prevails which was more abundant, and in a certain way embraces and includes the other. He writes there is no distinction of sex in this; for it happens whether the offspring be male or female. Therefore, whichever seed was more powerful and abundant draws the similarity to itself; hence it happens that sometimes the offspring displays the features of only one parent. But if the mixture was equal, he writes that the forms are mixed, so that the offspring appears either as a common blend or to resemble neither. He also thinks that disparate natures are created when the seed of the masculine stock falls into the smooth <note>or "light/left"</note> part of the uterus; for even if a male is begotten, he nevertheless displays something feminine: a softness of body, remarkable beauty, delicate limbs, exuberant whiteness, a slender voice, and a mind—

<margin>Aristotle.</margin> ...turning to alternating similarities. Aristotle writes in the seventh book of *The History of Animals* <note>original: "de natura animalium"</note> that a woman, through superfetation <note>conception of a second fetus while already pregnant</note> by different seed, gave birth to two children: one resembling her husband and the other her lover. He narrated the event but did not discuss the cause. However, he considers it possible for offspring to turn out resembling their grandparents rather than their parents, by reason of the various movements we mentioned above, as treated in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*. Indeed, in the seventh book, he brings forward the example of a daughter born in Sicily from an act of adultery with an Ethiopian; she did not reflect the father's color, but the son later born from her turned out to resemble his grandfather <note>i.e., the Ethiopian lover</note>. He judges that females are created for the most part similar to the mother and males to the father, yet he writes that the opposite can also occur. He also taught that similarity can occur part by part, and the offspring is accustomed to resemble the mother in one part of the body and the father in another. He also confirmed by the example of a mare nicknamed "the Just" from Pharsalus that by a law of nature, some generate offspring similar to themselves and others similar to their mates. But concerning the cause of this matter, he later discoursed more extensively in the fourth book of *The Generation of Animals*.

<margin>On the various forms of nutrition.</margin> But here, after a human is conceived and born through so many labors and hardships, in what way is he nourished after he eats food? Is it perhaps agreed upon? Certainly not in the least, as Cornelius <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, the Roman medical encyclopedist</note> asserts. <margin>Hippocrates, Erasistratus, Plistonicus</margin> Indeed, Hippocrates thought that very food was cooked <note>digested</note> by heat, which a great crowd of younger followers also believed. Erasistratus preferred the idea that food is not cooked in the stomach but ground down, which pleased many of his followers. Plistonicus, however, later than these—being a pupil of Praxagoras—judged neither to be true; he believed food putrefies rather than being cooked or ground, a view many agreed with. <margin>Asclepiades, Cornelius</margin> But none of these pleased the rivals and followers of the physician Asclepiades, for whom it was established that raw matter is distributed into the whole body exactly as it was taken in. Cornelius Celsus affirms that it is not understood by anyone's knowledge how that actually happens.

But let it be discovered how this animal is nourished; how long does it enjoy this life? How quickly does it reach old age, sought by all, yet soon hated or troublesome to almost everyone? <margin>On the varying length of life. Asclepiades.</margin> Asclepiades recorded that in Ethiopia, men are old at thirty years; in Britain, at one hundred and twenty. He attributed the cause to heat, which greatly parches the bodies of Ethiopians, making them thinner due to the sun's heat; he thought the bodies of Britons were more long-lived because they are denser due to the cold. <margin>Aristotle</margin> But Aristotle, discoursing on the shortness and length of life, records that those born in hot places are longer-lived than those in cold places, and he confirms this in two problems in the fourteenth section. He refers the cause to the firmness and durability of nature arising from dryness, and likewise refers it to moisture and heat, by which life is preserved longer, the destruction of which things is death. <margin>Stoics</margin> The Stoics ascribed old age to a defect of heat. Aristotle added many things elsewhere, mentioning the heart, heat, and moisture while discoursing on the length and shortness of life, and on old age, life, and death: of which heat there are two types of corruption, one violent and the other natural, arising from a lack of nourishment.

But though this span of life be long, is it supported by health or rather interrupted by a thousand diseases? <margin>On the discordant causes of diseases.</margin> <margin>Asclepiades, Alcmaeon</margin> Asclepiades rendered the causes as flowing particles <note>atoms</note> which, by stopping in invisible pores, block the way. Alcmaeon attributed them to a "monarchy" of qualities—when heat, moisture, dryness, cold, sweetness, or bitterness exceeds its bounds. <margin>Diocles</margin> Diocles attributed most diseases to an inequality of those elements which are in the body. <margin>Cornelius</margin> Cornelius teaches that some of the professors of wisdom thought likewise: namely, that ill health is created when something either exceeds or is deficient among the four principles. The same Cornelius affirms it was the view of <margin>Herophilus, Hippocrates, Galen</margin> Herophilus that all fault lies in the fluids <note>humors</note>. To Hippocrates, however, it lies in the breath <note>pneuma/spirit</note>. But Galen, in his *Introduction for Physicians*, says that Herophilus of Chalcedon and Praxagoras of Cos placed the causes of sickness in the humors. However, he states that Athenaeus and Archigenes placed them in the breath, whence they are called "Pneumatists" <note>original: "spirituales"</note>. To others, on the authority of Cornelius, it pleased them to say that sicknesses arise when blood is transfused into those veins which are adapted for breath, and excites an inflammation which the Greeks call *phlegmon*, and he wished such a movement to be produced by that inflammation.

In this manner, and regarding the short order of things, they hesitate and wander. It is most clearly seen in the writings of those who treat the Republic and its laws, for almost every man used to comment upon his own laws. Hence, even among the Latins, there is a wonderful variety; for although they wished justice to be done and for each person to be rendered their due <note>original: "suum unicuique reddi" — a classic definition of justice in Roman law</note>—and not only our people, but all nations desired this, as the whole system of civil discipline looks chiefly toward that end—nevertheless, there is great discord regarding the manner in which that very law (which is so called as if it were "just") ought to be distinguished. 

First, this is because the interpreters of the laws themselves followed various philosophers of different sects; indeed, some seemed to depend on the Stoics, others on the Academics and Peripatetics. <margin>Variety of Latin laws</margin> Labeo <note>Marcus Antistius Labeo, a famous Roman jurist known for his innovation</note>, devoted to Plato, introduced many innovations into Roman laws, of whom our Augustine makes mention, and the legal consultant Pomponius mentions extensively in the first book of the *Digests*. <margin>Interpreters of laws are imitators of philosophers</margin> Marcianus also, in the same book, follows Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> in defining law. Celsus embraces Theophrastus, who wrote on the office of legislators. Truly, Ulpian, along with Celsus (unless I am mistaken), affects a true philosophy; if he had marked it correctly, posterity would have owed him much. For as we have seen, there is much ambiguity and much discord concerning this matter. 

Furthermore, it has been ordained by varying law who ought to judge the law itself, who may act under that law, and who may reject it. Hence, diverse matters are treated concerning judgments, the jurisdiction of all judges, actions, and exceptions. Many duties are established for the plaintiff, many for the defendant and the advocate. There are many and varied kinds of punishments, and many prescriptions for acting and proving. There are almost no rules by common consent. Indeed, those who were not subject to the Roman Empire had their own laws; and not only cities and kingdoms outside of Europe have their own, but now in Italy itself, Venice and those cities and municipalities which are subject to the Roman Empire use their own laws and statutes by the authority of that very Empire. <margin>The proper and private laws of each city</margin> Although they sometimes refer back to the civil and ancient laws of the Romans, of which innumerable volumes were once written. 

But (to use the words of Tertullian) they have hewn down that whole "old and overgrown forest of laws" with the new axes of princely rescripts and edicts. It is written that even the most vain Papian laws <note>The Lex Papia Poppaea, regarding marriage and celibacy</note> were excluded by the Emperor Severus after the old age of such great authority. <margin>Outdated laws</margin> Nevertheless, they used to have volumes with a vast number of laws, which the Emperor Theodosius trimmed and reduced to a few. Then Justinian himself refined and digested those volumes; even to this day, lawyers fight most bitterly over them. This is because they are mostly either the responses of the wise, the edicts of Roman princes, or the decrees and consultations of the common people or the fathers <note>original: "plebis aut patrum scita" — referring to plebiscites and senatorial decrees</note>. 

For as in former times nations and peoples (as found in the *Epitome* of the historian Justin) were bound by no laws and the whims of princes stood for laws; yet when the Romans sent to seek laws, they returned to the Romans according to their own whim and responses, often so unjust that the Emperor Opilius Macrinus—as Julius Capitolinus recorded in his life—had determined to abolish all the rescripts of the ancient princes so that he might act by law and not by rescripts. He said it was an abomination that the wills of Caracalla and of unskilled men should be seen as laws. 

But even if one acts by law—even if confirmed by the consent of the commons and the fathers—there is nonetheless much ambiguity. Therefore, it does not harmonize exactly with the minds of all, since it is not entirely clear to everyone but only probable. Nor can a reason be given for all things which were introduced by our ancestors, as Julian writes in the first book of the *Digests*, under the title "On Laws and Senate Decrees and Long Custom"; nor is it proper to inquire into the reasons for those things which are established. Otherwise, many of those things which are certain would be subverted, as Neratius writes in the same title and book. For this reason, the ancient legislators—in order to prove their laws to those acting under them, whom human consensus might not have convinced—fabled that one had drawn his laws from the cave of Jupiter, another from the Pythian oracle, and another from Minerva. They did not think it enough if they themselves could be seen to derive their laws from the law of nature (which they had corrupted), whether by way of conclusions or by common determinations...

Xenophon, in his *Memorabilia* <note>original: "ἐπἀπομνημονεύμασι" (apomnemoneumasin). Xenophon was a student of Socrates; this work defends Socrates' character.</note>, indicated from their very discord that even those philosophers who sought sublime visions of nature were like madmen in their long and beautiful discourse. <margin>Xenophon</margin> These things were mocked by Lucian in his *Timon* because of that same contention; he joked that Jove's <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> ears were plugged by the shouts of disputing philosophers, and because of this, he could not hear prayers. <margin>Lucian</margin> This was also noted by the great censure of Seneca when discussing liberal studies: that philosophers descended to the pronunciation of syllables and the properties of conjunctions and prepositions, so that they knew how to speak more diligently than how to live. <margin>Seneca</margin> Fabius Quintilianus affirmed that most philosophers of his time labored not in virtue and study to be considered philosophers, but displayed a somber expression and a dress differing from others to hide the worst morals. <margin>Quintilian</margin> These same things were taxed by Cicero in his work *On the Laws* when he relates that the proconsul Gellius called together the philosophers who were then in Athens into one place, so that they might finally set some limit to their controversies. <margin>Cicero</margin> He suggested that if they truly desired not to waste their lives in litigation, the matter could be settled with him, and he promised them his assistance if any agreement could be reached regarding their dissension among themselves.

But how great, I ask, and how manifold and how unending is that discord? For we have seen—even if we do not claim to have collected all the disagreements, nor do authors write in a single way when describing those disagreements—how great and manifold is this dissension, teeming with various ambiguities. We have seen the leaders of the sects and their followers disagreeing both as a whole and in parts. Having described their dogmas individually, they have decreed variously and pugnaciously concerning the principle of things. Even in the causes of natural things and in nature itself and its material principles, they have been discordant. In the constitution of the world, in determining its end, in measuring its magnitude, in designating its shape, and in other matters of this kind, they are clearly found to be varied, inconstant, and combative. Now, when they discussed the parts of the world itself, the heavens and the stars, they uttered almost nothing with one voice. When they disputed concerning the lowest and atmospheric phenomena, they put on more faces than autumn. Truly, when they taught concerning man, they taught nothing; when they disputed concerning his soul, they did so so inconstantly that someone might suspect they lacked a soul themselves, and were not philosophers, but rather vanishing shadows and phantoms of the living. I pass over the various judgments on the functions and duties of the soul; I am silent on the body; I say nothing at all of man's happiness, the highest good, and morals—who could grasp it? Since in all these things they established nothing certain or peaceful, but poured out everything in a wavering manner, full of warlike tumult and utter foolishness. And so vainly that they even left it in doubt whether the truth of things can be apprehended at all.

Furthermore, their chief study was for one to attack another, and for whoever came later to vex those who wrote before him. For Plato, like a censor, noted all his predecessors, which he seems to have done especially in the *Theaetetus* and *Sophist* dialogues. <margin>Plato</margin> The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> accused Plato. The New Academics accused the Peripatetics and the Stoics. <margin>Peripatetics. New Academics. Stoics.</margin> These latter both rail against the Peripatetics and conflict among themselves; from their very beginnings, they seethed with factions, and as Numenius says, they were so divided among themselves that some confessed themselves to be Stoics more than others. The Sceptics argued against everyone, and the matter reached the point where war was entered into between the sects of philosophers not only with words but with fists (as the saying goes). <margin>Sceptics</margin>

Let us compare these things to the letters of the Old and New Testament, the sacred eloquence from which we seek our—that is, the Christian—discipline. <margin>Christian Discipline.</margin> In the former, we contemplate the truth under a cloud and veil of figures; in the latter, we perceive that same truth revealed in clear and manifest light. Let us compare, I say, our discipline, which truly—

...as is easy to see in the writings of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian who argued that Greek philosophy stole its best ideas from the Hebrews.</note>, who reports on these very matters. In the New Testament as well, many philosophers have labored, and even against their will have praised it, such as Amelius the Platonist <note>original: "Amelius platonicus"; a 3rd-century philosopher who famously commented on the Prologue of John's Gospel.</note> and others. Since much has been written on this subject both by others and by us elsewhere, it is better now to have hinted at a few things than to have explained many. Therefore, the dogmas of our faith, having been divinely handed down, were also divinely confirmed—not by any deceptive coloring of words or by the windings of syllogisms. For indeed, it was fitting for the greatest Judge of all things (as he says) not to argue, but to pronounce briefly and plainly. I add further: to confirm what was pronounced with signs and portents. For it is not fitting that if the principles are divine and above nature, the means by which they are proven should be held as of an inferior kind. Wherefore, being confirmed also by miracles above nature, the world’s greatest admiration arose from this, as did that veneration from the philosophers themselves. They would have wondered even more if they had perceived and turned their minds to the fact that the principles of our Christian religion are divinely handed down, that the means received strength from divinely produced signs, and that the end is eternal happiness. Thus, the first proposition, as it were, of this syllogism <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> possesses faith, revealed by divine light; then, as a second part, there follows an innumerable multitude of miracles to confirm that very faith and the works which proceed from it, perceived most clearly by that same light; and finally, a life of total happiness is gathered from these premises, perfected by that divine and most excellent light in the heavenly seat. Therefore, in the sacred scriptures themselves, which proceeded from God, there is truth, promised happiness, and constancy. In the books of the philosophers, who followed the senses and imagination most of all, there is vanity, uncertainty, and discord. We have largely enumerated these discords in the first book of this work, relying on authorities and using them as a history of opinions to be reviewed. Now, both the time and our promises demand that this same thing be done through reasons and disputations. In this matter, we shall not depart from the order observed by Aristotle in his teaching on animals. For he explained what pertained to their matter in several books using historical narration—whence those books are titled not "On Nature" but "On the History of Animals" in the Greek inscription—and that itself satisfies the question of the "fact of the matter" (or the "that it is"), which the moderns <note>original: "neoterici"; referring to contemporary scholastic philosophers.</note> are accustomed to call the *quia est*. But afterward, in other separate books, he treated the parts, and in others the generation of animals, so that he might investigate the causes—the final and the formal, which he judged to be nearly the same—in those books, while in these last ones, he investigated the parts pertaining to generation, especially that which receives the name of the "efficient cause." Thus, what history, resting on experiences, had opened up in certain books, the disputation relying on reasons might then discuss and confirm in the remaining books.

BOOK 53

Wandering here and there through winding paths for a long time, they were held back either by ignorance or by ambition, so that they did not reach the royal palace. The reason was that truth, sought after in the human fashion, was by its own nature exceedingly difficult to find; and once found, it was held in the highest price, heaping great praise upon its possessor, even though it remained unrefined and full of difficulties. These men themselves were also poorly suited to drink in the divine light because of the darkness of their vices, since they placed impassable clouds against that very light—which the Prophet <note>original: "propheta"; likely referring to King David in Psalm 4:6, "The light of thy countenance is signed upon us."</note> sang was sealed upon us, and which illuminates every man coming into this world—even if they could not entirely cast it away. Hence, they tried to abolish the notion of God, naturally implanted and branded into human minds, either through disputes or, if they could not do that, to eliminate it through their vices. The common crowd of the profane exploded the former attempt, but Paul condemned the latter, writing: *when they had known God, they did not glorify Him as God, or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and calling themselves wise, they labored in folly.* <note>A translation of Romans 1:21-22.</note> And indeed, what could the philosophers themselves wisely decree concerning other truths, when they hallucinated so imprudently regarding this one truth, so clear and innate from the birth of nature, doubting whether any true thing could be found?

<margin>How difficult it is to grasp the truth, by the testimony of the philosophers.</margin>

Yet they were not so blinded as to be deceived in this: namely, that it is difficult to know. For they said that truth was hidden and incomprehensible, yet they did not say they were entirely denied the ability to comprehend it. Content with eternal agitation, they caused trouble for others; they did not contend that they had found it, but remained nonetheless doubtful themselves, always searching. But those who thought they could possess the truth, and even that they had possessed it at other times, affirmed that it was sought with much zeal and great labors, so that they might make it appear a little less inaccessible to others—to the extent, clearly, that they might teach that it cost a great deal, even if they wished it could be bought for a small price. Thus:

One said it was submerged in a well, another that it lay hidden in horrific caves. And that famous man <note>Democritus, often called the "laughing philosopher."</note> laughed at the pursuits of men regarding it and disputed with himself in solitude, even becoming an inhabitant of tombs; while this other man <note>Heraclitus, the "weeping philosopher."</note> followed those same human pursuits with tears. Having testified at the beginning that he knew nothing, and at the end that he knew all things, he did so obscurely, however, so that he received the name "The Dark One" <note>original: "tenebricosi"; a reference to Heraclitus's nickname, *Skoteinos*.</note> from that very black bile with which Theophrastus writes he suffered. Hence his game of dice in the temple of Diana, hence his life spent in the mountains out of hatred for men, and hence an end of life not worthy of a philosopher. There were some, however, not long after, who contended that truth was more readily available; but their disagreement signified clearly enough that what they grasped was false. For some decided it could be apprehended and judged by the senses, many by the imagination, some by the intellect, and a part by all these modes. Others stood against them, both generally and specifically, pouring forth so much that the whole business of the philosophers regarding truth—whether it can be possessed or investigated by any means—was reduced to these three heads:

<margin>The triple sect in general concerning the judgment of truth.</margin>

So that some judged it necessary that every judgment of truth be abolished. Others judged it should be left alone, though this was contended by them in various ways. Others, adhering more to the first group, held to those very...

**SECOND [BOOK]                                XXXVIII**

We have been able to gather this clearly enough from the perpetual war of the philosophers. This has been shown both in a general sense and proven at least by the weight of authorities. Now, it must be demonstrated and confirmed both in detail and by rational arguments. However, there first occurs what is called by the Greeks the <term>criterion</term> <note>original: "κριτήριον"; the standard or benchmark of truth</note> of truth, for which we translate the term as "judicatory" rather than "judgment," rendering word for word. For just as the Latin Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> translate *criterion* in Aristotle as "sensory organ," and even "instrument of sensing," so let us also turn *criterion* into "judicatory," meaning the instrument of judging or the place of judgment. Therefore, whenever mention is made of the criterion, we shall use the name "judicatory," and it will be understood as the instrument by which some judgment is made, and also in some manner the place in which a cause or dispute is judged. Since that name can be taken in many ways, it seems it must first be explained so that we may grasp it in the specific sense that is proposed to us. The "criterion" is established for that by which we do anything or desist from doing it in performing the duties of an active life. Likewise, it stands for that which creates certainty for us regarding a matter.

**SECOND** [space] **39**

it is also established and prescribed that when they are affected by distress or soothed by joy, they possess something by which they perceive those affections to be true and not false or illusory. Nor can they deny this while they accept the laws of their fathers, for they are taught that they are by no means lacking in judgment, nor do they fail to possess some interior light by which they may distinguish whether they act well or ill, truly or falsely. They respond—those of the "judicatory" <note>The *judicatory* or *criterion* refers to the standard of truth used to judge reality.</note> whom we mentioned above—using many distinctions: they confess that, lest they be entirely without action or remain as "non-contributors" <note>original: *asymboli*; those who do not pay their share or participate in social duties</note> to human society, they accept certain things without discussion or controversy; but when these things come under the examination of philosophy, that is another question. For they have not gone so far as to deny what *appears* to be, but are led to action by that very appearance; yet whether that which appears is truly so, and is such as it appears, <margin>Arguments of the Sceptics against the Dogmatists.</margin> regarding this there is a great and manifold question. Indeed, it is so complex that it is always discussed and disputed by them, but never settled or decreed.

But indeed, against those who establish a "judicatory" of truth, the Sceptic family disputes in roughly this manner: I ask you Stoics and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> and whoever else is on this list, I call upon you who agree that there is a judicatory, yet do not agree on what kind it is or how many there are. Those who deny it, however, do not refuse the idea that it *appears* so, but they do not consent that it *is* so. We hesitate and continue to investigate. Can such a manifold discord be judged or not? If it cannot be judged, you must agree with us, withholding assent and philosophizing by searching; if it can be judged, in what way can it be done? Communicate this to us. But how are you able to do this, when it has not yet been decreed not only what it is, but whether there is any at all? On this matter, we ourselves are tormented by perpetual strife.

Again, so that the discord concerning the judicatory may be settled, we must already have an admitted and established judicatory, so that the discord itself may be removed, and it may be judged one way or the other whether the judicatory exists or not. And so that we may have a certain and constant judicatory, it is necessary at the outset that the manifold discord concerning that very thing be removed and judged. If, however, they say that a judicatory is judged by a judicatory, no one is found who does not know that the matter will go on to infinity. In the same way, the matter will fall into an infinite investigation if mention is made of "demonstration" (a subject we shall dispute at length). For demonstration requires a judicatory, as no demonstration will be fortified without the judgment of the senses, or the intellect, or both—as is openly known beyond all controversy to those who have read, not to say held in their hands, the treatises of the Peripatetics or Stoics concerning demonstration. If, however, the judicatory requires a demonstration, the matter, driven in a perpetual circle, will never be terminated, since one always requires the other, and each requires each.

But they say, even granted that some judicatory is held, they call it vain and useless, since whether the "true" exists by its own nature or not is not held clearly. <margin>How the ancient philosophers distinguished the "true" from "truth."</margin> For the ancient philosophers separated the *true* from *truth* in a threefold way: by essence, by constitution, and by power. By essence, because they said the *true* was incorporeal, while *truth* was corporeal. For the *true*, if we listen to the Stoics, is like a *lekton* <note>original: λεκτόν; a "sayable" or the meaning behind an utterance</note>—that is, a "thing said"—if we may translate it so, or an "enunciation."
