Whether the "true" itself actually exists or not is a matter of great doubt for many. And since truth—which is called a collection of many true things—is circumscribed within the "true" itself, nearly the same disputes and disagreements arise here as were brought up above. However, the doubt concerning this entire matter will be taken up and a careful weighing will be performed later in this very volume. 

But our own authors—among whom Augustine is foremost in the first book of his *Soliloquies*, where he disputes with his own Reason—distinguish truth from the true just as one distinguishes "chaste" from "chastity." He asserts that truth is more excellent than the true, for he argued that if anything is true, it is true by truth itself. 

Others among our authors (concerning which there is also a discussion in Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>) have accepted and defined truth and the true in three ways. First, they define that in which the true is grounded; thus Augustine said the true is "that which is," for being itself precedes the logic of the true as its foundation. Second, they define that which properly completes the logic of the true, in which way truth is called the "conformity of the intellect and the thing." For the thing is equated to the intellect. Perhaps it is from this that Aristotle said in his book *On Interpretation* <note>original: "perihermenias"</note> that speech is called true or false based on whether the thing is or is not. And in the fourth book of his *Metaphysics*, he says we speak the truth when it is said that what is, is, or what is not, is not. Third, the *effect* of the true is often called "true," in which manner Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers</note> judged the true to be "being made manifest," and Augustine taught in his book *On True Religion* that "that which is" is shown by truth, and that judgment is passed on lower things according to truth. 

Likewise, there is the thing, the intellect, and that which is the medium between them: the sense. The sense judges the things and is itself judged by the intellect, to which it is compared as a certain thing and an index of lower things. To put it simply, the name of "truth" is used to express the foundation of the true, its limit, and the very habit or relation between them. It is said by some to exist in the thing as in a cause, to be placed in the soul as in a subject, and to be expressed and indicated in speech as in a sign. 

However it may be determined, many things are designated by the names of true and false. We believe it has been sufficiently revealed above, and will be most clearly declared in the progress of this work, that the philosophers wish to pull the true, truth, and the judgment of these things into their own various opinions. Therefore, leaving our own authors aside for the present, let the dispute of the philosophers against the philosophers be recounted. 

For they say that since there is as great a controversy concerning the true and truth as there was concerning the "criterion" <note>original: "iudicatorio," the standard of judgment</note>—with different sects of philosophers denying, asserting, and doubting—how can the dispute be easily settled? For he who confesses that something is true, if he brings it forward without a demonstration, will not be believed because of the various opinions of dissenting philosophers. If he attempts to bring a demonstration, if it is false, it will be rejected; if he says it is true, the matter will revolve in a circle, because it will be asked *why* the demonstration is true. Whether that demonstration is again true or false must be made clear by another demonstration. Thus it will happen that this one is supported by that one, and that one by another, so that the inquiry will eventually reach no end. 

Furthermore, either only those things which are seen <note>perceived by the senses</note> are true, or those which are not seen; or of those things which are true, some are seen and manifest, and others are not. But they say none of these are true; therefore, nothing is true. For if only the things which are seen or appear to us are true, they will say either all such things are true or only some. But if they say all, the argument is turned around and subverted, for it seems to some that nothing is true, and no one will rightfully subordinate his own authority to another's judgment in an equal case. But if they respond that some of the things seen are true, if they answer this without a criterion, how will the matter be settled? For they will not be able to separate these from those so as to pronounce some true and some false. If they use a criterion, they will say that criterion is either manifest and apparent, or it is not. But they will by no means say the latter, for we are assuming for the present that only those things are true which...

<meta>This page continues the skeptical inquiry into the nature of truth and the possibility of a "criterion" or standard for judgment, likely from Sextus Empiricus's Outlines of Pyrrhonism, Book II.</meta>

->BOOK TWO<- <column-break/> ->40<-

...those things which are seen, which appear, and which are manifest. Therefore, they will contend that the manifest and the apparent are [the truth]. But when they say this, we shall press them thus: since the question is which appearances are true and which are false, the very thing taken as "apparent" or "manifest" to judge the things seen is itself part of the same dispute, insofar as it is an appearance. Therefore, it will need another apparent judge to determine whether it is true or false. And that will need another, and so on, one after another, so that the inquiry finds no end. But since we cannot judge an infinite series, we will also be unable to comprehend with certainty whether the things offered to us by an appearance ought to be judged as true by right and merit.

The same result will follow if we say that only those things which are not seen, which are not manifest, and which do not appear at all, are true. For they will not say that all such things are true; no one could reasonably say that the number of stars is even, nor could one rightly affirm that they are odd. <note>The "even or odd number of stars" was a classic Skeptical example of a "non-evident" matter where judgment must be suspended.</note>

And yet, if we judge one thing by another—saying these non-manifest and non-apparent things are true, but those are not—if we do not use some appearance as a judge to deliver a sentence, the same inconveniences mentioned above will surround us. But if we are to deliver a sentence using that which is not apparent as an arbiter, then we will need another non-apparent arbiter; for we are seeking which of the non-apparent things are true and which are false. Therefore, it will be necessary that this non-apparent thing (since it is also under discussion as it is placed among the non-apparent) be judged by another that does not appear. And if we judge this non-apparent, obscure, and unknown or non-manifest thing by another unknown thing, our argument will eventually run on to infinity. Thus it follows that obscure or unknown or non-apparent things alone should not be called true.

It remains for them to claim that of the things which are true, some are apparent and others are not; which would indeed be absurd. For whether they deem all things—both non-apparent and apparent—to be true, or say that some apparent and some non-apparent things are true, they will not avoid a double difficulty. For if they say "all things," their argument will again be overturned, for they must grant, whether they wish to or not, that things are both true and not true. For it will immediately be pronounced true both that the stars are even and that they are odd.

If they grant the second option <note>that only some things are true</note>, how shall we judge that among the things which appear, these are true and those are false? For if we use something apparent to judge, our argument will undoubtedly go on to infinity. But if we prefer to use a non-apparent arbiter: then since those things which are not apparent require a judgment, by what witness, by what judge, I ask, are we to judge? By the manifest or the obscure? By the apparent or the unknown? If by the apparent, the argument will always be driven in a circle <note>original: "circulo" - the logical fallacy of circular reasoning</note>. For this will be proven by that, and that again by this, and it will happen by turns and permutations; each will be proven by the other. If they say the judgment is made by the non-apparent, then the matter will proceed to infinity.

The same will happen if the same discourse is held concerning obscure and non-apparent things. Since if anyone attempts to judge the obscure by something obscure and unknown, an absolutely infinite argument will present itself to them. If he judges by the apparent and clear, then if he always assumes that which is apparent and clear, he will fall back into the inconvenience of infinite proof. If from this he makes a departure to the obscure, the argument will always be driven in a circle. Therefore, they maintain a vain and false position in saying that of the things which are true, some are clear or apparent, and others are obscure and little known.

From this they would have it that if apparent things are not true, nor are non-apparent things alone true, nor even some apparent and some obscure things true, then nothing at all is true. But if it is granted that nothing is true, then even the "criterion of judgment" <term>iudicatorium: a standard or tool for determining truth</term>, if any were found to be true, would be useful only in judging that; but since it is itself not at all...

SECOND [BOOK]                                                                XLI

<margin>The force of Xeniades' argument.</margin>

Next follows the opinion of Xeniades, whom Democritus also mentions. He wished to persuade others—though whether he persuaded himself, I know not—that all things are false, and that every mental image <note>original: "phantasia"</note> and every opinion is deceptive. He believed that everything which exists comes from that which is not, and likewise is defined and destroyed into that which is not. How much this opinion differs from or approaches that which is attributed to Xenophanes can be understood from this: if we grasp nothing of the truth, then for the sake of discerning falsehood—since a prejudice of falsity has already been introduced to all things—it will undoubtedly follow that no "criterion" <note>original: "iudicatorium"; the standard or yardstick for judging truth</note> is granted by which those things might be distinguished. Furthermore, he attributed the cause of why all things are false and of such a kind that they cannot be grasped or distinguished to the senses. The force of his argument is gathered in this specific point: If that by which other things are judged is false, it necessarily follows that all things are false; but that [the senses] is false, therefore all things are false. For the senses themselves pass judgment on all things, and they are fallacious; therefore, he says, what we intended is proven.

But Anacharsis the Scythian <note>A legendary 6th-century BCE sage from the Black Sea region</note> did away with the "grasping" <note>original: "comprehensionem"; likely referring to the Stoic concept of *katalepsis* or certain knowledge</note> that judges each art, being greatly angered at the Greeks because they had abandoned it. For who is it, he asks, who judges based on an art? Surely either a layman or a craftsman. If we say the layman, what absurdities follow? Being unskilled in those matters pertaining to the art, he will wander astray no differently than a blind man attempting things that belong to the sighted, or a deaf man attempting things judged by the ears. But if we grant the judgment of an art to one unskilled and ignorant of it, how would ignorance of an art differ from the art itself? Truly, if they say the craftsman judges based on the art, absurdities follow again: for he would judge either an equal craftsman of the same art, or a master of a different art. But how could one who is not of the same art pass sentence on a craftsman of a foreign art? For while he is knowledgeable and skilled in his own art, he will be considered a layman when transferred to a foreign one. Yet how can a worker of the same art approve or judge an equal to himself—that is, a craftsman of the same faculty? For this is the very thing we are inquiring: who is it who, among those established in the same art, may arbitrate with one and the same power? For if this man judges that one, it happens that the same person is both the one who judges and the one being judged, and the one to whom trust is both granted and denied at the same time. Insofar as he is of the same art, he is distinct from others who judge; but when he is judged, trust is not held in him, whereas insofar as he judges, trust was held in him previously. How can it be that the same person is both judge and judged? And that trust is both held and not held in him at once? Therefore, he thought it proven that no one is found who judges from art, from which he clearly thought the "criterion" was abolished.

Regarding the opinion and reasons of Protagoras, by which he wished the criterion of truth to be removed only in a universal sense; and there, an argument against Aristotle; and regarding the opinion of Dionysiodorus, Euthydemus, and Nausiphanes. Chapter Five.

Protagoras of Abdera, a Sophist <note>A paid teacher of rhetoric and virtue in Ancient Greece</note> rather than a philosopher, of whom much mention is made in Plato and a dialogue is inscribed with his name, was placed by ancient writers among those philosophers who wished the criterion of truth to be abolished. Protagoras was of the opinion that all imaginings and all opinions are true, and ought to be held as such. But not universally—only particularly. For the truth of them was among the number of things that are relative to something else. Therefore, everything that (for example) seems to me, is so for me. Whence he also exclaimed: "Man is the measure of all things; of those that are, that they are, and of those that are not, that they are not." He also confirmed his sentiment with a contrary opinion: for if, he said, you deny that, then it will be confirmed: because you who...

# BOOK TWO [space] XLII

For he considered it a characteristic principle that those who possess different dispositions should be judged differently by others. Thus, he maintained that neither the wise are fair judges of things done in madness, nor are those awake fair judges of the delusions suffered by those seized by sleep, nor are the old fair judges of the actions committed by children. For just as he thought that the experiences of the former do not appear the same to the latter, so too the actions of the latter do not appear the same to the former. Furthermore, he held that all things which appeared to someone were true to the person to whom they appeared. For this reason, he argued that if a man—whether insane or sleeping—was not a faithful and firm judge of his own actions while in that state, then once he became wise or awake again, he would likewise not be a fair judge of those previous states, since those conditions had then passed for him. From this it followed that a firm and constant criterion of judgment <term>iudicatorium</term> <note>The Latin term 'iudicatorium' refers to the 'criterion' or 'standard' by which truth is measured.</note> could not be maintained, since the very disposition by which judgment is rendered had shifted. But indeed, although Protagoras placed the criterion of judgment within man, he did so in a way that abolished a universal criterion of truth while leaving it intact for the individual. # BOOK

Being, or (if one prefers to say) that which is, and that which is not—although the ancient authors of the Latin language, and later Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a Roman rhetorician</note>, do not at all shrink from this noun *ens* <note>original: "ens"; the philosophical term for "being" or "entity"</note>. Nevertheless, there are some who, knowing nothing of philosophy and being poorly steeped in humane letters, dread that word worse than a dog or a snake. If a thing exists, he says, it is either being, or non-being, or indeed both being and non-being. 

But it is not being, nor is it non-being (as shall be stated), nor both being and non-being (as shall be taught). Therefore, it does not exist. For that which is non-being does not exist; for if non-being exists, it will simultaneously be and not be. Insofar as it is understood as non-being, it will not be; but insofar as it *is* non-being, it will, conversely, be. However, it is entirely absurd for something to both be and not be at the same time; therefore, non-being will not exist. 

Viewed another way, in this manner: If non-being exists, then being will not exist. For these things are opposites to one another; indeed, if it happens that non-being exists, it must happen that being itself does not exist. But if being does not exist, then neither will that which is non-being exist. And yet, neither will being exist. For if it is being, it is either eternal or generated <note>meaning "created" or "brought into existence"</note>...

either magnitude or body. But which of those should it be assumed to be? It will not be one. For if it is established as a quantity, it will be divided. If it were continuous, it will be cut apart; similarly, if it is understood as magnitude, it will not be indivisible. If it is proven to be a body, it will be threefold: in length, breadth, and depth. It is absurd, however, to think that Being is any of those; therefore, Being will not be a certain "one." And yet, neither is it "many": for if it is not one, it is not many either. For many things are composed of those things which are one, wherefore if the one is removed, the many are removed at the same time. Therefore, that it is neither Being nor non-Being, he <note>Gorgias</note> thought was made manifest from what we have said. That it is also not both at once is easy to gather. But so much for the first chapter of Gorgias, which we have interpreted almost word for word.

He added next that, even granted that Being exists and is maintained, it is not for that reason thinkable by man. <margin>The second chapter of Gorgias's argument.</margin> For if, he says, things thought are not Beings, then Being is not thought—and indeed (as he himself thought) with reason as the guide. For if, he says, it happens to things thought to be white, and it happens to white things to be thought, so if it should happen to things thought not to be Beings, it will necessarily happen to Beings not to be thought. Wherefore if things thought are not Beings, Being is not thought. Now, he wanted it to be presumed for a while that things thought are not Beings until he could prove it; therefore, he wanted to show that Being is not thought. He said it was clear from this that things thought are not Beings: for if things thought are Beings, then all things thought exist, whenever anyone has thought them. But this is absurd. For if someone has thought of a flying man, or a man running over the sea in a wagon, a man will not immediately fly, nor will he have driven a chariot over the sea. In addition to this, if things thought are Beings, then things which are non-Beings are not thought, for contraries happen to contraries. And certainly, non-Being is the contrary to Being, and therefore if it happens to Being to be thought, it will happen to non-Being not to be thought. But this is absurd: since Scylla, and the Chimera, and many of those things which are not, are thought of. Therefore, non-Being is thought. Furthermore, just as things seen are called "seen" for the reason that they are seen, and things heard are called "heard" because they are heard—and we neither despise nor reject things seen because they are not heard, nor do we eliminate things heard because they are not seen, for it is necessary for each one to be judged by its own sense and not by another—so also with things thought: even if they are not discerned by sight, nor heard by hearing, they shall nonetheless be grasped by their own proper judicial faculty <note>i.e., the mind</note>. If, therefore, someone thinks of wagons being driven about on the open sea, even if he has not seen these, he must think that wagons are running on the sea. This is therefore absurd; therefore Being is not thought or grasped.

But even if we should grant, says Gorgias, that Being is grasped, it nevertheless cannot be set forth to other men. <margin>The third chapter of Gorgias's argument.</margin> For if Beings are visible, audible, and generally sensible, and of those things which lie outside, some are visual and others are grasped by hearing, and not indiscriminately: then these cannot be announced to other men interchangeably. For it is speech <note>original: *sermo*, translating the Greek *logos*</note> which announces, but speech is not the underlying thing <note>the actual object</note>; therefore, we do not announce the things themselves to others at all, but rather speech, which is different from the underlying things. Just as, therefore, the visible will never become audible, and vice versa, so Being, which lies outside us, will certainly not become that which is our speech. Moreover, since it is not speech, it will not declare anything to another. For speech, he says, is constituted from those things which happen to us from the outside—that is, from sensible things—and is prepared by the movement of the lips. But if this is so, speech will not be the constitutor of that thing which lies outside, but the thing itself will be the indicator of the speech. And yet, it must not be said that just as visible and audible things lie there, so also does speech, and that for this reason, from the underlying thing and Being, those things which are underlying and Beings are announced. For even if speech is an underlying nature, it nevertheless differs from the rest of the underlying things, and visible bodies differ most greatly from speeches. For that which we call visible is capturable through one organ, and speech through another. Therefore, speech will not indicate many underlying things, wherefore neither...

<margin>Various things concerning Gorgias, which Aristotle and Sextus have handed down.</margin>

These matters having been discussed in this manner by Gorgias, it was concluded that there is no criterion of truth <note>Latin: *iudicatorium*, a standard for judging truth</note>; for he was one who would do away with existing things, and he wished to maintain that even if they existed, knowledge of them would be removed; and even if knowledge were left, he denied that it could be communicated to another. And indeed, these points concerning the disputation of Gorgias we have translated into our language from the Greek philosopher Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a Skeptic philosopher</note>; these are not entirely similar to those which Aristotle recited in a specific little work concerning the dogmas of Gorgias. For although Aristotle reports that Gorgias wished to establish those three points—that nothing exists, and if it exists it is not knowable, and if it is knowable it cannot be indicated to others—nevertheless, he pursues them in another way, interposes other dogmas of other men, and even argues against him. We have mentioned this so that the things which Gorgias himself properly proposed and took care to prove may seem more sincerely recited in the works of Sextus. However, our purpose in this place is to recite his dogma, not to disprove it, except insofar as it might repugn the true faith. But when we have reached almost the end of this book, we shall disprove all the opinions of the philosophers, or rather, we shall bring into the midst the Skeptics arguing against other philosophers. But there were also others who took away the criterion of truth, whose opinions, though varied, tended toward the same end. Metrodorus used to say that men know nothing, and do not even know this very thing: that they know nothing. In this part, he was opposed to Socrates, who affirmed that he knew only this: that he knew nothing. Furthermore, among Anaxarchus and Monimus, such a judgment was passed concerning the criterion of truth that existing things were compared to shadow-like sketches, and those who perceived them were compared to those who fall into madness and dreams.

### On the opinion of the natural philosophers who flowed from Thales; and on the opinion and reasoning of Anaxagoras, who were pleased that the criterion of the senses be taken away but that of the mind be left; and how falsely Aristotle insulted them. Chapter Seven.

<margin>The elements as beginnings.</margin>
<margin>Asclepiades.</margin>
<margin>Black snow according to Anaxagoras.</margin>
<margin>Against Aristotle.</margin>
The first natural philosophers who flowed from Thales brought the consideration of the criterion into the midst; and indeed, rejecting the senses as entirely deceptive in most matters, they established reason as the judge of the truth which is in things. Moving from this as if from a prison, they taught in order concerning principles and elements (these are called "beginnings" <note>Latin: *initia*</note> by Marcus Varrone in Cicero's works). They thought that the comprehension of these elements could be achieved by that very power [of reason]. Hence Anaxagoras, alleging the weakness of the senses because they were too obscure, gave the opinion that the truth cannot be judged by their unfaithful judgment. He wished this to be known by the mixing of two colors; for if, for example, white and black were taken, and an infusion were made drop by drop from one into the other, the sight would not be able to discern the smallest changes, even though they existed in nature itself. The physician Asclepiades did not shrink from this reasoning; indeed, he seems to have used it in some way in his first book on the prescription of wine. For he says, if we mix pale and dark wines, the sense will be powerless to discern whether the color subjected to the sight is simple or not. Therefore, Anaxagoras established the criterion of truth in reason alone. And there is also the argument that he said snow was black, though it appeared white, because he knew that water (from which it was gathered) was black, thinking this reasoning, such as it was, outweighed common sense. Concerning this matter, Cicero among others makes mention in the *Academics*. These were the views of Anaxagoras, who did not (as Aristotle ascribed to him in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: *primae philosophiae*, "first philosophy"</note>) assert that the prudence pertaining to reason and intellect was the same as sense, or that things were such as each person thought them to be. But this matter will be made clear more fully in the sixth book, when we dispute against Aristotle for having falsely reviewed the dogmas of the ancients.

On the opinion and reasoning of Empedocles regarding the judgment of truth, and how falsely Aristotle recites and attacks his opinion in the fourth book of the Metaphysics. Chapter ten.

<margin>Expositors of Empedocles</margin>
Empedocles, a follower of Pythagoras, wished for "like to be judged by like," but his commentators believed he established six instruments for judging truth. For besides the two efficient principles of things—Love and Strife—he also remembered the material principles: earth, water, air, and fire, and decreed these to be the judges. Furthermore, it is an ancient opinion confirmed by the consensus of many philosophers that "like can be perceived and known by like." Neither Democritus nor Plato shrank from this view, though they were moved by different arguments. There were also those who said Empedocles intended the judgment of truth to be attributed solely to reason <note>Latin: *ratio*</note> and in no way given to the senses. They claimed that within right reason there is something both divine and human; the first cannot be fully explained, while the second admits of explanation. In this matter, he rejects old age from the perception of truth, doing so in many beautiful verses. From this, one can sufficiently perceive that Aristotle did not 
<margin>Against Aristotle</margin>
correctly report his opinion in the fourth book of the Metaphysics, where he asserts that Empedocles considered sense and wisdom <note>Latin: *prudentia*</note> to be the same. For Empedocles distinguished sense from reason, and within reason, he decreed there to be both a human and a divine element. How falsely Aristotle imposed this view upon him can be proven from the very poems of Empedocles, in which he distinguishes the intellect from the senses. There, he mentions the intellect and sings that some things are so sublime that they can be grasped neither by sense nor by intellect. But we shall deal with this matter more extensively in the sixth book, where we will both cite his own words and translate them word-for-word, without regard for the elegance of Empedocles' verses. 
<margin>Note</margin>
For where truth is sought—especially against a man of such excellent genius and such great authority among philosophers—one must abstain not only from deceit, which must always be cast away, but from any suspicion of "colored" or flowery speech. Indeed, it will be shown that Aristotle condemns in Empedocles what he condemns in himself: saying that souls follow the body; and in his *Problems*, he says the judgment of reason is altered by the temperament of the body. One must consider that Empedocles, who gave wisdom to both humans and plants, gave it for different reasons. For he believed that divine inspiration <note>Latin: *respiratio*</note> comes to men, but that in sleep, men become forgetful of it, and in waking, they become wise again as the intellect enters through the pores or passages of the body—as if through doors—and recedes during sleep. Yet it does not recede so far that some remnants do not remain, like a root for breathing, to be revived later. Just as coals near a fire ignite immediately but are extinguished if they are far away—this is the opinion of Empedocles. Although this may be judged far from the truth itself, it is not recognized as having been refuted by Aristotle.

<margin>Against Aristotle</margin>
Nor did Heraclitus disagree with those we have mentioned, for he traced the judgment of truth back to the mind. Whoever says that he did away with it would be imputing this to him calumniously. For what Aristotle writes in the fourth book of First Philosophy <note>The *Metaphysics*</note>—that Cratylus only moved his finger, and that Heraclitus forbade entering a river twice, and Cratylus even once—does not contradict what we have said. For Heraclitus did not think that should be applied to all truth, but rather to hint at and signify the most difficult...

**SECOND** [space] **XLV**

I have found it to be most difficult to find truth in things that are continually flowing and slipping away; for this reason, he <note>Heraclitus</note> rejected the senses and placed truth in the divinely given intellect, writing: **"Eyes are bad witnesses for men"** <note>original Greek: κακοὶ μάρτυρες ἀνθρώποισιν, ὀφθαλμοὶ</note>. Yet, eyes stand out far among the senses, and many differences in things are shown through them, as Aristotle maintained in the first book of the *Metaphysics*. But Heraclitus also added that ears are not reliable, even though they are highly valued in the knowledge of things by Aristotle himself, since he claims that hearing is the sense of learning. However, he <note>Heraclitus</note> seems to have tempered his opinion by his manner of speaking, saying: **"and ears, for those who have barbarian souls,"** <note>original Greek: καὶ ὦτα βαρβάρους ψυχὰς ἔχοντων</note> unless he rather thought it the part of a barbarian and unlearned soul to have faith in the senses. Nor does this pertain to the intellect simply, but he judged that truth is perceived only by the common and divine—that is, by that intellect which is divinely given. What kind of intellect or reason the natural philosopher Heraclitus actually meant is conjectured by interpreters from Homer, for [Marginal note: Homer.] he sang: **"For such is the mind of men upon the earth, as the day which the father of men and gods brings upon them"** <note>original Greek: τοῖος γὰρ νόος ἐστὶ ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων οἷον ἐπ᾽ ἦμαρ ἄγησι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε</note>. And likewise from Archilochus, who repeated the same, writing: [Marginal note: Archilochus.] **"Men understand such things as the father of all brings to them day by day."** Euripides also used this sentiment. [Marginal note: Euripides.] Nor does this seem to differ at all from the opinion of Empedocles. But whether Heraclitus dreamed, or played, or falsely claimed that this common judgment assists everyone, is debated. For if anything appeared to one person that did not appear to others, he considered it untrustworthy and inconstant for that very reason. But it was altogether difficult once, and is now, to understand what Heraclitus wanted; for there was such obscurity of speech in the man that he drew from it the nickname "The Obscure" <note>Latin: scotini</note>. Plato writes in the *Theaetetus* that the followers of Heraclitus, when questioned, [Marginal note: Plato on the followers of Heraclitus.] usually respond with certain enigmas; if the reason or meaning of these were sought, they would not explain but increase the difficulty with another enigma.

Democritus, however, was not displeased by the idea that similarity is the cause by which truth is judged, since he noticed a certain gathering toward those things of a similar kind, occurring easily and of its own accord, both in living things and in those that are inanimate. For thus one may see (he says) cranes fly to flocks of cranes, doves to doves; so also lentils are gathered with other grains of lentils, and grains of barley are collected in heaps of barley. Truly, he took away those things which appear to the senses as uncertain, insofar as he did not think they could be truly comprehended. He left them, however, as probable and matters of opinion. But he thought the true and most certain things were the "void" and "atoms." Thus it happened that he thought, by a certain law of nature, there exist "sweet" and "bitter," "hot" and "cold," or as he says in his own words: **"By law sweet, by law bitter, by law hot, by law cold"** <note>original Greek: νόμῳ γάρ γλυκύ. καὶ νόμῳ πικρόν. νόμῳ θερμὸν. νόμῳ ψυχρόν</note>; [Marginal note: Against some.] while the cause of these is the underlying void and atoms <note>original Greek: αἰτίη δὲ, ἄτομα, καὶ κενόν</note>. Regarding this word, I marvel at his mention of "atoms," since it was handed down from the ancients that they were called "indivisibles" <note>Greek: ἀδιαίρετα</note> by Democritus, and only later called "atoms" by Epicurus, who was born many generations after him. In his book *On Ideas*, he did not put forward things entirely consistent with his earlier works. But in the book called *The Canons*, he established two types of cognition: of the senses and of the mind. Of these, the latter is brought in as faithful testimony for the judgment of truth, but the former he calls "dark": **"There are two forms of knowledge: one legitimate, the other dark. To the dark belong all these: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch"** <note>original Greek: γνώμης δὲ δύο εἰσὶν ἰδέαι. ἡ μὲν γνησίη. ἡ δὲ, σκοτίη. καὶ σκοτίης μὲν τάδε σύμπαντα. ὄψις. ἀκοὴ. ὀδμή. γεῦσις. ψαῦσις</note>. That is, there are two species: one indeed legitimate, the other truly dark; and to the dark belong all these: vision, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching. But he judged the legitimate to be that which is "hidden" from these. Hence I marvel that Aristotle, in the fourth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>The Metaphysics</note>, [Marginal note: Against Aristotle.] wrote that Democritus said either nothing is true, or it is not manifest to us, and this because of the variety of the senses; when nevertheless, as we have shown even by his own words, he called the cognition of the mind "legitimate."

These are the words of Cicero. How far he deflects from what Democritus intended by his own words is shown by those very words of Democritus, which were either unknown to or suppressed by Aristotle himself. This much is certainly known to almost all the learned, and recorded in many places concerning Heraclitus and Democritus: that one affirmed truth lies in a deep cavern, the other in a well, as if they wished to suggest by a riddle that truth can indeed be possessed, but only with great labor.

### On the opinion and reasoning of Plato in determining the judgment of truth, and how variously different men interpret it. Chapter Twelve.

We have run through the opinions and reasonings of almost all the ancient philosophers, and especially those who are called the "Physicists" <note>Natural philosophers who focused on the material world.</note>, concerning the judgment of truth. Plato follows, who, although he is multifaceted and usually explained in various ways (as was shown above), nevertheless did not seem to shrink from the Pythagoreans in the judgment of many, just as was established above when the treatise on their opinion was held. Plato himself in the *Timaeus* divided things into those which are intelligible <note>Things understood by the mind.</note> and those which are sensible <note>Things perceived by the senses.</note>. He established that the intellect becomes a sharer in those things called intelligible, as things which could be and are comprehended by it. But those things which are sensible, he thought were merely matters of opinion; wherefore some have thought that the judgment of things established by him should be referred to reason, which would both comprehend and take unto itself that clarity which is obtained through the senses. In this they differed from the sentiment of Democritus, because he decreed that obscurity, not clarity, was inherent in the senses. Therefore, those who have weighed the decrees of Plato himself placed in the *Timaeus* have moved toward this sentiment. For he says both that there is something which always is, having no beginning, and that there is something else which is generated <note>Brought into being/changing.</note> but is by no means "being" <note>True, eternal existence.</note>. <margin>What is comprehensible according to Plato.</margin> And they say that the former is comprehensible by intellection with reason, while the latter is comprehensible by opinion with sense. The Platonists say that "comprehensible" in his view is the name for reason common to both clarity and truth; they say it is necessary that reason be moved by clarity itself toward judging the truth, since the judgment of true things is made through those things which are clear and manifest. But clarity itself is not thought to be sufficient by itself for the knowledge of the truth; for if anything appears according to clarity, it does not necessarily subsist according to truth. It is necessary that one be present who may judge both what merely appears, and whether that which appears in that which is, is also supported by truth. This is done by reason. Wherefore they do not want both to concur at once: both clarity, by which reason is carried as if from the starting prison to the finish line <note>original: "a carcere ad calcem," a metaphor from Roman chariot racing.</note> of judging the truth; and reason itself to deliver the sentence concerning that clarity. Furthermore, to judge clarity and to distinguish what is true within it, reason cooperates together with the sense. For by the help of this [sense], receiving the "imagination" <note>The mental image or representation.</note> of the truth, it effects both notion and science; wherefore it is concluded that reason is the captor of both clarity and truth.

Next follows Arcesilaus, who, departing from the old school of Plato—which had belonged to Speusippus and Xenocrates—established the Middle Academy, which is also called the Second. <note>Arcesilaus (c. 316–241 BCE) was the founder of Academic Skepticism, shifting the Academy toward a philosophy of questioning all certainty.</note> However, Numenius, in his book *On the Dissension of the Academics*, argued that he was actually a Skeptic, and an Academic in name only. <note>original: "Numenius in libro de Academicorum dissensione"</note> Carneades followed him, who is regarded by many as both the author and founder of the Third and New Academy; or, if Lacydes was its founder, Carneades was undoubtedly its great expander. But first, let us examine the teachings of Arcesilaus, which may appear varied depending on how they are presented by his followers. For some have maintained that no criterion of truth was defined by him; others wish it to appear that a criterion was defined, but only for the purpose of contradicting the Stoics. <note>The Stoics believed in "kataleptic impressions," or certain perceptions of truth, which the Skeptics of the Academy sought to undermine.</note> Augustine, in his third book *Against the Academics*, thought that Arcesilaus believed truth could be perceived, but that he argued the opposite specifically to oppose Zeno, the leader of the Stoics, who had studied under Polemon at the same time as he did.

# **BOOK**

The interpreters and followers of this school believe in the "Apparition" <note>original: "Apparitione"; referring to the Stoic concept of *phantasia* or mental representation</note>; hence they have decreed that the affected imagination is a certain state of the living being, which is held to be the establisher of both itself and of another thing. For just as light shows both itself and everything that is within it, so also the imagination—since it is the leader of that notion which exists in the living being—ought, like light, to show itself, and also to make clear and apparent that by which it is established. 

But since it happens that it is not always truthful, but is also frequently found to be lying—inasmuch as it may disagree with the things by which it is impressed and report false news—it necessarily follows that the judgment of truth cannot be left entirely to every imagination. Furthermore, he adds many other points by which he weakens and removes both the imagination itself and all the senses from which it proceeds. These matters he himself later <insert>calls</insert> the judgment and [guide] in conducting life.

And it explains the matter much more clearly, as it seems to me, than those points recited from the first book of Clitomachus *On the Withholding of Assent* <note>Latin: *de sustinendis assensionibus*; this refers to the Skeptic practice of *epoche*, or suspending judgment</note> found in Cicero’s *Academic Questions*. It was clearly the view of Carneades that there are two kinds of appearances <note>The Greek term is *phantasiai*, translated here as "visions" or "appearances"</note>: in the first kind is this division—that some appearances are such that they can be perceived, while others cannot. In the second kind, however, some appearances are probable <note>original: *probabilia*; Carneades used the Greek *pithanon*, meaning "persuasive" or "trustworthy"</note>, and others are not. Therefore, whatever arguments are made against the senses and against clarity, those pertain to the first division; but against the second division, nothing ought to be said.

I say that this explains the business of Carneades more clearly than those passages of Cicero from Clitomachus—even those excerpts from the book dedicated to Gaius Lucilius <note>A famous Roman satirist and friend of the Academics</note>, translated by Cicero, written by the same Clitomachus (who remained with Carneades until old age, and was a man as sharp as a Carthaginian <note>Clitomachus was originally from Carthage before moving to Athens</note>, as well as being very studious and diligent). Those points are: that it pleases the Academics that there are such multitudes of things that some seem probable, while others seem the opposite; however, that is not a sufficient reason why some things should be said to be "perceivable" and others not.

**BOOK 52**

Whether a certain thing is white and sweet is not something individuals possess in common, since each person receives it from their own internal state <note>original: "affectu"</note>: for this reason, it may seem one way to me and differently to many others, due to the diverse dispositions of the senses. For we observe that what appears pale to some, appears crimson to others. But this, as it seems to me, can be attributed not only to the senses being affected by the occurrence of things, but also to the various temperaments established thus from the birth of one's nature. Truly, much more will be said on this matter in the fifth book of this work, when we shall dispute against Aristotle concerning the evidence and judgment of the senses. Setting out not from the silphium-bearing <note>Laserpiciferis: referring to the plant silphium, a major export of ancient Cyrene</note> Cyrene (as he says), but from the Lyceum of Athens itself. Now let us return to explaining the discourse of the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy founded by Aristippus, emphasizing pleasure as the supreme good</note>, who even extend these internal states to the ends of good and evil; some of these they decree to be pleasant, others harsh, and they likewise think others possess a certain middle nature. They consider those things to be good whose end is indisputably pleasure, and those things evil whose end incurs pain: the middle things are those whose end is neither good nor evil. Therefore, they thought that the internal states <note>affectus</note> of all things were both the judgments and the ends. For we live, he says, following our internal states and consenting to both "clarity" and "complacency" (as they say). Clarity pertains to the rest of the states, while complacency regards pleasure alone. Thus far the Cyrenaics, seizing upon the faculty of judgment more narrowly than the Platonists; for they circumscribe it with clarity and internal states alone, whereas it pleased the Platonists to measure it by clarity, but also by reason. Wherefore I wonder how it is that Cicero, in the second book of the *Academics*, writes that the Cyrenaics thought the judgment of truth resided in internal touch alone, whether of pain or pleasure. For we have shown that they admitted more criteria for judging truth, and it is most well-established that not everything we perceive, and even conceive in the mind, brings either pain or pleasure, but has taken on a certain middle nature between harshness and sweetness. Asclepiades did not shrink from the Cyrenaic opinion, establishing the faculty of judgment in the sense, by which he thought things themselves were grasped not by reason, if we believe what Antiochus reported.

**Concerning the opinion of the Stoics and the reasons for measuring truth and falsehood. Chapter Seventeen.**

The Stoics thought that the "grasping impression" <note>phantasia kataleptike</note> was the judge of truth. Although this was discussed above when dealing with Arcesilaus, something must nevertheless be commemorated in this place, because they say much and much is said against them. In this place, it will not be useless to have distinguished between assent and approbation. Likewise, between that which is uncertain and that which cannot be perceived, a matter which is also mentioned by Cicero in the *Academics*. Furthermore, to distinguish between perspicuity and perception, matters about which there is no small dispute between the Stoics and the later Academics. But because there is discord even among the Stoics themselves, let us set aside what they individually feel. "Phantasia" <note>impression or mental image</note> is not understood in only one way among them; for they define it thus: phantasia is *typōsis en psychē* <note>original Greek: τύπωσις ἐν ψυχῇ</note>, that is, a shaping or an impression in the soul. Upon this matter they immediately disagreed. For Cleanthes understood "shaping" according to equality and excess, like that shaping and impression which is made in wax by a ring; Chrysippus thought this was absurd. For it would happen that the same body would be formed with diverse figures around itself, just as that wax would be imprinted with diverse forms. Therefore, he took Zeno's word *typōsis* <note>original Greek: τύπωσις</note> not for "shaping," but for that which the Greeks call *heteroiōsin* <note>original Greek: ἑτεροίωσιν</note>. We (if it were permitted by the defenders of the Latin language) would call it either "alterity" or "alteration." Wherefore he himself [posited] another...

He himself introduced a definition with that word <note>likely referring to "phantasia" or "perception"</note>, which did not please those who came after him. From this, no small battles were stirred up in literature among the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude</note>, which would be too long and unnecessary to recount at present. Sextus Empiricus explained these matters diligently in the first volume of his work *Against the Logicians*, <margin>Sextus</margin> while Cicero, at the end of the second *Academic* book (which is also commonly called the *Hortensius*), <margin>Cicero</margin> relates that Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism</note> used to demonstrate this with his hand. When he showed his open hand with fingers extended, he said a "visual appearance" was like this. Then, when he had closed his fingers a little, "assent" was like this. When he had completely closed his hand and made a fist, he said that was "comprehension" <term>katalepsis: a central Stoic concept meaning a clear and certain mental grasp of an object</term>. From this similarity, he even gave the thing a name that had not existed before: *katalepsis*. But when he moved his left hand toward it and squeezed that fist tightly and vehemently, he taught that "knowledge" was such a thing, of which no one was master except the Wise Man.

Furthermore, the Stoics devised many differences among appearances. <margin>The various types of appearances or "phantasiai" among the Stoics</margin> For some appearances (or *phantasiai*) are said to be persuasive, others unpersuasive. Some are both, others neither. The first kind are those from which a smooth and steady motion arises around the soul, such as "it is now day" or "I am now writing." The second are those held in the opposite way, which withdraw us from assent, such as "if it is day, the sun is not above the earth." The third kind, which relate to diverse things, are sometimes held as such and sometimes differently, due to the varying relationship to which they refer, such as those drawn from ambiguous speech. The fourth are those in which not only is there ambiguity, but at no time can one part seem more probable than the other to human perception, such as whether the stars are, for example, even or odd in number.

Even of those named probable or persuasive, they say some are true, others false, some both, and others neither. They relate "true" and "false" to the nature of the proposition or predicate, which can be formed either this way or that—that is, truly or falsely. Therefore, a true proposition is one from which a true appearance will proceed, such as "I am now writing"; a false one is that from which a false appearance flows, such as "I am now resting amidst the watches of the soldiers." They think an appearance is both true and false at the same time in the case of the insane or those in a frenzy, such as happened to a certain foolish peasant we had at home. For when he saw his son, he indeed rejoiced, but called him by another name; insofar as he was moved by the present object, the appearance could be thought true, for he recognized his son, but insofar as he called him by another name, accepting him not as his son but as a stranger, it was certainly false. They considered those that were general to be neither true nor false, where the species are diverse and contrary, just as with "animal": one is rational, another irrational. But "animal" in general is not properly either this or that, nor can it be held as such.

Later, they made a distinction among true appearances; for they wanted some to be held as "grasping" and "comprehensive," and others not at all. The latter are found to occur through some disturbance in the mentally ill or those seized by "black bile" <note>melancholy</note>; even if they attract a true appearance, it is not a "grasping" one based on judgment, but rather something occurring from the outside and by some chance. Therefore, they are neither formed by them nor carried by assent. But they decreed the "comprehensive" appearance to be that which comes from an existing thing, and according to that which exists, is indelible and marked as if by a seal. The Old Stoics <margin>Old Stoics</margin> established this as the criterion of truth, which has such a property among other appearances as the horned viper <note>original: "cerastae"</note> has among other serpents. Many of the Platonists contradicted them, thinking it possible for a falsehood to be grasped unchangeably by a "grasping" appearance. But the Younger Stoics <margin>Younger Stoics</margin> added that it is necessary for that appearance to have nothing against it, since they judged it could lack trust and truth due to some external circumstance. They bring forward the stories of Admetus and Menelaus as examples. For when that King of Thessaly <note>Admetus</note> reasoned that his wife Alcestis had departed from life, and that the dead do not return to life, and he looked upon her whom...

And concerning every sect that, proceeding from Socrates and Plato, recognizes Socrates himself as a parent and does not shrink from Plato, we must now speak of Aristotle, who established a new sect and challenged Plato.

### On the opinion of Aristotle, Theophrastus, and their followers in determining the judgment of truth. Chapter Eighteen.

<margin>Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note></margin>
Aristotle and most of his followers established a twofold judgment of truth: the **sense** for sensible things, and the **intellect** or **mind** for intelligible things. However, Theophrastus imagines a certain common element to both, *the self-evident* <note>original: "τὸ ἐναργὲς" (to enarges) — clarity or self-evidence</note>, which we can call the clear and the lucid. In order, indeed, the sense precedes; in force and power, the mind does, although it is later in order and seems to follow the sense. But this is perhaps clearer in Theophrastus; in Aristotle, not at all. He always places the sense first, and in the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he asserts that one must believe the sense more than reason. We shall dispute this matter more extensively in the progress of this work. 

Certainly, the sense is moved by a sensible thing; and from that motion, which proceeds from the clarity of the sense in the souls of those living beings capable of self-motion, a certain motion arises which is usually called both **memory** and **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty by which the mind forms images of objects not present</term>. Memory is of the affection that occurs around the sense. Imagination, however, is of the sensible thing by which the sense is affected or suffers, and by which a certain trace is burned into and left in the souls. Therefore, it is defined by Aristotle as "a motion produced by the sense according to act." 

Furthermore, just as a footprint itself is made both *from* something and *by* someone—for example, from the position of a foot and by a friend—so too the same motion of the soul, whether it be a burning-in, an impression, or rather a trace, is made *from* some affection or suffering around the sense, and *by* some sensible thing whose likeness it even preserves. From this very motion, which has been given the names of memory and imagination, another motion arises in our souls, which is called both **thought** and **intellect**, due to different considerations of it. For insofar as it gathers and fashions images of things, they called it thought; but insofar as a certain clarity shines forth, they called it mind or intellect. 

For when the soul is able to compose, meditate upon, and collect in itself this or that notion of things perceived by imagination, it is called thought. But when it has performed this with wakeful clarity, it is named mind, or intellect—it is generally called *discursive reasoning* <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia)</note>. Moreover, from the intellect and thought are established both **Notion**, and **science**, and **art**. Thought occurs when sometimes species are conceived individually, and sometimes species and genera together. But the gathering of all phantasms in the intellect, and the collection of all particulars into one universal thing, is called a **notion**. In this gathering and collection, finally, both science and art are established. The former requires something exact and minimally variable, while the latter does not. 

Just as the nature of sciences and arts is later in generation, so too is that which is called **opinion**; for when the mind, struck by the sense, has consented to and acquiesced in the thing seen, then opinion is born. From all these things, it can be sufficiently gathered that the Peripatetics established the sense and the mind as the judgments of the knowledge of things; and indeed, that the sense holds the place of an organ or instrument, while the intellect uses it like a craftsman. And just as we would be unable to weigh heavy and light things without a scale, nor determine the straight and the crooked without a carpenter's rule or a plumb-line...

### On the opinion of Epicurus in judging the truth. Chapter nineteen.

After Aristotle and Theophrastus follows Epicurus, far inferior both in time and dignity, although he sharply attacked Aristotle himself. This same Epicurus, following the senses, favored the judgment of "phantasia" <note>original: *phantasiæ*; here meaning a mental impression or appearance</note>: which he thought was joined to opinion, and he called it "clarity" <note>original: *claritatem*; likely referring to the Greek *enargeia* or self-evidence</note>, and considered it entirely true, as that which showed the primary affections—that is, pleasure and pain. He believed that the former arose and was expressed from sweet and delightful things, and the latter from sad and afflictive things. And this same opinion was held not only universally, but also in detail and in relation to any singular thing. But he thought most people were deceived by the difference of the senses, when impressions seem to occur in which, for the sake of a foreign color or shape, a thing is presented differently than he thought. He even devised a way for differing and thus clashing impressions to occur, such that one was true and the other false. But he did not notice that "phantasia" differs from sense, as all good philosophers maintain, and as I myself showed sufficiently in a book on imagination <margin>The Author's book on imagination</margin> published many years ago. For one thing can be perceived by sense, and another by "phantasia." And where the sense has erred not in just one way but in six hundred, so to speak, it is manifest that "phantasia" can err just as often. But this is the place for explaining, not for refuting. However, he considered the opinions joined and related to these impressions to be likewise both true and false: true, those which were witnesses of clarity and did not have other witnesses to the contrary; false, those against which testimony was brought by clarity, and for which it brought none. Furthermore, that attestation which he calls *epimartyrēsis* <note>original: ἐπιμαρτύρησιν; Greek for "witnessing" or confirmation of a hypothesis by clear vision</note> is a comprehension through clarity, so that this "opinable" thing—for example, that some friend is approaching—is such as it was perceived by the opinion itself, with no other impression bringing a contrary judgment. Therefore, this attestation and non-attestation was called into counsel so that something might be true, and was placed in the seat of the judgment of truth. But that something was false, he said was discerned by non-attestation and counter-testimony. Moreover, the foundation and basis of all things was considered to be clarity itself. These things, in sum, were established by philosophers of every sect concerning the judgment of truth, against whom the Sceptics direct much contradiction, not indeed regarding one matter, but regarding many—indeed, the most numerous matters.

### That the Sceptic philosophers sharply contradict all others who established any judgment of truth, in a triple way and manner, where something deeper is found, namely concerning the excellence of the Christian faith. Chapter twenty.

We have seen and recounted in order all the sects of philosophers who did away with the judgment of truth, and we have seen all those who left it behind; and we have explained the various opinions not only of the former but also of the latter: which can be reduced chiefly <margin>Opinions on the judgment of truth reduced to five heads.</margin> to five heads. For some took the mind, others the sense, and others both as the judgment-seat. Others gave the primary place to "phantasia," but they disagreed on which "phantasia" was the captor of truth. Others used "phantasia" but as a servant and minister of either sense or mind. The Sceptics, intending to refute all these decrees at once, proceed in a triple way and manner.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Skeptical school's assault on the possibility of human judgment, likely following an introduction to the nature of truth or perception.</meta>

->BOOK 2<-

They proceed by considering that every capacity for judgment must come from someone, through something, and also occur according to something. Therefore, approaching the matter by this triple path, they strive to ensure that all judgment is abolished. First of all, they contend that the source from which judgment flows is unknown—that is, the human being who must deliver the judgment. Since the human is so little known, they argue that the judgment itself cannot be known, even though the consensus of all proves that judgment depends upon the human. Furthermore, even if they were to grant that what a human being is could be perceived, there is another "instrument of judgment" which they call the *through which*: that is, the person's senses and mind. They claim these are affected by so many influences that a judgment of truth cannot be expected from them. Yet, even if it were granted that both the senses and the mind could, for their part, deliver a verdict, they nevertheless wish to abolish that judgment which is named the *according to which*—that is, the <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "phantasiam"; in this context, it refers to the mental impression or "presentation" of an object to the mind</note>. They contend this is carried out neither rightly nor sincerely. Thus, even if other things were true by their own nature, the mental impressions would become false messengers, presenting by their own character things that are false rather than true. Therefore, since no opinion can be found to decree any judgment that does not proceed from the senses, the mind, or the mental impression, and since all these reside in the human being, they believe that once judgment regarding the human is removed, those other things will consequently be removed as well. But they labor to teach in great detail that even if the human being were known, a certain judgment of truth could not be established in his senses, his impressions, or his mind. Although this sect has done its best to destroy every other sect of the <term>Dogmatists</term> <note>Philosophers who claim to have certain knowledge of the truth, as opposed to the Skeptics</note>, it has vehemently attacked the Stoics, who thought themselves powerful in the great judgment required to discern truth. It also greatly vexes the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> in this matter, especially since they believed these three things—sense, intellect, and mental impression—concur to perceive the truth. These the Skeptics strive to disturb and thrust down from the tribunal and the seat of judgment with as many great engines of war as they can. But before we demonstrate and run through these three paths, I consider it worthwhile to reveal certain things by which the paths themselves may be found easier and less rugged.

<margin>Note on the zeal of ancient philosophers in contradiction.</margin> In ancient times, there was a very great zeal and care among philosophers for contradiction. From this, they acquired glory for themselves, for which they were most greedy. For this reason, some devised particular arguments or sophisms for themselves. Others endeavored to construct a formal art, as many did among the rhetoricians and philosophers—Aristotle, for instance, in the eight books he called the *Topics*. But these men presupposed both that truth could be possessed and that there was a means of judging it. Yet others attacked these things as false and rejoiced in removing what the former had established. Still others emerged who would deliver no judgment at all, yet they would contradict with all their might everyone else, especially those who boasted of having certain doctrine. They did not assert that they themselves spoke the truth, but only that "it so appeared" to them. They held that their own arguments and reasons could be removed by others—indeed, that they would be abolished by themselves, not unlike medicines which expel themselves along with the humors they drive out. These men employed perpetual consideration and always withheld their assent; they tried to uproot the principles of others' doctrines as if they were foundations, so that once dug up, the entire building would collapse. <margin>Pyrrho and others.</margin> Among these, Pyrrho <note>The founder of the Skeptical school (Pyrrhonism)</note> had great influence, and then Aenesidemus, and many others. The last of their sect, as far as I know, was Sextus Empiricus. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note> grieves that Sextus, along with many others, has been customarily introduced into our Church for the sake of pride and vain curiosity; and rightly so, since those vices should be extirpated, not fostered. However, for repelling the arrogance of philosophers and demonstrating the excellence of the Christian faith, they can be useful. Great and distinguished men of old were once held by a desire for this, as we have written elsewhere, when it was necessary to harm the enemies of our Church...

they are unable to harm. And if they were turned against the Church, they would possess no strength. For the principles of our faith <margin>Note on the principles of our faith</margin> do not depend upon man, but upon God himself; they are not grasped by the senses, nor by imagination, nor by human invention, but by divine revelation. They are not established by the sensible experiments of the arts, but by the light of faith and by wonders and miracles. Against these, neither Pyrrho <note>Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BC), the Greek philosopher credited as the founder of Scepticism.</note>, nor Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 AD), whose writings are the primary source for Greek Scepticism.</note>, nor any other philosopher could validly argue, no matter how great their genius or how heavy their abundance of learning. For so great is the force of divine truth that whatever weapons are prepared to attack it are blunted and recoil. Therefore, Sceptical consideration is not useful against our doctrine—that is, the Christian faith, which is more excellent and sublime in every way—but rather for demolishing or weakening the philosophy of the nations <note>original: "gentium philosophiam," referring to pagan or secular philosophy.</note> which was invented by human means. The goal of these Sceptics was to be in no way disturbed, which they achieved through the suspension of judgment. Indeed, they suspended judgment because of the contradictions found in opinions, in reasons, and in the diverse nature of things. They endeavored to oppose every reason with an equal reason, and they observed this in more than just one way. For they set appearances against appearances, and intellectual concepts against intellectual concepts; and conversely, they positioned the latter against the former from the opposite side. For example: the same tower is seen as round from a distance, but square when near. For both can appear true to men situated in different places. As for intellectual concepts against intellectual concepts: for example, to those who thought there was no providence because the good fared badly, it was opposed that there is a providence based on the order of the heavenly bodies, the right progression of nature, and other similar things. But against appearances they opposed intellectual concepts, after the manner of Anaxagoras <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously argued that because snow is made of dark water, it must be "black" despite appearing white.</note>; for when people said that snow appears white to the senses, he insisted that snow is frozen water, and since water is dark, snow must therefore be considered dark. They likewise opposed not only present things to present things, as in these examples we are discussing, but also present things to past or future things. Moreover, they prepared "modes"—which they also called "topics" <term>loci: traditional categories or 'places' used in logic and rhetoric to find arguments</term> and "types"—for the purpose of withholding assent due to the diversity of things, and subsequently for the purpose of contradiction. Some established more of these for themselves, others fewer. This was not only among the Sceptics themselves, but also among those numbered among the Academics <note>The "Academic Sceptics" of Plato's Academy, who were often distinguished from the "Pyrrhonian Sceptics."</note>. Cicero is the authority <margin>Cicero</margin> stating that Clitomachus wrote four books on the withholding of assent; and Aulus Gellius <margin>Gellius</margin> recorded in the tenth book of his *Memories* <note>The *Attic Nights*.</note> that Favorinus wrote ten books which he titled *Pyrrhonian Modes* <note>original: "πυρρωνίων τρόπων" (Pyrrhōniōn tropōn).</note>. But in the actual modes of restraining assent and sustaining the suspension of judgment, the Sceptics were, in my opinion, more diligent. All of these must be dealt with before their paths for removing the power of judgment are shown. For these may be regarded as the very doors of the ways, and even the keys of the Sceptics, in unblocking the doors of the philosophers.

Bury slaughtered bulls—the fact is known by sight—and from the rotting viscera, flower-bearing bees are born everywhere. Likewise, from the very ground, the warrior horse is the origin of the hornet. Similarly, from donkeys, beetles are born; from grubs, butterflies. For those wild grubs that are accustomed to weave the leaves of the forest with threads (a fact observed by farmers) change their shape into the death-bringing butterfly <note>The author uses "ferali" (deadly/funereal), perhaps referring to the "death's-head" appearance or the short life of the moth</note>. Since these things are established to rot within themselves (so to speak), what they are now is different from what they presented before by their own nature; they must display a likeness, an image, or a specter <note>Latin: *simulachrum, imaginem, spectrum*</note>, from which various and diverse phantasms <note>mental images or perceptions</note> are formed. Nevertheless, the common people will not see these as different, nor will those led by any more subtle consideration or doubt. Also, from a dead thing itself, a unique animal comes forth. If indeed there is one bird that restores itself and reseeds itself, the Assyrians call it the Phoenix. And in living beings and especially in humans, slippery worms are born <margin>Note.</margin>, nor are there physicians who lack the claim that human bodies are never empty of that "precious furniture" <note>A sarcastic or ironic reference to internal parasites</note>. For what has been omitted by the highest Creator of all things to instill modesty in the proudest animal and to force the recognition of its own humility? But of the animals born from coitus, some come forth into the light from a similar and uniform kind; others are joined and grow together from different kinds, such as mules and several of that same sort, about which Aristotle clearly discussed in his books *On the Generation of Animals*. Again, among living beings, there are those born alive, and those that lie hidden in eggs to receive life, where the heat of the sun and the mother together cherish them for some space of time. There are those that are neither brought into the light enclosed in eggs, nor break forth as living animals from a viviparous mother, but remain as an unformed little piece of flesh and are shaped by the mother's tongue, such as bears. For this is discovered and much repeated: "The cub which the bear has recently given birth to is not a cub, but poorly living flesh; the mother, by licking it, fashions it into limbs." From these principles of such diverse origins, they think it can probably be gathered that promiscuous, dissimilar, and conflicting qualities and properties flow out; and that different phantasms are formed for the bear. Animals are also reported which change their sex, as I have heard regarding hares. Certainly, Pliny reports females changed into males; and that poet sang: "And let us marvel that the hyena, which just now as a female endured the male upon her back, is now a male." Indeed, shall we not think that such great diversity of the principal parts of the body, especially in sensation, will produce for us a great diversity of either visions or phantasms? Shall we not judge it will provide great momentum both in withholding assent and in making opposition? For that animal, which is nourished by the winds and the breeze, immediately takes on whatever colors it touches, as that same ingenious poet <note>Likely referring to Ovid</note> sang. Furthermore, if we rub the eye even slightly and gently, the shapes, figures, and sizes of visible things will appear elongated and thin. Therefore, it ought to be considered highly probable that whatever animals have slanted and protruding pupils—such as goats, cats, and the like—imagine the things subjected to their senses differently. This would be much more so if they had double pupils, or a twin pupil in one eye, as Pliny reports of certain people in the seventh book of his *Natural History*. Their vision is entirely different from those endowed with a round and circular pupil. Even in mirrors, we see that if they are placed differently and arranged in various ways, they present the objects before them sometimes as small (as in concave mirrors) and sometimes as elongated and thin (as in convex mirrors). Some mirrors even show things with feet turned toward the sky and the head inclined toward the earth by a kind of trick, which otherwise stand in an upright position. Who would deny that because of these illusions of the senses, the imaginations of things vary? Whether they be men, dogs, lions, fish, elephants, or creeping things of the earth, things are seen otherwise than they truly are. I have said enough regarding sight.

<margin>**Hearing**</margin> But who has not observed the same in the remaining senses? One whose ear passages are narrow will be moved by hearing differently than one who has them wide and open. Also, sound will be presented differently to those whose ears are blocked by hair than to one whose ears are exposed. Those who lie on the ground at night receive sound differently than those who wander or walk about during the day.

<margin>**Smell**</margin> There is also great diversity in smell; for those who have a cold and are troubled by "distillations" <note>A historical medical term for mucus or catarrh</note> perceive scents differently than those who are healthy or those who abound in blood or yellow bile. Thus, what seems to smell good to one will seem foul to another.

<margin>**Taste**</margin> Is it not the same with taste? Willow leaves are bitter to men but sweet to goats; if you deny or doubt this because you have never been a goat, I know that the foolish "palingenesis" <note>The doctrine of rebirth or transmigration of souls</note> of the Pythagoreans makes you mock rather than consider it. Yet you must admit they are delighted by that bitterness, since the foliage of the willow is a most pleasing food to them, sought far and wide. Nor would the Sceptics admit the answer that it is unknown how things seem to cattle, but known that they are unpleasant to men: for either the varying temperament of the sheep and the man perceives things differently, or the goat kind is delighted by bitter things just as the human kind is by sweet. Sea water is salty and unpleasant to men, but sweet and pleasing to sea fish. But there are even among men those who are either delighted by the bitter, or find sweet what is bitter to other men. I knew those who ate dried and thickened aloe juice <note>Extremely bitter</note> just as if it were bread. 

<margin>**Albert's son**</margin> Albert, the son of Trimulus, was so delighted by a potion of rhubarb that he urged his nurse to offer it to him; nor did he seek it for the sake of expelling worms (for which reason it was first given to him). He was far from any concern for medicine, as his age did not yet allow it, but he was led by sense alone and a charming taste, though it is harsh and rejected by others. To those seized by fever and suffering from yellow bile, does not that which is sweet to others seem bitter? And wine, which is most pleasing to the healthy, is very troublesome to those inflamed with fever. This is true for almost everyone, except those who lie ill with the disease of pleurisy; for the more it brings destruction, the more it is craved. Indeed, pure wine is sometimes more pleasing to those seized by disease than to the healthy.
