# On the Diversity of Temperament

A great diversity of temperament is found among men. For there are those who, relying on a soft and well-tempered tongue and an even palate, taste well and with pleasure; there are others who, due to the roughness and hardness of the tongue and palate from their very birth, find little delight in nature. Likewise, those who possess a long throat take more pleasure <note>The author refers to the anatomical belief that a longer "path" for food increased the duration of sensory pleasure.</note>, which Aristotle condemned in the prayer of Philoxenus <note>Philoxenus of Cythera, a famous glutton, famously wished for the neck of a crane so he could enjoy the taste of food longer. Aristotle critiques this as a purely bestial desire in the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, though not correctly, as some have decided. 

And truly, since there is such great diversity of both limbs and humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term> in man, and many variations can exist in appearance, and a thousand in intensity and relaxation, countless diversities of humors can coalesce and be repeatedly transformed. 

Even from nourishment, if it be the same and uniform, various things are produced. For we observe one and the same rain sent down from heaven and received by trees, turning into leaves in some and into branches in others. So too, in us, now the blood is increased, now it is diminished; and from nourishment likewise come yellow bile, and black bile, and phlegm. I omit those things which can bring about a greater change, such as the abstemious, the drunken, and—

...men are [affected] by the sight of them, not only by eating them, which pigs pursue in order to devour. If a viper is touched by a branch of a beech tree <note>original: "phagi"</note>, it remains stunned; the same happens to an owl if it is touched by a leaf of a plane tree. The elephant flees from the ram, the lion from the farmyard cock, and both the tiger and sea monsters <note>original: "cæte," likely referring to whales or large marine creatures</note> dread the sound of drums. It would be a long task to recount what discordant things literature has handed down concerning living creatures. Let us gather only this: that diverse perceptions <note>term: phantasias — here meaning sensory impressions or mental images rather than "fantasy"</note> arise in animals, proceeding from the things presented to them. But what judgment do we have concerning them? For can we say what a thing appears to be to us when it is present? But how shall we determine what it is in its own nature? How shall we judge between our own perceptions and those of other living creatures? Since we ourselves are different from them, and are a part of that very difference. Hence we would rather need another judge, who might teach us what the difference is between us and them. From this, we can also prove the divinely revealed doctrine which was given to man as a guide while he dwells in such darkness of errors and in so great a conflict of sense and perception.

But more on this matter elsewhere. Now, a few things in passing against Aristotle, although the last three books of this work are destined for the weakening of Aristotelian doctrine. Aristotle himself, in the fourth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>, while admitting the greatest diversity in the senses of living creatures and also diverse "sensings" (if I may put it so) often in the same creature—which could be judged neither by many nor by few—nevertheless later struggles to affirm that there is a "true sense." Although we do not deny that this is so when it is not deceived and when it is not varying (as we shall dispute at length in the fifth book), we nevertheless do not admit that we can be compelled to assent by Aristotelian reasons.

These [reasons] are: that what is in motion can be perceived because it participates in boundaries—both that from which it recedes and that toward which it tends. All of this seems to increase the doubt of sensory judgment rather than remove it; for it is subject to continuous motion, and the nature of the boundaries is diverse. Nor does that other reason seem effective: that the form <note>original: "speciem"</note> of a thing remains even if the quantity is changed. For the external sense perceives neither the form of the thing, nor even properly its quantity; for the former pertains to the intellect, and the latter to the "common sense" <note>term: sensum communem — the internal faculty that integrates data from the five individual senses</note>. For the external senses dwell only upon accidents—that is, qualities—which qualities lead, perhaps from a distance, to the essence and form of the thing, or are to be apprehended by conjecture alone. And Aristotle himself, in the first book of *On the Soul*, seems openly to deny that form and substance are known entirely by the senses, when he wrote that accidents contribute in large part to the knowledge of "that which is" the essence of a thing. Furthermore, what he adds concerning the heavens does not carry much weight: because even if it is not changed...

On the second grounds for withholding assent, established from human diversity, wherein also some points are raised against Aristotle. [space] Chapter Twenty-Three.

The time has come for us to insist upon demonstrating the second point, which is taken from the diversity of human beings: from which also those things which were said against Aristotle <note>The author is likely referencing the Skeptic tradition (Sextus Empiricus) which challenged Aristotle’s reliance on universal sensory truths.</note> will be strengthened. For even if we were to willingly grant that faith should be placed in men regarding the judging of other animals, which men, I ask, shall we acquiesce to when they disagree among themselves? For since we are composed of two things, soul and body, we disagree with one another in both. For just as bodies are diverse, so are men diverse. Nor do I wish to bring up here that diversity of the human race which Pliny mentions in a long discourse in the seventh book of his *Natural History*, when he cites cannibals <note>original: "anthropophagos"</note>, Cyclopes, Laestrygonians, Shadow-foots <note>original: "sciopodas" - a mythical race of people with a single large foot used as a sunshade.</note>, snake-born men, androgynes, and even pygmies (on the authority of Aristotle). For I pass over these common tales: instead, I adopt a diversity that is either fortified by reason or reported by established and not-worn-out authors. First, let the diverse temperaments <term>temperamenta: the balance of bodily fluids or "humors" believed to determine health and personality</term> of men be considered, flowing from the diverse seed of parents, from diverse regions, from various nourishments, and from daily habit. These are the cause for diverse mental images <term>phantasmata: appearances or impressions formed in the mind via the senses</term> to be both presented and brought forth. From this also come diverse affections of the souls and diverse judgments. Scythians differ in bodily form and temperament from Ethiopians and from Indians, and those from our own people. Hence, various mixtures of humors suggest various characters, arising not only from various inclinations of the heavens <note>i.e., astrological influences or climate</note>, but from the seeds of parents; from all of which come various senses and various mental images, and from these, various opinions. Hence some desire things which are an abomination to others. Ethiopians seek black and flat-nosed wives; for the blacker and flatter-nosed they are, the more beautiful they are judged by them, on the authority of Sextus <margin>Sextus.</margin> <note>Sextus Empiricus, a Pyrrhonist philosopher who used these examples to argue for the relativity of perception.</note>; on the contrary, the Persians judge those who are fairer and with more hooked noses to be of more excellent form, while they judge those who are clearly similar to Ethiopians to be the worst. And hence many things are pleasing to many, from which others shrink away as much as possible. But if any of the physicians should bring forward species or degrees of temperament, and of a more placid and temperate inclination of the sky, to which they might attribute more reliable mental images, let them first explain—it is worth the effort—how he who has approached nearer to one of the two extremes of latitude does not differ from another who is judged closer to the other? For who could find a "point-like" <note>original: "punctalem" - meaning a perfect, singular point of ideal balance</note> temperament, so to speak? Then let them declare how individual differences do not render the judgment of the mental image in some way varied and diverse? Who is able to enumerate those things by which man differs from man? Let those things we said above come to mind: concerning Mithridates <note>The king who supposedly made himself immune to poison by taking small doses.</note>, concerning the girl nourished on poison, concerning rhubarb, and concerning the bitterness of aloe—wonderfully loathsome, which nevertheless seemed sweet bitterness to someone. The juice of aloe itself, when sent down into the stomach, is accustomed to loosen the bowels and draw out red bile, and this in most people. But I know a man, excellent in both learning and character, a physician by trade, who, if he wishes to harden and make firm a fluid and soft belly, swallows pills or "carapocia" <note>A type of medicinal pill or bolus.</note> made from aloe, which thing stops the bowels for him, while it loosens them for others. Just as there is a juice deadly to men, with which the people of Marseille used to kill criminals, and by which Socrates, the father of moral philosophy, was killed <note>The author is likely confusing hemlock with another substance or referring to a specific regional tradition.</note>

...was extinguished by the Athenians <note>Likely referring to hemlock, the state poison of Athens</note>, it was consumed without harm not by quails or starlings, but by humans. Some have tolerated four draughts. An old woman of Attica even endured thirty without any detriment to her life, according to the same sixth author <note>original: "eodem sexto Authore," likely referring to a specific book of Pliny or a similar naturalist</note>; and a certain servant of Alexander named Demophon, who presided over the tables, used to freeze in the sun and the bath, yet sweltered in the shade. And to pass over the Psylli, those peoples of Africa who do not perish when bitten by serpents and asps, Athenagoras of Argos felt no pain when struck by venomous spiders <term>phalangiis</term> <note>A type of venomous spider described by ancient naturalists</note> and scorpions. Those called the Tentyrites, inhabitants of Egypt, move among crocodiles with impunity. There is also a certain race of Ethiopians opposite Meroe, extending as far as the river Hydaspes, who eat scorpions, asps, and other creeping things of that kind without any danger; not only are they not harmed by them—which even Aristotle might admit, who writes in the eighth book of the *History of Animals* that in Pharo and other places scorpions do not sting.

A certain Ruphinus in Chalcis, having drunk hellebore <note>A toxic plant used as a purgative in antiquity</note>, was not purged in whole or in part, but as if he had taken a customary drink, he digested it and was nourished by it. Soterichus the Surgeon, whenever he smelled the fumes of a sturgeon <note>original: "siluri," likely the sheatfish or a similar large fish</note>, was troubled by bile. And (as we have done above) let us mix examples of our own time with the ancient ones. My kinsman Oliverio, Bishop of Sabina <note>original: "hofriensis," likely a corruption of Hostiensis or referring to his Neapolitan origins</note> and Cardinal of Naples, who passed away a short time ago as an old man to the great sorrow of wise men, was nearly killed every year by spring flowers (for that was said to be the cause), though others are usually greatly delighted by them. Andron the Argive persevered so well without thirst that even if he made a journey through parched Libya, he did not seek drink.

In our own town of Mirandola, there was a woman who, before she was joined to a husband, never drank water or wine. This matter should not be attributed to illness, for she enjoyed good health, had a ruddy complexion in her face, and always performed the duties of a strong woman. However, once joined to a husband and having conceived a daughter, she drank. I shall pass over those marvelous stories of virgins who in our age lived many years without food or drink, and the abstinence of a certain hermit, whom I heard had tasted nothing for nineteen years not far from Cologne; this was verified by the testimony of several soldiers who stayed in his hut for many days, sent by the bishop of the city to explore the truth of the matter. For things believed to have happened by divine miracle are not to be numbered among human examples, even if Aristotle reports there was a man who did not eat in his whole life.

I can easily return to the records of nations, which reveal many things present in men so different from others that there is always a supply of examples to oppose to the customary ones. Tiberius Caesar could see in the darkness of night; for his senses were not deceived at night when a visible object was presented, though the senses of other men were deceived. This diversity of his particular nature had placed a diversity in his visual power. A phantom of a man always stood by a certain Thasian—Aristotle is the author—yet others did not see it. Seneca also writes in the first book of *Natural Questions* that there are some who seem to encounter themselves, seeing their own image everywhere; he refers this first to ill health, and later offers this cause: that the weak power of the eyes cannot break through the air even close to them, but is resisted by it. Since, therefore, there is such great diversity inherent in human bodies, will there be a communion of phantoms and judgments in their minds? Especially if we stand by Aristotle, who determines that souls follow those things which inform the bodies. But the writings of the multitude of philosophers give us greater evidence of disagreement, especially those who profess to hand down dogmas; for they disagree about everything, and contend and battle most of all over what we ought to follow and what to avoid, choice and flight...

And since avoidance and pursuit depend largely on pleasure and pain, which are derived almost entirely from sensation and imagination—with Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotele"</note> himself agreeing that animals are governed chiefly by memories and imaginations—it follows that when they choose some things and shun others, we must believe they are not moved by these same mental images <term>phantasmatibus: mental representations or appearances</term> in the same way. Indeed, if the case were otherwise, things would be desired similarly or avoided without distinction. This provides a great opportunity for the suspension of judgment <term>assensus cohibendi: the skeptical practice of 'epoche' or withholding assent</term>, since the senses, being varied in most cases, cannot deliver a proper or pure verdict in all matters, despite what Aristotle believed. For we must either give our assent to all opinions or only to some. If we surrender to all, even when they are contrary and contradictory, we fall into absurdity; if only to some, I ask: who shall say to whom the "palm of victory" <note>original: "herba sit porrigenda," a Roman idiom for admitting defeat</note> should be given?

The Platonists will answer that we must listen to Plato; the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> will advise that we should sail with full sheets into the harbor of Aristotle’s embrace. He will refer you back to the senses; but if you think even the slightest bit of reason should be demanded from them, you will be expelled from his "Elysium." This is because, by contradicting that decree set down in his *Metaphysics*, you would be seeking a rational explanation for things of which there is no rational explanation. 

But who will satisfy the objections brought forward above? <margin>Against Aristotle.</margin> Namely, the diversity of temperament which produces differences in the senses—varying from man to man—as we shall dispute more extensively against Aristotle himself in the fifth book of this work. This is evident from the almost total natural similarity to those with jaundice <note>original: "ictericis"</note>, from those born with that disease, and from things judged to be similar yet not entirely so, from which variety arises. A much greater variety is seen in the eye due to a greater diversity of temperament than in the sensible thing seen—that is, color. According to Aristotle’s own testimony, color is composed only of two things: whiteness and blackness. It happens, therefore, that from the intensification, relaxation, and various mixing of these, almost infinite species of colors are produced. How much more, then, can the judgment of things appearing to the eyes vary based on a temperament composed of many humors and qualities? From these, diverse mental images are formed in just proportion, from which, finally, it is both certain and well-established that various judgments flow. 

But enough of Aristotle for now. If you consult other philosophers who are led by the senses, they will send you back to their masters: the Epicureans to Epicurus, affirming the prize must be given to him who (as Lucretius <note>The Roman poet and Epicurean</note> authored) "purged the breasts of men with truth-telling words." <margin>Against Lucretius.</margin> As I sing it, however, "he defiled the breasts of men with false-telling words." So too the Stoics point to Zeno, and even in our own times, different schools have different leaders to whom they decree every kind of crown. Therefore, while this perpetual litigation continues, the Sceptics say: "we shall suspend judgment." <margin>Objection.</margin>

And if someone thinks we should stand with the majority, the answer is that judgment in the matters of philosophers is not the same as in those things decided by a majority of a chapter in Canon Law <note>original: "pontificia lege"</note>, <margin>A manifold solution.</margin> or what happens by a majority vote of the people in a republic. In those cases, one can discern how many or who are being asked for their opinion. But among philosophers who speculate on the universe and the nature of things, it must not be done so. For when they differ concerning men, unless they know the specific properties of every individual, they can decree nothing exactly or beyond controversy. 

But who, I ask, knows all men across all nations and peoples? And even if he knew them, who is able to perceive what pleases each nation? For it can happen very frequently among some people what is rare among us; and conversely, those things which seem rare to us can be most frequent among other nations. Who doubts that things they perceived most clearly remain hidden from us, and things that were hidden from them are manifest to us? Indeed, many nations remained unknown, as has been made clear by the voyages that occurred in our age, <margin>Regions recently discovered.</margin> when a vast land to the west, unknown to prior centuries and filled with many peoples, was discovered by the Spanish fleet; of which...

We were once as ignorant of those inhabitants as they were of our own regions in which we dwell; and in our own age, the Portuguese sailor, relying on the southern stars, has also sailed to Ethiopia <note>The author likely refers to the circumnavigation of Africa and the voyages of Vasco da Gama</note> and penetrated as far as India, and saw Cannibals <note>original: "Anthropophagos"</note>, and learned many things which prior ages did not know. <margin>The voyage of the Portuguese.</margin> But even if it is granted that nations and peoples are known individually, is there not also such great diversity among individual men that we can gather nothing certain or universal that cannot be specifically weakened by the examples of other men? ### Concerning the third topic raised for the withholding of assent, based on the diversity of the senses, where there is also something said against Aristotle. Chapter 24.

The Sceptics devised another topic to refute the Dogmatists <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Dogmatists" refers to those who claim to possess certain knowledge, such as followers of Aristotle</note>, thinking that they act wrongly when they believe they can pass judgment on other things, however different they may be, while they themselves are tossed about in this dance of disagreeing and differing things. They say it follows that when they wish to pass judgment on those things which are seen and appear, they—before they even begin the act of judging—accept the very things under judgment as already decided. And since most people established reason in man as that to which they wished the judgment to be credited, the Sceptics contradict this and restrain their assent, placing the opposite of the third mode in the differing affections of each sensory organ. They took care to infer this: that if the senses do not correctly grasp those things which are outside us, then neither can the mind, which uses the service of the senses, grasp them. First, therefore, they demonstrate that the senses themselves differ among one another. So much so that if we follow the senses, diverse judgments are made as to whether the same thing is beneficial or harmful, or whether it pleases or displeases human nature. From this it is also gathered that we are in no way able to know the nature of any thing unless we have drawn out all its affections through each individual sense. If the elements of letters are referred to sight, some seem equal to others, some seem to sink, others to excel and stand out; but if they are referred to touch, no distinction will be recognized between them. Honey is sweet and pleasing to the taste, but placed upon the eyes it is heavy and painful; therefore, if it is asked absolutely whether honey is sweet or not, they cannot answer unless a correct distinction of the senses is first made. Fragrant ointments, and those especially made of myrrh, please when moved to the nostrils but displease the taste. Euphorbium <note>A toxic succulent plant used in medicine</note> is painful to the eyes, but not at all unpleasant to the rest of the body, by which it happens that we cannot say absolutely whether by its own nature it harms or profits human bodies. Rainwater helps the eyes but irritates the windpipe and the lung, and as it is said by the Greeks, *it makes it rough* <note>original: "τραχύνει" (trachynei)</note>. The marine torpedo fish <note>An electric ray</note> numbs the extremities of bodies when applied to them, but is harmless to the other parts. From which it happens that we are unable to state what the nature of such things is, though perhaps we can state how it appears. Indeed, whatever things are presented to us offer themselves to our senses in various ways. In an apple there is smoothness, scent, sweetness, and color; yet it is not clear or uncontroversial whether it has only these qualities, or only one within itself? For if it is referred to the senses, it will be proved to have even more qualities than those mentioned. Therefore, just as we said above regarding nourishment, it can happen that one single thing, being received diversely, produces diverse effects; so that the apple may be uniform in itself, yet appear multiform to the diverse apparatus of the external senses. But it is also possible that more qualities than those seen by us are held in the apple...

...that this is possible is proven in this manner. Let us conceive in our minds a man who, from the beginning of his nature, possessed the senses of touch, smell, and taste, but could neither hear nor see. This man would most easily believe and conceive in his mind that nothing exists from the start that is visible or audible; rather, he would think there are only those three kinds of qualities which he himself is able to draw in through those three sense organs. We, who are empowered with only five senses, try to persuade ourselves that we can only perceive those qualities for which we are capable through our sense organs; but it is also possible that other qualities may fall upon other sense organs which we ourselves do not share in. But someone will say that it was brought about by nature itself that the senses are commensurate with sensible things. <margin>Removal of an objection</margin> What indeed, say the Skeptics <note>The author refers to the Pyrrhonist tradition which questioned the possibility of certain knowledge.</note>, is this "nature"? Since such great discord and such an unjudged lawsuit still persists among the Dogmatics <note>Philosophers who assert certain doctrines as true, contrasted here with Skeptics.</note> concerning nature itself. For he who judges whether this very thing is "nature" is either unlearned—and through this he will not be trusted—or he is a philosopher, and thus, since he is a party to the case and has an adversary in the lawsuit, the judgment shall not be handed over to him, inasmuch as he ought to be judged, not to judge. Likewise, who knows that there are not more than five senses? <margin>Discord concerning the number of senses: Democritus, Plutarch.</margin> They will respond that this is asserted by the philosophers: I shall also bring forward philosophers who prefer more. For Democritus did not think there were only so many, as we have said before; and Plutarch also, in his *Natural Opinions* <note>Original: "placitis naturalibus," referring to the *Placita Philosophorum* attributed to Plutarch.</note>, reports that there are not as many senses in man as are said to be held, but he thought that more are present in both the Gods and other irrational living beings and wise men than are established by us. To this can be added the testimony of Simplicius the Peripatetic <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his third commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, <margin>Simplicius.</margin> where he does not entirely deny that sense can in some way be attributed to the celestial bodies, provided it is different from the way in which we and other mortals perceive; in like manner, he does not entirely eliminate imagination from them, nor does he contend that sense cannot be attributed to plants, though it be more obscure and, as Plato says, "sleeping." John the Grammarian <note>Also known as John Philoponus.</note> also, <margin>John the Grammarian, author of the commentary on the third book of Aristotle's *On the Soul*.</margin> among some Platonists and Peripatetics debating the sensation of celestial bodies, was unwilling to settle the dispute; concerning which matter we have discoursed at length in our own commentaries on the third book of Aristotle’s *On the Soul*. Thus, the disagreement concerning all the senses causes the judgment of the mind to waver as well; nor ought we to judge that those things which we ourselves least know do not exist in the nature of things. Lorenzo Valla, <margin>Lorenzo Valla.</margin> whose opinions in his *Logical Institutions* we have often refuted, was a noble grammarian and almost the avenger of the now-faded Roman tongue. But when he heard something being said which he himself had either not read or did not remember reading, he almost immediately thought it was not Latin; <margin>Note.</margin> nevertheless, those who afterwards examined the writings of ancient authors more diligently found to be Latin those things which he had set aside as barbaric. So too, it is necessary for wise evaluators of things to abstain from headlong judgment, and they ought not to affirm that what they themselves do not know is unknown to others, or immediately expel from the nature of things those matters of which they have never heard mention made. Thus also Aristotle devised only some modes by which the judgment of the sense could be deceived, <margin>Against Aristotle.</margin> thinking they could err in no other way. We, however, have said that there are as many modes or species of the sense itself as there are temperaments of men, and in the fifth book of this work we shall prove more exactly that a certain rule for judging a sensible thing can hardly be drawn. Indeed, we shall show in that same fifth volume of this work that the judgment of the sense is also uncertain for the most part by its own rules. Nor does Nicholas of Cusa <margin>Nicholas of Cusa.</margin> seem to have shrunk far from a difficulty of this kind, when he said that the sense does not judge except "sensibly," and reason except "rationally," so that for that reason he thought it always judged otherwise than the thing is—that is, by conjecture—if it should ascend to examining those things which belong to the mind, in the way he affirms that reason judges two and three, and five.

### Chapter XXV. On the fourth mode of restraining assent, which is drawn from circumstances or dispositions.

<note>The "modes" or tropes are classical Sceptic arguments used to show that certain knowledge is impossible, leading to a suspension of belief (epoché).</note>

The fourth mode is established in circumstances, which are also called "dispositions" by the Sceptics. They contemplate this very mode in that which is either according to or contrary to nature: in the state of sleeping or being awake, and in the state of being in motion or at rest. To these are added being a child, a youth, a young man, or an old man; likewise loving, hating, needing food, being full, being heavy with drunkenness, or being vigorous in sobriety. Furthermore, not only the dispositions themselves, but the causes that preceded them must be weighed; for it is necessary to take into account both boldness and fear, and to remember both sadness and joy. And so that we may repeat and explain each point in a fitting order from the beginning of these things we have reported: unequal images of things strike those men who are moved according to nature and those who are moved contrary to nature. For to the frenzied and to all those captured in mind <note>i.e., the mentally ill or delirious</note>, many things seem to be heard, or seen, or tasted, or smelled, or touched, which do not appear so to the healthy. Furthermore, some are so affected that they say they are seized by the scent of storax or frankincense, which others do not perceive. The same water poured on inflamed areas will seem to boil to one person, but to others it will seem cold. The same garment will be judged red by one who suffers from the disease which <margin>Concerning the healthy and the sick.</margin> the Greeks call *ikteros* <note>original: ἴκτερον; jaundice</note>, but to us it will appear otherwise. The same honey seems sweet to me, but bitter to those with jaundice; to others, neither this nor that—a matter discussed more extensively in the fifth book.

<margin>Response. Refutation.</margin> Now, if anyone should say that the cause is a mixture of humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</note>, so that dissimilar phantasms appear to those acting contrary to nature from the underlying objects, let him first know and learn that those who are considered healthy do not always possess a perfect balance of humors. Therefore, it is possible that both external things and those which are "according to nature" are actually such as they appear to those said to be "contrary to nature," and appear entirely different from their own nature to those who are healthy. For to say that poorly mixed and wrongly tempered humors give the power of varying the images of underlying things, but that those who are differently composed from a "bad" disposition do not, they say is seen as entirely fictitious and vain. For just as the healthy possess by their own nature what belongs to a healthy man, but find what belongs to the sick to be contrary to nature, so also the sick possess by their own nature what belongs to the sick, but find what belongs to the healthy to be contrary to nature.

<margin>Concerning those sleeping and waking.</margin> Likewise, different images are produced by waking and sleep, since phantasms are not presented during rest in the same way as when we are awake, nor vice versa. Therefore, it is fitting to measure these imaginations not absolutely, but as related either to sleep or to waking. Thus, the things that become present in dreams do not persist in waking; and let the order be reversed: when waking phantasies are abolished by succeeding sleepy ones, which are so varied that they cannot be distinguished in sleep itself, since we even dream that we are awake, and we even reason in our dreams that we are not sleeping but waking.

BOOK TWO [space] 58

If it lacks a demonstration, how can it be worthy of our agreement? But if he prepares a demonstration, it must be true, otherwise persuasion will not arise from a falsehood; for a false demonstration is not even worthy of the name, let alone capable of creating any certainty in itself. He will therefore say that the demonstration is true so that it may be believed. But how is this done? By a judgment or not? For if he has not previously judged that very demonstration and found it to be true, will he be worthy of persuading us with it? But if he has weighed and judged it beforehand, he will clearly say he used a criterion of judgment <note>Latin: *iudicatorium*, referring to the standard or instrument by which truth is measured</note>, yet we are seeking a demonstration for that very criterion, and we also demand a criterion for that demonstration. Thus, they say there will always be a need for the demonstration to be confirmed by a criterion, and the criterion by a demonstration, to show that it is true. But they maintain it is impossible for a sound demonstration to be established if some true criterion does not exist, nor can a criterion judge what is true unless a demonstration has been previously provided. Thus, a fall and a slip occur in the manner of what is commonly called a "circular argument" <note>original: *promiscuus*, here referring to the *circulus vitiosus* or circular reasoning</note>, when one proves the one by the other, and again the other by the one; the matter itself is led in a long circle and ends in frustration. For if there were a demonstration of a demonstration, its principle would go on to infinity, and Aristotle teaches in the *Posterior Analytics* and in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* that this ought not even to be sought. If, however, it is prepared without a demonstration, one must rely on a simple assertion, which is not believed. But if the matter is resolved by the judgment of the senses, it has already been sufficiently shown above that this is weak and deceptive. But now the consideration of the fifth "mode" <note>The "modes" or *tropes* are the classical arguments used by Skeptics to justify the suspension of judgment</note> demands our attention.

¶ Concerning the fifth mode prepared for the convenience of withholding assent, drawn from the location of things and explained by distance. Chapter Twenty-Six.

Things appear differently than they actually are because of their location, their various positions, and the distance of the places in which they are situated. The same portico, if viewed from one end, will be perceived by the sight differently than if it is viewed from the middle. The same ship, if seen from afar, will appear both small and stationary; if near, it will appear large and agitated by motion. The same tower seen from a distance will be believed to be round, but square when close by. From a different position, too, the face of things changes: the light of a lamp placed in the sun appears dim, but in the dark it is brilliant. The same oar in the sea will appear broken and curved, but on land whole and straight. The same egg is tender and soft inside the bird, but hard in the air; the urine of a lynx <note>A common medieval and classical myth that lynx urine hardens into a gemstone called *lyngurium*</note> is liquid in the animal, but in the air it becomes so dry that it turns into stone. Coral also, as we have said, we see among us as something hard and stony, and yet it is well known that it lay hidden beneath the waves as a soft plant. The same human voice will be perceived differently if poured out through the mouth, through a pipe <note>original: *siringam*, a panpipe or syringe-like tube</note>, or through a flute. The same image, if lying flat, will appear level, but if the back is turned, parts of it will seem to project and others to sink. Even the necks of doves will appear to have different colors from different positions. Since, therefore, whatever is seen must be seen in some place, and at some interval, and according to some position or site—each of which brings a different change to the imagination and appearance—it follows that one happens to rein in assent and restrain the headlong rashness of the mind in delivering a judgment. For whoever wishes to judge some imaginations or appearances and distinguish one from another will do so either without a demonstration, by a simple affirmation of words (in which case he will not be believed), or he will employ a demonstration. If the latter, he will either bring forward a false demonstration, and then he will claim less credibility for himself, or a true one, and then for the construction of this truth there will be need of a demonstration, and for the confirmation of this...

### Concerning the sixth and seventh modes prepared for leading men away from judgment: of which one is established from mixture, the other from quantity and composition. Chapter XXVII.

**A**bstaining likewise from judging what things are and of what sort they are, the Sceptics warned that we ought to do so for many reasons; and from this they prepared the **sixth mode**: because none of those things which lie outside ever strike our senses alone and pure, but always mixed with something. Therefore, they say, perhaps one could say what the nature of the mixture is—both of the thing placed outside and of that through which we observe it—but we are by no means able to clearly assert what the thing itself is, which is located externally. From this it happens that it always appears to us differently than it actually is. For our own color, to begin with sight, appears one way in warm air and another way in cold; therefore we cannot say what our color truly is, but only what sort...

SECOND [BOOK]                                                                                                                             LIX

<meta>Continuing the discussion of the Ten Modes of Scepticism, specifically the seventh mode concerning quantities and compositions of substances.</meta>

they argued that [appearances] arise from the quantity and preparation or composition of a thing. For they claim that regarding the quantities of things and the compositions of their preparation, it happens that the very things which lie externally as subjects become so confused that they cannot be clearly perceived. For example, if the shavings scraped from a goat's horn are viewed by themselves as tiny scrapings, they will appear white; yet in the horn itself, where they are grown and embedded, they appear entirely black. Likewise, silver filings, which have been finely filed away, appear black when viewed separately, but if they are considered in the whole mass, they will appear otherwise, for they will seem white. So too, many will think that fragments of Taenarian stone <note>A famous black or dark marble from Cape Taenarum in Greece.</note>, if discerned by themselves, are bathed in whiteness; yet viewed in the intact marble, they will appear yellow. Even grains of sand, if handled separately, feel rough, but if touched together when gathered into a heap, they will be felt as smooth to the touch. Even Hellebore, if taken when it is fine, budding, and covered in down, [causes] suffocation, but [acts] in another way [if prepared differently]. Wine, if taken in moderation, strengthens the powers; if moderation is lacking, it dissolves the body. Even the quantity of food brings forth diverse effects: for if we are filled with too much of it, it weakens us and oppresses us with indigestion and almost infinite other diseases; if taken moderately, both life and health are preserved. Therefore, in all these things, how shall judgment be firm? For we can say, if we look to quantity and composition, what sort of things they *appear* to be; but what they are in truth or what they are like in their own nature, how [can we say]? Namely, because of the diverse fantasies or appearances which spring from diverse quantities and compositions. Does it not also appear universally that things which would help by themselves, harm because of excessive quantity, and conversely, things which would harm, do no damage in the smallest quantity? The medicines of the medical art also bear witness, which if prepared rightly are one thing and produce certain effects, but are different if not so treated. If they are mixed correctly and exactly, that which is compounded and forged from them helps; if diligence is neglected, it will sometimes turn out no longer useful, but harmful and destructive.

->**On the eighth mode, which concerns relativity, in which something is said against the Sceptics.**<-
->**Many things [are said] in their favor. Chapter XXIV.**<-

So they also taught that the greatest diligence must be applied so that relation—or that which is usually called "relative to something"—is always considered. By this they wish it to happen that a way is always provided for us to abstain and to withhold assent. For they write that we can always say what sort of thing a matter appears to be in that which is referred, or said to be referred, to something; but what sort of thing it is in itself and in its own nature, we can by no means set forth clearly and openly. Moreover, they wish all things to be "relative," and they take this in a twofold sense; they use the word "to be" itself, both in this matter and in others, by a certain misuse for that which is "to appear." For they do not affirm that anything *is* or *is not*, but that it *appears*; and they inquire, consider, and weigh what it might be. Therefore, the Sceptics do not take this which we call "relative" in those modes properly and significantly as the dialecticians, philosophers, and younger theologians following Aristotle are accustomed to do, and concerning which we have discussed abundantly (unless I am mistaken) in the second book of the *Institutions of Logic*: <margin>The Author's *Institutions of Logic*</margin> unless perhaps insofar as relation defines the order of one thing to another. But they proceed by a different path, and the "relative" itself, as we said, is taken by them in two ways: for first, they refer that which is judged to the one judging, for the thing which is the external subject and is judged appears so to the one judging. Second, they refer those things which we contemplate together, such as the right to the left. Therefore, they prove that all things are relative, either according to that which judges—since the things themselves will appear so to this animal, and to this man, and to this sense, and according to this or that circumstance—or according to those things which [are contemplated] together...

**BOOK 2**

We observe things as they appear specifically in this mixture, in this manner, in this composition, in this quantity, and in this position. Furthermore, they attempt to conclude more specifically that all things are "relative" <note>Latin: *ad aliquid*; a technical term in logic referring to things that exist only in relation to something else</note> in this way: either those things which are described as distinct by way of difference differ from things that are relative, or they do not differ. If they do not differ, then they themselves are relative; but if they do differ, since everything that differs is relative (for it is spoken of in relation to that from which it differs), then even those things said to differ from relative things are themselves relative. In addition to these points, among all things that exist, some are "supreme genera" <note>The highest, most general categories of being</note> according to the opinion of the dogmatic philosophers, others are "ultimate species," and others are both genera and species; yet all of these are relative, therefore all things are relative. Again, of all things that exist, some are manifest <note>Evident to the senses</note> and others are hidden; some are signifying and others are signified; but that which signifies and that which is signified are relative, therefore all things are relative. It follows that of all things that exist, some are similar and others are dissimilar, and these indeed are—

**BOOK TWO [space] 60**

The sea, at first sight, strikes those watching it with a sense of wonder. It terrifies those who are not so experienced or skilled, being unaccustomed and raw to such a sight. The beauty and exceptional form of the human body, presenting itself suddenly and unexpectedly to the eyes, moves one more than those things which are accustomed to delight the sight. For things that are rare and precious are usually more pleasing. Indeed, if we very rarely beheld water, given for so many human uses, and if we most infrequently contemplated that silvery brightness of hers, so suited to delighting the eyes, we would easily be compelled to chime in with Pindar when he sings: <note>original: "ἄριστόν μέν ὕδωρ"</note> *Water is best.* On the other hand, if it were granted to possess gold most frequently and at will, as something found everywhere among discarded stones and rubble, we would not agree with the same poet when he sings: <note>original: "ὁ δέ χρυσός"</note> *But gold [is like a blazing fire]...* and what follows. By these things we are reminded that we can only state how a thing appears to us based on its rarity or frequency; however, we cannot say what that thing is in itself—whether it is precious in its own essence or a natural arouser of admiration.

To this very point, the tenth "mode" <note>The "modes" or "tropes" were ten arguments used by ancient Sceptics to induce a state of suspended judgment.</note> is attached by the older Sceptics, which also partakes in this idea of <margin>The tenth mode.</margin> frequency and infrequency, but which inclines more toward active rather than contemplative philosophy. For it gathers evidence concerning the choice and institution of life, customs, laws, legendary beliefs, and the opinions of philosophers. They used to oppose each of these either to itself or to another; for example, they compared customs to customs in this manner: the Ethiopians brand marks upon infants, but we do not; and the Persians indeed think it decorous and dignified to use floor-length and embroidered garments, while we consider it both indecorous and frivolous. The Indians also couple with women in public, whereas most people consider that custom both shameful and obscene.

They opposed law to law in this way: among the Taurians <note>An ancient people of the Crimean Peninsula.</note> the law was to slaughter guests in the sacrifices of Diana; among us, the law is that a man who has fled to a sacred place, even if guilty, shall go free in safety. Among the Romans, it was provided by law that no son who had surrendered his father's goods could be compelled to pay his father's creditors; among the Rhodians, even he who had renounced his father's estate was held liable for his father's debts.

They opposed choices and institutions of life to other institutions, such as if one were to oppose what Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, known for extreme poverty and social defiance.</note> had decreed to the decrees of Aristippus <note>A philosopher who advocated for seeking pleasure.</note>. Or if one set the decrees of the Spartans against the decrees of the Italians. They placed legendary beliefs in opposition to others in the same way: they told the tale that Jove was the father of both men and gods; yet they also told the tale that <margin>The author's declaration on the Homeric poem. Alexander of Aphrodisias.</margin> Oceanus was the God of origin and Tethys the parent—a Homeric poem which is not, I think, sufficiently known to everyone, and upon which even philosophers do not agree. For who would not think that Homer says water is the principle of all things, since by the names of Oceanus and Tethys he affirms water to be the parent of things on both sides?

But Alexander of Aphrodisias, in his commentaries on the *Metaphysics* of Aristotle (allow me, both now and hereafter, as I think has been allowed before, to use certain terms already accepted among the modern philosophers), in his commentaries on the *Metaphysics* or "First Philosophy," Alexander explains Tethys as the Earth, which is like a <term>titha</term> <note>From the Greek 'tithe', meaning a nurse or wet-nurse.</note>, that is, the nurse of corruptible things. So too among the Platonists, "prime matter" is also called "nurse" and "mother," as is easily seen in Alcinous <margin>Alcinous the Platonist.</margin> who reviews her titles.

Furthermore, they managed the opinions of philosophers so that they resisted one another; as if one were to say there is only one element, by the authority of many philosophers, while another said many were established by others, and some even said they were infinite. It was no different regarding the soul, which some proved immortal, while others said it was mortal. And so it goes with the remaining topics usually treated in philosophy. Finally, they opposed customs to laws in this way: the Persians were accustomed to abuse boys, but...

However, Roman law has taken precautions so that this does not happen. Among us, adultery is likewise forbidden; yet among the Massagetae <note>An ancient nomadic confederation in Central Asia</note>, if we agree with Eudoxus of Cnidus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note>, the custom is treated with indifference. Among us, laws likewise prohibit sons or brothers from being joined in marriage to their mothers or sisters. Yet it was the custom in Persia for mothers to marry sons, and the custom in Egypt for sisters to marry brothers. Customs were opposed to established institutions in this manner: it is a human institution and a consensus of nations that when men wish to have intimate knowledge of their wives, they seek out more private places out of a sense of shame. <margin>Augustine</margin> And our own Augustine, in his books *On the City of God*, relates that this was received as a consequence of the sin of our first parent <note>Referring to Adam and the Fall of Man</note>. However, it was the custom of Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a Cynic philosopher</note> to couple openly with his wife Hipparchia; she, being a Cynic philosopher herself, did not blush at this. The first mode is therefore established from the disagreement among authors. For when a matter is proposed for discussion, we find such great diversity and such great dispute concerning it—always debated and never settled—that since it is not sufficiently clear what should be chosen and what should be rejected, we abstain and suspend our judgment. <margin>First mode</margin> <note>The "modes" or "tropes" are formal arguments used by ancient Skeptics to show that certainty is impossible.</note>

The second mode is established by the fact that the clarity of proof runs on into infinity. For whatever is brought forward as proof for something else requires its own proof, and that in turn requires another, and this happens so frequently that no discourse can find a certain end. <margin>Second.</margin> For in the end, one recurs to the senses, which have been shown in many ways to be deceptive; for humanly speaking, no principle can be given that either is, or is held by all to be, beyond controversy.

The third mode is supported by relation, when—either from the perspective of the one who judges, or from the perspective of the things being considered together—it can be said what the thing under scrutiny and subject to debate appears to be to me, but what it truly is in its essence remains unknown. <margin>Third.</margin>

It is clear, therefore, and should be held as beyond controversy, that whatever disagreement regarding a **sensible object** <note>A thing perceived through the physical senses like sight or touch.</note> is presented to us, we are able to reduce it to these five modes. And if the matter concerns an **intelligible thing** <note>A concept understood by the mind or intellect rather than the senses.</note>, and we wish to weigh the business carefully, it will easily be established that whatever it may be, it can be referred to these same modes. For if it is said that there is a controversy regarding that very thing, whatever its nature, which has neither been decided nor can easily be decided, then the permission to **abstain from judgment** <note>original: "abstinendi"; the skeptical practice of Epoché, or withholding assent.</note> will be granted to us, even if we do not ask for it. 

If, however, someone decrees that it can be judged, and attempts to achieve this, he will either provide proof by means of another intelligible thing—from which he will slip into an **infinite proof** <note>The "infinite regress" where every proof requires a new proof, never reaching a foundation.</note>—or by means of some sensible thing, which will result in him falling back into the **reciprocal mode** <note>original: "praemiscum locum"; likely referring to the circular reasoning where the sense proves the intellect and the intellect proves the sense.</note>. For that very sensible thing which he wished to use as a witness is itself ambiguous.

They have striven to demolish the definition of man, adding this further point: those things which fortify a definition are understood either in act <note>original: *actu*; referring to something currently happening or fully realized</note> or in potential <note>original: *potestate*; the capacity to become something</note>. If not in act, does it not follow that he who has not attained perfect learning is not a man? And that he who does not excel in perfect reason, and is subject to the very state of dying, is not a man? For this is that *mortal* <note>original: θνητόν (*thneton*)</note> which the Latins translated as *mortale*. But if it is by potential and not by act, then he who possesses perfect reason, and excels in intellect and knowledge, will no longer be a man—which is even more absurd than the previous disadvantage. For they were taking that potentiality only by itself, and the Act also by itself. Furthermore, when we say that anything is susceptible to a certain thing, we do not thereby declare its essence; for we judge nothing more regarding what the thing itself is, as far as its own nature is concerned. But Plato, who had devised that famous definition of his—*a wingless, bipedal animal with broad nails, susceptible to knowledge*—is rejected by these same thinkers. <margin>Other arguments of the Sceptics against the definition of man.</margin> Beyond this, they say he did not speak firmly and consistently regarding the definition of man, but rather used a certain probable manner of speaking. For if he had believed he had established this consistently, they say he would have wandered far astray. For even if they say man can be thought of, he cannot, however, be grasped <note>original: *compræhendi*; to be fully understood or perceived by the mind</note>. For the Dogmatists <note>Philosophers who claim to have found the truth, as opposed to Sceptics</note> constitute him from soul and body; if neither of these is graspable, then man, who is fused from both, will not be grasped either. <margin>The Sceptics' argument against the definition of man brought by Plato.</margin> That the body cannot be grasped, they argue thus: those things which are accidental to something are different from that to which they are accidental. Whenever, therefore, either color or something similar is presented to us, it is consistent that the accidents of the body are presented to us, not the body itself, which they say is composed of a triple dimension. <margin>The Sceptics' argument that the body cannot be grasped.</margin> We ought, therefore, to have grasped length, breadth, and depth, if we could rightly affirm that the body is grasped by us. Since, however, we cannot do that, and it is necessary to dwell upon those accidents, it will surely happen that he who contends that the body is correctly discerned by us from them acts no differently than one who would say that from the color of gold itself, a silver vessel smeared with gold could be judged to be gold and not silver. Yet that can by no means happen; wherefore, if we cannot discern a golden vessel from a silver one that is gilded by those accidents, so also they will not judge other bodies by their accidents. I add that point brought forth by Aristotle in the first book of *On the Soul*: the accidents of a thing do not declare its essence, yet they contribute in large part to knowing what the thing itself is. As if he were saying—if we think he felt correctly—that a handle for investigating and conjecturing the substance is offered to us from the knowledge of accidents; and this is as far as it pertains to the body of man, and as far as the present business is concerned. But as for the soul? In what way shall it be grasped? <margin>What the Sceptics argue against the grasping of the soul.</margin> Which some have said does not exist, such as Dicaearchus the Peripatetic and his followers; others say it does exist; others refrain from both affirming and denying. If the Dogmatic philosophers think this disagreement cannot be decided, they will consequently think it cannot be grasped; if they contend it is decidable, in what way can that be done? Let them show us. By sense? Not at all, since they say it is intelligible <note>perceivable only by the mind, not the senses</note>. But if they prefer it to be decided by the mind and intellect, they will say (the Sceptics say) that nothing in the soul is more controversial than the mind, since many who think the soul exists harmoniously are not in agreement regarding the mind itself. And if they wish to grasp the soul by the mind, they will also wish to decide the discord about the mind itself, and thus try to determine and strengthen that which is more sought after by that which is less sought after, which is absurd. But indeed, even if we grant (they say) that man is graspable by the mind, it does not therefore follow that things ought to be judged by him. For he who attributes judgment to him will either use a demonstration to affirm it...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of Christian doctrine against Sceptical arguments, specifically addressing the reliability of human judgment and the authority of Plato.</meta>

SECOND [BOOK]                                                                                              LXV

<margin>**Note.**</margin> These matters are argued most fiercely and subtly by the Sceptics. Even if these arguments might hinder Plato—who judged that he should stand by his positions only insofar as he, being a somewhat more sacred man, had decreed something else, by which he seemed to judge himself superior to all men—they do not, however, hinder us. For we do not say that men have manifested the truth to us, but God, the wisest of all, the fountain of all knowledge and (if I may put it this way) Truth itself. In Him we have faith; in Him we believe; and we grant our assent to all those who have drawn from Him what they have poured out into us: namely, the most soul-healing <term>dogmata</term> <note>original: "dogmatica"; here referring to established religious doctrines or principles</note> for attaining a happy life.

<margin>**For Plato.**</margin> Those who love Plato more dearly could excuse him from arrogance by this one fact: that he was in Egypt and learned divine things; therefore, he thought that what he had drawn from divine writings should take precedence over all human inventions. <margin>**Something also in Plato.**</margin> But whatever may be decided on this matter, I certainly affirm this: those things were not entirely and sincerely divine, but in many places less than human, and infected by the perverse superstitions of a malignant demon.

But let us return to the Sceptics, adding this to the previous points: even if they were to grant their adversaries that some wise man is wiser than another, and that such a man exists, has existed, or will exist, they still will not grant that one must therefore "descend with hands and feet" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to support a motion or opinion with total enthusiasm or by a formal vote.</note> into his opinion. This is because wise men, as they are called and held to be, are never without an ambition for honors; they are accustomed to give authority to trivial things just to show off their own cleverness. Therefore, we shall not hold the judgment he has made of things to be any more sound than any other, since it cannot be certain to us whether things are so by their own nature, or whether they only first attained that estimation through the judgment of that "wise" man.

Furthermore, if some were to go so far as to say that judgment ought to be handed over to the consensus of the majority, one can easily weigh from the following how vain that is. First, truth is perhaps found only rarely; therefore, it is possible that one man may be wiser in perceiving it than many. Secondly, in every court of judgment, more people will stand against those who agree with one another. For those who abandon any particular judgment will bring forward another that seems to agree with them, and they will oppose the multitude with their own.

To this, those who come together into one agreement are either affected by different dispositions in that matter, or by one and the same. If by different ones, they will by no means come together into one and the same judgment at all. If by one—since both the one who brings a different view has one disposition and habit, and those who come together also have one—then, as far as it pertains to that by which we say judgment is brought by God, no difference is found in the multitude itself regarding the disposition itself. From this, it follows that it is not necessary for us to have faith in the many rather than in the one.

The multitude of disagreeing judgments is also incomprehensible, since we can grasp particular men in no fixed number, nor run through their individual differences. From this, it is also gathered that we cannot discern toward which side the majority inclines. Therefore, they wish to conclude from all this that a judgment based on a multitude of judges is vain if it is referred to the nature and universality of men—which, of course, cannot be grasped by man. And if we are not to rest even in the multitude, we shall find no one at all from whom a judgment of things may be safely brought. And from this, they deduce that the knowledge of truth is "hardly graspable," if the one by whom it is said to be graspable cannot be grasped at all.

But even if all these things (they say) about which controversies have been raised were granted freely and peacefully to our adversaries, they would still not possess the means by which they could safely and securely pass judgment on matters. If, however, these things are not granted at all, then everything will be immediately undermined, since everything else is either a part, a state, or an action of a human being. it would be necessary to ascend to the understanding. However, because the function of the mind itself is not sufficient for finding and judging the truth, the Pyrrhonists <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis, the founder of Greek Skepticism, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> have brought many arguments into the open. For they say the mind is difficult to grasp, since Gorgias <margin>Gorgias.</margin> <note>A famous Greek Sophist and rhetorician.</note> decreed that the mind itself is nothing, and Dicaearchus <margin>Dicaearchus.</margin> <note>A student of Aristotle who argued that the soul or mind does not exist as a separate entity from the body.</note> even did away with the soul. Others, on the contrary, ask: who then shall settle the dispute? For it cannot be settled by the mind acting as an intermediary. For they would be assuming the very thing that is under question. And what other thing, I ask, will they take up by which a distinction might be made? Therefore, it remains a matter of controversy whether the intellect exists or not. But even if it were granted and held as clear that the mind exists, a judgment concerning things still could not be rendered. For if the mind does not even perceive itself exactly, but a dispute is waged over its very essence, its origins, and the place in which it resides, in what way will it be able to diligently apprehend anything else? They say it is certainly necessary first to know what the mind itself is and how true it is, if it is to be held as the rule of truth itself. And it must first know itself to be the rule of truth before it judges the truth, just as an architect distinguishes the straight from the crooked only after the carpenter's rule is known. What, then, is the mind itself? Philosophers have not yet agreed. For Dicaearchus, as was mentioned, said it was nothing else but, in a certain way, the body. Others have said it exists, yet is not contained by the body itself; of these, some—like Aenesidemus <margin>Aenesidemus.</margin> <note>A Skeptic philosopher who revived Pyrrhonism.</note> following Heraclitus—have thought it to be outside the body. Others say it is in the whole body, as some followers of Democritus do; others say it is in a part of the body, and among these there are also manifold and various opinions. For some thought it differs from the senses, while others thought it was the same as the senses, as if falling through certain locations of the sensory organs; of this disagreement both Strato the physicist and Aenesidemus stood as leaders. Furthermore, if it is established that the mind is the judge of things, since there is such a great and manifold difference between minds, in what way shall we judge by means of it? For the mind, or thought, or opinion, or notion of Gorgias is one thing—for so I might easily call that which the Greeks call *dianoian* <note>original: "διάνοιαν" - meaning thought, intellect, or the capacity for discursive reasoning.</note> as I said a little while ago—the mind of Gorgias, I say, is one thing, according to which he says nothing exists. The mind of Heraclitus is another, according to which he says all things exist. In what way, therefore, shall we judge this very difference of minds by the mind? For we shall not be able to say rightly that this mind must be approached, that one departed from, or that we must stand with this one against that one. For if we should dare to render a judgment by some mind, by taking a side in the discord, we have seized upon the very thing that was being questioned: that which had been denied at the start and brought into controversy as ambiguous, we have taken as confessed and certain. Aristotle does not admit this mode of arguing. But if we settle the dispute by something else which is not the mind, we shall be found deceptive, since we have already ordained that things ought to be measured by the mind alone. And indeed, from those things said above concerning the "criterion" <note>The standard or tool for judging truth.</note> to which the name "in which" has been given, they believe they can show that we will not be able to find any mind more skillful or superior to others in judging; and even if some more skillful mind were found than all others that have been in the past or are at the present time, since it is not manifest whether there might be some more skillful mind in the future, it would by no means be proper to yield to that one. But if we should establish a mind most skillful of all and most subtle, which excels all others in its discourse, shall we then yield to it, and are we to commit ourselves securely to its judgment? For there is a danger that it might be deceived by the excessive speed of the mind, mixing in something false, which nevertheless it might persuade us is true by that extraordinary sharpness; and I will add that it is possible for it to change its opinion for various reasons. It remains for them to say that judgment is made by both, that is, by sense and mind. This can likewise be refuted without much labor. For the senses themselves do not precede the mind and lead it by the hand, as it were, to the comprehension of the truth, but they themselves are frequently opposed to it. Certainly honey seems sweet to some, but bitter to others. I add that it does not seem sweet to those who are unwell.

It argues that if the mind cannot understand its own essence or location, it cannot be trusted to judge external reality or resolve contradictions between different philosophical schools.</summary>

BOOK 32

<margin>How great is the disagreement regarding tastes.</margin>
As we have said before, honey appears bitter only to those suffering from jaundice. We do not here bring forward the honey of Colchis <note>A region on the Black Sea, famous in antiquity for "mad honey" that caused hallucinations.</note> which is reported to be steeped in bitterness, nor Sardinian honey which is said to be spread with a harshness as if tainted by wormwood; nor even the Pontic variety which, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40-90 AD) whose work was the primary text on pharmacology for 1,500 years.</note>, is most deadly in certain years. For such honey ought not to seem sweet even to healthy people, since they have experienced it to be bitter, harsh, and ruinous. But we are speaking of the honey of other regions—of Asia, Greece, and Sicily—which everyone pronounces sweet upon tasting, yet others have judged differently and claimed to perceive the honey itself in a diverse manner, according to Sextus <note>Likely Sextus Empiricus, a physician and philosopher who recorded the arguments of the Skeptics.</note>.

<margin>Democritus and Heraclitus on honey.</margin>
Democritus said it was neither sweet nor bitter; Heraclitus said it was both sweet and bitter. And regarding the other senses and other sensible objects, the judgment is the same. Thus, the thought and opinion of the mind proceeding from the senses is forced to decree diverse and clashing things, which is entirely foreign to a proper judicial faculty. Indeed, it can be seen how the senses hinder the judgment of the mind; for just as if a body falls between the sight and the object seen, it will not allow the sight to comprehend the visible thing, so if the sight—which is itself without mind—intercedes between the notion of the mind and the object lying outside, it will not permit the notion of the external object to be perceived. And so it is with the other senses which are neither internal nor endowed with reason, such as taste, hearing, and the rest. Therefore, the mind placed within and overshadowed by the senses will be unable to deliver a correct opinion on things placed outside. This becomes even more evident if we notice that things are not presented to the mind for inspection except through the service of the senses, which report only their own affection or passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the way a sense organ is "acted upon" or affected by an external stimulus.</note>. For example, the touch heated by fire does not present "fire" to the mind, but rather the present sensation of heating, of which it is properly the master; the mind is not. Otherwise, the mind would not be distinguished from the sense if it were moved in a sensory way.

Therefore, the apprehension of a thing through the sense is different from the thing itself, and much more so is the notion of the thing itself conceived by the mind, even if it is claimed to be similar. For who does not know that the notion of a sensible thing differs greatly from the thing itself? For the notion of fire does not burn, but fire burns. Therefore, how do we grasp that fire is burning from the mere notion of it? And a whip inflicted upon the flesh affects the flesh with pain, yet the whip itself is not pain, nor does pain dwell within it. In the same way, if honey affects the sense with sweetness, wormwood with bitterness, and fire with heat, you cannot pronounce beyond controversy that fire is hot, honey sweet, or wormwood bitter.

<margin>The authority of the Skeptics.</margin>
Just as you might think or assert—following the authority of Aristotle and the agreement of the entire Lyceum <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle in Athens.</note>—that the sun is falsely called "hot," yet you will correctly say and feel that you are being warmed by it. I have brought forward this very example which seems to support the Skeptics. Therefore, if you pronounce such things to be so, you pronounce by conjecture based on a perceived similarity, but not by certain and exact reason. It is as if you had never seen Socrates, but had looked upon an image of Socrates; you would never know if that image was truly like him. Thus it happens that the notions of things cannot be perfectly judged by the sense.

<margin>The response of the Dogmatists.</margin>
But some of the Dogmatists <note>Philosophers who claimed to have arrived at certain truth, as opposed to the Skeptics.</note>, who confuse the parts of the soul and assert that just as honey is both moist and sweet, so the soul is both intellectual and sensory—and that this part is moved by the senses, while that part is moved by the intellect—say nothing at all that pertains to the question at hand.

<margin>Refutation of the Skeptics.</margin>
For it cannot be denied that there are different powers and that each one is delegated to perform its own duty; otherwise, the soul would be considered both rational and irrational at the same time, with no distinction made regarding the same object. Do they not see this in material things? Honey is both yellow and sweet; yet one quality employs the sight, the other the taste, and neither sense communicates with the other in performing its own duty. And surely such diverse judgments of the mind cannot be made to unite into one through the service of the senses. Therefore, either they are diverse themselves, or lest they be diverse—
