->SECOND<- <column-break/> LXVII

the notions of the mind do not hinder them. Were there not philosophers who removed everything spoken of as either false or ambiguous, such as the followers of Democritus? Were there not those who established certainties, like the Epicureans and the followers of Protagoras? Were there not those who wished some things to be removed while others remained, like the Stoics and the Peripatetics? Therefore, do they judge things by all the senses and all their differences, and likewise by all the understandings and notions of the mind, or only by some? If they say by all, they speak of impossibilities, since so many disagreements have appeared in the senses, and so many battles in thoughts and understandings. For reason would be overturned and destroy itself—especially if the thought of Gorgias <note>Gorgias was a pre-Socratic nihilist who argued that nothing exists, or if it does, it cannot be known.</note> is added, by which it is denied that one ought to assent to either sense or thought. 

But if they assert that things ought to be judged by only some of these, in what way will they distinguish which senses or mental opinions nature requires us to approach, and which to avoid? For as of yet, it has not been decided by common consensus what exactly ought to be held as the <term>judicatory</term> <note>original: "iudicatorium" - the faculty or standard used to judge truth.</note> which must be used in the discord of the senses and the battle of minds. For if they decide that senses or opinions are to be judged by sense, opinion, or thought, they will be taking the very things under question as if they were already settled. For it is still being asked whether a verdict can or should be brought through a judicatory of this kind. 

But the Skeptics say this must not be omitted, so that it may be pressed upon the <term>Dogmatic</term> <note>In this context, "Dogmatic" refers to philosophers like the Stoics or Aristotelians who claimed to possess certain knowledge, as opposed to the Skeptics.</note> philosophers: for they must judge either senses and mental thoughts by the senses, or senses and thoughts by thoughts, or thoughts by the senses, or senses by thought. If they wish to judge by both the senses and the mind, let them choose whichever they prefer, and those difficulties cited above will follow them. 

But if they wish to distinguish, separate, and judge senses by senses, or thoughts by thoughts—since the senses are combative and oppose other senses, and thoughts oppose other thoughts—which one will they choose from the combative senses to serve as the judge of the other senses? And which thought will they choose to bring a verdict concerning the others? For they do not mention "common sense" in this place, but I believe they would have disputed against it as something diverse, just as they did regarding thought and <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "phantasia" - the mental image or impression through which we perceive the world.</note>. Certainly, they would be taking what was being sought as if it were granted, seizing it not with the adversary's consent, but while he is protesting and fighting back. For that part which is taken as settled is actually part of the disagreement; a controversial matter would be decided as if it were a judged matter. 

If, however, thoughts are to be judged by the senses, and senses by thoughts, that circular <note>original: "promiscuus... locus" - referring to a circular argument or "diallelus".</note> reasoning which was rejected above will be introduced. According to this, in order for the senses to be judged, it is necessary to have already judged and decreed thoughts; and so that thoughts may be approved, the senses must be pre-judged. Since, therefore, neither like things can be judged by like judicatories of the same kind, nor different things by those of the same kind, nor those of the same kind by different ones, it will not be possible for us to judge truly and beyond controversy either mind by mind or sense by sense. 

And this is roughly the dispute of the Skeptics concerning the second judicatory, which does not hinder us at all, <margin>For the faith of Christ.</margin> who draw the principles of our discipline not by sight or taste, but by hearing—which is also properly called by Aristotle the sense of learning. For the Apostle says, "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" <note>A reference to Romans 10:17.</note>—of the man, that is, and of God, who neither deceives nor can be deceived; which word has been confirmed by infinite signs beyond all sense and human reason.

To these things, <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; here meaning the faculty of imagination or the mental image itself</note>, by the imagination of some thing, is the effect of the thing imagined. For a phantom and likeness of the thing placed externally is imprinted on the mind by the mediating senses; wherefore when the mind applies itself to desiring anything, it then conceives a certain effect and, as it were, an image of the thing placed externally—that is, the <term>spectrum</term> <note>a mental apparition or vision</note>, the <term>phantasia</term>, the <term>simulacrum</term> <note>a representation or likeness</note>, the image—not the thing itself within itself. Because if anyone should say that the mind, persuaded by affections and discourse, reaches toward things placed externally, many difficulties which were brought up above will surround him. For either the things placed externally are the same as the images of them which we conceive in the mind, or they are similar. If they are the same, in what way can it happen that the same thing is both the effect and the cause of the same thing? For one is different from the other; for we have shown that the thing placed externally is the cause of the thing conceived by imagination. If, however, they are similar, certainly that which is similar is different from that to which it is similar; that is, it is not the same as it. Wherefore the similarities of things which lie externally, not the things themselves, will be conceived by the mind. But in what way will the mind know those things to be similar? But how can it happen that it is known whether it is similar to the thing, if the thing itself has not been known? Moreover, in knowing the thing, so that the <term>phantasia</term> may arrive, in what way will it arrive at knowing itself? This is proven by the rejection of things that are apparent; for we are not moved to grant assent to the conception "it is day" when the sun's rays illuminate the air in the same way as we are to "it is night" while that same brightness persists. Nor is it the same to say "Socrates the Athenian is disputing in the Lyceum" as it is to say "Socrates met his end by drinking hemlock." So too will it appear in "consequents," which the Greek Stoics called *synēmmena* <note>original: συνημμένα; meaning "connected" or "linked" propositions</note>, and the ancient Latins called <margin>Connected. Consequent.</margin> "connected" and "joined." But the younger writers call them conditional consequences: "If it is day, there is light," or "If you walk, you are moved." Who doubts that these are true? And who can say these conceptual fantasies should be condemned? On the other hand, false ones are: "If it is day, it is dark," or <margin>Sextus Empiricus.</margin> "If you walk, you are not moved." I pass over much that Sextus Empiricus <note>A physician and philosopher (c. 160–210 AD) who recorded the arguments of the Skeptics.</note> discusses both copiously and subtly against the logicians in his first volume regarding fantasies. He is concerned not only with overturning the idea that all are true, but also that all are false, using nearly the same arguments. For if all are false and none are true, it will be true that none are true; and if it is true that none are true, it clearly proves that *something* is true. The distinction between fantasies is itself manifest: for by some we are pulled away from assent, and by others we are driven to assent. Were this not so, neither experience nor inexperience, nor any art, nor any ignorance of things would seem to exist. But so that some should not be judged true and others false, he labors much, deeming this to be more a wish of philosophers than the truth. For if we speak of the "grasping fantasy" <note>The Stoic term *phantasia kataleptike*, a perception so clear it compels the mind to accept it as true.</note>, which is drawn from an existing thing insofar as it exists, and is as if branded into the soul—the kind which could not be extracted from a thing that does not exist, as the Stoics decree—<margin>Carneades</margin> Carneades <note>A skeptical philosopher (c. 214–129 BC) who headed the Academy in Athens.</note> contradicts this. He thinks it possible for visions or fantasies to be drawn from things that do not exist in the same way they are usually drawn from things that do exist; and that many people are accustomed to assent to the former no differently than the latter in actual practice. Thus, in dreams, he who drinks because he is thirsty is delighted by a false image, and he who fears cries out with vain dread. So too in madness, one thing is taken for another. Assent is granted to false imaginations no differently than to true ones by those whose minds are alienated. In this way (as it is in the myths), while Hercules was raging, he joined action and deed to the fantasy by which he conceived his own sons to be not his own, but those of Eurystheus; namely, by killing those whom he falsely conceived to be the sons of his enemy. Yet, recognizing the bow which he used, he had a true fantasy, and he mixed this true one with the false one regarding his sons. If, therefore, there are "grasping" fantasies or imaginations insofar as they lead us to assent and action, since false ones also achieve this, one cannot <margin>Author against the Stoics</margin> safely grant judgment to such a promiscuous and ambiguous power. I would add, bringing help to the Platonists and Sceptics against the Stoics in this part as I often do, that such "grasping" fantasies occur not only in those driven by madness, but also in those who are sane—not only from external causes, but internally, namely by the changing of the four parts of the year. For we often conceive of things one way in spring, another in autumn, another in winter, and another in summer, because the humors are moved, and the temperament, being variously affected, presents various phantasms. For who would doubt that when the West Wind <note>Zephyrus</note> pushes forth the buds, when the woods are in leaf, and the year is at its most beautiful, more cheerful fantasies that nourish delightful things are stirred up than in winter? In summer also, when the buds swell on the joyful vine-shoot, other fantasies arise, different from those impressed by the North Wind <note>Boreas</note> while it shook the honor from the leaves. Even in the same month, they are changed by wind, or rain, or clear skies; for the habit and state of the body is changed or even disturbed. This happens not only in humans but also in brute animals—and more so in them, because they lack the reason that might stand against those images, to say nothing of the diversity of natural temperament. <margin>Virgil's poems.</margin> For "when the weather and the shifting moisture of the sky have changed their courses, the appearances of their minds turn, and their breasts conceive movements, now of one kind, now of another, as when the wind was driving the clouds; hence that chorus of birds..." <note>A quotation from Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 1, describing how animals react to weather changes.</note>

the harmony in the fields, the joyful cattle, and the crows exulting with their throats; I pass over the thoughts of things both past and future in men. I am silent regarding the various conditions of gluttony, hunger, sobriety, drunkenness, sleep, wakefulness, different regions, motion, rest, and other matters by which various images and various phantasms are conceived. Finally, I omit the inspirations of celestial minds, from which arise express, fixed, and certain phantasms—which often oppose other imaginations of the same man that were at other times held as certain. I return to the Academics <note>The Academic Skeptics, who followed the later philosophy of Plato's Academy, arguing that nothing can be known with certainty.</note> who lead the Stoic philosophers out from the Portico <note>The "Stoa Poikile" or Painted Porch in Athens, where the Stoics met and from which they took their name.</note> into the sun. They take two eggs that are entirely identical and present them to be inspected one after the other, swapping them in turn, so that the Stoics might finally declare without error, if they can, whether it is one and the same egg shown repeatedly, or different ones? They carry the matter to such an extent as to show that a phantasm <note>term: phantasia. Here used as a "mental impression" or "presentation" of an object to the mind.</note> can be received from a non-existent thing, as well as from that which exists and is evident. They also suggest that if anything of any matter were "graspable," it would especially be through sight. For sight seems to capture and grasp colors, magnitudes, shapes, and motions. But they say it is not so. For men change by the hour, in their actions, nature, ages, circumstances, health, sickness, sleep, and wakefulness. I add that the phantasm of the same thing varies so often that it could be said without injustice not to be the same; indeed, it is frequently foreign to that image which was previously captured by the mind. For when that prior one has vanished, another succeeds in its place, not similar to the thing itself from which it was drawn (as the prior image was similar), but more truly similar to the image than to the thing—or at least not entirely dissimilar, insofar as it leads in some way to the remembering of that very image. Therefore, the "grasping phantasm" <note>original: "captatrix phantasia," translating the Greek "kataleptike phantasia," the Stoic term for a clear and certain perception.</note> will not rightly be held as the criterion of judgment. For just as that which adapts and harmonizes with the crooked cannot be a judge of the straight, so the phantasm itself cannot judge without danger, since it sometimes assents to false and ungraspable things as if they were true and rightly conceived. Furthermore, the Stoics err in that they prove one thing by the other; <margin>Against the Stoics</margin> for in defining the "grasping phantasm," they posited an existing thing. But when they define an existing thing, they employ the "grasping phantasm." For what is an existing thing? When asked, they themselves say "that which exists" <note>original: "τὸ ὑπάρχον" (to hyparchon)</note> is that which moves the grasping phantasm. However, the Academics seem to err in this matter because they establish as the judge a phantasm that is not "grasping," but which they call "persuasive" <note>original: "πιθανὴν" (pithanen), often translated as "probable" or "credible."</note> <margin>Against the Academics</margin> because either through it they gather useful dogmas for conducting life, or because they track and discern the truth in things by its aid. They wander first because no single [phantasm] is uniquely useful for the actions and duties of life, but each one is useful if frequent observation is applied, according to which one will be persuasive for this reason, and another for that—as they themselves say, "through the wandering and undistracted" <note>original: "διὰ ἐξοδευομένην & ἀπερίσπαστον" (dia exodeuomenen kai aperispaston). These are technical terms for a refined, scrutinized impression that the Skeptics used to guide action.</note>—that is, both traveling through and unshakable. But then they are deceived because the persuasive phantasm alone shall be the judge of truth. For it is necessary, in order for this to be found, to have run through much beforehand, lest the mind, relying on suspicion and conjecture in place of certain judgment, judge the false for the true. Just as they themselves condemned the Stoics because certain things could be confused and mixed with vain ones, and changeable things with firm ones in the "grasping phantasm," so they themselves are to be condemned, who provide nothing certain and constant in their "persuasive" phantasm, into which some falsehood might not be mixed by that very lack of discourse and, as it were, the wandering of the mind in capturing examples. Finally, they reject the idea that a criterion can be established because the straight can be a judge of itself and of the crooked alike—which is seen in a ruler, a balance, and other things. This is childish...

### Chapter XXXV. Concerning the truth, which the Sceptics have discussed in general so as to render it ambiguous.

Even if it is granted, they say, that a faculty of judgment exists, it will nevertheless be seen to be useless if the truth does not exist, and if that which is shown to be true is found to be inconsistent. We have shown that the philosophers, especially the Stoics <note>The Stoics were an ancient Greek school of philosophy that emphasized logic and natural law.</note>, distinguished "truth" from "the true" in a threefold way, and differently than we are accustomed to do. We must deal with "the true," which they take to be a sort of dignity or a "signifiable" statement <note>original: "enunciabile" — a technical term for a proposition that can be expressed in language</note>. They think that "truth" is the science of all such signifiable statements.

<margin>What "the true" is and how far it differs from "truth" according to ancient philosophers.</margin>
Therefore, among these authors, "the true" encompasses "truth" in such a way that truth is a collection of true things, which is clearly destroyed if the true itself is removed. Furthermore, the Sceptics attempt to render "the true" itself ambiguous in two ways: first in general—concerning which we did some work at the beginning of the second volume, though we shall deal with it more accurately here—and then more specifically and exactly.

Therefore, since there is a controversy regarding the true (says Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a 2nd-century physician and philosopher whose works are the primary source for ancient Scepticism.</note>) even among the dogmatic philosophers—since some admit that a certain truth exists, while others say none exists—it certainly does not seem possible for the matter to be settled. For those who affirm it, if they affirm it without demonstration, they will not be believed; for a thin and weak negation is the proper response to a thin and weak affirmation. This is because the true is already disputed and pulled apart by various opinions.

If, however, they bring forward a demonstration, and if they admit that demonstration is false, they will themselves revoke their own assent. If they say the demonstrations are true, they fall into a common trap: a true demonstration will itself need a demonstration, and so that this one may be proven true, another will be needed, and then another, so that finally no limit can be found. Who can doubt that infinite things cannot be demonstrated?

And he adds: the "whatness" itself, or "being" <note>original: "ipsum quid, siue ens"</note>, is so general that it encloses all other things in its vast circuit; it is either true, or false, or neither true nor false, or both true and false.
If they grant the first, they will admit all things are true. For if that which encompasses all categories is true, it is easily proven that the things enclosed under it are true. And nothing would be false, by which the true is distinguished; for one is recognized by the other.
If they grant the second, all things will be false by the same reasoning we brought above, from which they deduce that nothing is true—and through this, nothing is false, since one both establishes and removes the other. If the false does not exist, neither will the true be found, for one is known by comparison to the other. And besides, if all things are false, it is necessary to confess that something is true: namely, that it is true that nothing is true.
If they admit the third, they must also admit that all particular things—which are said to be neither true nor false—will not be true, and it will be obscure

<margin>Rebuttal of the objection.</margin>
and doubtful to us whether truth can be found in the nature of things. But if they answer that things are neither true nor false because "good" and "evil" exist in things, while "true" and "false" consist in the intellect—and therefore there is a need for composition and statement—let them now hear that what is said of each individual thing is also said of the composition itself, since both the extremes and their conjunction do not escape the circuit of "being." But a particular dispute on whether truth is not found even in statements will be undertaken shortly hereafter.
If, however, they admit the fourth, each particular thing will be both true and false, from which it will be deduced that nothing is true by its own nature...

by its own nature. For that which has such a nature that it is true, cannot be entirely false at all, so long as that nature stands and remains. To this, either only those things which appear or are seen (as was said at the beginning of this second book) are true, or only those things which are not seen are true. Or, of those things which are true, some appear or are seen, and some do not appear. If they grant only those things which are seen, they must grant either all of them or some of them. If all, then reason is overturned, for it seems to some that nothing is true; and those things seen through sleep or madness <note>The author refers to the skeptical trope that dreams and hallucinations are indistinguishable from reality to the person experiencing them.</note> are not true. If they answer "some," then that very thing cannot be decided without a means of judgment <term>judicatorio: a criterion or standard of judgment</term>. Moreover, this means of judgment will either be seen and apparent, or it will not be seen—this they could in no way say. <margin>What [unclear]</margin> For it is now supposed that only those things which are seen are true; if it appears, since it is asked which appearances are true and which are false, when the means of judgment is counted among the appearances, we will again need another apparent means of judgment, and likewise another, unto infinity. But who can judge infinite things? If, however, one accepts only those things which are not apparent or not manifest as true, he will not be counted among the number of the dogmatists <note>original: "dogmaticorum" — referring to philosophers who assert positive doctrines, as opposed to skeptics.</note>, who quarrel over such non-manifest and non-apparent things, such as the principles of natural things and those things which are composed and grow from them. <margin>[unclear] what.</margin> And furthermore, they will be forced to admit that contradictory things are true at the same time, such as that the stars shine in the sky in an even number and also in an odd number. But if they prefer "some" [of the non-apparent], by what means will they decide those things, so that some non-apparent things are true and some are false? For they will not use an apparent thing. If they use a non-apparent thing, we will ask which of those non-apparent things are true and which are false? For this non-apparent thing will need another non-apparent thing by which it may be judged, and that another, so that the excursion proceeds to infinity. It remains for them to say that of those things which are true, some are apparent and manifest, and others are not at all, which will also be refuted. For either all apparent and non-apparent things are true, or some apparent and some non-apparent. If all, again the speech and discourse are overturned, since it will be true, and nothing will be true. For it will be said to be true that the stars are even, and odd. But if some of those things which appear and some of those which do not appear are judged to be true, how shall we judge 

¶ that of those things which appear, some are true and others false? For if we use an apparent thing, the discourse will run on to infinity. If a non-apparent thing—since those things which are not apparent need judgment—this non-apparent thing will again be judged by another; and if that be an apparent thing, a circular and mutually vicious mode of proof <term>vicioſe procumbit: a circular argument or "begging the question"</term> will be introduced. <margin>concerning showing [unclear]</margin> If, however, it is not apparent, the proof will be banished to infinity. Furthermore, they say that the truth itself, about which the question is made, is either of those things which consist by their own nature and are established by their own difference, or of those things which exist in relation to another. If the first is given, that absurdity follows: that things which consist by their own nature exhibit their appearance similarly, not differently and variously. For that which, for example, is hot, equally heats all who are capable of receiving heat; it does not indeed heat this one while affecting another with cold. But truth is not so, but one and the same thing appears true to this person and false to that one. But if they prefer to give the second [option], since such things are established by intellect and thought, and with no change made to the thing, they receive different conditions, even adverse and fighting among themselves, it will happen that truth does not exist through itself, but exists in the way it is conceived, leaning only on thought and not on the substance of the thing. And that same thing will happen: that the same thing is true and false at the same time. For just as the same column is both on the right and on the left—on the right if it is referred to this person, but on the left if compared to another—and just as the same thing is both below and above—above if compared and brought together with that which is subject to it, but below when compared to the superior—so the same truth [is] different...

<margin>Aenesidemus</margin> ...if it is referred back to conceptions, it will be found to be both true and false. Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a physician and philosopher who recorded the arguments of the Skeptics.</note> adds many things from Aenesidemus <note>Aenesidemus was a Greek Skeptic philosopher of the 1st century BCE who revived Pyrrhonism.</note> in the second volume of his work *Against the Logicians* <note>original: "contra logicos"</note>, of which these seem to be the principal points: either the truth is perceptible by the senses, or it is intelligible by the mind, or it is both. The first is by no means the case. For if the visible is perceived by sight (the audible by hearing, the odorous by smell), then truth would also be perceived by a sense, which is absurd since the senses lack the reason <note>original: "ratione"</note> by which truth is said to be captured. The second is not the case at all. For either the intelligible is common to all, or it is private to certain individuals; it is in no way common, because then every inquiry would be abolished, and this is also least credible, and furthermore, it is a matter of conflict and controversy. The third option will also be least accepted, for either every sensible thing and every intelligible thing is true, or only a certain sensible thing and a certain intelligible thing are true. If they grant the first, they grant it by no reason at all, for it can by no means happen: and furthermore, sensible things conflict with sensible things, and intelligible things with intelligible things, and again, sensible things with intelligible things, and intelligible things with sensible things; and if all things of this kind were true, the same thing would both be and not be, and the true and the false would be proven at the same time. But if they answer that it is something else, it will be a matter of controversy, for it will be asked and disputed what that thing is and of what nature it is. To these points, regarding the cause of truth, he added several things to show that it would be done away with. In what way, he asks, do they grasp this cause? As something appearing to them? Or as something least seen and manifest? If they say it is as something appearing, they will be lying when they teach that truth does not subsist according to that which appears and is seen. But if they say it is not as something appearing and seen, I will ask how it became known to them? From itself or from another? From itself is indeed impossible, for that which is not seen is not comprehensible from itself; if he says from another, I will ask again about that: was it appearing or not appearing? And thus, with the investigation receding into infinity, the truth will never be found. What is it, then, that persuades us whether it is true? But what kind of essence does it have? Sensible? Or intelligible? Or both? But these we have already left among the doubtful, ambiguous, and controversial things. For if the truth persuades, yet since it does not persuade everyone, therefore we will not all grant (they say) that it exists, but rather that it both exists and does not exist, and is simultaneously true and false; for insofar as it persuades some, it will be true and exist; but insofar as it does not persuade others, it will be false. But it cannot happen that the same thing is and is not at the same time, and is judged to be both true and false. Therefore, the truth will not persuade.

<margin>Removal of an objection.</margin> Unless perhaps they say that what persuades the majority of men is true: Shall we then pronounce honey to be truly sweet because it persuades the majority of healthy people that it is sweet, even though it does not persuade one person who is jaundiced and feverish? This is indeed like old wives' tales: for when we inquire about the truth, we ought not to look to the consensus of the multitude, but to the dispositions themselves: for the sick man uses one disposition, and all the healthy use another, yet we should not yield to the latter more than the former. Because if we proceed in reverse, we will be convinced to say that honey is not sweet, having respect for the multitude: for let us suppose that many...

BOOK TWO                                                                                             LXXI

Furthermore, the Sceptics descended toward more specific arguments in order to oppose the various sects of philosophers, especially those of Democritus, Plato, the Stoics, and those who did not differ far from them. Now, Democritus and Plato <margin>What Democritus and Plato said concerning the truth.</margin> said that only intelligible things <note>Things understood by the mind rather than the senses.</note> are true, yet they held this opinion for different reasons. For Democritus wished for no sensible thing <note>Objects perceived by the senses.</note> to be underlying in nature to the atoms, since nature is destitute of every sensible quality. Plato, however, held this because sensible things were always becoming and never truly *were*; they exist like a rapid torrent, so that they cannot remain or be grasped even for two tiny particles of time, nor can they even be pointed out because of the velocity of their flux, as Asclepiades used to say. But indeed, Aenesidemus <margin>What Aenesidemus thought of the truth.</margin> devised a certain difference among sensible and apparent things: those which appeared commonly to everyone were true, while those appearing only to a specific individual were not. Epicurus, however, <margin>What Epicurus thought of the truth.</margin> said that all sensible things were indiscriminately true and existing, defining the "true" in this way: the true is that which is in such a state as it is said to be, and the false is that which is not in such a state as it is said to be. He said the sense was the receiver of those things which fell upon it, neither adding anything, nor diminishing, nor transforming. He wanted the sense to be entirely truthful, and to capture the thing just as it was by its own nature, and not to be deceived when the "images" <note>original: *simulacra*; the thin films of atoms Epicureans believed flowed from objects to the eyes.</note> of things excited it. Nevertheless, he maintained that opinions differed from all sensible things (even if the latter were true), for of opinions, some were true and others false, both in reality and in how they were held. The Stoics, truly, wanted some sensible things and some intelligible things to be true; <margin>What the Stoics thought of the truth.</margin> however, they did not pronounce sensible things true immediately of themselves, but according to their relation to the intelligible things which were composed by and adjacent to them. They defined the "true" as that which existed and was opposed to something; the "false" as that which did not exist and was not opposed to something. And this indeed was the difference among these sects of philosophers concerning the true and the false. There was also that disagreement where some placed the true and the false around the *signified* <note>The meaning or concept behind a word.</note>, as did the Stoics, who wanted these three things to be joined together: that which signifies, that which is signified, and the actual object encountered. They said the first was the voice; the second was the thing itself declared through the voice; the third was the thing placed externally, established in itself and its own nature. Of these three, they decreed two to be bodies <note>Physical matter.</note>: the first and the third; but the middle one was incorporeal—that is, the thing signified and enunciated, which could be both true and false. And this was not entirely common to all, but some were "deficient" and others "perfect," which would be called a "proposition" or "value" <note>original: *dignitas*, translating the Greek *axioma*.</note>. Their description of it was this: a value (they called it an *axioma* <note>original: ἀξίωμα</note>) is that which is either true or false. Others, however, such as Epicurus and Strato the physicist, placed the true and the false in the voice alone, casting aside the other two; others placed it in the movement of the mind and thought. Among these Aristotle can be placed, <margin>What Aristotle thought of the truth.</margin> who ordained that the true and the false are in the intellect, of which words are the signs, just as written marks and characters are the signs of words. But because the Pyrrhonists <note>Followers of the skeptic Pyrrho.</note> contradict these, they will easily be seen to contradict Aristotle as well, although a place is prepared for me to dispute against Aristotle in the last three books of this work—taken not from the Pyrrhonists, but from the Lyceum itself. Therefore, the Sceptics condemn first of all Democritus and Plato, <margin>Against Democritus and Plato.</margin> who despise the senses and do away with sensible things by clinging only to intelligibles; they say these men confuse things and expel not only the truth of things, but the very notion of them. For every notion arises from sense, or not without sense, and either from an incident or not without an incident—namely, the encountering of the "image" of a thing placed externally. Whence we shall not find those fantasies which are called false in sleep or madness to be entirely alien to those things known to us through the senses according to the encounter made to us by an image. For he who imagines for himself certain bloody Furies and girls entwined with dragons, does so from those things which are known to him...

It specifically highlights the debate over whether truth resides in physical objects, the mind, or the language used to describe them.</summary>

...shapes and fashions their form: and he who perceives a flying man in his dreams does not do so without having seen a man, nor without having beheld some winged creature; that image creeps into the mind during rest.
<margin>From what sources notions or thoughts are formed in the mind.</margin> And to speak briefly, it is impossible to find anything according to a notion <note>Latin: *notio*, a mental concept or general idea</note> or thought which does not already have something known, by that very encounter with an image of which we spoke. This is captured either according to the likeness of those things which appeared in the encounter itself, or according to addition, or according to subtraction and decrease, or according to composition. According to **multiplicity** indeed—for example—from the already seen image of Socrates, we conceive in the mind the man himself even when he is not seen. According to **increase**, however, when from the common notion and concept of a man, we are moved and excited to imagine not a man as he is, but of a more majestic stature, such as the giants were, or such as Polyphemus <note>The one-eyed giant from Homer's Odyssey</note> is depicted, who is made huge, towering, and "strikes the high stars." <note>A poetic reference to Virgil's Aeneid, describing the giant's height.</note> According to **subtraction and decrease**, as when from the common appearance of men we revolve the idea of a pygmy in the mind. According to **composition**, however, just as when from the sight of a man and a horse, we fashion a centaur in the mind, even though such a thing has never happened upon us, nor has ever been observed by our eyes. Therefore, every notion must be preceded by some image falling upon us through the senses, by which it happens that if the sensible object is removed, every notion is rightly considered to be removed likewise. To this, those who say that all things which appear are false, and that only intelligible things <note>Things understood by the intellect rather than the senses</note> exist according to truth, either say this content with a mere assertion, or they also join a demonstration to it. If they contend this by assertion alone, they shall be repelled by a mere denial; if they prepare a demonstration, we shall subvert or undermine it for them. For they either use something apparent and recognized by the senses, or something not seen at all and unknown. They will by no means say the first, since they wish all such things to be removed; but if they say the second, this absurdity follows: that it is proper for the unknown to be indicated and known by the manifest and the known. Wherefore the opinion of Plato and Democritus is by no means to be admitted (as they wish).
<margin>Against Epicurus.</margin> Epicurus is an exception, whom they also think should not be admitted because it is false that the senses are not deceived when images <note>Latin: *simulachra*, the thin "films" or "idols" Epicurus believed flowed from objects to the eyes</note> strike them. When Orestes <note>A figure from Greek mythology driven mad by the Furies</note> thought he saw the Furies and the Erinnyes with their uncombed black snakes, his senses, moved and excited by the images, were true. For the images themselves were underlying them, but the intellect, thinking those images were solid things and true Furies, was deceived. And furthermore, when he says some fantasies <note>Mental impressions or appearances</note> are true and some false, and distinguishes "opinables" from true sensible things, by what means does he prepare this? For it is not by an apparent and seen thing—for such things are what are being questioned—nor even by an unknown and least apparent thing. For through that which is clear and known, obscure and unknown things are made manifest. But indeed, Epicurus has unwillingly fallen into a similar doubt; for if he confesses that some fantasies are drawn from solid bodies, and some from naked and vanishing images, and thus separates opinion from clarity and truth: Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, the skeptical philosopher whose work this text likely discusses</note> asks, I say, how he judges between them? For it is not by clarity, for that is what is being questioned; nor by opinion, which is made credible through clarity: for it is absurd for those things which have less ambiguity to be proven by those which are more doubtful.
<margin>Against the Stoics.</margin> Less assent is also granted to the Stoics, because they cannot bring forward what those "grasping" or "comprehensive" fantasies are, extracted from the underlying objects; and which are from the things themselves not insofar as they are such, but insofar as they *seem* to be. What difference do they establish between true and false, whether they be sensible or intelligible things? For they confess that some proceed from the underlying objects, yet not according to the underlying objects themselves, such as those which befell the raging Hercules. For they were drawn from his sons, but not insofar as they were his own sons, but insofar as they seemed to be the sons of Eurystheus; otherwise he would not have killed them. Therefore, they cannot bring forward a distinction for when fantasies are grasped rightly and when they are grasped wrongly.

<meta>This page continues the skeptical critique of Stoic logic, specifically focusing on the nature of the "enunciable" or "proposition" (lekton), following the previous discussion on the criteria of truth.</meta>

-> SECOND BOOK <-                                                                                                                              72

But if a transition is made to the truth itself, does it consist in the enunciable <note>original: "enunciabili"; the underlying concept is the Greek *lekton*</note> in a proposition, or in the voice, or in the mind? A multifaceted battle and controversy will be found; for the *lekton* <note>original: "λεκτον"; literally "that which is said"</note>, as they call it, which we can call the "dictum" or, if you prefer, the "enunciated," they decree to be that which exists as constituted according to a rational phantasy <note>original: "phantasiam"; in Stoic terms, a mental impression or representation</note>. Now, a rational phantasy <margin>Rational phantasy according to the Stoics.</margin> (as they would have it) is that according to which what is conceived by the phantasy is constituted by reason. Furthermore, many species of the enunciated are brought forward: the deficient, the perfect, and of the latter there are many differences—commanding, denying, questioning, wishing, comparing—and some of these they call *axiomata* <note>original: "αξιώματα"; usually translated as "axioms" or "propositions"</note>. Cicero would call them "pronouncements" <note>original: "pronunciata"</note>; he says in the first *Tusculan Disputation*: "Every pronouncement—for so it occurs to me at present to call the *axioma*—I shall use another later if I find a better one." That, therefore, is a pronouncement which is true or false; so says he. Others call it "dignity" <note>a literal translation of the Greek *axioma*</note>: but the Stoics intend it to be that *axioma* which is either true or false. This enunciated, then, which the Stoics call incorporeal, they also want to be distinct from the signifying voice. By what means, ask the Sceptics, shall we establish this? Either by itself—and the Stoics will say this exists, and thus establish it by their own authority—or they are going to confirm its substance by some demonstration. If the first, then it will also be permitted to the Sceptics to bring forth a contrary opinion by their own authority; for they say no more faith is owed to them than to us if authority alone is brought to judgment. But if they bring themselves to the tribunal of demonstration, a certain worse doubt will befall them. For if a demonstration is a speech, and speech is constituted from enunciations, it will happen that they conclude some enunciation exists by means of enunciations; for he who does not grant one enunciation will by no means grant many enunciations. Moreover, for those who are to seek enunciations in a demonstration, if they decree them to be so by their own nod, another will deny them to be so by his own refusal. But if they attempt to prove it through demonstration, the discourse will go on into infinity. If indeed a demonstration is required for those enunciations which are comprised in the second demonstration, and they bring a third for those concluded in the third, a fourth will be desired, and thus no end will be found. The Sceptics also find fault with that point stated by the Stoics: that a perfect enunciation consists in the composition of a noun and a verb; yet they contend that nothing which is composed and divisible can be incorporeal, and for this reason they do not admit the noun, just like the enunciation, to be incorporeal, because it is clearly composed of syllables. But they say no enunciation subsists by itself, since part succeeds part in the act of enunciating, and before the latter part is brought forth, the former slips away. A nearly similar reasoning is used by more recent <margin>Our theologians.</margin> Theologians who are accustomed to dispute concerning the words of the consecration of the host in the fourth book of the *Sentences* <note>referring to Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, the standard medieval theological textbook</note>; yet they themselves truly dissolve the opposing arguments, being imbued with true divine mysteries which the gentiles were ignorant of. To relate their disagreements so that they may be refuted, we must return. Furthermore, the Sceptic philosophers rebuke the Stoics because they busy themselves explaining the unknown by the more unknown, or at least by the equally unknown. For when asked what that is which subsists, they say it is that by which the "grasping phantasy" <note>original: "captatrix phantasia"; translating the Greek *phantasia kataleptike* or "kataleptic impression"</note> is moved; likewise, if we inquire about this same phantasy, they return to that which subsists, answering that a grasping phantasy is that which proceeds from that which exists, insofar as it exists; and so they fall into a promiscuous and alternating place of indicating and declaring themselves. But indeed the enunciation itself, whether it is simple—which they divide into the "determinate," to which a sign of showing is connected, such as "this man," "that man," "yon man"; and the "indeterminate," to which a singular sign is not added, but a common and indefinite one, such as "someone," "somebody," and the like; and the "middle," to which neither of those is added, for example "a man sitting," "Socrates disputing"— <margin>Concerning the enunciations of the Stoics and the junior dialecticians.</margin>

...state, whether it is not simple but composite, which they call either *connected* <note>original: συνημμένον (*synēmmenon*)</note>, that is, joined together, or *interwoven* <note>original: συμπεπλεγμένον (*sympeplegmenon*)</note>, that is, complicated, or *disjoined* <note>original: διεζευγμένον (*diezeugmenon*)</note>: that is, disunited or separated. First, note that the Stoics say a "connected" proposition consists of "if," "or," or "since," such as "if it is day, it is light." The <term>Modern Dialecticians</term> <note>referring to the "Neoterici," likely the later Scholastic or Renaissance logicians</note> call this a "conditional consequence" in our language. That "interwoven" type, note, is formed by "and"; our people would call it a "copulative" statement. The "disjoined" type is truly forged by the particles "or," "whether," or "either"; our people would call it a "disjunctive." In all of these, they themselves have a preceding statement, to which they give the name *leading* <note>original: ἡγούμενον (*hēgoumenon*)</note> and *first* <note>original: πρῶτον (*prōton*)</note>. This is the "preceding" and "first" part; they also have a "consequent" called by them *ending* <note>original: λῆγον (*lēgon*)</note> and *second* <note>original: δεύτερον (*deuteron*)</note>. This is the "defining" and "second" part. They also have an "inference" which they call *bringing-on* <note>original: ἐπιφοράν (*epiphoran*)</note>. Therefore, they find fault with this statement, whether simple or composite, in many ways: they contend that no "demonstrative" (if I may use the term) simple statement can be verified, since under the act of showing, they do not provide the very things they strive to show. Rather, only certain particles are present which, by right and merit, by no means sustain the truth and predication of the whole statement. But if this cannot be done in a demonstrative statement, much less can it be done in the two remaining types which are far more removed from "showing." But they especially bring forward the disagreements of the dialecticians of great name, **Philo** and **Diodorus**, regarding composite statements. For the former [Philo] wanted a "connected" statement to be true in three ways: that is, when it begins from a truth and ends in a truth; likewise when it ends in a falsehood starting from a falsehood; and when starting from a falsehood it ends in a truth. But it is false in only one way: when it begins from a truth and ends in a falsehood. **Diodorus** contradicts him in almost all points, a matter about which I myself have discoursed at length in the fourth book of my *Logical Institutions*. Others also bring forward two other modes of "connected" statements, about which words will be made in the following book, while those things which the **Skeptics** brought against the logicians are related. So, they ask, how shall we learn in which statement truth is located? Concerning the soundness and truth of a statement, it ought first to have been established. But how shall it be established while the lawsuit is ongoing? For shall we agree with all statements? Or with certain statements as if they were true, and with signs and judges of the truth itself? It is not possible for us to agree with all, for we would be agreeing with conflicting things. For things that conflict cannot be equally persuasive. If we are to do this with certain statements, we will do it either by our own will and without evidence, or with reason, showing us the soundness of the speech. If the first, why are we to agree with this one more than that one? If the second, the speech will either conclude and terminate the question, or not at all. If the latter happens, it will be without faith and vain. If the former, certainly it will be because the conclusion follows those things which were assumed. Thus it happens that through inference and some consequence, that very statement is proved. But the "consequence" would have to be proved again, the truth of which was being sought in the joined statement. Therefore, this will be such as that which falls into a <term>circular argument</term> <note>original: *promiscuum locum*, likely referring to the "reciprocal" trope of the Skeptics</note>, when one thing is usually proved by the other. For if the "joined" is to be proved from the "consequence," since in this business it is necessary to run through a certain speech, and this speech, in order to function with soundness and be held as true, must have a consequence ready and confirmed through which what is true may be judged—then the whole matter is left in ambiguity. They doubt no less concerning the "copulative" statement, in which they want all parts to be true for it to be true; but they want that which is forged from all false parts to be false; while that which is composed of false and true parts, they say is no more true than false. And if indeed they are allowed to decide according to their judgment and will, and to give instructions concerning the things themselves: let it be granted that the "interwoven" and "copulative" statement which has one false part be pronounced false. But let it also be allowed for others to oppose and say that what is joined from many true parts and one false part is true. If, however, they think they must adhere to the nature of things, that which is composed of both is no more...

they will pronounce it no more this than that: just as we would assert that something mixed from white and black is no more white than black. The Stoics will respond that the similarity is supported by very little force. <margin>Response of the Stoics</margin> Indeed, if a garment is for the most part whole, yet some part—even the smallest—is torn and gnawed away, it ought to take its name not from the greater part, but from the lesser, and be judged as "shattered" and "broken." The Pyrrhonians <note>Followers of Pyrrho, the ancient Greek skeptic who argued that we must suspend judgment on all things.</note> stand in opposition, <margin>Refutation.</margin> conceding that it is permissible for the common assembly of men and for common life to use names loosely and with the least proper expressions, but not for the philosopher; for the common people do not look exactly at the nature of things, but at opinion. For in this way, the common man speaks of "digging a well," "weaving a garment," and "building a house," yet not properly. For if it *is* a well, it is not being dug, but has already been dug; and if it *is* a garment, it is not being woven, but has already been woven. But our logicians <note>original: "dialectici"</note> would decree that one must look not at the nature of the thing itself, but at the inference, <margin>Opinion of the author.</margin> and that truth is either proved or falsehood rejected in the consequence itself. For in such joined statements, neither that which precedes nor that which follows is considered, but that which is connected. But what either our people or I might say in this matter is not the place to report, since the business is being conducted between the Stoics and the Sceptics, as to whether truth is proved or disproved in the meaning of a proposition. Furthermore, the Sceptics press the Epicureans and Strato, <margin>Against the Epicureans and Strato.</margin> since they decreed that truth exists in the voice. For they ask: is truth in the expressed voice or in the suppressed voice? For it seems impossible to think otherwise. But it is in neither this nor that; therefore, they have decreed falsely. They prove the latter assumption regarding the lower part thus: that which is expressed does not subsist <note>i.e., it does not have a permanent existence in time</note>, therefore truth cannot subsist in it. Regarding the second, they argue thus: truth is not in the suppressed voice because it does not yet exist; therefore, truth shall be placed in no voice at all. Moreover, they say if truth is in the voice, it is either in the shortest voice or in the long and drawn-out one. Not in the shortest, because it is indivisible, but truth is not indivisible; nor in the long and drawn-out, because it does not subsist. For when its first part is uttered, the second is not yet; when the second is uttered, the first has slipped away. To these points, if truth is in the voice, it is either in a signifying voice or in one that signifies nothing. Not in the latter—for how can it be that in a sound like *blitiri* or *schindapsus* <note>Nonsense words used by ancient logicians to illustrate sounds without meaning.</note>, which signify nothing, any truth or falsehood can be found? If they say truth is in the former, they are about to receive this blow: that no voice, insofar as it is a voice, signifies the same thing to everyone. For it would be necessary that everyone who receives the voice with their ears—whether Greeks, Latins, or those from the furthest barbarism—would also perceive its meaning if that were the case. Furthermore, some voices are simple, others are composite (for no other division is given). Simple, such as "Socrates"; composite, such as "Socrates walks." Truth will be in either these or those; but it is found in neither, therefore in none. Not in the simple, according to most philosophers, for whom truth is usually placed in the proposition, which is entirely composed of words. Likewise, not in the composite, since it has already been shown above that no composite voice can subsist; for when we pronounce the first part, we do not yet produce the second, and when we utter that, the first has vanished, disappearing into the thin breezes. Furthermore, the Pyrrhonians contend against most philosophers that truth does not exist in the notion and concept of the mind. If it were so, they say, nothing of those things which are outside would be rightly held as true, which they think is absurd. For the concept of the mind is within us, not outside us: in which things alone they place the truth. Again, they say there would be no truth common to all, since each person's own mental concept is his own, in which truth has established its seat. But if it be conceded that there is no common truth, it will follow that all things are obscure, and nothing at all manifest and clear; for those things which [appear] to this man...

### That truth is found in the Sacred Scriptures, and is to be drawn from there; where much is said concerning the truth and perfection of Christian discipline, and in passing, several points against the obstinate Hebrews. Chapter XXXII.

Without strife, however, are the sacred letters of both Divine Testaments, from which we seek our discipline—that is, the Christian one. There, truth exists without dissension, without wandering and anxious discourse; there is the knowledge of the one God, the rejection of the superstitions of many gods, and the refutation of the vain and conflicting dogmas by which philosophers thought the path to happiness lay open. For concerning God himself—that He is one, and that all the gods of the nations are demons—and that one goes to God, in whom is true happiness, through holy character and the observation of divine precepts, Moses, divinely taught many centuries ago, had already revealed. In those times, not only were there no celebrated authors among the nations (especially in Greece), but even the very letters <note>The alphabet or written literature.</note> were not yet in use, which some prefer to think were imported into Greece from Phoenicia and others from Egypt; but more truly they migrated from the Hebrews. Of this matter, among others, Gregory of Nazianzus <margin>Nazianzus against Julian.</margin> <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), a Church Father who wrote orations against the Emperor Julian the Apostate.</note> made mention in his first book against the Emperor Julian.

Certainly, Moses revealed these things and proved them by signs and wonders, not by the vain syllogisms of philosophers: when Egypt was struck in manifold ways by the portent of the rod; when by that same rod the Red Sea was divided; when by the striking of that same rod water flowed from the rock; and when many other miracles were performed, so that most evident signs—not of human darkness, but of divine light—were offered to men both for living well and for hoping for the best. The most celebrated philosophers of the nations—Pythagoras, Democritus, and Plato—followed his doctrine, or rather, they obtained it; yet, led either by the error of the multitude or persuaded by fear of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens.</note> and the city, they both marginalized it and mixed it with their own fables.

That same Moses, looking out for the hard and obstinate people of the Hebrews, and speaking to those same unrefined people who were most persistent in their errors, suggested that another prophet was to be sent by divine providence <margin>That Christ is the Messiah.</margin>. If they listened to his word, it would be well and blessed for them; if they refused to listen, divine vengeance awaited them. That this one promised to the Hebrews was Jesus Christ, the blood of the martyrs has clearly testified, reason has proven, events have shown, peoples and nations have agreed, miracles have confirmed, and an innumerable crowd of evil demons has confessed. And finally, if Judea itself does not stop up its ears and wishes not to depart from the Mosaic and prophetic monuments, it cannot fail to hear. Regarding this matter, many have written, but among others, Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, wrote excellent books to which he gave the title *On the Evangelical Demonstration* <margin>Eusebius on the Evangelical Demonstration.</margin> <note>A 4th-century work by Eusebius of Caesarea defending Christianity against pagan and Jewish objections.</note>. Therefore, in these testaments of divine literature, the truth must be sought—a truth which is undoubtedly easy to find, <margin>How easily sacred literature is understood.</margin> for it is proposed to be held by faith, which many reasons and innumerable miracles have confirmed. No long period of time is required for this, such as is designated by philosophers for perfecting human knowledge. The matter is handled by hearing; for "faith comes from hearing." <note>A reference to Romans 10:17.</note> If we assent, we have already attained great fruit. No loftiness of intellect is necessary, no specific bodily temperament, and no sex is excluded. Both a decrepit old woman and a boy are as capable of this matter as is sufficient for happiness. No necessity of household affairs hinders it, and no occupation in performing the duties of an active life repels anyone. It is available to all, without price or reward, and is acquired with few words; and finally, no vanity is mixed in. There is no ambiguity of opinion regarding the truth of the Mosaic literature, no conflict, and no contradiction in its history. There is absolutely no disagreement concerning the truth of the events, a disagreement with which all history of the nations is full. In the *Commentaries* of Caesar, Asinius <note>Asinius Pollio, a Roman critic who famously doubted Caesar's accuracy.</note> desired a more sincere and truer narration. And he was silenced, being convicted by manifest witnesses. I pass over those histories which can be considered akin to fables among the Greeks, such as the death of Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine, struck down by Zeus for bringing the dead back to life.</note>, a matter about which the skeptical commentators on the poets fret while they rail against the grammarians. But regarding Roman history, even in the most well-explained and commonly accepted accounts, what shall we bring forward? If anyone were to ask about the founder of Rome, would he not be answered immediately that Romulus was the parent, founder, and establisher of the city? This is based on that common opinion on everyone's lips: that Rome was named after Romulus. No one would dare to oppose this history, which is strengthened by such public consensus. Yet, in this very matter, more ambiguities, weaknesses, and controversies are found than in any other history of nations. Many Latins disagree with many Greeks; the Greeks vary among themselves; nor do all the Latins agree with one another. Some wish it to have been founded by the companions of Aeneas, or even by Romus, the son of Aeneas. Others claim it was founded by a certain Aeneas and named after a Trojan woman named Roma. Others prefer that both the city and its name came from Romus, the son of Circe and Ulysses. Some say from Romus, the son of Italus; others from Evander; others say other things.

However, these disagreements and variations are far removed from the histories of the Old and New Testaments which we have received. For no true Hebrew ever doubted even the smallest letter of the sacred text. Josephus is the authority <margin>Josephus, Philo, the Christians.</margin> that this text was preserved in uncorrupted monuments through so many captivities, so many exiles of the people, and so many disasters, by the public consensus of the Hebrews. Philo confirmed that not a word had been changed in two thousand years. Indeed, we Christians are so unable to doubt the truth of both Testaments that if we did not choose to face death rather than hesitate, we would be judged unworthy of the name Christian. Therefore, we all agree, and with unanimous consent, we believe, speak, and assert that whatever is written in both instruments <note>original: "instrumento" — a common term for the Testaments of the Bible.</note> is true. We are persuaded not only by innumerable reasons arising from the outcomes of events and by a vast number of miracles, but we are inwardly moved and stabilized by the very light of faith and confirmed by divinity. By the benefit of this light, we do not doubt that all things enclosed under faith are true. We do not seek the darkness of the senses, nor the dark and opaque clouds of any shifting or deceptive imagination, nor any twilights of arguments. For we consider nothing to be more certain or unshakable, since we know divine things by divine light. To this light, reason is subject, and all inferior nature serves as a handmaid.

<margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine teaches Romanianus and Lucinianus to beware lest they think they know anything unless they have learned it as clearly as knowing that one, two, three, and four, when added together, make the number ten. But if they believe Him who said in the Gospel, "Seek and you shall find," <note>Matthew 7:7</note> the knowledge of what those numbers signify will become even more manifest.

<margin>The nature of the difference between Christians and Hebrews, and how the Jews are surpassed.</margin> There is, however, a disagreement between us Christians and the obstinate Hebrews regarding the meaning of the sacred scriptures. But we easily convict them by an examination of those very letters which they revere: by the course of their long captivity, by the timing of the promised Prophet, by the perfection of the Gospel, by the religion of the nations in worshipping Christ, and by the miracles proving all these things.

<margin>That among Christians there is no entirely stubborn dispute in matters necessary for salvation.</margin> There is also sometimes a dispute among Christians themselves, though not an entirely stubborn one. These disputes were largely produced by the doctrines of the philosophers, while our people thought it useful to mix their disputations with divine scripture to explode various heresies. But all our people cling harmoniously to the foundation of the letter and the clear sense, and we revere it with the greatest simplicity.

SECOND [BOOK]                                                                                             LXXV

you may know that you have entered into an inexhaustible store of wealth; for by following the literary context, you will be able to build up whatever truth you find elsewhere, and most learnedly derive connections, and penetrate—both by divine grace and the light of your own intellect—into matters where the unrefined and those destitute of such light could not penetrate at all.

### Epilogue of the Second Book. Chapter XXXVIII and last.

How variously and how contentiously the philosophers of the nations <note>original: "gentium," referring to non-Christian or pagan thinkers</note> have discussed the truth, we have revealed throughout the entire course of this second book. From this, it is easily gathered that if so many brilliant minds labored through so many centuries in search of it—either in vain or with little fruit—it is by no means easy for human effort alone to grasp that very truth. Indeed, those who dedicated themselves to its inquiry confirmed, no less by their deeds than by their words, that truth lay hidden in caves and in the deepest wells. They also made it clearly understood that what Augustine pronounces concerning them in his work *The City of God* is true: <margin>Augustine</margin> that those same philosophers disagreed not about fields or houses, or any financial matter, but about those things by which one lives either miserably or blessedly. In these discussions, even if some true things were said, false things were uttered with the same license, so that not without reason did such a city receive the mystical name of Babylon <note>Augustine uses Babylon to symbolize the "City of Man," characterized by confusion and worldly discord</note>. These are the words of Augustine, and they are undoubtedly excellent. And certainly, when they disagreed about God himself or about nature in general—since it was necessary to pursue this through the highest speculation of the mind—if those same philosophers had not perceived it rightly, or exactly and perfectly <note>original: "ad amussim," literally "according to the carpenter's rule"</note>, the sublimity of the subject might have shielded them from reproach, lest they be blamed in the name of ignorance or negligence. If, when they disputed about the heavens and those things which happen on high—the generation of winds, lightnings, and storms—and likewise when they commented on the movements of the earth, springs, rivers, the sea, and finally those things which occur in the hidden caverns and bowels of the earth, they had not used a true plumb line, pardon would be easily granted; for those things, being remote from the senses, could be thought beyond human capacity. But when they cast doubt upon all morals and vices, what manner of conducting life did they leave behind for their present disciples or for posterity? And since they neither knew nor demonstrated any end of good things <note>the "summum bonum" or highest good</note> by which this animal <note>man</note>, born for happiness, might be blessed: what could they utter concerning universal philosophy that was not raving? Or perhaps did Aristotle excuse them, teaching that as each person is, so does the end appear to him? <margin>Against Aristotle.</margin> Or rather, should he have blamed this human race, by whose common consent a goal has not been established for all, toward which they ought to tend? How much more, therefore, were they wandering under a fog of ignorance while searching for the paths of truth and goodness in detail—paths through which access to that ultimate goal of truth and goodness would have been opened? Furthermore, when they doubted whether there was any truth at all, and brought forward so many reasons for that doubt, what handle of excuse, I ask, remained for them? O singular mercy of God! O human blindness! O pestilential arrogance of those who thought they knew something without the divine light! <margin>Note, reader, the most excellent wisdom and goodness of God.</margin> For while the philosophers of the nations were wandering as if in a dark and unlit labyrinth of nature, pleasing themselves too much and delighting in their own blindness, a light appeared from heaven by which the exit to heaven might lie open; and from there, threads were let down <note>A reference to Ariadne’s thread, used to navigate the labyrinth</note> by which that ungraspable and inescapable error might be made known. Truth itself came to men—Christ, both God and man, the source and origin of all truth. Nor did He come before the philosophers of the nations themselves confessed that truth had been long sought but not clearly and exactly found. "I," He said, "am the way, the truth, and the life," and elsewhere, "For this I was born, and for this I came into the world."

<note>original: "LIBER"</note>

...that I might bear witness to the truth. In what way could we have received a testimony of truth among the philosophers of the nations <note>The "nations" or "gentiles" refers to non-Christian, specifically ancient Greek and Roman, thinkers.</note>? For even those who were most illustrious among them would plainly concede that they did not recognize that very truth. It is manifest that one cannot bear witness to what one is ignorant of. Therefore, the philosophers, following the wandering tracks of human wisdom, were distracted among many sects and, as if mangled and torn apart into diverse opinions, they lacked the light of the true. And while the entire world was full of ignorance, and all the sects devoted to capturing the truth were merely hallucinating it, the discipline of Christ revealed that very truth by drawing back the shadows.

<margin>Two principal benefits from Christian discipline.</margin> From this discipline, we have been able to gather two principal benefits in general: both how the nations were wandering in error, and how the law divinely given to Moses was to be understood—not as the Jews thought, but spiritually. Both the Gospel and its sacred commentators have opened this up clearer than light, and have set before good minds the very sea of truth to be navigated. Therefore, in this sea of truth, the truth is both to be sought and to be cherished; when you have tasted it, give thanks to God, in whose light you have begun to see the light. And reveal it to others in the words of the Apostle, lest they walk as the nations do in the vanity of their own senses. To discuss their vanity more explicitly, let us close this second book and begin the third.

->**THE THIRD BOOK OF GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, LORD AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA, ON THE EXAMINATION OF THE VANITY OF THE DOCTRINE OF THE NATIONS AND THE TRUTH OF THE CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE.**<-

**PREFACE**

<margin>A</margin> **I**t is recorded in memory that Apelles, that most celebrated painter, when he had painted a horse with marvelous skill, attempted to add foam to its mouth. Frustrated by his lack of success in the matter, he threw the sponge with which the colors were wiped from the brushes at the tablet; by its contact, the foam which the best master of the art could not produce happened by chance. If I were to say that this happened to me in large part in a dissimilar matter, I would perhaps not be justly blamed. However, I wish what I am about to say to be attributed not to chance, but to certain causes and ultimately to divine providence. I had long been of a doubtful mind whether I ought to commit to paper what I had conceived regarding the philosophers of the nations and hand it over to others to read. Many things moved me this way and that: I judged that critics <note>original: "zoilos" — a reference to Zoilus, a harsh ancient critic; a "nitpicker."</note> would not be lacking, and I perceived by more than average conjecture that many would arise to pluck at such a bold deed. But I was also stimulated by public utility and urged by the love of truth, which it is right to prefer above all else. I thought it would be more excellent if I brought forth what I had conceived in my mind, which would be not unwelcome, if perhaps not to many, then certainly to some. While these things were perhaps turning in my mind, and no hope of accomplishing what I had desired flourished, behold, suddenly a certain whirlwind, as it were, seized me; and while it seemed to elevate me on high, it drove me a little less than headlong. For Julius II, the Supreme Pontiff, a man of vast and terrible spirit, while he prepared war against Alfonso, Prince of Ferrara—whom he had interdicted from all sacred rites and had punished by arms with the loss of several towns of Emilia and the city of Modena—was about to attack Ferrara itself in the middle of winter amidst great snows. I, for whom the ninth year of exile was now passing, was in my homeland <note>Mirandola</note>, which was conducive to the attacking of Ferrara...
