# BOOK <unclear>TWO</unclear> <note>The Latin 'LIBER' is followed by an illegible numeral, likely 'II' based on the transition from the 'previous book' mentioned in the text.</note>

### That two sects of philosophers, the Epicurean and the Pyrrhonian, held the liberal disciplines in no esteem, and for what reasons, and how they differed from one another. Chapter One.

->**Q**<- uas much as the philosophers of the nations have decreed variously, diversely, and contentiously concerning truth itself and its judgment, I believe I have sufficiently explained in the previous book; therein we reviewed not only their opinions, but also the arguments by which they were moved and the reasons by which they were persuaded to make such decrees. It remains for us to follow through with the liberal arts and every part of philosophy: declaring how controversially, how variously, and how discordantly they have also decided concerning all those things which are usually held in the highest esteem for the cultivation of the mind and the notion of truth. 

And to begin with the liberal arts, I find that they were valued either not at all or certainly very little by two sects of philosophers, though for different reasons. For Epicurus and most of his followers thought they had no importance for the perfection of wisdom. Most scholars think this was done by them for a twofold reason: either to hide their own ignorance—since Epicurus was thought by many to be unrefined and unlearned—or because they did not wish to agree with Plato, Aristotle, and others who were, and were held to be, most learned, acting as if out of a certain resentment. These are the causes usually brought forward, one or the other of which Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman rhetorician.</note> perhaps indicates; these are his words in the second book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: "For concerning Epicurus, who fled from all disciplines, I am not surprised." 

But another reason is also not passed over in silence: that Nausiphanes, a follower of Pyrrho and a teacher of Epicurus, was studiously engaged in the disciplines and instructed youths in them, especially in rhetoric. Epicurus, who listened to him, was moved by a certain enmity toward his master; so that he himself might seem to be **self-taught** <note>original: "αὐτοδίδακτος" (autodidaktos)</note>—that is, taught by himself—and a philosopher **by his own nature** <note>original: "αὐτοφυής" (autophuēs)</note>, he therefore became a despiser of the disciplines. 

The Pyrrhonians <note>Followers of the skeptic Pyrrho of Elis.</note>, however, did not themselves value the disciplines, but for entirely different reasons. It was not as if they thought those arts did not lead to wisdom; for if they had decreed this, they would have been counted among the "dogmatists" <note>Philosophers who assert certain truths as certain, whom the Skeptics avoided joining.</note>, from whom they wished to remain separate with great zeal. Nor did they think the arts should be rejected because they themselves lacked learning: for no sect was more learned, being most diligently versed in all the sects of other philosophers and the most experienced of all. Nor was it for the sake of anger or pride, since they were held among the other sects of philosophers to be both humane and mild. 

But in this matter, they experienced what they did in all other doctrines: they decided to wish for nothing on either side, but preferred to dispute on either side out of a desire for finding the truth. And when they perceived reasons and arguments on this side and that, it seemed more excellent to them to modestly suspend judgment rather than to deliver a sentence either impudently or arrogantly. Yet they themselves excelled in those disciplines, even if they did not value them too much. So also our <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine: who held them correctly? In his book *On Order*, although he had attributed much to the liberal disciplines themselves, in his book of *Retractations* he approved of this less, since many holy people are quite ignorant of them, and those who do know them are not holy. However, he did not therefore withhold his assent in the manner of the Pyrrhonians.

BOOK THREE [space] 77

The Pyrrhonists <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis, the founder of Scepticism</note> themselves brought forward arguments by which they professed to suspend judgment and not to cling to the dogmatic philosophers who extol the liberal arts so wonderfully. They proceeded by a twofold path: first, generally or universally; then, specifically. They first considered that if any discipline exists, four things must be established: the matter which is taught, the one who teaches, the one who learns, and the method of instruction. Against all of these they first dispute so that the discipline itself may be left in doubt as a whole. Soon they bring the specific disciplines—grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astrology—into controversy. Therefore, as far as it pertains to the matter which is taught, they argue in roughly this manner: that which is passed on in instruction either is, or is not; likewise, it is either true or false. If the first <note>i.e., if it does not exist</note>, since it does not exist, how can it be taught? For instruction is not of those things which do not exist. And if false things were taught, what would be the future utility of the instruction? <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin> Indeed, how great a stain on the mind if, for example, that were passed on as truth instead of being false. And even if being, insofar as it is being, is said to be taught because it is such: it will become manifest that not all instruction proceeds from certain confessed and manifest things. But if they say that not being as such, but something else is taught, let them hear that there is nothing which escapes that vast circuit of being. <margin>Method of apprehension</margin> If that which is passed on is said to be true, then they say that how easily any ambiguous truth can be found can appear from those things which were brought forward when we were dealing with the criterion of judgment. Furthermore, the matter which is passed on in instruction either appears, or it does not; it is either clear or obscure to cognition. If you grant the first, there will be no need for a discipline, for those things which are clear appear equally to all. If the second, since those things which are not manifest are under dispute because of their ambiguous and least-judged nature, how shall they be taught? <margin>Whether body or incorporeal</margin> Moreover, that which is passed on by instruction and perceived through a discipline is either a body or incorporeal, and each of these suffers from difficulty. For a body, according to the dogmas of the Stoics, is not counted among those things which can be taught; for only propositions <note>original: "enunciata"</note> are of such a kind as to be grasped by a discipline—that is, things which are not bodies—and they say these are not sensible things either, and that this is proved by the notion of them, since it is either a combination of magnitude and figure and resistance <note>original: "ἀντιτυπίας" (antitypias)</note>, or it is divided threefold by width, length, and depth as pleased the mathematicians, or it is the triple dimension itself with resistance <note>original: "μετὰ ἀντιτυπίας" (meta antitypias)</note> as it seemed to Epicurus, so that from this he might define a vacuum. Or it is a resistant swelling, as others have wished. Therefore, its nature is not one and simple, but is a combination of many things fashioned by the intellect. But if this is granted, it will not be a sensible thing, and even if that is conceded, it will not be grasped by instruction, insofar as a sensible thing does not need instruction to be perceived by the mind—just as one does not learn in order to see white. <margin>The sense does not need instruction</margin> Therefore, we shall observe from this whether it will be perceived as an intelligible thing and whether it be true. For if neither width by itself is a body, nor likewise length by itself, nor depth: that which is conceived to be constituted from all these will be a body. Or is a body made from incorporeal things? Incorporeal things also do not fall under the senses, from which the mind is accustomed to form a notion. And furthermore, they say that of bodies, one kind is sensible, or another is intelligible, and there is no other supreme difference between them. Not the former: because that would be confessed by all endowed with sense; nor the latter, because there is a fight among all philosophers on this matter. For some say atoms; others say indivisibles; and among these, some divide these into infinites, others into the smallest and impartible parts. Incorporeal things are also not manifest, such as Platonic Ideas, or the propositions of the Stoics, place, vacuum, time, and other things of this sort, which some say exist, others say do not exist, and others abstain from assent. <margin>The author responds to the sceptics</margin> By these and similar attacks, the Sceptics [present] things which are not at all true, yet have the appearance [of truth].

But when they <note>The Sceptics</note> think that not only is what is handed down in a discipline ambiguous, but they also believe it should be done away with entirely—so that the duty of teacher and student, so celebrated among the Dogmatics <note>Philosophers who claim to hold certain truths, as opposed to Sceptics</note>, is no longer practiced—they generally argue as follows: Either a master teaches a master. But in what way does one require the instruction of the other? Or he instructs a master who lacks skill—but whoever said that would provoke laughter. Or one without skill teaches another without skill—but how could the blind lead the blind? Or he who excels in art and would grasp it by art establishes it—but how shall he excel in art by his own nature, as if he brought the art with him from his mother’s womb? Not in the least. For by what way, since he is without it, shall he become a participant and possessor of the art? For either a single contemplation <note>original: "speculatio"; a focused mental observation or theory</note> can effect this, or not at all. If the first, it will be possible to deduce by a good connection that art is not a collection of comprehensions and notions. And furthermore, who would endure that a man be called a master who held only one single precept of an art and was imbued with only a single contemplation? But if someone should say that one can perfect a heap of others and bestow the name of master: let him take heed, for it is not accounted in an unnumbered way by which and by how many contemplations each art is completed. Therefore, he will never know what is lacking to perfect the art. Indeed, all things are not grasped collectively, but individually, even if it be granted that they can be grasped. Therefore, let them say in what way a master is established? Even one who is established doubts the precepts of that same art and is attacked by others. Furthermore, as for him who is said to learn an art without skill, insofar as he is without skill, let them see to it that they do not learn just as the blind learn colors and the deaf learn sounds. Otherwise, is he both a participant and devoid of the same art? Devoid indeed, since it is so supposed; a participant because he has a comprehension of the theorems of the art. But the Sceptics are deceived in the way we mentioned above, in that which is "simply" and "in part," for he who learns is in some way a participant in the art by power—that is, by potentiality and aptitude.

Hitherto the Sceptics add many things regarding those matters which they bring into the open while they dispute against the physicists: when they argue against the transforming and receiving cause, and they allege generation and corruption. Likewise, they think the method of teaching will be destroyed if neither one who learns nor one who teaches can be found. Specifically, they insist thus: Either it consists in clarity or in speech. But if the former were true: since clarity belongs to those things which are shown and manifest, they would already be understood by everyone, and there would be no need for any teaching. But in what way by speech? For either it signifies something, or not at all; they are certainly not going to say the latter. Otherwise, how would anything signify by its ministry and use? If indeed it signifies, it is either by the position and will of men, or by its own nature. Certainly not the latter, otherwise all men would use one language; therefore, it is the former. But what, I pray, would that teach him who otherwise remains entirely ignorant of what it signifies? Does it not rather bring back to memory, as if by certain signs, those things which he had learned before? Furthermore, they want the comprehension instilled for the sake of the teacher to be equal in the one who learns, which they judge will be destroyed by many arguments. Regarding the studies of life and the virtues, and especially prudence <term>prudence: "prudentia," the practical wisdom or moral discernment required for virtuous living</term>, they doubt whether it comes from the prudent or the imprudent, or the opposite? And similar things which were brought up above concerning the master and the one ignorant of art, adding this: If prudence is established as the knowledge of good, evil, and neutral things, when the imprudent man hears the words, will he understand the matter? Will he perceive it? If he perceives it, he will not be imprudent; if he does not perceive the matter, though he holds the words, and you judge him prudent, you must also admit that imprudence is the knowledge of those things of which there is prudence. Thus say the Sceptics. But this does not hinder us, for prudence is acquired more by use than it is learned, and there is a light within us marked upon us...

### Chapter III. What the Sceptics are accustomed to dispute against Grammar, where also many other things from other authors are found.

        Nevertheless, the Sceptics poured out those very arguments against those who professed to be engaged in the disciplines and to know many things, as if against the whole world. And so that they might show from this that everything which those men established could be destroyed, they did not run through their individual dogmas—for that would have been a work of infinite labor—but they thought their paths should be blocked and their foundations, as it were, cut away; once these were undermined, whatever had been built upon them would fall in a single ruin. Therefore, they took care that the principles, or those things which flowed from the principles, and the more notable methods or ends, should be abolished. They began from Grammar. Now, this was spoken of in two ways: <margin>Grammar in two ways.</margin> for one is the knowledge of articulate voices of whatever kind, the other is that which, as a part of this, is reduced to order and art in some manner, and is like a certain part and species of the former, about which among the Greeks, Crates, Aristophanes, Aristarchus, and others have taught. Among the Latins also, some have followed in their imitation. So also Medicine, which among the Greeks was given the name *iatrikē* <note>original: ἰατρική</note>, <margin>Where Medicine comes from among the Greeks.</margin> was called in ancient times from the "removal of arrows" <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν ἰῶν ἐξαιρέσεως. A folk etymology linking the Greek word for doctor to the word for arrows or poisons.</note>. Now, however, it is equipped for expelling other diseases and disturbances of the body, being more strongly supported by art. And Geometry, which formerly took its name from the "measuring of lands," <margin>Where Geometry comes from.</margin> has now drawn its nomenclature from much more subtle things. Or as it pleased Asclepiades, that name is from "letters" <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν γραμμάτων</note>, that is, from literature; or from "writings" <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν συγγραμμάτων</note>, that is, derived from compositions. Therefore, the Sceptics attack that which has claimed for itself the name of art and learning, but not before they have defined what it is. In this matter, they by no means despised the opinion of Epicurus, <margin>The opinion of Epicurus.</margin> by which he decreed that nothing can be sought or doubted without a concept <note>The Epicurean idea of *prolepsis* or "preconception" necessary for inquiry.</note>. Therefore, Dionysius Thrax <margin>Dionysius Thrax.</margin> conceives of and defines Grammar as *empeiria* <note>original: ἐμπειρίαν</note>—you might say "experience" or "skill"—in those things which are said for the most part by poets in verse and by historians in prose. For the Grammarian interprets what Homer, Pindar, Menander, Herodotus, and what Virgil, Horace, Plautus, Livy, and moreover what the rhetoricians and philosophers have handed down. Ptolemy the Peripatetic contradicted him, <margin>Ptolemy the Peripatetic.</margin> arguing that it is not that kind of skill and experience, because the latter is established without art and without reason, by the mere observation and practice of a single thing, whereas this [Grammar] truly is and is held to be an art, and has also obtained the name of an art; concerning which matter Sextus wrote much in his *Empirical Commentaries*. <margin>Sextus. Metrodorus.</margin> Metrodorus wished that there be no skill which considers its own end except philosophy: taking "skill" there to mean "art." But it is chiefly used for the knowledge of many and various things. Just as old men, because they have seen much and heard much, are said to be "experienced in life." But indeed, as for those who excel in that skill: if it is of all things—since all those particulars are infinite—the Grammarian will be held to be skilled in infinite things; if it is of some things, he will not be skilled for that reason, since even those who are not Grammarians know some few things of the poets and historians. If they say "the most part," let them declare which things they are, so that we may discern how far the skill extends. But if they wish to determine and number them, let them confess that there is need of some finite and determined number; yet if "the most part" is contained therein, and if one unit is taken away, they will still say it is "the most part," for it is absurd for something to be called "the most part" or "not the most part" by the addition or subtraction of a single unit. But if this is done repeatedly, the matter will come to the point where there is no "most part" number: by which it will happen that neither is that [Grammar]...

grammar, for "the many" and "the few" are relative terms. For if a "great number" of known things constitutes grammatical skill, then a "few" things—being not many—will not constitute it. Furthermore, it is false to say the grammarian knows "the most" things, since there are far more things of which he is ignorant. To this we add that "skill" <term>peritia: practical knowledge gained by experience</term> concerns things perceived by conjecture, such as the faculties of navigation or medicine. Grammar, however, conjectures nothing. Those who preferred not to include that word "most" did not remove the doubt but rather increased it. To this is added the fact that voices change in every way through the course of ages. <meta>This page continues the critique of the liberal arts, specifically focusing on the "artificial" or technical part of grammar. The author is engaging with Sceptic arguments (likely Sextus Empiricus) regarding the nature of elements and letters.</meta>

->THIRD [BOOK]<-                                                                                              LXXIX

The task of judging is found to be manifoldly complicated, if one considers that the understanding of poets cannot be obtained without art and historical skill, and that neither of those two can be perceived without the other. Therefore, these things are not distinct or clearly separated from one another. And from this, it could also be concluded that if one of them were removed, the others would be abolished because of their mixing, shared nature, and entanglement. Yet they nevertheless strive to abolish each one separately, beginning with the **artificial** part. They attempt to show that this part is without art, without method, and without foundation, starting from the **elements** <note>original: "elementis"; here referring to the letters of the alphabet as the fundamental building blocks of language</note>. Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a Pyrrhonist philosopher who argued against the professors of various arts</note> objects to the division of these as vain and useless. For he contends that the so-called "double" elements, <margin>Against the artificial part.</margin> **ζ** [zeta], **ξ** [xi], **ψ** [psi]—inasmuch as they are composed of **σ** [sigma] and **δ** [delta], or **κ** [kappa] and **σ**, or **π** [pi] and **σ**—ought not to be called elements. Let him use the example of Greek letters, since among Sceptic writers there was no use of the Latin language. But since they share many points in common with Latin grammar, I will also mark many things from that when the opportunity arises. Therefore, a double element, because it is gathered from two, ought neither to be called nor held to be a simple element. For if the things that constitute a double element are themselves elements, then the thing constituted from them will not be an element. To these, they argue by similar reasoning that those which are called "two-timed" <note>vowels that can be either long or short</note>, and liquids, and common, and ambiguous, and changeable—**α** [alpha], **ι** [iota], **υ** [upsilon]—are not elements. For either the element itself or the letter by its own nature announces such a common and ambiguous faculty, or it does so by the addition of an **accent** <note>original: "accentu"; here referring to marks of prosody or vowel length</note>, by which a syllable is either shortened or lengthened. How will they say the first is possible? Namely, that a simple letter should indicate by itself its own common nature or condition and faculty—that is, both long and short—when one of these is the opposite of the other. But if they say the second, this inconvenience follows: that while it can signify either long when it is so, or short when it is so, by means of an accent, how will the "common" nature be announced by the accent itself? Is there any mark among grammarians by which the ambiguous nature of a letter or syllable is suggested to the mind of the reader? But if they respond that they are called <margin>Response.</margin> "common" by their own nature because they are susceptible to both times, namely long and short, they will return to the same point. For that which is susceptible to something is not the thing itself <margin>Refutation.</margin> for which it is susceptible. For bronze is capable of becoming an image or a statue, yet it is not itself the statue; therefore, if they receive long and short time by turns, they themselves are neither long nor short, nor do they indicate the commonality of both. This is even more true because "long" is the opposite of "short," and they are not established at the same time; when length is removed, shortness is established, and length is placed only when shortness itself is removed. For this reason, it is impossible for a **circumflex** mark to turn out short, since by the very "flex" <note>the shape of the accent mark</note>, length is necessarily established. Therefore, if an element is "two-timed" by nature, it will either establish the power of both length and shortness under one single thing, or according to a part. How the first? Since around the same vocalization, by itself and according to the same thing, opposing powers would be established: namely, stopping and extending. Can the second ever be persuaded? For who does not know that when the accent sign is long, it is not common to both length and shortness? A similar mode of attack would apply to the **intense** and **aspirated** <note>referring to breathed or emphasized consonants</note> sounds, and those common to both, but let it suffice to have shown the mode of attacking. From these things, it follows that each of those elements is double, not simple. For which reason it happens that there are not merely seven vocal elements—of which two are long, **η** [eta] and **ω** [omega]; two are short, **ε** [epsilon] and **ο** [omicron]; and three are the "two-timed" ones we are discussing—but ten: five of which are long (**η**, **ω**, **α**, **ι**, **υ**) and five of which are short (**α**, **ι**, **υ**, **ε**, **ο**). In the same way, if a consideration of accents is made, the vowel letters will be multiplied beyond measure; for those two short ones, since they [are] five...

<note>The author is discussing the phonetic properties of vowels and how they carry different accents and breathings.</note>
They are considered the recipients of these qualities: short, acute, long, thin, and thick <note>referring to vowel length, pitch accents, and "breathing" or aspiration</note>. Two of them are always long and likewise receive those five qualities, and in addition, they admit the circumflex vocalization. Those which are called "common" <note>vowels that can be either long or short, like 'a', 'i', and 'u'</note> each receive seven of these qualities. When these are multiplied by the logic already described and the consonants are added, one finds not twenty-four, but sixty elements. Some also gather fewer vowel elements than the grammarians say, on the grounds that if 'a' is either shortened or lengthened, it is not a different element but one common one; and so it ought to be. They argue that alpha, upsilon, epsilon, and eta <note>original: ".α.υ.atq;.ε. & .η."</note> are one and the same from the same common power. Since the power in both is the same, as when a shortened 'pi' is made with 'epsilon' it is of equal power, and an extended 'pi' becomes 'eta'; they decree that the same happens in the case of 'omicron' and 'omega'. 

Likewise, many of the philosophers establish that there are more vowel elements than are commonly thought, such as the diphthongs 'ai' and 'ou' <note>original: ".αι. & .ου."</note> and those of the same nature. For an element is judged to be an element primarily from an uncompounded and simple sound of a single quality, such as 'o' or 'e'. But since the diphthong 'ai' is held to be a sound of simple and single quality, it shall also be held as an element. The sign of a simple voice is if it is uttered equally from the beginning to the end. For that which is composite affects the sense of hearing differently at the beginning than at the end. For example, the sound "Ra" affects the sensory organ differently at each extreme; for at the beginning it is moved more by the 'R' itself, and at the end more by the 'a'. But 'o' affects the sense equally, so that the hearing which was moved at the beginning is in no way changed at the end; and the same judgment shall be held for the remaining diphthongs. 

Furthermore, regarding the three elements called "common" because they are susceptible to both brevity and length: should not all elements be called common in the same way, since they are all susceptible to gravity, sharpness, thinness, and thickness? These are both held in the place of accents and are counted as such. What has been said of Greek letters can be said even more so of Latin ones, since all vowels in the Roman tongue are held to be common, and 'x' and 'z' obtain the force of a double consonant; and as for accents, though they are not in common use, the art and knowledge of them is maintained. 

But let us now pass from letters to syllables. These they call both long and short: long either by nature or by position, and this in many ways, as will become clear in the course of the text. But if any short syllable is to be rightly established, it must be established in the minimum amount of time. However, time cannot be divided into a minimum, since it is divisible unto infinity, as will be made manifest; and that which can be divided cannot be a minimum. Therefore, a short syllable, which ought to be measured by a minimum time, will not be found. If someone should say that a syllable is called short and the same is a minimum—

<margin>Response.</margin>
—not because it is such by its own nature, but because it is so judged in relation to our senses: 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
he will increase the difficulty, not diminish it. For those syllables which are called short by the grammarians, we find that by the judgment of the senses they are held to be divisible, not minimal. For when we perceive the syllable "ER" (for example) being uttered, the force and power of the 'e' itself is felt before that of the 'R'. The power of the 'e' itself affects the sensory organ first and runs through its own sound. Nor does it happen otherwise if we invert it and express it as "RE"; for the 'R' is felt by the ear before the 'e'. Where there is a prior and a posterior part in relation to the sense, shall we judge that of which those are parts to be a minimum and indivisible? And although musicians have perhaps devised certain "irrational" times and augmentations of voices, that depth is not granted to the grammarians, who distinguish all syllables generally into short and long. We have already shown the short syllable to be inconsistent; let us show also that the long syllable has no standing. They say it consists of two times. But two times do not exist simultaneously. For if they are two, they are by this very fact divided...

...there are two things, of which one exists and the other does not. If indeed one of the two remains while the other does not remain, both can by no means exist at the same time. Therefore, if a long syllable consists of two <term>times</term><note>original: "temporum"; in classical prosody, a "time" or "mora" is the unit of duration for a short syllable; a long syllable equals two morae.</note>, its first time will exist when the second does not, or conversely, the latter will only exist when the former has been abolished; but both together, never. If indeed someone were to say <margin>Response.</margin> that this is achieved by memory—namely, that from the sound which preceded and that which follows, one single thing is established to which the name of "long syllable" is given—that person would himself be admitting that a long syllable cannot exist as a stable entity. For if <margin>Refutation.</margin> it were to exist, it would have to exist either in that which is uttered first, or in that which is brought in after; but it can happen in neither, because if you take either one separately, it does not exist as a whole. For when one utters the first part, the second does not yet exist; and when the second is uttered, the first has already preceded it and vanished. Who would not notice that from that which is and that which is not yet, nothing can be established, grow together, or exist? By the same reasoning, the way is opened for disputing against words and the other parts of speech, and that common argument is brought against speech itself: either speech is something other than <margin>What the Sceptics argue against grammatical speech.</margin> its own parts, and the parts themselves are different and separate from it, or speech is the very collection of those parts. If the first is granted, who does not perceive that if all the parts are removed, that which is "other" than them would remain? But so far is it from the case that speech is not destroyed when all its parts are removed, that even if you take away just one, the whole perishes. For example, this line of speech: *Sing to me, Muse, of the wrath of the fierce son of Peleus*<note>original: "Iram pande mihi pelidæ muſa ferocis"; a Latin translation of the opening of Homer's Iliad.</note>; if it is diminished by even one word, it will no longer be considered a verse or a complete speech. If, however, the second option is taken—so that speech is nothing other than its parts collected into one—it will seem to follow that the parts are considered parts of each other. For if there is no "whole" underlying them besides the parts themselves to which they belong, then one part will be the part of another. This cannot happen, since parts are usually included within that of which they are parts; just as in a man there are feet, hands, and a head; in the feet and hands there are fingers; in the head, eyes, nose, ears, and the rest, which are considered parts of the man himself. But the parts of speech are by no means contained in a part in this way; for "sing" is not enclosed in "wrath," nor the reverse; nor is "to me" contained in "son of Peleus," or vice versa. <margin>Objection.</margin> But it could be said on the contrary what Aristotle says in the *Metaphysics*, when he judges that a composite is a certain "third thing," different from the two parts that compose it; he uses this example: the syllable *ba*, which is neither *b* nor *a*, but *ba*. But the Sceptics <margin>Response.</margin> would respond by providing that it is already assumed and peacefully accepted that the letters *b* and *a* are considered parts of the syllable, which they themselves would bring into dispute, perhaps for this reason: that a whole and its part regard each other such that one cannot be understood without the other. However, *b* and *a* exist separately both by nature and by time before the syllable *ba*; and thus one must judge the parts of speech by the same proportion as the parts of a syllable. And furthermore, they ask, when it is affirmed by the grammarian that the word "wrath"...

<margin>On the imposition of names.</margin>
<margin>That names are not the same for all who use the same language.</margin>
<margin>Whether masculine and feminine names exist by imposition.</margin>
<margin>Response. Refutation.</margin>
<margin>Response. Refutation.</margin>

[Main Text]
...of all things, let that, if you please, be what is called a "name." Some names are called masculine, others feminine, and others neuter; their numbers are singular and plural, and among the Greeks, even dual. If this was done by nature, it was surely either established by those ancients among whom the first mention of a name occurred—who also expressed the cold by which they were affected and the pleasures by which they were soothed with certain sounds proceeding from nature—or it has come to pass because they naturally move the sense of each individual in the present, so that this is judged masculine and that feminine. 

If they say the former, whence then arises that question: do names consist by imposition <note>Latin: *positione*; referring to "convention" or man-made choice</note> or by nature? For it would be ended by a simpler discussion, which the philosophers would admit, among whom there is much dispute on this matter, argued with almost equal reasons on both sides. For if names existed by nature and not by imposition, would they not signify the same things to everyone—Greeks, Latins, Hebrews, and others? And if they moved every individual [the same way], what controversy would there be regarding this matter? For we would all feel ourselves moved in the same manner, just as we are all affected by fire and by cold. 

And yet, names are not the same for everyone, even for those using the same language. The Athenians utter "tin" <note>original: *stannum*</note> in the feminine, while the Peloponnesians use the masculine, and each of them believes they speak correctly. So too with "dome" <note>original: *tholus*</note>; some prefer it to be masculine, others of a different gender. And besides, they even write many names differently according to the manner, and sometimes some use one way or the other, because they have known it to be so instituted and positioned. Indeed, as for *limon* <note>original: λιμὸν; Greek for "hunger" or "famine"</note>, which name signifies "famine" in Latin, many of the Greeks pronounce it with both a feminine and a masculine voice. 

But if they should say that there are some things masculine by nature and some feminine, to which names of the same reasoning are fitted—so that masculine names denote masculine things and feminine names denote feminine things—[this is refuted]. For a masculine name is fitted to female mice, eagles, gnats, beetles, and scorpions; for all those—*mys, aetos, konops, kantharos, skorpios* <note>original: μυς, ἀετός, κωνωψ, κανθαρος, σκορπίος</note>—are pronounced among the Greeks for the females just as they are for their males. Conversely, the swallow, the tortoise, the crow, and the shrew-mouse are of the masculine sex, yet they are called by a feminine name among the Greeks: *chelidon, chelone, korone, mygale* <note>original: χελιδών, χελώνη, κορώνη, μυγαλή</note>, and many others besides could easily be found. 

Therefore, if no name is feminine or masculine by nature, but they consist by imposition, in what way do the grammarians decline names in the manner we have said? You will say, perhaps, that those which are of the other sex or gender are made into the other by the force of the article; but if by nature there is no such thing, will it not rather be indifferent whether it is uttered in this gender or that? But someone might say it has happened by usage that they were uttered now in this way, now in that; therefore, it was not a systematic reasoning <note>Latin: *artifex ratio*; literally "craftsman-like reason"</note> that did this, but a misuse.

And since observation has established this, they attempt to demolish both. Regarding the first point, it is sufficiently clear that they hand down an art in vain which is accepted by no one—much like someone wishing to bring outdated and rejected coins into the forum, which not even the traveling vegetable-sellers would accept. Regarding the second point, since usage and custom are varied, nothing fixed or entirely constant can be adopted. For according to the variety of minds, there have been various opinions, as Sextus <note>Likely referring to Sextus Empiricus, the skeptical philosopher whose work *Against the Grammarians* is the source for much of this argument.</note> is the author of this view. Nor were there lacking those who called Demosthenes, Thucydides, and Plato "barbarians." Aeschines also condemned Demosthenes for barbarism, and an Attic old woman called Theophrastus a "stranger" <note>original: "hospitem"</note> because of his affectation of a single word (if we also stand by the Latin authors). <margin>Note.</margin> But indeed, regarding the art of speaking itself, whether in Greek or Latin or any other way, what can be brought forward that is fixed and perpetual? Since all things are referred to custom, which is varied and diverse. For if they say they possess the art itself, they must say they hold and possess it either without an art or by some other art. If they proffer the former, they fall back upon custom supported by use but not by art; if the latter, there will be need for another art, and again another, until the discourse finds no end. For it will always be asked of that art: does it consist of any craftsmanship or not at all? Again, since among those things called arts, some are true arts and consist of their own principles—such as statuary or the military art—while others are not arts at all but exist in name only and in vain promises, such as astrology <note>original: "genethliaca," the casting of nativities</note> and geomancy <note>divination by earth or dots</note>, a judicial faculty will be needed to distinguish whether this property we are speaking of—the ability to differentiate correctly and significantly in every idiom—should be placed here or there. Moreover, this judicial faculty will prove the matter either properly and by art, discerning the right from the crooked, or without art. If they say the first, those inconveniences we taught above will occur, hanging from infinity. If they bring forward the second, what else would it be but custom, which requires no art? Furthermore, since speaking correctly in either Latin or Greek is nothing other than what we learn among the grammarians, that will surely be either clear and conspicuous, or obscure and unknown. The first cannot be said, because it would be harmonious and constant, not varied and disagreeing. And besides, in perceiving that which is clear, there is no need for art, just as we do not use art when we sense and perceive what is white or sweet or hot. But if the second is brought into the midst, it will happen that since it is obscure, it must be made manifest through something else; it must certainly be manifested either by some natural judge—whereby, with nature as a guide, Latinity or Greekness is distinguished from barbarism—or by some custom of speaking which is the highest and most perfect among all customs, or by every custom and every practice of discourse gathered together into one. He will by no means give the first, because among those who believe they speak Latin, some speak one way and others another, both in the genders of nouns and the inflections of verbs; no less among the Greeks, among whom the Attics say *the pickled fish* <note>original: "τὸ τάριχος" (neuter)</note> while the Peloponnesians say *the pickled fish* <note>original: "ὁ τάριχος" (masculine)</note>, and some utter *the pebble* <note>original: "λύσαμνον"</note> while others say *the pebble* <note>original: "τὸν σάμνον"</note>. Wherefore, how shall the grammarian prescribe or learn from this how one ought to speak? Since the particular customs of different people are established neither by art nor by nature. If, however, they choose one above the others, which they call the highest and perfect, they will say this either by simple assertion or by employing demonstrations and methodical proofs. If the first, we ourselves will say to the contrary that one ought to assent to the many rather than the one. If they bring forward the second, they will be forced to confess that this method is the norm and index by which the distinction between speaking correctly and incorrectly is made; since this cannot be done, it remains that it must yield to common custom. This, however, is attributed to common observation, not to a rule of analogy. Indeed, speaking Latin or Greek consists either by position <note>convention</note> or by nature. <margin>What is analogy.
Sextus.
Gellius.</margin>

that which is sanctioned by law will be more correctly understood by one who grasps it through use than by one who has hunted for it through **analogy** <note>The linguistic principle of regularity where words follow predictable patterns.</note>. But indeed, is not analogy itself derived from custom? If it is nothing other than the comparison of many similar nouns, as **Sextus** <note>Likely Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic philosopher who critiqued grammar.</note> defines it, or the consideration of equals and unequals as is written by the same author, or as **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius, author of 'Attic Nights'.</note> writes, the inflection of similar words. In his work, one can see that there was no small controversy even among the ancient and most highly approved grammarians, **Crates** and **Aristarchus**; while the latter defended analogy, the former defended **anomaly** <note>The principle that language is naturally irregular and unpredictable.</note>, that is, the inequality of inflection. **Marcus Varro**, in the eighth book of *On the Latin Language*, agreed with this and taught that there is no consistent observation of similarities, even if he defended analogy in other matters. 

Will analogy, I ask, be derived from custom and common usage? If it is the observation of many nouns. For nouns consist of custom; whence analogy is also considered indebted to custom. Since it depends on custom itself, if you take custom away, you have taken away analogy itself; if you accept custom, analogy will be judged in no way necessary. Furthermore, if we must stand by antiquity, who is a more ancient authority than the Greeks and Latins? That is certainly not sufficiently clear, and many things now antiquated are no longer received by common consent—into which consent, finally, all approved modes of speaking and all equally faulty speeches are referred, as if to a judge and arbiter of all speech. 

So from this, it is clear that those who define **barbarism** <note>Errors in a single word.</note> and **solecism** <note>Errors in grammatical construction.</note> remember custom; since they shrink from it, they are condemned as a vice. Moreover, this custom applies either to the consideration of each and every noun, or to some, or to many. Not to every single one, because they are ungrasped and innumerable. But if it applies to only some, it will not be universal; for what happens to certain nouns does not therefore happen to all. If it applies to most—from which some were babbling that a universal rule is falsely constructed—will those who speak thus not notice that what is understood universally differs from what happens frequently or for the most part? For the former is always the same way, while the latter sometimes fails and varies. 

For so it often happens in nouns as in the things of nature, that certain things are excepted which are not similar to others: such as the **magnet** among stones; **horned vipers** among serpents; the **Elephant** among quadrupeds; and among fish, that which the Greeks call the *galeos* <note>original: "galeon" - likely a type of shark or dogfish.</note>. Therefore, just as the magnet is set apart from other stones because it alone attracts iron or follows iron; and the Elephant from other animals because it alone is powerful with a trunk; and the horned vipers from serpents because they bear horns; and that fish from other fish because it is considered a viviparous animal <note>One that gives birth to live young rather than laying eggs.</note>: so nouns possess a certain peculiar inflection, so that they cannot be numbered among the rest as similar; and thus analogy is established. 

But if they retort to us that customs are also varied, that will not hinder us, but rather those who make themselves teachers of grammar. We shall throw that very thing back upon their own analogy: if it is indeed the observation of similarities, and the "similar" comes from custom, but custom is unequal and inconstant, will they not admit that analogy is, and ought to be held as, inconstant? 

<margin>Concerning etymology.</margin>

And if **etymology** claims to distinguish or judge for itself, they will say either that this very thing harmonizes and agrees with analogy, or not at all. If the first, it will be drawn from analogy. If the second, there will be no need for it, just as we said above concerning analogy and custom. Furthermore, regarding a noun which etymology must judge—whether it be Latin, Greek, or barbarian—it either has all preceding things subject to etymology itself, or it does not. If they grant the first, they will easily arrive at a certain infinite progress without any beginning, so that the beginning remains unknown, whatever is finally established, and to which language it ought to be ascribed; since it is not given to know from which word it finally [comes]...

First, let us consider how a word is derived. For example, the word "stone" <note>original: *lapis*</note> is believed to be a Latin name because it is so called because it "hurts the foot" <note>original: *laedit pedem*. This is a folk etymology common in Roman grammatical texts, linking *lapis* to *laedere* (to strike/hurt) and *pes* (foot).</note>. In turn, one must ask about that very word "hurts"—from what is it derived? And was that original term itself called by a Latin, Greek, or foreign <note>original: *barbara*</note> voice? For who can investigate, let alone establish and determine, the very first and highest principle from which a word has flowed?

If, however, they grant the second point, it will be easy to say—just as he says regarding those things which have no etymology. They admit that the very things containing a principle of etymology are referred back and resolved; they accept them and hold them as Latin or Greek not because of their etymology, but because of some worn-down habit and common usage. Thus, that which is accepted by its "true meaning" <term>etymon: the underlying "true" or original meaning of a word</term> and is therefore placed among Latin or Greek words, ought to be accepted not from etymology, but from use and custom. 

But indeed, it sometimes happens that the same things are called by two names: one which is powerful in its etymology, and another which is far removed from it. Surely you would not reject the latter as foreign while embracing the former for that reason alone?

[Sextus Empiricus] reports that he was of the family of the Elians, a disciple of Chrysippus of Cnidus <note>A famous 4th-century BCE physician</note>, and the teacher of Erasistratus. To him was born a son named Aristotle, from Pythias, the daughter of Aristotle himself. What art or method, I ask, exists in such matters? In matters, I say, which are in a certain sense infinite, and so varied that almost everyone holds their own opinion on them.

Take, for example, that story of Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note>, who is considered the inventor of the medical art among the Greeks and was killed by a lightning bolt. Some, like Stesichorus in his *Eriphyle*, claim he was struck from heaven because he raised certain men from the dead who had fallen in the Theban war. Others, such as Panyasis, say it was because he raised Tyndareus; others because he had recalled the son of Tyndareus to life. Polyanthus of Cyrene claims it was because he restored to health the daughters of Proetus, who were driven mad by the wrath of Juno <note>original: "Iunonis ira"</note>. Staphylus says it was because he cured Hippolytus as he was fleeing from Troezen. Phylarchus says it was because he brought aid to the blinded children of Phineus, intending to do a favor for their mother, Cleopatra. Telesarchus claims it was because he wished to raise Orion

<meta>This page continues the author's skeptical critique of the liberal arts, specifically targeting the claims made by grammarians regarding the necessity of their field for a virtuous or happy life.</meta>

### BOOK THREE <column-break/> PAGE 83

It is argued that grammar provides the opportunities for living most commodiously and contributes greatly to the attainment of happiness, and for that reason, grammar is necessary for us. To this, a response can be given: there is no truth in the premise, nor is that truth found in the conclusion (if it is taken as a consequence). For poets provide no fewer opportunities for evil, drawing men toward vice as much as toward virtue; they have written on diverse subjects, sometimes loosening the reins of vice and sometimes restraining them. This is easy to see if anyone takes them into their hands, even if one poet is more inclined toward virtue and another more prone to narrating or extolling vice. Therefore, a "little distinction" <term>discerniculo: a small tool for sorting or distinguishing</term> will be needed, which is sought not from grammar but from philosophy, which distinguishes poet from poet and passage from passage during the reading itself.

Furthermore, the art of grammar will not be necessary for this reason, since the noble sentiments found in poets can be drawn out without its assistance. For who would not notice either the warnings or the supreme precepts without grammar? Just as the common people commit many things to memory for the use of life—even those spoken enigmatically—or speak proverbs, or admit into the inner chambers of the soul and the recesses of the mind certain remarkable deeds from foreign histories perceived with a keen ear.

But regarding that part which they say contributes to happiness, I do not know whether it is because they define happiness correctly and teach the method and way of finding it? Or because they judge it useful for life? Perhaps because it was once useful for increasing wealth or attaining leadership; but whichever they prefer, even if they take both at once, no advantage for a blessed life comes to them, and there is no increase in happiness. For what shall I say about defining happiness? When many think that Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher often associated (sometimes unfairly) with the pursuit of pleasure</note> drew the idea that the highest good is in pleasure from Homer; that many had the opportunity for impiety from Euripides; that many sought the fuel for impure and obscene love and a drunken life from Alcaeus and Anacreon; and there are those who would have it that they drank the precepts of anger from Archilochus and Hipponax. It would be a long task to recount every instance where some have rushed headlong into ruin because of things they learned wrongly from the poets.

If they say it is useful at times, and therefore opens the path to happiness, they are far mistaken; for that which is useful to life at one time is not so always, nor does it lead to that ultimate end. Otherwise, dancing would also contribute to happiness, since it was once useful to Sostratus in liberating his homeland of Priene, when Antiochus granted him that very gift because of his dancing. For even some mechanical arts are held to be not only useful but necessary among men, yet they in no way provide happiness.

But lest we utterly reject the idea that poetry is in some part useful for the sake of life, and seem to completely refute other arts that greatly serve man, let us examine those who say grammar is necessary to those very arts as a "knower" and "judge." Upon what foundation do they lean? A solid one or one of sand? For all poetry and all history which is submitted to the grammarian to be "winnowed" <term>eventilanda: literally to fan or winnow grain, here meaning to critically examine</term> is composed of the words declaring and the things declared. Therefore, it will be necessary for the grammarian—if he has any art of discerning and judging poets and historians—to know either the words alone, or the things alone, or both.

But how shall the grammarian recognize the "things"? For some are physical, others metaphysical, others mathematical. Will anyone understand physical things besides the physicist? They are so involved, complex, varied, and inconstant. Or shall he know mathematics who has not previously been engaged in their speculations? How much less, then, those things which are above sense and human imagination? Shall the grammarian then be altogether wise and, as is said in Greek, *all-wise* <note>original: "πανσοφος" (pansophos)</note> and skilled in every science? But if he is blind in these matters, he will certainly be no less blind in the poems which are produced from them.

This was the case among the Athenians, <margin>Laws of the Athenians.</margin> so that for this reason Plato, the author of the Old Comedy <note>Not the famous philosopher, but a comic poet of the same name.</note>, wrote that if anyone were to travel abroad for three months, he would no longer recognize his own city. They even command sometimes that laws should be read according to an *apocope* <note>A technical term for a "cutting off" or shortening of a word or phrase.</note>, and that some concept or understanding should be composed from those parts which are left. Frequently, indeed, they distinguish between ambiguous words, choosing a meaning useful to themselves, and six hundred other beggarly deceits. In this way, they wish a rhetorician to be deservedly condemned if he excels in fostering unjust causes, <margin>The Refutation.</margin> but they hold that this is a fault of the human mind, not of the art itself. Nevertheless, the detractors of rhetoric stand their ground, contending that a "wise man" of the kind they describe is either never found or found only very rarely. Therefore, they argue that such a rhetoric cannot exist if such men do not exist, or only as rarely as a prodigy. They also reject the example of the warrior or the athlete; for those men do not teach others to do wrong, though they may sometimes do so themselves. The rhetorician, however, gives instructions in his art on how great things may become small, how small things may grow into great ones, how just things may become unjust (and vice versa), and how they may turn black into white. Furthermore, since rhetoric itself is constituted from contrary reasons and speeches, and since the unjust is contrary to the just, it follows that such a rhetorician devotes himself to injustice.

Furthermore, they have wished to argue that rhetoric is not an art based on the material it deals with: first, from those things which were disputed against the grammarians concerning words and speech; and second, from the quality of the speech itself. For if speech is not useful, but harmful, or a mixture of the harmful and the useful, the art founded upon it should be considered an evil rather than worthy of the name of an "art"—just as those things concerning unhealthy or deadly...

->BOOK THREE<-                                                                                                LXXXV

If a person were to administer deadly drugs, or mixtures composed of both deadly and healthful substances, that practice would not be called medicine or an art. In the same way, a faculty that is slanderous and a disturber of civil life should not be graced with the name of "art." Furthermore, "speaking well" <note>original: "benedicere"</note> does not only pertain to the rhetorician, but is common to all fields of learning and disciplines. Moreover, the very phrase "speaking well" suffers from much difficulty regarding how it ought to be understood: whether it means announcing useful things, or using words proper to the language in which one is engaged, or explaining a matter briefly and concisely. For rhetoricians know little or nothing of the actual subjects themselves, and both common custom and the liberal arts also claim the propriety of language for themselves. Indeed, they are so far from speaking briefly that they employ long periods and exclamations <term>epiphonematibus: a striking concluding sentence or exclamation</term>, and they avoid the clashing of vowels, and search from afar for words with similar endings—to such an extent that if anyone wished to use common speech in the way they do in their orations, he would be laughed at. They also stir up controversy regarding the very goal <note>original: "fine," referring to the 'telos' or ultimate purpose</note> of rhetoric.

Furthermore, rhetoric does not pursue that which is "persuasive" in a way that is common to both truth and falsehood; for in that case, falsehood is intertwined, which is something a true art <term>art (Latin: ars/Greek: techne)</term><note>In this context, an 'art' refers to a systematic body of knowledge with a reliable method, not just a creative skill.</note> by no means accepts. If it is an art, how can it have a purpose in common with other arts and with other things that are not arts? For "to persuade" is common to many things, since many people are persuaded by riches, by glory, by uprightness, and even by physical gifts. 

Moreover, rhetorical speech—engaged as it is in rounded periods and the artificial harmony of words—is not necessarily persuasive; for a simple style of speech is often more persuasive. Indeed, the speaker who possesses nothing "juicy" <note>original: "suci" - referring to a lush or overly-ornamented style</note> and nothing of craftiness more easily wins over the judge and almost every kind of listener. Whatever is taken from a hypothesis to establish belief in a matter is either firm and stable, or weak and feeble. If it is firm and stable, then whatever is taken against it from a hypothesis will also be firm and stable; therefore, we shall be positing conflicting and contradictory things. If, however, that which is against and opposite to what was taken from the hypothesis is not going to establish belief without a demonstration, then the hypothesis itself will likewise fail to establish belief in that matter; therefore, let us suppose neither. It can be gathered from this part, therefore, that nothing should be taken from a hypothesis or a supposition. Furthermore, the very thing which is supposed to be is either true or false. If it is true, let us not seek it nor demand that it be granted to us—namely, by fleeing to a hypothesis, a thing full of suspicion—but rather [let us take it] of our own accord... <note>The text breaks off mid-word at "cap-", likely "capiamus" (let us take).</note>

Those who observe the things that appear to the senses will find that if no sign <note>original: "signum," here meaning a geometric point</note> or boundary appears among sensible objects without dimension, then we must also perceive and think the same regarding those things which we grasp through the imagination. Therefore, if nothing is found among sensible objects that lacks dimension, it is consistent that no such thing would be found among the things we imagine for ourselves. For indeed, every sensible object—however much it may be a boundary or a sign of something—is not without dimension. For the extremity and the outermost limit of a thing both exists and is held to be such; moreover, every such thing is conceived as being a part of that object, for everything from which its extremities are removed is diminished. That which is a part completes that of which it is a part; furthermore, that which completes a length increases it entirely, and that which acts as an increaser of magnitude is recognized as being by no means lacking in that very magnitude. ->THIRD<-

we shall accept it as being without parts and without dimension. To this, when they themselves say that a straight line proceeding from a center and rotated to its extreme end or boundary describes a circular *surface* <note>original: ἐπίπεδον (epipedon)</note>, that is, a plane. How can they escape the fact that a point must have parts, must not be indivisible, and must not lack dimension? For the highest point, or the extreme, or the end of the straight line itself is a point, which, when drawn in a circle, describes and measures the circumference; from which it is recognized to complete that very circumference. This circumference, however, has distance <note>In this context, "distance" refers to spatial extension or magnitude.</note>; therefore, the point which completes it is understood not to lack all distance. Furthermore, if it is entirely accepted by geometers that a sphere touches a plane at only one mark or point, and when rolled creates a line, it will be manifest from those very meeting points that a line is completed. Therefore, if the point is the maker of the magnitude of a line out of itself, then it too is not devoid of magnitude. Nor was that response of Eratosthenes <margin>Eratosthenes</margin> <note>Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276–194 BC), a polymath known for measuring the Earth's circumference.</note> sufficient against these arguments: that a point neither occupies a place nor measures the distance of a line, but that while it "flows," it creates a line. For in what way can it be understood that anything flows which, having departed from one place, does not seek another place? Therefore, if we imagine a point to flow, it follows that we should not only think of it as partless, but rather as being composed of contrary parts.

And so much for the point. Concerning the line, even if the point existed, they dispute it in such a way that they think it cannot stand. If, they say, it is the flow of a point and a length without breadth, it is either a point extended in length, or many points lying in order and continuous among themselves. But it is neither this nor that; therefore, a line is not granted in the way they establish it. For if the first is said—namely, that it is a point—it will either have only one place, or it will change places, or it will be stretched out from one place to another. If the first, it will no longer be a line but a point, which constituted a line while it was flowing. If they answer the second, it is surely consistent for them to understand one of two things: namely, that having left one place it seeks another, or it is stretched from the place it holds and occupies into another. If the former, as we said, it will not be a line but a point; for by the same reasoning that it was a point while occupying the first place, it will be considered a point in the second place. But if they say the latter—that it is transferred from the place it occupies into another—let them also say whether it is stretched through a divisible place or an indivisible one? If through an indivisible one, it will no longer be considered a line but a point and a mark. For that which contains an indivisible place is indivisible, and that which is indivisible is judged a point, not a line. But if through a divisible place, it will now also have parts, since it is co-extended with the whole place; but that which has parts co-extended with the parts of a place is a body. <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin> Wherefore the mark itself will be judged to be both divisible and a body, which is as absurd as anything can be. From all these things it can be gathered that a line is not a mark or a point extended in length.

But that it is not many points placed in order can be gathered from this: these points themselves will be understood either to touch one another or not to touch. If they do not touch, they are separated by certain intercepted places; but things that are so divided will by no means compose a single line. But if they are said to touch and be connected to one another, surely they are joined either as wholes to wholes, or as parts to parts. <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin> If they say the latter, it follows that none of them is without dimension and without parts. For whatever mark (for example) is conceived to be the middle of two marks: it will touch the mark which is before it with one part, and the mark which is behind it with another part; therefore, since they differ so much in their locations, it will be judged not a partless mark, but one with many parts. But if the marks are joined as wholes to wholes, it will be manifest that marks are contained within marks and concluded in the same place. But indeed, having excluded every reasoning of the mark and the point, they still attempt to remove the line from the midst; for it is, as the geometers wish, a length without breadth.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of geometric dimensions, specifically questioning the existence of a "length without breadth" (a line) as defined by classical geometers.</meta>

XXXVIII
BOOK I

Let us look and diligently observe whether any length without breadth can be found among sensible things <note>Objects perceived by the senses</note> or among the objects of the intellect themselves. Indeed, in sensible things, whenever we begin to perceive a sensible length, breadth immediately presents itself to our conception along with that very quantity. In intellectual or imaginary things, the same occurs, insofar as we can conceive in the mind one length to be thinner or narrower than another. However, when we divide breadth in our thought while keeping the length equal, and then divide it again, we will always think of a smaller and smaller breadth. But once we have deprived length of its breadth entirely, we will no longer imagine length at all; rather, it will be immediately removed and the notion of it will vanish. For if we turn over in our minds all the **modes of conception**, we will find that we fall into none of them that allow us to correctly conceive of length without breadth. For such a length does not strike the senses, nor do we infer it from sensible things, nor do we transfer it by similarity, composition, or analogy—whether by increase or decrease. For it is well established that there are neither more nor fewer modes of conception than these. To which sense did a length without breadth ever occur? Or to whom did it occur in the mind to transcend things perceived by the sense and, by a certain metaphor, pluck out this very idea? By similarity? But can any similarity be found for that which cannot exist? For we see nothing among sensible and apparent things that lacks some breadth, from which we might be moved by its similarity to conceive of such a thing in the mind. For that which is similar is similar to, and possesses the quality of, something already known. How can it be that we find a similarity to that which is not known? Or perhaps by composition or analogy? But let them tell us which of those things known to the senses they will compose with another to track down a non-broad length—just as from a man and a horse, which are animals known to the eyes, they composed a centaur in the mind. Let them also say what analogy they can use, either by increasing or decreasing, to fish out this length without breadth. For those things conceived according to analogy have a certain similarity and agreement with that from which they are conceived, whether you increase or decrease: as from seeing a man of common size, you fashion a Cyclops, or from that same man, a pygmy. However, you will be able to find nothing in common, nothing similar, and nothing fitting in proportion between a broad length and a non-broad length, which itself has never in any way appeared to human senses.

<margin>Modes of conception</margin>

<margin>Removal of the response</margin>

Nor will that device of the geometers profit them at all: the idea that through continuous extension and the thinning of a wide breadth, one can arrive at a non-broad length. For it was shown above that the universal and absolute deprivation of breadth is the destruction of length, which clearly cannot exist without it. For even if someone could arrive at the thinnest and narrowest breadth through extension and reduction, if anything remains, it will be breadth, however tiny and almost vanishing. Otherwise, as we said, the length will perish, for it cannot stand if you take away breadth entirely.

<margin>Removal of the response</margin>

Nor does that famous analogy of Aristotle's <note>Aristotle often used the example of a wall to explain abstraction</note> avail to support the geometers—the idea that we can grasp in the mind the length of a wall without considering its breadth. For since the knowledge of things not manifest comes through the notion of those things which are seen, Aristotle (says Sextus) <note>Sextus Empiricus, the Skeptic philosopher</note> wandered from the truth and played with a sophism. For when we think of the length of a wall without breadth, we do not think of it without *any* breadth at all, but only without that specific breadth which is established in the wall itself. Therefore, length can be thought of without *this* or *that* breadth, but it cannot be thought of without *any breadth whatsoever*. But indeed, since geometers say that a line is the limit of a surface, come, let us speak of both at once in this way...

<margin>Sextus against Aristotle</margin>

->BOOK THREE<-                                                               LXXXVIII

For a smoother path will be paved toward that discussion which is to come concerning the body. If a line—which is defined as being length without breadth—is the boundary of a surface, it will be evident that when surface is joined to surface, either two parallel lines will be created, or both will become one. If they argue for the latter, it follows also that two bodies would become one body. For if a line is the boundary of a surface and a surface is the boundary of a body, and from two lines one line is formed, then from two surfaces one surface will also be formed. Furthermore, from two surfaces forming one surface, one body will be made from two bodies; but if two bodies result in one, the composition will not be a composition, but a union. This is as absurd as anything can be, especially when we see in composite bodies that certain things can by no means become one. Moreover, it would be necessary for separation to occur not only through the extremities themselves, but through various torn-away parts so that corruption <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the philosophical concept of a thing's destruction or change in essence.</note> would be introduced. We see nothing of the sort, since we are permitted to observe the boundaries and extremities of bodies before composition, and after separation they appear just as they appeared in the composition. 

<margin><unclear>Note regarding composition</unclear></margin>

If, however, two lines become parallel by the composition of two bodies, that which is formed from the two lines will be greater than a single line. If this is granted, it follows that each line must have breadth, since with the other it creates a greater distance; and thus a line will not be length without breadth. Therefore, we can introduce one of two conclusions: either the evidence of the senses must be discarded, or the "imagination" <note>original: "phantasiam"; here meaning the theoretical constructs or mental models used by mathematicians.</note> of the geometers—that a line is length without breadth—must be held in low esteem. 

<margin><unclear>Note on parallel lines</unclear></margin>

But departing from this, let us show that even if their own hypotheses are granted to them, it does not follow what they strive to conclude from them. Indeed, that dogma of his—that a line is length without breadth—conflicts with that other dogma: that a straight line turned upon itself describes circles with all its parts. For if a straight line, drawn upon itself, is naturally suited to circumscribe a circle, it will not be length without breadth. For when a straight line drawn from the center is turned upon itself and describes a circle by its own motion, then either the line itself is carried through all parts of the breadth included in that circumference, or not through all of them. If you say the latter, you can never say that it describes a circle if it is carried through some parts but not at all through others. If you answer the former, then it measures the entire breadth of the circumference. But that which measures breadth is not lacking in breadth itself, to which it is, of course, commensurate. Therefore, a line will be a length with breadth. 

This is shown even more clearly by their own dogma when they affirm that the diagonal <note>original: "obliquum... latus"; literally the slanted side, referring to the diagonal of a square.</note> of a square, when rotated, measures the parallelogram and the surface. 

<margin><unclear>Note on the diagonal</unclear></margin>

If indeed it is length without breadth, the diagonal side of the square, when rotated, will not measure the parallelogram surface of the square by itself; for that which measures breadth ought not to lack breadth. They say, moreover, that a plane is touched by a cylinder along a straight line; which, being rolled along one part after another, measures the plane by its position, whence the plane is constituted from straight lines, and the surface of the cylinder is likewise fashioned from straight lines. Thus it happens that since the plane has breadth, and the surface of the cylinder similarly is not without breadth—which is the "constitutive element," so to speak, of breadth—the line itself ought to be endowed with breadth. 

<margin><unclear>Note on the cylinder</unclear></margin>

It is manifest, therefore, that the straight lines from which breadth is joined together are by no means lacking in breadth. Furthermore, even if we grant that a line is length without breadth, the consequences of this would be clearly more absurd. For just as a flowing point <note>The "flowing point" (punctum fluens) is a classical geometric concept where a line is imagined as the path of a moving point.</note> constitutes a line, so also a flowing line, according to their dogma, constitutes a surface, which is the boundary of a body endowed with two dimensions: namely, length and breadth. If, therefore, the surface is the boundary of the body, and the body is entirely...

...determined: for if it is the case that when two bodies are joined together, then either the boundaries are touched by boundaries, or the things bounded are touched by things bounded. If you grant the first point, it follows that you cannot grant what comes next: that is, that the bounded things (the bodies themselves) are not touched by the bounded things, which is absurd. If, however, we concede that the bodies themselves touch one another, but that their boundaries do not touch each other, then those bodies will be established outside of their own boundaries. But if the boundaries are touched by boundaries, and the bounded things are joined to the bounded things by that contact, we stir up a doubt; for where the boundaries touch each other, the bounded things will not touch each other. 

But if they do touch, we shall place the bodies outside of their own boundaries, since a boundary is a surface, while that which it bounds is a body. Furthermore, many of the principles that the geometers themselves consider to be established and firm can be brought into dispute by the philosophers of other sects. First, Aristotle defines the point differently than Euclid does. For Euclid says: "A point is that which has no part." <note>original: "punctus est cuius pars non est"</note> But Aristotle defines it as: "An indivisible thing having position within a continuum." <note>Aristotle, Metaphysics Book 5</note> He evidently used "indivisible" as the genus to include both the unit <term>unit: the basic building block of number</term> and the point, but added "having position" to distinguish it from the unit.

For things that have position also have those attributes which necessarily follow from position, and especially "place," which is numbered among the continuous quantities. Indeed, there have been those who believed that a continuum is composed of indivisible points, such as many of the Platonists, among whom Robert Grosseteste <note>original: "Robertus lynconiensis," the 13th-century Bishop of Lincoln and scientist</note> and Bonerus are numbered. <margin>Robert of Lincoln</margin>
