...many of their arguments and those of the people commonly called "calculators" <note>original: *calculatores*; likely referring to the Oxford Calculators or similar scholastic logicians who applied mathematical methods to physics</note> would be mocked when they mix mathematics with natural and sensible things. This is not permitted by Aristotle among the pagans—who for that reason rejected certain ancient philosophers—nor by the most approved theologians among our own people. Augustine says in his book *Soliloquies*: "It seems to me that one could sooner sail upon the land than perceive geometry through the senses," although those first learning it may seem to be helped a little bit. Nor is it an obstacle when some say that the intellect is not deceived simply because it conceives of a thing differently than the thing actually is; for the intellect possesses an abstracting power, conceiving united things separately, divided things together, material things without matter, and singular things universally. This does not interfere with the truth, because a question would then arise concerning the "reflective act"—namely, whether the intellect would know it was being deceived or not. 

For even if a line without width is present in the intellect—as a concept of length with no breadth—because the definition of length is different from the definition of width, the intellect does not perceive it to exist in reality in the same distinct way they are defined. Otherwise, it would be lying. However, it does not fall into falsehood because of the pure presentation in its first glance. Since it is moved in one way by length and another by width, even though both truly and properly exist in the same line and surface, it follows that even if it conceives a thing differently than it is, it does not *judge* it to be otherwise than it is. Therefore, there is a difference between "conceiving a thing differently than it is" and "conceiving that a thing *is* different than it is." The first pertains to the first office of the intellect <note>simple apprehension</note>, and the second to the second office <note>judgment or composition/division</note>. In the first, there is no falsehood; in the second, there is a lie. 

Therefore, when someone abstracts in such a way that he believes the thing itself is actually divided within itself just as the intellect distinctly separates it, he is greatly deceived. And if he later wishes to insinuate this falsehood to others, he is openly lying. These abstractions serve only for easier understanding and for discerning that in one and the same thing, there are different "reasons" <note>original: *rationes*; formal concepts or aspects</note> by which the thing can be apprehended; and there are almost as many of these as there are accidents. For who can deny that every sensible line—from which the mathematician abstracts the "insensible" line—is merely imaginary? In itself and in its own nature, it is truly a surface and does not lack width when joined to length, even if the definition of length is one thing and width another. Likewise, a sensible point has parts, and so on for the rest in equal proportion.

It may be objected that no number is understood to exist in a subject except for the things actually numbered. If they <note>likely referring to the Platonists or Pythagoreans</note> respond according to the second [argument], a great difficulty arises: it would follow that the [Idea of Unity] itself is many, because it is shared by many and almost infinite things. For just as "Man" in the universal sense—which most understand as a "mortal rational animal"—is neither Socrates nor Plato (since if it were, no other human besides that one could be called a man), nor does it exist by itself, nor solely with Plato and Socrates (since "Man" is grasped by us as a concept of the mind); so too "The One" is understood neither as existing solely with individually numbered things, nor as subsisting entirely by itself. In the same way, one must argue concerning the numbers two, three, four, and the rest. Let us also question the mathematicians <term>arithmeticos: those who study the theory of numbers</term> thus: Is the Idea of the One, by whose participation something is called "one," a single Idea, or are there many Ideas of the One itself? If the first is granted, it cannot be shared by many. For if, for example, "A" possesses the entire Idea of the One, then "B," not participating in it, will not be "one." Yet it will not be composed of many parts either, so that many things could exist which participate in it; for among them, the unit is understood to be indivisible. If this last is granted, then duality certainly does not arise from the placing of unit next to unit. But the number ten is not something different from the ten units themselves; for if those units are removed, the ten is also clearly removed, and if you remove the ten, you have also removed the units themselves. If, however, the ten is the same as the ten units themselves, it is manifest that if a subtraction of a unit is made from the ten, it is made from every single unit. For whatever is taken from each unit of the nine particular units that constitute the number nine is taken from the nine itself. <margin>Concerning doubtful suppositions.</margin> First of all, it is sufficiently clear that those who measure celestial matters utilize certain suppositions <note>The Latin *suppositio* here refers to the underlying mathematical or theoretical assumptions used to build astronomical models.</note> which can be denied with almost the same ease with which they are usually affirmed. <margin>How many disagreements there are regarding the motion of the eighth sphere.</margin>

All of this must be refuted, either in the revolving motion of the sphere itself—which is indeed most irregular and of an ungraspable, changeable variety—or in the fallacy of all instruments used in detecting the stars, or in the falsity of some star detected and observed long ago, where no care was taken for the past centuries in which it might perhaps have been observed more faithfully. If any of this is conceded, then any exact and clear judgment concerning the motion and observation of all superior bodies perishes—even if a ninth or tenth sphere is established against the authority of Plato and Aristotle. For they referred all their observations to this very "eighth sphere," shimmering with innumerable stars, as the supreme visible body. If its motion is so varied that it has not been detected beyond controversy, which of the mathematicians shall we consider competent? So many professors, for so many centuries, laboring in vain, whom later ages have always corrected!

<margin>An effective argument from the lack of consensus.</margin>

If the instruments deceive, in what way shall that which is erroneous be corrected? Moreover, it seems it cannot be denied that they do deceive, as both experience and reason testify. Experience indeed shows this when, using the same instruments, one person disagrees with another by twelve or thirteen degrees in noting a star. Reason shows it because (as the *Summarium* writes and Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note> the uncle proves) before you can behold a star by the aid of an instrument, you must define its location; and once that is found, you must use a kind of calculation in measuring its course. But how are you to detect the location so that you do not fail in defining it? For the instrument will not respond to the senses with more subtlety or exquisite precision than what the observer himself can suggest. Indeed, one must take into account the proportion between the circumference of the instrument and the circumference of the universe, and the distance between the star and the place where the instrument is located; the senses cannot rightly judge the relationship between these parts and the parts of the universe.

<margin>Giovanni Pico.</margin>

Henry of Mechelen and Abraham <note>Likely Abraham Zacuto or Ibn Ezra.</note> in the preface to his tables, and others looking out for posterity, agree with this: that no instruments can exactly detect the locations of the stars. But if the instruments deceive, how will posterity know that the ancients wandered from the truth? For the same question will be asked of their instruments, and the same judgment will be passed. This same thing easily happens in measuring the magnitude of the stars through instruments: that is, finding either a larger or smaller circuit due to the fallacy of the tools. I will pass over those who, relying on Holy Scripture, discuss the magnitude of the stars differently than the consensus of Astrologers has established. Among these, Franciscus Maronius <note>Francis of Meyronnes, a 14th-century scholastic.</note>, in his second volume on Augustine's commentary on Genesis, determines that the moon is larger not only than the earth, but than any of the stars.

by which he could have perceived that the same sphere was sometimes carried from the east to the west; thus it happened that Azarchiel <note>Arzachel, an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer</note>, who applied himself to more ancient observations, discovered that after a certain space of time had passed, it was carried back toward the east by a backward motion. I shall respond by denying that these things can be asserted with such ease as they are brought forward; then I shall ask of them that they produce those most ancient observations, so that I may both correct those upon which Ptolemy relied, and judge those upon which Azarchiel depended. If they take refuge in the Flood, I shall first inquire into the historical reliability of such a celestial positioning; for they are not going to bring forward any observations of the stars from Sacred History <note>The Bible</note>. Then I shall desire that the observation with which the stars first began to be shown be exhibited, so that all things may be clearly corrected by it. But when they excuse themselves by the waters of the Flood, saying they cannot travel back that far, I know they will bring forward certain "birth-charts of the world" <note>horoscopes for the moment of creation</note>—various, inconsistent, ridiculous, refuted by many, and contributing nothing to their case. But however they may be, they were certainly made public before Ptolemy, and before all those who discussed the varying motion of the eighth sphere; yet they could not bring about agreement among mathematicians. And even if all things were granted, what are they to say about the observations of Thabit <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer</note> and others who, in measuring the course of the eighth sphere, accepted neither Ptolemy nor Azarchiel, but refuted them and discovered new motions themselves? But so that we may gather this and other conflicting opinions of mathematicians in a brief and easy order regarding the remaining spheres which have been devised above the eighth sphere, and regarding the planets—and collect into one their various dogmas concerning their number, position, and motion—let us begin here. Nor shall we use any other witnesses than its most celebrated professors; since they have never been found in agreement in detecting the number of celestial bodies, in asserting their order, or in measuring their motion, it follows that this art <note>astronomy/astrology</note> ought to be considered uncertain by us. Indeed, so many great men have sweated in vain with such great zeal, leaving to posterity the same desire for attaining certainty by which they themselves were held.

<margin>Controversy concerning the number and motion of the stars.</margin>
First of all, it is sufficiently established among them that stars are divided into the "fixed" and the "wandering" <note>planets</note>; yet it is not established how many wandering stars there are, nor was it established in the time of Emperor Hadrian, nor in later ages; nor is it established in what manner those which are not wandering, but fixed in their places, behave and move. Next, it is not established by what motion they are driven—their own or another's? And do the planets rotate within their own spheres, or are they carried along by some larger or smaller orb? They do not even agree on the uniformity of the solar motion (the chief among the planets), nor on its velocity, even if it is held to be uniform. And those very stars which are usually considered non-wandering: do they revolve in the heavens with the same continuous tenor, or do they also move backward with an uncertain motion? So that it is uncertain whether the star-bearing heaven itself "wanders" or not. Then, whatever motion you prefer to ascribe to it, there is no small controversy as to whether that motion is proper to that orb or belongs to a higher orb, either a ninth or a tenth.

<margin>Controversy concerning the number of spheres.</margin>
For they do not agree on the number of spheres above the planets. There are those who want more, and those who want fewer, having conjectured this mostly from the varying motion of the eighth sphere; concerning which, does it move toward the east or the west? Toward the north or the south? And if it moves, is it by a non-uniform or a uniform course? And if uniform, at what velocity? Much discord flourished in the past and flourishes most especially now. Let us explain all these things, or at least the more notable ones.

<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
Favorinus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher</note> thinks it possible that there are more than seven planets (which Nigidius called "wanderers"). But they may be hidden either because of their height or because of the excellence of their light.

<margin>Alpetragius.</margin>
This very point could be confirmed by the authority of Alpetragius <note>al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer</note>, who decreed that there is a motion in the heaven that is unknown; for there can also be some body as yet undetected to which that motion belongs—which can by no means be considered absurd by the younger generation, who have discovered so many motions, as they think.

**THIRD [BOOK] 93**

<margin>How great are the disagreements concerning the seat of the sun and the other planets.</margin>
In previous centuries, they discovered spheres surrounding the others that were unknown [to the ancients], about which antiquity said nothing at all. Regarding epicycles and eccentrics <note>Epicycles are small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles (deferents); eccentrics are circular orbits whose center is offset from the Earth.</note>, the controversy is well known, as is the debate over the multitude of spheres that serve the planets, and the assertion of a ninth and tenth sphere, of which we shall make mention. But for the present, not departing from the planets, we assert that neither their order nor their motion has been grasped by a certain principle. Ptolemy, following the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note>, affirmed the sun to be in the middle in such a way that it had three planets above it and three below. Plato and Aristotle, following the Egyptians in this matter, placed it above the moon with no intermediate [body]. But you will say that we must yield to Ptolemy, who, being so many centuries later than Aristotle and Plato, was able to explore the matter more clearly. By this same reasoning, we ought to yield to Theon, the disciple of Ptolemy, and to Tiberius, who think the sun is second from the moon and ought not to be established in the middle of the planets. The reasoning on both sides is traditional and vague. We must also agree with Alpetragius <note>Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer.</note>, who wished Venus to be the middle of the planets and placed the sun beneath it—that is, immediately above Mercury—as we also related in the first book. But indeed, such varied [opinions] concerning the seat and use of the sun were brought forward by the first philosophers that Metrodorus of Chios, Crates, and Anaximander even placed it above the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "non errantium siderum," literally "non-wandering stars."</note> and made the moon closest to it, and between the moon and the other planets, they placed the fixed stars in their own sphere. Aristarchus, however, although he granted the first place to the immobile stars, nevertheless thought the sun held the second place and was higher than the other planets. The position and order of Venus and Mercury are likewise uncertain. Concerning Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, it is equally uncertain in what order they are placed: for although he thinks they should be established higher than the sun, he confirms that the order is neither known nor can be known, on account of the great diversity of their appearances. Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides.</note>, following the opinion of Abubacher <note>Ibn Bajja (Avempace).</note>, also asserted the order of the planets to be uncertain.

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
<margin>Solution to the arguments of Ptolemy and Alpetragius concerning the seat of the sun.</margin>
Certainly, whatever arguments are made in determining the place or position of the sun, which holds the princedom of the planets, are easily refuted. For the reasoning of Ptolemy does not hold, who judges that the sun ought to be placed in the middle because the three he considers "superior" move away from it in longitude, while Venus and Mercury always follow it. For the moon departs no less from the superior ones than it does, so that the reason does not establish the sun as a middle point between those that depart and those that follow and do not separate. Moreover, the reasoning of slowness devised by Alpetragius—that the lower ones should be faster in motion—is not satisfactory; for it would follow that Venus should be considered higher than the sun, which, even if he himself wished it, others do not admit.

<margin>Solution to the argument brought forward for the opinion of Plato and Aristotle.</margin>
Furthermore, the reasoning brought forward to prove the opinion of Plato and Aristotle is easily solved; it is that the sun is never snatched from us by the interposition of Venus and Mercury, and therefore it must be placed beneath them. For the smallness of Mercury and the proximity of Venus, intercepted by the solar rays, can be the cause [of this], so that even if they are opposite the sun, they nevertheless do not snatch its body from our sight. This can also be attributed to the thinness of the essence of those planets, so that the light is not taken away as it is from the moon, which, though more remote, [blocks light] on account of its thickness and quasi-earthly density.

<margin>How great a variety [of opinion] concerning the motion of the sun and other planets.</margin>
But if the place of the sun in heaven is found to be imagined and [un]certain, what shall we decide concerning its motion? Which Ptolemy, in the *Great Composition* <note>The Almagest.</note>, calls the most manifest of all, and by which he declared the others must be measured as by a fixed and certain standard. I wonder how he wrote this, when previously both Hipparchus and mathematicians older than Hipparchus had varied in measuring it. For they completed the return of the sun and finished the year in three hundred and sixty-five days with a fourth part of a day added. This opinion is also followed by Augustine in the second [book] *On Genesis*. Others wished more than a fourth to be added to return to the same point of the zodiac; Hipparchus thought that less than a fourth part ought to be added, but he did not decree how large that part should be.

<margin>Controversy concerning the number and motion of the spheres.</margin>

...we have shown that their number, position, and motion are uncertain and unperceived; let this same thing be shown regarding the stars fixed to their own heaven. Accordingly, the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Plato, Aristotle, and Hipparchus established the eighth sphere <note>In the geocentric model, the eighth sphere is the firmament containing the "fixed stars," located beyond the spheres of the seven known planets.</note>, sparkling with innumerable stars, which is said to be placed above the orb designated by the name of Saturn as the outermost and highest of all. Ptolemy also joined their opinion (although others think differently), as he proved. Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the author’s famous uncle and a renowned Renaissance philosopher.</note>, my uncle, in his eighth book *Against Astrologers*, noted that Alfonso <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the "Alfonsine Tables" in the 13th century.</note> is considered the first to have calculated the positions of the planets according to a ninth sphere. Others introduced a ninth sphere because of a newly discovered motion <note>This refers to "precession" or "trepidation," where the stars appear to shift slowly over centuries.</note>, since it does not seem consistent with reason that two opposite motions should be attributed to the same body—such as those seen in the eighth sphere, moved (as they say) from west to east, and again revolved with the rest from east to west. They think the first motion is proper to the eighth sphere, while the second belongs to a higher sphere which carries all the lower ones from east to west. However, this reasoning did not sway Leo the Hebrew <note>Levi ben Gerson (1288–1344), a Jewish philosopher and astronomer known for his critical approach to Ptolemaic astronomy.</note> or the Platonist Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on mathematics and astronomy.</note>, both highly skilled in mathematics, from contending that the eighth sphere is the highest of all. Indeed, there are those who deny the reality of that double motion and completely dismantle the reasoning for it. For there are some who do not accept that the stars move from west to east, as we shall show below; there are others who ascribe the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note> motion to the *aether* <note>The "fifth element" or substance of the heavens.</note> and say it is perpetual and not divided into spheres, and that all these—the eighth as well as the seven lower wandering stars <note>The "planets" (from the Greek 'planētai', meaning wanderers).</note>—revolve with their own motions from west to east. On the contrary, Leo the Hebrew assigned that motion to a lower sphere. There are some who constitute the whole heaven from all the spheres as if it were a living animal made of all its members, and they refer the motion of the whole heaven to a single universal motor, while attributing the individual motions of the spheres to their own specific motors. For this reason, they think it is not necessary to seek a ninth (and thus new) sphere by reason of the diurnal motion, since that motion is not proper to the eighth sphere—so that it would be said to rotate with two motions—but is common to all, and is clearly referred to a common motor.

But indeed, there are those whom the reasoning of the double motion, now dismantled, persuaded to introduce yet another sphere because of another discovered motion; and so they did not make the ninth the outermost, but placed a tenth above it, as Alfonso, Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), an Italian mathematician and astronomer.</note>, Leopold <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note>, Messahalla <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note>, and Albertus <note>Likely Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century polymath.</note> believed. But even regarding the ancient motion, a new opinion emerged a few days ago. For our friend Theriacus <note>Benedetto Tiriaco, a contemporary humanist and physician.</note>, lately debating with me, affirmed that it did not seem to him that it is carried from west to east in a straight path, because the same point on the orb would be moved by a contrary motion at the same time—since it is also said to be carried by the higher sphere from east to west—and compared to another point, it would simultaneously approach and recede. Instead, he believes it moves along the path of the sun, that is, the way of the zodiac <note>Latin: "signifer", the circle of animal signs (the ecliptic).</note>, so that it is carried by its own motion from the Tropic of Capricorn to the Tropic of Cancer.

->**BOOK THREE**<- [right]**95**

...[it to be] <note>original: "certam"; completing a sentence from the previous page where the author likely refers to the "mathematical" part of astronomy.</note> certain and noble, and most honorable within its own limits, and highly approved by the authority of the most learned men. For it could be called certain in itself—that is, as far as its nature pertains, not as far as it concerns us. Likewise, it is certain in some way and partially, though not entirely; certainly so in comparison to rustic and nautical astrology, and much more so than divinatory astrology. Finally, it is certain as long as it contains itself within its own limits: namely, distinguishing the opportune times for conducting affairs due to the inequality of days and nights, the division of months and years, and the observation of the solstices. For this reason, it is praised by learned men and considered a most honorable thing for maintaining fixed and solemn ceremonies—both in the ancient law of the Hebrews due to various observations of lunar motion, and in our own law for the celebration of Easter, about which there were many disputes at the beginning of the rising church. 

But these matters do not require an entirely exact and "punctual" certainty, so to speak; otherwise, how would we read those things we cited above from the most sacred book of Job? <note>Referring to Job 38, where the limits of human knowledge regarding the heavens are humbled by God.</note> Nor is there any exceptional utility from it for leading a civil life. For in Xenophon, it can be seen that Socrates thought there was little <margin>Xenophon.</margin> utility in learning astrology <note>The term "astrology" here encompasses what we now call astronomy.</note> but a great waste of time; he advised that it should be learned only for this reason: so that we might more exactly perceive the days and nights, hours, months, and years. But he disapproved of those who strove to grasp the exact motions of the planets and their distance from the earth, although he himself was not unlearned in that matter. And lest anyone should think he was speaking about divinatory astrology, he himself attacked that more sharply and judged it so impossible and impious that he openly decreed the gods would take punishment from those who kept watch over it, if what Xenophon himself recorded for posterity in the book *Memorabilia* <note>original: "de dictis socraticis," literally "on the Socratic sayings."</note> is true. 

Our Augustine also, who was a most fierce <margin>Augustine.</margin> enemy and attacker of divinatory astrology, when he made mention of this astrology of measuring motions both in his *Confessions* and in his books *On Christian Doctrine*, wrote there: "I do not care to know the transits of the stars." Here, indeed, he taught that it is more healthy and honorable to despise it, since it is close to the error of those who sing of foolish fates. Even Columella, in the first book of *On Agriculture*, indicated how uncertain it is <margin>Columella.</margin> when he writes that many are persuaded that by the long duration of time, the quality and state of the sky are changed; and he adds that Hipparchus, the most skilled professor of astrology, predicted there would come a time when the hinges <note>The "cardines" or poles of the world.</note> of the world would be moved from their place. If this has been fulfilled, ancient observations have perished; if it happens in the future, later ones and the rest will perish. Since even if one celestial thing is varied by even a small amount, it is necessary that those dogmas and decrees of astrologers which were founded upon it should also be varied. And enough about astrology; let us now proceed to examine music.

**What the Skeptical philosophers argued against the art of music, and what can also be said against them regarding this matter. Chapter Nine.**

**M**usic was about to be condemned by the Skeptical <note>original: "ephectici," referring to the Skeptic school of philosophy that suspended judgment.</note> philosophers, but since they were approaching an unpopular task, they first set forth the various meanings of the name itself. First, by the name of music, they took that faculty which was concerned with melodies, sounds, and rhythms; therefore, those who excel in that art are called musicians. Next, they called the skill of instruments "music"; and therefore they called those who used flutes and psalteries <note>An ancient stringed instrument.</note> "musicians." Also, by a certain misuse of the term, they called a well-composed work "musical." However, concerning music taken in its first sense only...

They <note>The author is likely referring to the Skeptics or Epicureans, who often argued against the value of the "liberal arts."</note> say this, and they proceed to do so in two ways. For first, they endeavor to show that music is not useful for achieving happiness, but is rather useless and harmful. Then, they attempt to uproot the very foundations of the art by overturning its principal hypotheses. In the beginning, they busy themselves by proving that there is nothing in music that naturally stirs the soul, but that all of its power is to be attributed to human opinion and estimation. For one person is delighted by a sound, another not at all; therefore, it is not in the nature of music to affect listeners with delight. Indeed, the very same sound will often excite horses but will not excite men; and perhaps the melody itself will not be an awakener for horses, but rather something that makes them tremble. From this, they wish to conclude that music is not useful for life. For it does not possess a faculty capable of directing the human mind or thought toward virtue, but rather restrains it in some way. Therefore, when such melodies cease, the mind—not being at all liberated by them—returns to its original unhealthy state. Just as wine and sleep do not dissolve sadness but instead bring about forgetfulness, so too melody and harmony do not correct or restrain the sorrow of the soul, nor do they calm an angry mind; rather, they pull it away for a time, so that music might be seen to grant a kind of truce. And in this manner, it merely distracts. When Pythagoras is said to have restored drunken youths to their senses by the harmonies <margin>The example of Pythagoras.</margin> he ordered to be played, he perhaps distracted them from their madness for a little while, but he did not make them sober. Otherwise, one would have to admit that flute-players have more power than the precepts of philosophers regarding the virtue of sobriety and the correction of wicked morals. For nearly the same reason, <margin>The example of the Spartans.</margin> the Spartans entered into battles with the flute and the lyre. For just as those who carry heavy loads, or those who row, or those who endure some other troublesome labor, try to turn their minds away from the consideration of the labor's hardship with a rhythmic voice or a kind of groaning; so too soldiers used trumpets and flutes in war, not because there was something in the harmony that excited the mind or instilled courage, but because they strove to recall the soul into itself away from agony and turmoil. So too certain barbarians are accustomed to wage war with the noise of horns and drums, which nevertheless do nothing to aid courage. Furthermore, when it is commonly said that Achilles, when he was raging and seized by love, turned to melodies, it is no wonder, since he was afflicted by an imbalance of the soul. And these things are handed down in fabled stories—just like the claim that heroes, when they left their homeland, used to leave singers behind to guard their wives. How "beautifully" those singers used to instruct them is witnessed by Clytemnestra <note>original: "testis est clytemnæstra"; Clytemnestra famously murdered her husband Agamemnon despite the presence of a court singer assigned to keep her virtuous.</note>. But those who wish music to be of use to poetry, <margin>Objection</margin> so that they entwine it entirely with it, do not thereby prove it useful, because <margin>Solution</margin> even poetry, when discussed as a part of grammar, can be considered useless. And even if poetry is established as useful, it does not follow that music is granted to be useful, <margin>Objection</margin> because the latter merely soothes the senses, while the former also instructs the mind. <margin>Solution</margin> If indeed we turn from the poets to the philosophers and hear that Socrates <margin>Objection</margin> and Plato cultivated music, we will not for that reason confess that it contributes to happiness, because <margin>Solution</margin> other philosophers have denied it, calling it idle, a lover of wine, and a servant of pleasures. If anyone should say that those skilled in the art are more delighted than the unskilled, and that therefore one must apply oneself to harmony, it could easily be refuted by the common people, for whom there is great delight in food and drink if they are wasting away with hunger and thirst, without any knowledge of the cause of why it is so, and without any training in the art of cooking or winemaking. For in this way, infants—relying on no skill in the musical art—fall asleep charmed by melodies, and many irrational animals are soothed by flutes and pipes. In the same way, dolphins, delighted by the harmonies of flutes, swim alongside ships as they are rowed, affected perhaps with greater pleasure by songs and sounds than Aristoxenus, Philoxenus, or Timotheus <note>Famous ancient Greek music theorists and composers; the author argues that animals feel the "pleasure" of music just as much as these experts, suggesting music is a sensory rather than intellectual or moral good.</note> ever were, who are celebrated for their discipline in harmony.

The author uses historical and mythological examples, such as Pythagoras and Clytemnestra, to suggest that music's effects are sensory and fleeting rather than intellectual.</summary>

THIRD [BOOK]. 96.

...celebrated. Nor do the Skeptics admit that the world is governed by harmony; and even if they were to admit it, they do not want it to follow that music contributes to happiness. And these things, in summary, are what the Ephectics <note>original: "ephectici"; a term for Skeptics who "suspend judgment" rather than making definitive claims</note> say. I do not agree with them in all things, since it is well enough established by common sense <margin>The author’s argument against the Skeptics in favor of music</margin> that almost no man can be found so barbaric and inhuman who is not delighted by some form of music, even if not every kind. This music could be called a "concordant discord" of sounds and voices, just as beauty is a concordant discord of parts, health is a concordant discord of the humors, and the beauty of the world is the concordant discord of the upper and lower spheres. It has been employed in sacred rites by the consensus of the entire world—not merely by the custom of nations, but by divine decree, as is quite apparent in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament where hymns and songs are frequently used. 

However, the second way the Skeptics use to demolish the art of music is by subverting its principles. For they say: if music is called the science of melodies and non-melodies, of rhythms and non-rhythms, and if we show that melodies and rhythms do not truly exist, then we shall have removed every science of that kind. Voice, they say, is the specific object of the sense of hearing, just as color is the specific object of sight. Of voices, some are high and others low; this is clearly by a metaphor of the senses related to touch. For that which pricks and cuts the touch is called "acute" <note>sharp</note>; that which presses and breaks <margin>High voice. Low voice.</margin> is called "grave" <note>heavy</note>. Thus, that which in some way cuts and pricks the hearing is called a high voice, and that which, as it were, presses and breaks it is called a low voice. 

When, therefore, a voice is carried equally toward some pitch so that it causes no tearing of the sense—neither toward heaviness nor sharpness—such a sound is called a *tone* <note>original: "φθόγγος" (phthongos)</note> by the Greeks. Therefore, musicians describe it thus: <margin>Tone.</margin> a tone is a falling of the melodic voice upon a single pitch. Furthermore, some tones are called "equivocal" or "uniform" by the Greeks <note>original: "ὁμόφωνοι" (homophonoi)</note>. Others are not equivocal; the former differ from one another in sharpness and heaviness, while the latter do not. But from both groups, some are called high and some low. And again, among the non-equivocal ones, some are called *diaphonous* <note>dissonant</note> and others *symphonous* <note>consonant</note>, if we may say so; for if the ears hear "dis-voiced" or "con-voiced" sounds, they either simply could not bear them, or would do so with great displeasure. Dissonant sounds are those which move the hearing in an unequal and more distracted way. Consonant sounds, however, move it in a more equal and undivided manner. <margin>Consonant and dissonant tones; likewise symphonous and diaphonous intervals.</margin> 

They also define certain intervals according to which the voice moves, either rising and stretching toward something sharper, or sinking and relaxing toward something heavier. For this reason, by a certain analogy or proportion of these intervals, some are called consonant (or symphonous) and others diaphonous. The symphonous ones are those contained by symphonous tones, and the dissonant ones are those contained by dissonant tones. Of the consonant intervals, musicians call the first and smallest the <margin>Consonants: Fourth, Fifth, Octave. Diesis, Semitone, Tone. Character.</margin> *fourth* <note>original: "διά τεσσάρων" (dia tessaron), meaning "through four"</note>. That which is larger than this is the *fifth* <note>original: "διά πέντε" (dia pente), meaning "through five"</note>; and that which is larger still is the *octave* <note>original: "διά πασσῶν" (dia pason), meaning "through all"</note>. Again, the smallest and first of the dissonant intervals is called by them a *diesis* <note>a small interval, often a quarter-tone</note>. The second is the *semitone*, which is double the diesis. The third is the *tone*, which is double the semitone. 

Furthermore, just as every interval in music has its existence in tones, so too does every *character* <note>original: "mos," referring to the Greek "ethos" or musical mode</note>; this is the genus of the melody. For just as some human characters are sadder and ruder (as is recorded of ancient men), while others are inclined toward love and drinking parties, or even toward mourning and lamentation, so too a certain melody produces honorable and refined motions in the minds of men, while another produces viler and degenerate ones. Such a mode of melody is commonly called "character" <note>original: "mos"</note> among musicians, since it is in a way an affector of morals. Of this common melody, one kind is called <margin>Chromatic, Enharmonic, Diatonic.</margin> *chromatic* <note>original: "χρῶμα" (chroma)</note>, another *enharmonic* <note>original: "harmonia"</note>, and another *diatonic*.

The harmony <note>original: "harmonia"; here referring specifically to the Enharmonic genus, the most difficult and prestigious of the three Greek musical scales</note> of these is thought to be the preparer of a certain austere character, and in some way, of an honorable one. The *Chroma* <note>The Chromatic genus, characterized by half-steps</note>, however, presents something sharp and mournful, while the *Diatonic* is harsh and somewhat rustic. Again, the Enharmonic melody is held to be indivisible. The Diatonic, however, has two variations: the Soft Diatonic and the Intense <note>original: "Syntoni"</note> Diatonic. The *Chroma* consists of three variations: the "Victorious" <note>original: "uictrici"; likely a translation of "hemiolic," a specific mathematical ratio in the Chromatic scale</note>, the Semitone, and the Soft. From all these things, it can be well enough established that the whole study of the art of music has its foundation in the pitches <note>original: "phthongis"; the Greek term for discrete musical notes or sounds</note> themselves, which, if you take them away, you have taken away music. 

But how will you take away pitches, someone will ask? Since they are, according to their kind, voices <note>original: "uox"; here meaning sound or speech</note>. Yet many of the dogmatic philosophers, and not only the Skeptics, have removed the "voice" as something that does not truly exist. For the Cyrenaic philosophers said that only "affections" <note>internal feelings or sensations</note> or passions exist; hence, since the voice is not an affection but a cause of an affection, it is not numbered among things that truly exist. The followers of Democritus and many of the Platonists, rejecting everything that can be perceived by the senses, also wished to reject the voice, which appears to be a sensible thing. 

Indeed, this voice is either a body or incorporeal: it is not the former according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, nor the latter according to the Stoics. Moreover, if there is no high or low voice, there is no voice at all; but it was shown that neither exists during the discussion against the grammarians, when we were disputing about syllables and speech. Furthermore, voice is conceived of neither in its effect and end, nor in its substance, but in its generation <note>the process of being made</note> and its extension through time. However, what we observe in the state of "being generated" does not yet truly exist. Thus, we do not rightly say that a house or a ship *is* a house or a ship while it is (so to speak) in the very act of being made. Therefore, if the voice is removed, the pitch does not exist; and if you remove the pitch, neither harmony nor melody will remain.

To this we add: that which is said to be composed of non-existent things does not itself exist. Such is time, composed of the past (which no longer is), the future (which is not yet), and the present. The present is either divisible or it is not. If the first is said—that it is divisible—then since every divisible thing is measured by some part of itself (as a cubit is measured by a finger), it would be necessary for us to measure the present by some part of it. But we cannot measure other times by the present, otherwise the present would be the same as the past and the future: the same as the past because it measures it as a part, and in the same way with the future; and vice versa, we could not measure the present by other times for the same reason. 

If it is indivisible: how can one part of it be past, another present, and another future? And indeed, what is indivisible cannot become divisible, as Timon <note>A famous Skeptic philosopher and poet</note> writes. Furthermore, if the moment of present time is indivisible, it will have neither a beginning from which to start, nor an end in which to cease, and because of this, no middle. And thus the present will not exist. Now, as far as it concerns the Skeptics, let us graze upon their arguments. Since they think they can demolish demonstration, they care first and foremost to overturn the "sign" that demonstrates. For they admit a distinction which the famous schools of later philosophers in the Peripatetic family also admitted: that some signs are "commemorative" <note>original: "rememoratricia"</note>—let me call them what they call *hypomnestika* <note>original: "ὑπομνηϛικὰ"; signs that remind us of something previously observed, like smoke reminding us of fire</note>—and others are "demonstrative," called *endeiktika* <note>original: "ἐνδεικτικὰ"; signs that point to something naturally hidden, like sweat being a sign of pores in the skin</note> by them. The former are said to be valid for indicating those things which are not manifest at the moment: things which indeed have an evident nature but are obscured by certain external circumstances. The latter, however, are said to be valid for judging those things which are not manifest by nature—things said to be of such a kind that they cannot appear clear to us by their own nature, and are therefore both tracked down and held by demonstrative signs. They profess to wish to argue against these [demonstrative] signs. Against the others, not at all: for they are approved by common life, though they wish these signs to be understood differently than was later customary. For they say "commemorative signs" are the smoke of a fire and the scar of a wound, which in some way preserve their clarity along with the thing of which they are signs. But "demonstrative signs" are those which, from the equipment of their own nature, indicate that of which they are signs—as bodily motions are signs of the soul. Therefore, they attempt to bring these signs into controversy in this manner. They wish for "propositions" <note>original: "pronunciata"; in logic, these are statements that can be true or false</note> to be "expressions" <note>original: "dicta"; the Stoic term 'lekta', meaning the underlying meaning of what is said</note>. If they choose the first, an opposite negation, also arbitrary, will be set against them, possessing entirely equal strength. ...held. Therefore, if the demonstrative sign is cast into doubt, the demonstration itself is also brought into controversy, no differently than if someone were to doubt whether an animal existed in the nature of things; he would immediately also doubt whether man himself was found in the nature of things. These and other arguments, both against signs and in favor of signs, are what the Skeptics <note>A school of philosophy that practiced "epoché" or the suspension of judgment to achieve peace of mind.</note> are accustomed to discuss, so that they may make the matter doubtful from both sides. For this reason, they want it concluded that a decision must be made regarding demonstration (which is a species of sign), and also regarding syllogisms <note>A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note>. The definition of a syllogism is almost the same among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on systematic logic and biology.</note> as the definition of demonstration is among the Stoics; therefore, if they are the same, the same conclusion can be reached. If, indeed, demonstration is a species of syllogism, as is established among the Peripatetics, once the syllogism is removed, the demonstration itself collapses. Furthermore, the syllogism can easily be classified under the "sign," since it consists of propositions or assumptions which are established from signifying terms.

They also construct both particular and general arguments against demonstration and against the syllogism—and especially against the Stoics, whose definition of demonstration (as I said) is almost the same as the Peripatetic definition of the syllogism. For the Stoics propose four modes of speech that do not "gather or collect" <note>referring to invalid argument structures</note>, <margin>The Stoic doctrine.</margin> but five modes of "indemonstrable" speech <note>These are the fundamental, self-evident argument forms in Stoic logic, such as "If P, then Q; P; therefore Q."</note>, which are said to be of such great strength that all other things can be demonstrated through them, and which, if removed, would overturn the entire power of dialectic in connecting and joining propositions. But the <margin>The Skeptic opposition.</margin> Skeptic endeavors to show that all these modes can be reduced to a single mode of "not concluding" <note>showing that they fail to actually prove anything new</note>, and they insist on this as a common principle. They ask: are the connections from which something is demonstrated either manifest <note>obvious or self-evident</note> or doubtful? If the latter, we will not grant the conjunction itself, nor will we concede it as manifest. If the former—since we have granted the antecedent part of the conjunction—we will suddenly also have granted the following part. For if we concede that it is day, we simultaneously concede it is day because it is inferred by its own nature; therefore, it is concluded that both this and other modes are reduced to a mode condemned by them, which is called *by attraction* <note>original: "Κατὰ παραλκὴν"; a Greek logical term suggesting the conclusion is "dragged along" or redundant because it was already implicit.</note>.

Regarding the categorical syllogisms of the Peripatetics, they say the same, using this example: *The just is beautiful; the beautiful is good; therefore, the just is good.* Either it is confessed and manifest that the beautiful is good, they say, or it is doubtful and unmanifest. If it is said to be doubtful, it will not be conceded through interrogation, and because of that, the syllogism will not be "collected" or concluded. If the first is true—that is, it is manifest that everything beautiful is good—as soon as it has been admitted that something is beautiful, it will simultaneously be admitted that the same thing is good. Thus, this interrogation would be enough: *The just is beautiful; therefore, the just is good.* And that other assumption, in which it was said that the beautiful is good, is "drawn along" <note>rendered redundant</note>. They say the same also in this discourse: *Socrates is a man; every man is an animal; therefore, Socrates is an animal.* For if it were not manifest in itself that everything which is a man is an animal, the universal proposition would not be conceded, nor would we have given it to the questioner. But if, from being a man, it follows that he is an animal, and for that reason what is conceded is true, then that proposition "every man is an animal" would be inferred at the same time it is uttered—namely, that Socrates is a man and the same is an animal. Therefore, this interrogation by itself would be more than enough: *Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is an animal,* and that proposition "every man is an animal" is merely "drawn along" <note>again, the Greek concept of "paralkē" or redundancy</note>. 

Furthermore, they say that "true speech" is not found, both for the reasons stated and because it must end entirely in truth. However, whether a conclusion is true or not cannot be discerned, because it is either manifest or it is not. It cannot be the first, since it would not need to be made manifest by propositions if it were clear from itself, no less than those things from which it was inferred. If they say the second—since there is a controversy regarding those assumptions, as has been indicated enough above—the conclusion would be uncomprehended and controversial; and through this...

### BOOK THREE. [space] 99

For how can it be that one thing is contained by diverse things in the same way, such that we might behold the whole or the universe in each of those things in which it is said to exist? If they say it is according to species, first, it does not follow that every genus <note>A "genus" is a general category, while a "species" is a specific type within that category.</note> belongs to the species, as they think; for not every animal will be a human, but a part of the animal genus, just as not every animate substance will be stationary <note>original: "sessilis," likely referring to organisms like sponges or plants that are alive but fixed in place.</note>. Then, even if it is said that all species participate in a part of their own genus, that part will be either the same or different. If it is the same: how can this be affirmed because of what has already been said? If it is different, the species will not be similar according to their genus, and that is considered absurd by the Dogmatists <note>Those who assert certain truths as absolute, here referring to mainstream Aristotelian logicians.</note>. Each single genus would also be infinite, dissected into infinite parts—not only species, but also the individuals in which it is pronounced to exist after its species. For not only is a human an animal, but Socrates, Plato, and others are also animals. Many other things have been poured out both against these very points and against other dogmas of the dialecticians. Since I believe all of these can be resolved with very little difficulty, and many of them could be defended by the distinction between the clear <margin>The author argues for the logicians.</margin> and the obscure, the known and the better known, or simply and in part, I do not think they need to be explained more diligently. I wonder, however, that they did not also mention that Socratic saying reported by <margin>Xenophon.</margin> Xenophon in his book *Memorabilia* <note>original: "de Soc. dictis" (About the Sayings of Socrates). Xenophon was a student of Socrates and a historian.</note>, that Socrates used to advise that logic should be learned only to the extent that one would not disapprove of great study and much labor being spent on it. But let us next turn our attention to what the philosophers themselves have brought forward to weaken metaphysics, physics, and ethics.

### What and how multifaceted is the disapproval of the highest part of philosophy—which many call metaphysics, others first philosophy, and others the theology of the nations—devised by the skeptics; and therein also something against them. [space] Chapter eleven.

After the liberal arts, the Skeptic philosophers <note>Philosophers who practiced "epoche," the suspension of judgment, to avoid the distress of conflicting opinions.</note> attempted to render the very parts of philosophy, which were thought to remain, full of contention and dispute. They began from the first causes and principles of things, as they call them. Since the nations <note>A term often used for the non-Christian or pagan world.</note> especially numbered their gods among these causes, the Skeptics thought they should deal with the gods first—not because they did not worship them themselves as far as the laws of their country commanded or permitted, but insofar as they had been introduced either by the authority of philosophers or by the evidence of the senses and the investigation of conjecture. Of those things which we think about (they say), we ought to be able to conceive of their essences—for instance, whether they are corporeal or incorporeal—and also their species. For no one can rightly conceive of a horse, for example, who does not first know its form or figure. But since among the Dogmatists some say the gods are corporeal and others incorporeal, some say they are figured with human features and others not at all, and again some place God in a location while others do not; and of those who said he is in some place, some placed him within the world and others entirely outside it—how can we have a concept of him? For the philosophers agree neither on his essence, nor his form, nor his location. As for the fact that others consecrated men themselves because of things they discovered that were useful to the human race, and discussed those below <note>Referring to the deification of heroes or the inhabitants of the underworld.</note> in their own way, this is entirely vain. For they do not thereby teach how men arrived at the belief that gods exist, especially since they have thought differently about them. For the <margin>Persians.</margin> Persians said fire was God, the <margin>Egyptians.</margin> Egyptians said water, and others said other things. And if men thought that people became gods after death, how did they have that initial conception of gods to which they would refer the souls of the deceased? But even these ideas perish in a short time. For those things in which men falsely trust remain only while they are living, but are abolished as quickly as possible once they are dead. One can see many who were consecrated to memory while life accompanied them, but were plainly despised after death. Nor could the conjecture of <margin>Democritus.</margin> Democritus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the idea of gods arose from terrifying natural events.</note> suffice to bring forth the gods from earthquakes, lightning, and thunderbolts, nor that of Epicurus from the images... <margin>Removal of a silent objection.</margin>

But among many of the Greeks, certain spirits and the divine nature itself were discussed; and one was called "eudaemon" <note>from the Greek 'εὖ' (eu, meaning "well") and 'dæmon' (spirit)</note> if they had a well-disposed spirit. Therefore, they say that before we can recognize blessedness, it is appropriate to first have knowledge of God and of the spirit. Thus, each requires the other. These and many other points differ from the opinion which men are first said to have held concerning the gods. 

Then, they disputed at some length whether the gods themselves actually exist, since an opinion or estimation can be held about something which does not actually exist, such as a Scylla or a centaur. Many have said that gods do not exist, <margin>Euhemerus. Callimachus.</margin> such as the arrogant old man Euhemerus, who composed wicked volumes; to paraphrase a half-verse of Callimachus: he wished for the gods to be fictions created by powerful and prudent men so that they might restrain the men subject to them through fear. <margin>Critias. However, there were those who argued the opposite and believed that gods do exist, relying chiefly on these four foundations: the consensus of mankind, the order of the world, the many absurdities that follow the opinion of those who remove the gods entirely, and finally, the easy dismissal of the arguments that oppose them. There were also philosophers who remained silent when asked about the gods; for this reason, unless I am mistaken, the Skeptics could place them neither among those who affirmed the gods nor those who denied them. <margin>Thales. Tertullian. Furthermore, among those who affirmed and those who denied, the Skeptics thought they acted more securely by taking a middle path. They would "accept" the gods "without dogmatic opinion" <note>original: "ἀδοξάστως" (adoxastos), a key Skeptical term meaning to follow custom without intellectual commitment to its absolute truth</note>—to use their own word—and would worship according to the laws of their fatherland, but would decree nothing according to philosophy. Therefore, they wrote much: sometimes in favor of the gods, following the Pythagoreans, Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics; and sometimes against the gods, following the footsteps of Carneades and Clitomachus. It is not profitable to recount all these things, <margin>Cicero. # THIRD BOOK. ->C.<-

...Yet it seemed appropriate to have reported these few things so as not to abandon the order of the book. Certainly, Iamblichus writes that the knowledge of the one God is innate and, as it were, branded into men, <margin>Iamblichus</margin> and he speaks of a "touch" of divinity that is, as he says, far better than any mere knowledge. He asserts that the plurality of gods was rejected even in antiquity by fine minds, and unity was affirmed. Many others of our side have shown this, and I myself have clearly demonstrated it both in my books *On the Foreknowledge of Things* <note>original: "de prænotione rerum"</note> as much as I was able, and in the book *On Providence*. <margin>Works of the author in which he argues against the plurality of gods.</margin> In that book, unless I am mistaken, all the arguments of both Carneades and Clitomachus <note>Sceptic philosophers of the New Academy known for challenging religious dogmas</note> are easily refuted. 

But I return to the Sceptics. So that they might not be accused of impiety—since they seemed to do away with the gods as the makers of things—they took care to more generally and universally do away with the causes of things, or at least leave them in doubt. The majority of Dogmatic <note>In Sceptical philosophy, "Dogmatic" refers to any philosopher who claims to have found the truth, such as the Stoics or Aristotelians</note> philosophers attempted to establish these causes of things; but those Sophists who thought they could remove local motions and changing causes from our midst believed they did not exist. The Sceptic philosophers argued that it is more likely they do not exist than that they do, raising arguments on both sides so that they might finally introduce doubt and ambiguity to this matter, as they do with all others, and withhold their assent.

Therefore, they were accustomed to argue against the existence of causes themselves, or to review arguments devised by others: <margin>Arguments of the Sceptics against the causes of things.</margin> If a cause exists, it belongs to the category of things that are <term>relative</term> <note>original: "ad aliquid"—a philosophical category where a thing's identity depends on its relationship to another, like "father" depends on "child"</note>; that is, it is the cause of something. Now, things which are said to be relative exist indeed in our thought, but not at all in reality. Furthermore, if anything is said to be the cause of something, it cannot exist if that of which it is the cause does not exist. But many things are said to depend on their causes which not only do not depend on them, but do not exist at all, as will become clear. 

Besides, a cause as a cause cannot be known unless the effect is recognized as the effect of that cause. Therefore, for a cause to be understood, it is necessary to have foreknown the effect insofar as it is its effect; and for the effect to be foreknown, it is necessary to have prior knowledge of its cause insofar as it is a cause. Thus, each is known by the other, and it does not sufficiently appear where the starting point should be. And from this is introduced the "circular" argument <note>original: "locus," referring to the Sceptical 'trope' or mode of circular reasoning</note> which has already been rejected. 

To this they add: if there is any cause, either a body is the cause of a body, or an incorporeal thing is the cause of an incorporeal thing, or a body is the cause of an incorporeal thing, or an incorporeal thing is the cause of a body. But none of these is the case; therefore, there is no cause. For if the first is granted, since both possess the same nature, why would one be the cause of the other rather than the reverse? If both were causes, there would be no effect or "patient" <note>the thing being acted upon</note>; and where that is conceded, there will be no efficient cause either. If the second is granted, by the same reasoning, it would follow that there is neither an efficient cause nor a recipient. If the last two are brought forward, then that which acts must touch the matter in order to act, and the "patient" matter must be touched in order to be acted upon. But an incorporeal thing can neither touch nor be touched. Therefore, they argue that a body cannot be the cause of an incorporeal thing, and vice-versa. 

But this last point would be very easily solved by our people through a distinction <margin>The author's theological solution.</margin> between "bodily contact" and the contact of "power" <note>original: "uirtutis"</note> or "sense" and "spirit." However, Aenesidemus <note>A famous Sceptic who revitalized Pyrrhonism</note> argues against causes in this way: <margin>Arguments of Aenesidemus.</margin> if a body is the cause of a body, it is either ungenerated—like the atom according to Epicurus—or generated, as is commonly said; and this is either manifest, like fire or iron, or unmanifest, like the atom. Whichever of these is said to be the cause, it can produce nothing; for it either produces something while remaining according to itself, or not according to itself but by joining with another. If you say the first, you must also say that it cannot do more than its own nature allows; if the second, you will not rightly say that a third thing is produced by it which was not previously present in it. For how can it be that one turns into two, or two into three? In this way, something...

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the Sceptic critique of divine providence, the author now addresses their specific logical arguments against the concept of causality (cause and effect). He transitions from Iamblichus’s defense of the "one God" to the Sceptics’ attempts to undermine all deterministic origins.</meta>

BOOK.

[Marginal note: The author's theological solution.]

...would prevent infinite things from being produced from one; and by the same reasoning, this could be asserted and brought forward regarding the incorporeal without difficulty. In addition, they [the Sceptics] say that nothing is the cause of anything if both exist at the same time, because one is no more a cause than the other; nor can one be the cause if they occur one after the other. For if the cause exists while the effect does not yet exist, it cannot be called a cause of that thing. For a "cause" is defined in relation to its effect; and things that are relative in this way must exist simultaneously. They usually argue in a nearly identical way regarding the "mover" and the "moved." But the solution is readily available: therefore, it is not useful to explain these arguments further, since the division is not complete. From one eternal and omnipotent cause, many causes and effects could be produced in different ways. However, that Divine Cause is not a cause of an effect in the same way as others are; rather, it is infinitely exalted above every cause that we humans properly conceive and understand. Our theologians prove that this same Cause is present in all things, even the lowest.

The Sceptics also attempt to remove causes from our consideration by showing that causes ought not to be said to exist any more than the effects themselves. They ask: is a cause, by its own nature, entirely and perfectly responsible for producing a thing, or does it require some cooperating power from the effect itself? If you say the former, it would mean that everything must be attributed solely to causes—a notion that almost all philosophers agree is a common error. For if you grant this, you will find no cause that exists purely by itself, since the effect should be attributed to the nature of the object as much as to the cause.

For example, if fire is the cause of burning, it would be so either by its own nature and through itself, or because the material being burned cooperates with it. If the first were true, fire would burn everything it touched; but it is not so, for it burns some things and not others. Therefore, it does not produce burning by itself, entirely and absolutely. If you answer with the second option, how can we say the fire is the cause of the scorching, and not also the property and fitness of the wood? For just as there is no burning if fire is absent, there is also no burning if the material that can be scorched is missing. Therefore, if a "cause" is defined as something which, if present, an effect is produced, and if absent, it is not, then the material's property for receiving the fire's impression is just as much a cause as the fire itself.

They put forward many other similar logical proofs <note>original: "epichiremata," a technical term for a complex syllogism or proof</note>, by which they say the Dogmatic philosophers <note>Dogmatic philosophers, such as the Stoics or Aristotelians, are those who claim to have found the truth, as opposed to the Sceptics who continue to search.</note> are so constrained that they must almost admit that the "sufferer" [the passive object] is not different from the "agent" [the cause], but that the effect happens through their meeting. Just as the melting of wax depends not so much on the heat as on the nature of the wax itself, since one cannot cause the melting without the other. The wax is no more melted because of the heat than the heat "melts" because of the wax. Therefore, they want to conclude it is absurd that something which depends on two things should be attributed to only one as the cause.

They add this also: those who claim there is a cause either state it simply without any rational reason, or they are persuaded by "suitable causes" to believe it. If the first, they deserve no credit. If the second, they are "begging the question" <note>original: "petunt id quod principio negatum est," a logical fallacy where the proof assumes the truth of the very thing it is trying to prove.</note>. For they are assuming the existence of causes to prove that causes exist, while the existence of causes is the very thing under doubt. Sextus [Empiricus] himself discussed these and many other things regarding cause and effect in Greek for the Sceptics, both in the third book of the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* and in the first part of the book *Against the Physicists*. I have brought these few points forward in Latin to maintain the order of the book and keep my promise, and I have omitted the rest.

<meta>This page continues the Sceptical critique of physical reality, moving from the impossibility of identifying causes to the impossibility of defining "matter" and "body" themselves. The author is likely summarizing arguments from Sextus Empiricus or a similar source to show how Sceptics undermine the foundations of physics.</meta>

### BOOK THREE. 101.

They have also brought matter itself, and all those things which depend upon it, into the realm of controversy. By disputing at length regarding material principles and the very elements of corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> things, they have hinted—through the extremely fierce battle of philosophers over these very principles—that the truth about them cannot be comprehended. This is evident since some philosophers have wanted there to be only one principle, while others argued for many. Among those who argued for many, some said they were finite and others infinite; and among those who argued for one, some chose earth, others water, others fire, and others different substances, as I have reviewed for the most part in the first book of this work.

Starting from that point, they consider that those things which are called either corporeal or incorporeal cannot be comprehended, since they claim that neither the body nor the incorporeal can be understood. <margin>Against the definition of body.</margin> Therefore, if a body is (as some define it) "that which is capable of acting or being acted upon," they judge it to be incomprehensible for this very reason: they have already sufficiently attempted to show above that neither an "agent" <note>the thing that acts or causes change</note> nor a "patient" <note>the thing that is acted upon or receives change</note> can be comprehended.

If, however, a body is defined as a "triple dimension" <note>having length, width, and depth</note> that is capable of resistance, they attempt to dismantle that definition with this argument: The thing called a "body" is either something else besides these very things—namely length, width, depth, and resistance—or it is merely the gathering and coming together of these properties. If they say the former, they would also have to say what that "other thing" is, which is nonetheless excluded from their own definition. If they assert the latter, then if all the individual parts that make up the definition are removed, the body itself is immediately taken away as well.

If there are certain boundaries of bodies, these must be either lines, surfaces, or other bodies. Whichever of these is asserted, it will be said to either exist by itself or to be considered only within the bodies themselves. If the first is claimed, it will seem like a dream. If the second is asserted, it will immediately be granted that by its own nature, it does not actually form a body. For it is necessary that whatever is rightfully affirmed to produce something else must have some essence of its own. Therefore, these boundaries will not be found to exist within the bodies themselves, which is also revealed by the difficulties surrounding the concept of "touch."

For if joined bodies touch one another, they touch by their outermost boundaries or ends—that is, by their surfaces. Therefore, surfaces as a whole will not be united to each other in their entirety through touch, because touch would then be a "mixture" or a certain merging of the things that are in contact, which is not what we observe. If, however, a surface touches the surface of the body placed against it with some of its parts, but is united with the body of which it is the boundary with its other parts, then no one will be able to observe a length and width around the body that lacks depth—and therefore, no surface at all. 

Similarly, if we suppose two surfaces are joined together according to their extremes—where they end according to the length said to be in them, which is to say, along lines—then the lines themselves, through which the surfaces are said to touch each other, will not be united. For they would be mixed and confused in some way. If, however, each of these lines touches the line of width placed against it with some parts, but is united to the surface of which it is the boundary with other parts, then it will not be "without width," and thus it will not be a line. If, then, there is neither a line in a body, nor a surface, then neither will width, nor length, nor depth be within it.

<margin>Argument that touch is not comprehensible.</margin> He further asserts that touch is not comprehensible in this way: things that touch each other do so either as "wholes" (as I might put it) or by "parts." Not the first, for then such things would be united to one another rather than merely touching. Not the second, because the parts themselves, when compared to the whole, are "parts," but when compared to their own sub-divisions, they are found to be "wholes." Therefore, since these wholes are parts of others, they will not be touched as wholes by other wholes (for the reasons already stated), nor will parts be touched by parts; for these parts are themselves "wholes" when referred to their own smaller parts. Therefore, neither wholes are joined to wholes, nor parts to parts, by touch. From this, touch is asserted to be incomprehensible, and by that opinion, "resistance" is removed—which is the property by which a body is affirmed to be composed beyond the three dimensions themselves.
