BOOK.

<margin>Concerning incorporeal things.</margin> ...defined. They also believed that incorporeal <note>things without physical bodies, such as the soul or time</note> things are eliminated once the body is removed, just as "privations" <note>the lack of a quality, such as blindness</note> are erased if you remove the "habit" <note>original: *habitum*; here meaning the state or presence of a quality, such as sight</note>. Furthermore, they say that if something is incorporeal, it is either perceived by the senses or by the mind. If the first is granted, it will be considered incomprehensible due to the differences between animals and humans in perceiving, and because of the differences among the senses themselves, the circumstances, the mixtures, and other such things—subjects we dealt with in the second book when discussing the "ten modes" for withholding assent <note>the Sceptical arguments used to show why we should doubt our perceptions</note>. If, however, the second is proposed—that it is understood by the mind—since the sensible leads to the knowledge of the intelligible, and since the reliability of the senses is already in dispute, what will they achieve? To be sure, they would achieve something if they could climb toward incorporeal things using the methods our own thinkers have used. But while they differ on these and many other matters, they eventually come to the subject of "temperament."

<margin>Response of the author.</margin>
<margin>Concerning temperament.</margin>
The "younger" philosophers <note>likely referring to the Stoics or contemporary medical theorists</note> call these "complexions" <note>the specific balance of qualities like heat and moisture in a body</note>. They argue that these are placed in a state of uncertainty because of the multitude of clashing opinions. Among other things, they use this mode of reasoning: things that are "tempered" <note>mixed together</note> are said to be composed of "substance" and "quality." Therefore, one might say that either their essences are mixed but their qualities are not, or conversely that the qualities are mixed but the essences are not, or that both are united with each other, or that neither is mixed with the other. If neither the substances nor the qualities are mixed together in any way, then "temperament" is unthinkable. For how can a single sensation arise from a temperament if nothing is composed in any of the ways we have mentioned? If, however, someone says that one quality is simply placed next to another, while the substances are mixed, he would surely be speaking nonsense. For we do not grasp these temperaments by discarding the qualities that exist in the temperaments of bodies; rather, we perceive them as a single thing fashioned from those elements which have been blended. But if, on the other hand, someone asserts that the qualities are mixed while the substances are not, he is undoubtedly asserting the impossible: for the essence of qualities resides within the substances themselves. Therefore, it will be seen as ridiculous if he claims that qualities—separated from their substances—are mixed privately and on their own.

<margin>Response.</margin>
What if it is answered that both the qualities and the substances are blended together in the temperament, and that this blending constitutes the temperament itself? They will persist and press their point,

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
contending that this could only happen if the mixture occurred solely through "power" <note>original: *potestate*; meaning the influence or effect of a thing rather than its physical presence</note>, or that it could never happen unless an equal amount of each of the things to be mixed (as they say) were provided. For if someone mixes one "cyathus" <note>a small cup or ladle used as a measure</note> of some juice with ten cyathi of water, they would not deny that the juice is mixed with the water. If, then, a tiny bit of this mixed thing is taken, one will find it full of the power and virtue of the juice. But if part is mixed with part in such a way that the whole is "coextended" <note>spread out through the same space</note> with the whole through the passing of quality and essence, then they will be equal; and then either the one measure will be equal to ten, or the ten to one. These are the sorts of things they say, along with several others, to which a response would not be difficult through the arguments the younger philosophers make regarding temperaments.

<margin>Concerning motion.</margin>
Next, they attempt to "move motion from its place," so to speak <note>a play on words: they are trying to displace the concept of movement</note>. Although it is said that there are six species of motion, they begin with that motion which is called "local" <note>change of place</note>. There are two species of this: either when a body moves according to the whole, or according to a part. An example of the first is when someone changes their location by walking; of the second, when someone extends and contracts a hand, or when a sphere rotates around its center, while one part and then another always changes its location and stands in a different relation to the point fixed in the very heart of the sphere. However, three opinions regarding motion itself have been tossed about in ancient controversy. Some, such as Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Epicurus, and the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, decree that motion exists. Others, such as Parmenides, Melissus, and Diodorus Cronus, say it does not—unless perhaps Diodorus might concede that something "has moved," but by no means that it "is moving." Indeed, he is numbered among those who abolished motion. The Sceptics, however, say "no more this than that," nor the opposite. Insofar as they look at the things that "appear" <note>the evidence of the senses</note>, they do not deny that there is motion...

### BOOK THREE. 102.

...perhaps persuaded by Antisthenes the Cynic <note>a student of Socrates and founder of the Cynic school, known for his emphasis on practical ethics over theory</note>, who, when he was questioned about the nature of motion, responded not with words <margin>Antisthenes.</margin> but with action—namely, by standing up and walking around. However, insofar as motion is investigated by philosophical reasoning, the Sceptics <note>followers of Pyrrhonism who sought tranquility by suspending judgment</note> argue that it does not exist. Therefore, when they bring into the light both the arguments usually made in favor of motion and those made against it, and they oppose these logical reasons to appearances and common sense, they withhold their assent <note>original: *assensum cohibent*; the Sceptical practice of refusing to agree that a proposition is definitely true or false</note>. They judge that motion exists "no more than it does not exist," because of the discord among various opinions and reasonings. The arguments that are led against motion are generally of this sort: if something moves, it is moved either by itself or by another. <margin>Arguments against motion.</margin> It is not moved by itself, because everything that is said to move something else moves it either by pushing, by pulling, by thrusting it upward, or by pressing it down. If a thing pushes itself, it must be behind itself; for every such thing that pushes something before itself is...

### [possibly 115] BOOK.

[uni]ty being taken away: for unity is indivisible, and therefore cannot be taken away. Nor can it be taken from the nine that remains <note>Latin: *relicto*; the OCR reads "felicto," likely a printing error for the number nine remaining after subtraction</note>. For that which is taken away does not leave the thing from which it is said to be taken whole; however, the number nine is not diminished when a single unit is taken away from a ten <note>The logic here is that "nine" is a distinct essence; if you take 1 from 10, the "nine" doesn't change its nature, it only begins to exist as a result</note>. That addition also cannot occur can be proved from this: that which is added is added either to itself, or to something already existing, or to that which is constituted from both. For example, let a ladle <term>cyathus; a small liquid measure or ladle used in ancient Greece and Rome</term> be added to four ladles. I ask: to what is the addition made? Not to the ladle itself, because that which is added is different from that to which it is added, and nothing is different from itself. But neither is it added to that which is composed of both. For how can an addition be made to something that does not yet exist? And the composition of one and four ladles does not yet exist before the addition of one to four occurs. If, however, the addition is said to be made to the pre-existing four ladles, it would follow that the single ladle itself is equal to the four ladles, because that which is extended and co-extended to something else must be equal to it. Therefore, neither addition is sufficiently established, nor subtraction; and through this, neither is transposition, which clearly arises from addition and subtraction. For these reasons, they assert that motion does not exist.

To these, Diodorus Cronus <margin>Diodorus Cronus.</margin> <note>a Greek philosopher of the Megarian school famous for his logical puzzles</note> argues in this way: If something moves, it moves either in the place where it is, or in the place where it is not. It does not move in the first, because it remains there and fills it; it does not move in the second, for it is not in that place. It would be absurd to say that what is in Rhodes is moving in Lesbos. He also affirmed that nothing is *moving* <note>original: *moueri*; the act of being in motion</note>; nevertheless, he affirmed "having moved" <note>original: *motum*; the completed state of motion</note>, even though it was not currently in motion. He said this because he claimed an indivisible thing is contained in an indivisible place, and is found now in this place, now in that. This concept <margin>Response of the author.</margin> seems not entirely unlike that which some of our own writers have treated when they discussed the motion of angels <note>The author likely refers to Medieval Scholastic philosophers who debated whether angels move through space instantaneously or continuously</note>.

But indeed, I know that the first argument can be easily answered by the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note> regarding the motion of a sphere in the same place, and the distinction between the "point from which" and the "point to which," so that a body is said to be partly in one and partly in another. But the Sceptics press on regarding the parts of that same sphere not moving in the same place, and they attempt to do away with the distinction of motion, whether taken in a broad sense or a strict sense—for example, in a house, or in the air surrounding us. They speak of "proper place," that is, the surface of the air hedging us in; in which nothing moves, if it is truly said to be in it. For a body is not rightly said to be in any other parts of the surrounding air except those by which it is enclosed. Therefore, the doubt that was brought up before returns.

Many other arguments are brought forward, both in the third book of the *Pyrrhonian Outlines* and in the work *Against the Physicists* by the author we have often cited <note>Sextus Empiricus, the primary source for ancient Scepticism</note>. In discussing growth <margin>On the whole and the part.</margin> and diminution, they throw against common sense the argument regarding the inconstancy of things, whose essence flows and changes so constantly that you cannot affirm it is the same. Furthermore, they contended above that addition (by which growth happens) and subtraction (by which diminution happens) are to be abolished.

There is also a great dispute concerning the "whole" and the "part," not only because the Stoics <margin>Stoics.</margin> <margin>Epicurus.</margin> wanted "the whole" and "the universe" to differ. For these words, they substitute "the whole" <note>original Greek: *to holon*</note> and "the all" <note>original Greek: *to pan*</note>. They say "the whole" <note>*holon*</note> is the world, but "the all" <note>*pan*</note> is the void outside the world together with the world as one. Therefore, the former is finite, while the latter is infinite. However, Epicurus and most others confuse these and accept them interchangeably. I say this not only for those reasons, but because there is much dispute about how the whole and the parts differ, and how the parts differ among themselves. Many strive to do away with the "whole" and "parts" entirely, or at least leave them in doubt, of which these few points may suffice: If addition is abolished (as we did above), the "whole" is abolished, which is constituted from the meeting of parts. And even if subtraction is granted, if one or some parts are taken away, it ceases to be a whole. To these things, if there is any whole, it is either something different from its parts, or the parts themselves are the whole. If the first is granted—that it is something other than the parts—it follows...

### BOOK THREE. 103

...it follows that once the parts have been removed, the whole itself would remain—which we do not see happen in any case. If the second option were true, the "whole" would be merely a name and an empty label, supported by no essence of its own. Furthermore, if there are parts, each will either be a part of the whole, or they will be parts of each other, or each will be a part of itself. 

It cannot be the first, because there is no "whole" apart from its parts; thus, the parts would effectively be parts of themselves, since each individual part is said to contribute toward the completion of the whole. It cannot be the second, because a part is understood to be contained within that of which it is a part <note>Logic dictates that if A is a part of B, B cannot simultaneously be a part of A, as containment is a one-way relationship</note>. Nor can it be the third, because a thing would be both greater than itself and smaller than itself—being both that which contains and that which is contained—if it were said to be a part of itself. 

<margin>On natural change.</margin> Natural change as well, which the more recent philosophers <note>Latin: *iuniores*; likely referring to the Stoics or other later schools who refined the terminology of physics</note> are accustomed to call <term>alteration; *alteratio*, a type of change where the substance remains the same but its qualities change, such as a cold object becoming warm</term>, is called into doubt. For either it is a body that is transformed, or it is something incorporeal; or it is changed according to active or passive causes—but all these matters have long since been brought into controversy. Furthermore, that which is changed is said to be changed in some span of time; but it is changed neither in the present time, nor in the pre[vious time...]

...has been made, or not at all; this they by no means affirm. For it is said to be formed and perfected by that which is placed within the body itself. But if they say this, they are going to say it because when a body is in a place, then there is a "place" in which that which is placed within it is already said to be; but it is already called the place of that specific body which is put into it. Finally, it is either a body or it is incorporeal, but both positions are called into question above. Just as they also wish for **time** <margin>On time.</margin> to be considered under the same scrutiny. For as far as we follow those things which appear to the senses, they say that time seems to be something; but when the arguments usually brought forward from various sides are placed under examination, they have argued that it is nothing at all. This is true whether one brings forward the definition of those <margin>Many ancient definitions of time.</margin> who wished for time to be a certain dimension of the world's motion, or of those whose consensus is that it is the "number of what is before and after" in motion <note>This is Aristotle's famous definition of time from his *Physics*.</note>, or of those who called it the measure of motion and rest, or those who asserted it was chance, or those who thought it a body, or those who thought it incorporeal. For truly, all definitions of this kind cannot be true because they fight against one another and destroy themselves. And which of them is false? Different people decide differently. Since, however, everyone seems to adopt motion, rest, and number, they wish it to be easily understood that if these are removed (as was attempted before), time will be removed as well. Furthermore, they raise the question: is it finite or infinite? And they weave arguments for both sides. They also inquire whether it is divisible or indivisible. If the second is answered, they oppose it with the division of the present, past, and future. If the first is answered—since everything that is divided is said to be measured by some part of it—they assert that no time can be measured, because one part has already passed, one part is in the future, and that which is present is held to be indivisible <note>The argument is that you cannot measure something that has no width (the present) or something that does not exist (the past and future).</note>. Moreover, they say it is neither created nor corruptible, because that which is generated must be made from something that is in the process of becoming, and it must also be destroyed in something that is becoming; nor is it uncreated and incorruptible, because one part does not yet exist and the other has passed away. And since everything that is generated or happens is said to happen *in* time, if time is made, it will be made in time. Therefore, either it will be made in itself, or one in another. If the first—that it is made in itself—the same thing will simultaneously exist and not exist; for it is necessary for that in which something happens to pre-exist the thing that happens within it. If they answer the second—that one happens in another—then the present will happen in the future, and the future will happen in the present. These and many other things are disputed by them concerning time, but these remarks on it are enough, as are those on every difficulty they bring against physical things. Now let us look at what they have prepared against moral doctrines.

...bringing forward what will seem to us to fit the matter we are dealing with, as we have often done in this work to show that nothing in human philosophy is so firm and stable that it has not had fierce attackers and destroyers. First, the question of how life is to be led and with what morals is usually brought into controversy from the various opinions of philosophers and the assessments of different nations. Regarding this matter—since in the first book we reviewed many things pertaining to this: the highest good <note>original: "summo bono"</note>, the disagreement of philosophers over goods, evils, and <term>indifferents</term> <note>Things that have no inherent moral value, like wealth or health, which can be used for either good or evil.</note>, and concerning human virtues and laws; and in the second book also some points while mention was made of the <term>tenth skeptical mode</term> <note>The "tenth mode" of the Sceptics focuses on ethical systems, customs, and laws, showing how they differ across cultures to argue against absolute moral truths.</note> of contradiction—we will not repeat all those things at present. Instead, to introduce those things we must now dwell upon, we shall keep them in mind.

Some define the Good itself as that which effects happiness, others as that which completes it, others as that which leads to attaining it, and others as that which is to be chosen for its own sake. Plato, in the first book of *The Laws*, separated goods into divine and human. He said divine goods are wisdom, temperance, justice, and courage. Human goods are health, beauty, strength, and wealth. Others defined it otherwise, for as each person desired for themselves or possessed what was desired, they measured the good; hence perhaps Aristotle says "the good is that which all things seek." <note>A reference to the opening of Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>

But indeed, the Sceptics do not want the essence of the good to be known, but rather certain "accidents." <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature—like a person being tall or short.</note> These accidents either belong to the good alone or to other things. If they belong to other things, they do not constitute the good itself, nor do they separate it from things that are not good (if I may speak so) in such a way that they properly signify and shape the good. But if these accidents belong to the good alone, it still cannot happen that we thoroughly know the good itself from them. For just as he to whom a horse was unknown, and who did not yet know what it is "to neigh," would not come into knowledge of a horse through the act of neighing unless he first encountered a horse while it was neighing. So he who was unaccustomed and ignorant of the good, and asked what the good was, would be unable to know what was properly and solely in the good itself unless he could understand the good from the good itself. For first it is necessary to know the nature of the good itself, and then to know that it helps, and for that reason is to be chosen, and that it promises or provides happiness.

That accidents of this kind do not suffice to declare the nature of the good, the <term>dogmatic philosophers</term> <note>Philosophers who claim to have found the truth and hold certain doctrines as absolute, as opposed to the Sceptics who continue to search.</note> themselves will be witnesses. Even if they concede all those things, when they are nonetheless asked what that thing is to which those very accidents happen, they will stir up incredible fights. For some will devise virtue, others pleasure, others freedom from pain, and others something else to be that which helps, which is to be chosen, and which effects happiness. They will decide no differently about evil and about that which is indifferent, since they also wrangle and war over its nature.

Furthermore, they argue from this that nothing is by its own nature either good or evil or indifferent. Whatever affects someone by nature affects all equally who possess the same nature. For fire heats and burns all wood; snow affects all living bodies with cold; and so for the rest. But good, evil, and the indifferent do not so affect those by whom they are said to be known; therefore they cannot be counted among those things which are such by their own nature that they are rightly judged to be so. For to pass over the unlearned common people—some of whom think health of the body is the good, others to be immersed in crowds of harlots, others to be addicted to gluttony, others to gorge on wine, others to spend the night in games, and others even worse—many of the philosophers establish three types of goods. Yet they are not in agreement in dividing them, since the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note> and the <term>Stoics</term> divide them differently. But also some have placed pleasure among the goods (though not held as such by the others), not only placing it among goods but as the first of goods, while there are nonetheless those who place it among evils to such an extent that...

One of them exclaimed: "Better to be insane than to feel pleasure," <note>original: "μαίνεσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἥδεσθαι"</note> which is to say, to be mad rather than to be delighted. Truly, he who says one must walk partly this way and partly that, so that the strife of the philosophers disputing this matter might be avoided, would himself become part of the strife, by which he would be opposed either to one side or the other; he himself would also require someone to judge and decide whether he had chosen rightly or not at all. Since, in truth, no judgment for deciding the truth exists that is undisputed, clear, and accepted or received by all—as we discussed in the second book of this work based on the opinions of these philosophers—they say it is better to **abstain from assent** <note>This refers to the Sceptical practice of *epoché*, or suspending judgment, when faced with equally weighted but contradictory arguments.</note> rather than to decide rashly and without clarity. 

They also add this: that which is called "good" is either the act of choosing itself, or the thing which we have chosen. It is not the first [the act of choosing] by its own nature; for we do not hasten and desire to choose something, and pursue it, unless we might fall away from that very desire—that is, so that we do not have to choose anymore. For we do not long to choose wine or bread when we are thirsty or hungry, except so that we may be freed from the distress of hunger and thirst, by which we were affected when we longed for and chose the bread and wine. Therefore, to desire and to choose is not good in itself, but is more truly a trouble, <margin>Sextus / Aristotle</margin> since the hungry man busies himself to obtain food for no other reason than to lack the trouble of hunger; and thus one must judge concerning all other appetites. 

If the good is said to be according to the thing we choose, <margin>Plato / Aristotle / 1st Book of Ethics</margin> this is certainly either outside of us or around us. If it is outside, it surely either works some affection in us, or nothing at all. If nothing, it will not lead us to choose it. If it does work an affection, then it is no longer the thing itself outside of us that is to be chosen by us, but rather the disposition implanted in us from it. If, however, it is around us, it will be either around the body alone, or around the soul, or around both. If it is around the body alone, it will escape our knowledge: since we only know by the soul, <margin>Common opinion</margin> not by the body alone. If they say it extends from the body all the way to the soul, it is necessary that what is chosen is either known or remembered insofar as it is judged by the mind or thought—not by the irrational body. It remains, therefore, for them to assert that the good exists around the soul alone. 

But this is also a matter of controversy even among the **Dogmatists** <note>Philosophers who claim to have discovered the truth, as opposed to the Sceptics who are still searching.</note>, since some say the soul does not exist. Others say that if it does exist, it can comprehend nothing, as was widely disputed when the Sceptics examined the question of the "criterion of judgment"—a question pregnant with many things. 

Certainly, **Epicurus** assigned the good and the end of life to pleasure; <margin>Epicurus</margin> yet he said the soul consists of atoms, just like everything else. In a heap of atoms, how can pleasure be formed, or assent, or judgment? And how can we affirm, if we are of sound mind, that "this is to be chosen and is good," or "this is to be fled and is evil"? 

How shall we agree with the **Stoics** as well? <margin>Stoics</margin> For they say the "good arts" are in the soul, and that they are formed from practiced concepts; but they affirm that since concepts are centered around the **principal spirit**, <term>hegemonikon</term> <note>The 'ruling part' of the soul in Stoic philosophy, which they believed was a physical, breath-like substance (spiritus or pneuma).</note> we must seek the collection of knowledge and art in that very spirit. But one impression deletes another, and a prior shaping will be abolished by a later one, since the spirit itself is in some way fluid...

...they are carried by a certain impulse; for if they are driven, they do not choose. Nor are they always driven, and brute animals lack the reason that humans possess, which they ought to use to restrain their pleasures. These pleasures should not be considered among the "goods" because they produce evils and are the causes of pain, poverty, disgrace, and death. Moreover, bodily labors are often opposed to pleasures, while honesty of the soul frequently prepares true pleasures. Truly, if anyone considers how diverse and varied the decrees of tribes, nations, and almost all schools of philosophers have been regarding goods and evils—how they pursued some and fled others—he will see that nothing certain can be found in human morals even among the philosophers themselves. For what some considered a "good," others placed among "evils" or categorized as *indifferent* <note>original: *indifferentia* – things that are neither inherently good nor bad, such as wealth or health, which depend on how they are used.</note>. 

Let us examine, therefore, what was held to be shameful or not, what was lawful or unlawful, pious or impious, according to their laws and customs. Among us, it is considered shameful and wicked—rightly and deservedly so—to have sexual relations with boys. Yet, among the ancient Germans, as <margin>Sextus. Aristotle.</margin> Sextus [Empiricus] says, and also among the Gauls (according to Aristotle and the older Isidore), it was not considered shameful; indeed, by their custom, boys were publicly "married." Among these same <margin>Julius Caesar. St. Thomas.</margin> Germans, robbery was once not considered infamous, as Julius Caesar writes, and after him, St. Thomas [Aquinas]. But let us not believe that this vice of male lust belonged only to one nation. Among the ancient Cretans, it became a deep-seated habit; hence the grammarians believe Virgil was referring to this when he mentioned <margin>Virgil. Cicero.</margin> Cydon. Among the Thebans, too, the love of boys was not condemned. I believe the cause of this crime lay in the laws of Lycurgus, which loosened the reins on the shameful love of boys. These laws, along with their author Apollo and their admirer Plato, were condemned by <margin>Theodoret.</margin> Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop who wrote extensively against pagan philosophy and laws.</note> in his book *On Laws*. I will not mention now how this wicked and most destructive vice migrated into Italy and other regions; for even if it is committed there, it is still considered shameful and is punished by the severest laws. 

But among those ancient peoples, as I said, it was not considered shameful—just as among the Persians it was not shameful to abuse boys (as we said in the previous book). Similarly, among the Massagetae, it was not considered shameful or obscene for women to be shared publicly and engage in adultery. Among the Persians, it was not shameful for mothers to marry their sons or fathers their daughters; for according to the laws of Zarades <note>likely referring to Zoroaster</note>, as found in Theodoret, this was permitted—not only for sisters to marry brothers (which was legal among the Egyptians). But while these acts between male and female do not shrink from nature in the same way, it is even more surprising why this very crime of male lust was not exploded <note>meaning "driven out" or "rejected with hissing"</note> by all the philosophers. 

On this point, the <margin>Cynics. ...[even if they] held to it in words, were they not found to be strangers to it in their deeds? For must we not examine this: did the philosophers not admit that their own morals were at war with their speech and doctrine, a point asserted by many? Or did they act legitimately and according to reason? For instance, when Pythagoras <note>A famous Greek mathematician and philosopher (c. 570–495 BC).</note> sought tyranny among the Tyrians, or Zeno <note>Likely Zeno of Elea or Zeno of Citium; here accused of political ambition.</note> among the people of Priene. Or when Anaxagoras refused to return a deposit to his enemies. Or when Aristotle <note>The famous student of Plato and tutor to Alexander the Great.</note> shamefully caused his friend Hermias to be cast out with a joke, or when he basely fawned over Alexander, or sold the oil in which he had bathed, or performed sacred rites for a woman he loved as if she were Eleusinian Ceres <note>The goddess of the harvest; the author is accusing Aristotle of deifying his wife or mistress, Pythias or Herpyllis.</note>. Or when that insane and rabid Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was a critic of Christianity.</note> wished to kill himself, restrained only by Plotinus. Indeed, it seems so: even Cicero <margin>Cicero.</margin> reported that their lives and vices fought marvelously against their speech. So too did Cornelius Nepos <margin>Cornelius Nepos.</margin> <note>A Roman biographer (c. 110–25 BC).</note> write that he had seen many of those who, in the schoolroom, taught most cleverly about modesty and restraint, yet lived in the grip of every lustful desire. Before him, Cato the Censor <margin>Cato.</margin> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC), known for his strict morality and opposition to Greek influence.</note> attacked the deceits of philosophers who fashioned empty shadows of words—those who (to use his words from the *Attic Nights* <note>original: "in Atticis noctibus repetitis"; a reference to Aulus Gellius’s work.</note>) say they have nothing and yet lack nothing and desire nothing, even as they burn with having, lacking, and desiring. 

Therefore, they were condemned not merely for the sake of perpetual disagreement and contention—as we showed sufficiently in the epilogue of the first book—but perhaps they were carried so far into wickedness that, because of it, they were expelled by decrees of the Senate. This happened both while the Roman Republic stood and while the Emperors held power, as was indicated earlier in this very book. Nor were they left unattacked by their own kind. Surely Seneca <note>A Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note>, in his refutation, compared them to doctors whose labels claim to offer remedies while their jars <note>original: "pyxides"; small boxes or jars used by apothecaries.</note> hold poisons. 

<margin>The benefit of divine law.</margin>
O, the greatest benefit of the divine law! That which the competing philosophers of the nations have never defined without controversy through so many centuries, this law has taught and explained in few words and with peace: what is good? what is evil? what must be done? what must be avoided? And this was done first under the shadow of the Mosaic beginning <note>The Laws of Moses in the Old Testament.</note>, and then in the most splendid light of the perfect Gospel. Those who preached this Gospel did not overturn it by living a contrary life; instead, to defend it, they endured crosses, racks, and fires. In this Law, whatever is commanded is a rule for living and an art for attaining happiness, because it is the word of God—always true, always holy, always to be observed. 

In contrast, what the nations have handed down is either false, or profane, or either always or often harmful. I ask you, what fixed law for conducting life can be found among them? For they have not yet agreed among themselves what is to be judged as good, what as evil, or what as neutral or indifferent. Whether you enter their path of doctrine or of morals, you will find as many opinions as there are heads. Even in the laws themselves, which many have attempted to overturn, Cicero confessed that no solid and expressed image of true law or genuine justice is held—only shadows and sketches <note>original: "umbram & imagines"; literally "shadows and images."</note>—and he said, "If only we would follow even those!" Indeed, many have disapproved of those laws for the very reason that each nation established laws for what was useful to itself. As for the morals of the philosophers, they are as varied as the common people; if they belong to different sects, they are utterly different; if they are followers of the same sect, they are still not the same. But also, as that author said, their speech fought marvelously with their morals and their life. Therefore, the "art of living well and blessedly" cannot be found among them, since no art is found in their studies and schools that is not full of difficulty and teeming with their brawls. For there is not one art, but many, and they fight against each other in turn. Therefore, men cannot follow them all, since they are opposed to one another; and whichever one is proven to be closer to the truth by human reason will also be disproven by human reason. Nor can there be any appeal to a Lydian stone <note>term: Lydian stone <gloss>a touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here a metaphor for an absolute standard of truth</gloss></note>. Nor can a sect be led sincerely by common human inclination...

### Epilogue of the third book of the examination: in which it is shown that all the sects of philosophers attained some shadow of truth only insofar as they, even from afar, emulated the divine dogmas of the sacred scriptures, in which whatever is scattered unclearly and thinly in those profane books can be seen to be collected eminently and purely. Chapter 14 and the last of the third book.

**H**itherto I have reviewed for the most part what the nations <note>The author uses "nations" (Latin: *gentes*) to refer to the non-Christian or pagan world.</note> have attempted while warring among themselves with literary weapons for so many centuries, so that I might show that nothing firm and nothing constant can be found among them. Wherefore, not content with what most people bring forward while insisting only on well-worn and common controversies—and not unrolling more remote and, as I judge, more effective matters—I myself have attempted to approach the dogmas of the ancient philosophers (unknown to not a few people), not merely citing their doctrines, but looking at complete and finished volumes written in Greek. I have looked especially at the works of the Sceptics, who argued pugnaciously and subtly against all the rest. Although I do not approve of these Sceptic philosophers in most things, nevertheless I do not disapprove of them insofar as they blunted the arrogance of those who professed to know and hold all or most things. It is, however, very easy for one considering human nature more subtly to see clearly that in all the sects of philosophers there is something notable which is not common to the others; if you compare these into one, you will plainly find all those things much more eminently and purely in the sacred scriptures which we Christians revere. 

The Sceptics <margin>Sceptics</margin> <note>original: "Sceptici". These are the followers of Pyrrho, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> disapprove of other philosophers who profess to know anything by the power of human philosophy. Does not sacred scripture do this much more clearly, effectively, and truly? For it despises the empty philosophy of the nations and warns us lest we be deceived by it. The Sceptics take up the laws of their country and acquiesce to their ancestral customs simply and without any inquiry. Do not our people do this, but more securely and holily? For they command that divine voices be admitted without a scrupulous examination of reason; they are led by simple faith to believe and hope in eternal things, and to behaviors either commended by divine law for keeping, or condemned for casting aside. 

The Dogmatic <margin>Dogmatics</margin> <note>original: "Dogmatici". In this context, this refers to philosophers like the Stoics or Aristotelians who asserted certain truths as certain.</note> philosophers, on the other hand, say they know; they are indeed to be admitted if they understand that they know only some things and in a human manner, and through the intermediate senses which often deceive. Otherwise, our senses were given to us for learning in vain—that is, if they always deceived; but if they never deceived, what falsehood would there be in human affairs? Whence would any praise for truth be found? Whence would any reward be found? Is it not so that in the sacred scriptures, discipline is sometimes praised, and at other times the excessive desire for searching is condemned, while we are warned not to be wiser than is fitting? <note>A reference to St. Paul's letter to the Romans (12:3): "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think."</note> 

As for those who wish that nothing be known, the Academics <margin>Academics</margin> <note>original: "Academici". Specifically the "New Academy," which followed a tradition of extreme doubt.</note>, insofar as they uncovered in their disputes many things which were thought to be true but were false, they are indeed to be tolerated and approved. This is as Solomon instructs: that a fool must be answered according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself. <note>A reference to Proverbs 26:5.</note> But insofar as they asserted that they knew only this one thing—that they knew nothing—in that respect they are not to be imitated, but rather...

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book I of the new volume. It continues the author's argument that secular philosophy is inherently unstable and that true certainty is found only in the "divine light" of Christian Scripture, a theme established at the end of the previous book.</meta>

BOOK I.

Bitter contention must not be held, by that same precept of Solomon <note>Proverbs 26:4: "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him."</note>, by which we are ordered that a fool must not be answered according to his folly, lest we appear like him. We have spoken in general about this pursuit of grasping the truth among the various sects of philosophers: of which some asserted that they held it, others that it could by no means be held, and others that this was no more true than that. However, if other matters are also examined, it will certainly become manifest that if they possess anything of the true or the probable within themselves, it all depends entirely on the sacred letters <note>A common Renaissance term for the Bible or Holy Scripture.</note>. In these, all those things are found most eminently—along with many other things besides—about which the philosophers of the nations <note>The "nations" (Latin: *gentes*) refers to the non-Christian or pagan world.</note> did not teach, as if they were entirely unknown and separated from human knowledge. 

<margin>In the principles</margin> Therefore, in the first principles, Scripture offers precepts of faith which none of our people reject as certain, and there are those who agree they are evident. Much more so than any things said to be humanly and evidently observed; some would attribute this to that firm inclination by which we are sincerely carried toward believing divine things, while others attribute it to signs above nature <note>Miracles.</note>. Indeed, they hold that it is received from the light of faith, from which they assert a more certain knowledge is derived, through an internal brightness sent down freely from God. By this light, eternal things are seen and assent is granted to miracles—things from which those who are destitute of that very light shrink away. I say that the sacred letters offer their pronouncements much more firmly than the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their reliance on logic and empirical observation.</note> or others from the dogmatic philosophers. 

<margin>John Duns Scotus</margin> John Duns Scotus <note>A major medieval Franciscan theologian and philosopher (c. 1266–1308).</note> thought, in his fourth commentary on theological sentences <note>Referring to the *Sententiae* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> (question three of the fourteenth distinction), that the truths of our faith ought to be held as more excellent than others because the natural light of mortals does not reach them. They are also more certain because they come from that Truth which can neither deceive nor be deceived at all. By this, he intended that what has been revealed in the divine letters ought to be held more certainly than that which any intellect can reach by natural light. Add to this that those very matters of which we have spoken at length have not seemed to everyone to rely on truth, nor have they been admitted by a harmonious opinion. 

<margin>Plato</margin> And add, if you please, that saying of Plato in the *Laws*, that it belongs to God alone to approve those things about which many feel doubt, so that we may be able to prove the certainty of divine eloquence even from the words of the nations. For we were able to see above how ambiguous the pronouncements are among most philosophers, and how full of quarrels they are. Our truths, however, are celebrated both by the consensus of nations and by wonders. 

<margin>In morals</margin> They also prescribe the duties of cultivating morals, which no sane man would fail to see as most worthy of being observed. They are so far from being attacked by quibbles or clouded by ambiguities that—unlike those matters which do not pertain to this—the <term>Sceptics</term> <note>Followers of Pyrrho or Sextus Empiricus who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> do not consider them worthy of being insisted upon. Thus, we can easily withhold assent from them much more than from the disputations of Aenesidemus, Nausiphanes, or Sextus. 

<margin>The Pythagoreans</margin> The Pythagoreans assented to Pythagoras in such a way that they held what he had said as certain; nor did they offer any other proof for it than that "he himself said it" (referring to Pythagoras). And as they themselves used to speak in the Doric dialect, "He himself said it" <note>original: "αυτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha)</note>. We, however, say that God and those who spoke by God's inspiration must be believed. 

<margin>Gregory Nazianzen</margin> As Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> says in his first speech against the Emperor Julian: among them it was said, "He himself said it"; among us it is said, "Believe." Or to use Nazianzen's own words: "Among us, believe" <note>original: "παρ' ἡμῖν πίστευσον" (par' hēmin pisteuson)</note>. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans, the old Platonists, and others among the more recent ones who transferred their studies to divine matters, suggested that Pythagoras’s secret "Quaternary" <note>The *Tetractys*, a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, which was sacred to Pythagoreans.</note> indicated a divine nature. I easily think this happened in Egypt, where he stayed for a long time and where he learned many Mosaic things. He even learned of circumcision and underwent it, according to the authority of Theodoret <note>An influential theologian of the School of Antioch (c. 393–458 AD).</note>, which circumcision we read in the historians of the nations was a custom of the Egyptians. Thus, Pythagoras could have held in his secrets the name of four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the four-letter name of God in Hebrew.</note> by which the essence of God was most famously signified among the Hebrews. This can even be confirmed by the fact that he was accustomed to swear an oath by that very Quaternary...

...they succumb. Therefore, we ought to embrace those writings <note>Referring to the Sacred Scriptures and the works of the Church Fathers.</note>, by whose study we both ought to and can follow truth while rejecting falsehood, and attain happiness while sending away misery. These are the very writings that the philosophers of the nations <note>The "nations" or "gentiles" refers to the non-Christian/non-Jewish pagan world, specifically the Greeks and Romans.</note> sought out by undertaking travels and exiles; and if any of that liquid which the soul, thirsty for truth, desires has ever watered their own literary monuments, it all flowed from the fountain of those sacred writings. This is evident since **Plato** sought out Egypt, and from there the streams of the Academy and the Lyceum flowed forth, though they were somewhat murky, having been drawn through the superstitions of Greece. Even before him, **Democritus** and **Pythagoras** dwelled in Egypt; and even earlier **Orpheus**, who commanded Musaeus to maintain the worship of one God, though he himself had previously been a worshiper and advocate of many gods. Indeed, Orpheus obtained a greater fruit from his travels than Pythagoras or Plato, who lived in later ages; for by their time, the Egyptians had already begun to gradually admit many superstitions of multiple gods alongside the noble monuments of **Moses**. Add to this that both eloquence and the knowledge of reality flourished among the philosophers of the nations, though handled in diverse ways, as can be seen in the volumes of the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, and among the Stoics and Sceptics. Among our own theologians, you will find both distinguished eloquence and a more exact knowledge of things, made manifest by a greater and clearer light. Furthermore, in those ancient theologians and the proclaimers of our Christian law, there was a pure and naked truth, confirmed by supernatural signs, which the nations lacked. Then, many men of excellent talent and learning arose, both among the Greeks and the Latins—not to add strength to the truth (which is self-sufficient), but to reject those who attempted to stain the sincerity of our faith. By their efforts, they contributed a great deal to the propagation and adornment of theology itself. For while they interpreted and declared the sacred writings, they brought forth such vast and deep rivers of wisdom that anyone delighted by divine matters could draw from them as if from channels. For who is ignorant that **Peter Lombard** compiled his *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* (c. 1150) was the standard medieval textbook of theology.</note>—over which all younger theologians have toiled in explanation—and that **Gratian** compiled the *Concord of Discordant Canons* <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, a foundational collection of Canon Law.</note>—in explaining which the interpreters of pontifical law have labored—from those very ancient theologians? Even the Decretal letters of the Popes were confirmed by their testimonies, so that one might eventually return to the sacred writings by way of those intermediate theologians. But when the study of literature entirely ceased in Greece, and when the cultivation and proper use of the Latin tongue withered among the Italians and foreigners, the continuous flow of style was changed into a concise form. Those ornate figures of speech, drawn from the workshops of orators, gave way to the naked syllogisms of dialecticians <note>Logic-choppers or practitioners of formal scholastic logic.</note> and mere propositions. The result was that while the later writers followed the dogmas of the ancients, they could in no way match their style of writing. Finally, so that nothing should be lacking, and so that we might even surpass the nations in this regard, there were some who—not ignorant of oratory, logic, and all philosophy—acted as mediators between those ancient orators and these modern logicians. They undertook the task of manifesting the truth so that a much easier return might be offered to those most esteemed and ancient writers who should be read and learned by heart, by whom the sacred writings were more sincerely explained. Although we excel in neither eloquence nor knowledge, we nevertheless desire to follow them; for this reason, we have already examined so many and such great volumes, both among the Greeks and the Latins—some long neglected and many unknown to most people. But because in our own time not many people either know or care for these ancient things—considering these styles of speaking to be antiquated—they only recognize or admit **Aristotle**. They go so far as to think him the only philosopher, and they imagine all his dogmas are true and conform to the sacred scriptures. Perhaps they are not unlike those of whom **Lucilius** spoke: "Like infant children who believe that all bronze statues are alive and are real men." <note>Lucilius (c. 180–103 BCE) was a Roman satirist. This quote mocks people who mistake lifeless imitations for reality.</note> Come now...

<meta>The previous page introduced the author's intent to scrutinize Aristotle's reputation. This page continues that preface, with Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola justifying his critique by contrasting Aristotle's pagan authority with the supreme truth of the Christian Gospel, while referencing his own history as a former defender of Aristotelian thought.</meta>

BOOK. <unclear>faded text</unclear>

I do not deny—indeed I confess—that if I assert that his doctrine, when weighed as if on a scale and examined at length, does not possess the weight that most have believed it to have; if I show it to be frustrated without true philosophy, to be uncertain, and in many places false, let them excuse me. Let them instead ascribe this to a love of truth and the pursuit of piety. Will Christian men and brothers, who share in the one true religion, deny me this request when they have granted it freely and without mediation to Aristotle, a foreigner enslaved to profane and superstitious nations? A certain idolater <note>Likely a reference to Cato the Elder, who famously distrusted Greek influence in Rome.</note> could not endure a Greek city among the Roman citizens; he could not tolerate the delusions of the Egyptian land located so far away. Shall I, a Christian man among Christians, and before their very eyes, endure that the volumes of Aristotle be either preferred to or equated with the Gospel of Christ? These books are so refined and so highly esteemed that you will not easily find one among the proud cultivators of letters who does not strive to be called an "Aristotelian" rather than a "Christian." They think the former is the title of a learned and distinguished man, while the latter is a name for the unrefined and the common. They are so unpolished and so utterly lacking in true reason that they are deluded into thinking <margin>What [to think] of Aristotle in general.</margin> everything in Aristotle is certain, firm, and unshakable—as if nothing more certain or more supported by truth could ever be found.

There is much (and I do not deny it) in Aristotle that is erudite; there is much elegance in his writing, and perhaps even much truth. But there is certainly no small amount of vanity. Use a balance, and notice which side weighs more. Use it often, so that the husk may be separated from the grain, and the empty chaff may be tossed to the West Wind. Why are you angry? I ask nothing of you except that, having departed from there, you seek better things, and lift yourself up from human things to divine things as if on the wings of faith and love. Or are you looking at me with a grim expression because I have called Aristotle’s doctrine "vain"? Why are you not first and more angry with those who called him a "quack doctor" <note>original: "pharmocopolam". Critics sometimes slandered Aristotle by claiming he was a failed druggist before becoming a philosopher.</note>, as reported by Aristocles the Peripatetic, and by Eusebius, and by Athenaeus? Why not be angry with Theocritus of Chios? As recorded by the same Aristocles, and by Diogenes [Laertius], and by Eusebius, he called Aristotle "vain"—and the Greek word he used, *vain-minded* <note>original: "κενόφρων" (kenophron)</note>, sounds even sharper. 

But those who have learned in the Book of Wisdom that "vanity" is the charge against anything lacking the knowledge of God, and those who have read in Solomon <note>Referring to the Book of Ecclesiastes, attributed to Solomon.</note> that "all things are concluded under vanity," ought to be much less angry. If some place my own study under that same heading, I shall not take it poorly, provided they themselves make progress and acknowledge the truth. Otherwise, I ask you, what have I to do with Aristotle? I follow the truth, and I exhort others to follow it. 

Indeed, I once explained his dogmas in commentaries dedicated to the rational soul and the "appetite" of prime matter. And when certain ill-mannered men attempted to falsely ascribe to him an impiety regarding divine providence to excuse their own crimes, I spoke on Aristotle's behalf. I showed that providence was affirmed by him, though not sincerely nor in all respects; for this reason, his teaching on that subject was called *small-minded* <note>original: "σμικρολόγον" (smikrologon), meaning trivial or petty.</note> by both Gregory of Nazianzus and Theodoret. Nevertheless, having discussed all his works to the best of my ability, I revealed in the first part of a long work composed on that subject that he supported rather than detracted from divine providence. At other times, I defended Aristotle against certain ancients and against Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century humanist who critiqued Aristotelian logic.</note> for the same reason. In my book *On Imagination*, I even called him the "interpreter of nature." In that book, as in many others, I followed him frequently—either because the facts seemed to be as he had determined, or because his authority was so great that it did not occur to me to question the truth of his doctrine. For most people considered him not just a philosopher, but the very law of philosophy. And yet, I was never so burning with zeal for his study, or that of other philosophers, that I did not recognize their doctrine as largely uncertain...

<meta>This page begins Book Four of Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s "Examen vanitatis doctrinae gentium" (Examination of the Vanity of Pagan Doctrine). The author transitions from a general critique of ancient learning to a specific, systematic assault on Aristotle. He prefaces this by discussing his personal hardships—exile and war—during the composition of the work, attributing his ability to write amidst such chaos to divine providence.</meta>

**BOOK FOUR**

<margin>That the author wishes to attribute whatever good exists in his works to God.</margin>

In performing this duty, if any true or good things should shine forth, I would wish them to be credited not to me, but to the Father of Lights <note>A reference to James 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights."</note>. While I desire this in all my other books, I most especially hope for it in this fourth book of this work, and in those which follow—the fifth and sixth <note>The OCR reads "quarto" (fourth) again here, but the context of the work's structure indicates the fifth and sixth books.</note>. This should not be taken as a mere display of modesty, but rather as a matter of truth, for I hardly dare consider myself fit to carry such a burden. By some means, I have been led to a task I might otherwise never have hoped for. This began during the most bitter time of my exile, when it would have been more appropriate for me to handle weapons to resist injustice, to implore the aid of kings and princes, and to secure the friendships of my peers. Later, it continued during the defense of my homeland, recovered after a four-year war, where we who had returned suffered no less labor than we did when we were twice exiled in foreign lands. Nevertheless, amidst those very hardships, everything judged necessary for completing this work was present, granted by divine favor. For even during my travels, the spirit to work by lamplight was there; in foreign cities, libraries of various languages were not lacking; and in defending the walls we had gained, even amidst the siege engines <note>original: "machinas bellicas"</note> and dangers, there was often such tranquility and peace of mind that one could hardly have desired more in a time of peace and leisure. Who could rightly doubt that these benefits, occurring amidst such calamities, were orchestrated by God? And who could fail to credit them to God himself, from whom all true and good things are derived, as if from the very fountain of truth and goodness, by His marvelous providence? But now, in this fourth book which we have at hand, let us attempt to reveal the vanity of Aristotle in general. In the fifth and sixth, however, we shall strive toward that same goal more specifically and (as I believe) more effectively.

**That the doctrine of Aristotle, when weighed in the balance, shows more emptiness than true weight, and that it suffers from a threefold vanity. Here also, the order of the three following books is explained in detail. Chapter One.**

<margin>The first vanity of Aristotle’s doctrine is explained at great length.</margin>

So, are we to weigh the doctrine of Aristotle in the scales? O, what a labor, exposed to the many bites of slander! But with piety as my leader and truth as my companion, nothing is to be feared. This first point (unless I am far mistaken) is certain: if in one scale we place Aristotle’s diligence, his elegance of style, his sharpness of wit, his vast reading, and his great learning, we could place little else in it besides. But if in the other scale we place a threefold vanity, I might easily believe that the former does not outweigh the latter, but rather is tossed high into the air by that weightless momentum. For where there is superstition, uncertainty, and falsehood, what solid weight can there be? What is not empty? What is not vain? When we have detected this vanity throughout the whole work, we shall be unjustly accused of a false examination. Therefore, it will be possible to see that his doctrine staggers and is even now on the verge of collapse because of this threefold vanity, the meaning of which we discussed in the first book of this work. To begin, we must deal with the vanity of the beginning and the end, and with deceptive means. This is done both to preserve order and so that this dispute does not bring us hatred, but rather brings shame to those who would condemn our undertaking to commit these things to writing—should wise judges of affairs consider it so. Both the unlearned and the scholarly believe that the beginning of philosophy depends upon the Highest Good, and that its very end is placed in the attainment of that Highest Good. It was the consensus of all who are well-regarded in literature that this cannot be possessed except through religion. Nor was Aristotle himself averse to this, who, both in his *Ethics* and in the republic which he established...

"God is an eternal and most excellent living being." <note>original Greek: "τὸν θεὸν ζῶον ἀΐδιον ἄριστον." **Alexander.** From this definition, perhaps, Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A highly influential commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD); Pico accuses him here of "delirium" for identifying God with the physical universe.</note> drew his delirium, teaching that God is the world. But what need is there to distort the philosopher's meanings with interpretations that are hardly firm—not to say inept? 
**Response** For they bring into the discussion that word "we say" <note>original Greek: "φαμέν" (*phamen*). <meta>This page continues the critique of Aristotle’s theology. On the previous page, the author began dismantling the idea that Aristotle's definition of God as an "eternal living being" aligns with Christian truth, suggesting instead that it leads to pantheism or physicalism.</meta>

->FOURTH BOOK<-                                        113.

...Aristotle argued in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, while speaking of the first mover who is pure act <note>original: "actus purus." In Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to a being with no untapped potential, often identified by medieval scholars as God.</note>, that he was not speaking of the altogether first being whom we call God, but of the whole class of separated movers. Petrus Aureolus <note>Peter Auriol (c. 1280–1322), a Franciscan philosopher known for his critical stance on earlier medieval traditions.</note> contends that Aristotle's opinion on separated substances <note>Non-physical beings, such as angels or the intelligences that move the celestial spheres.</note> contradicts the faithful truth in three ways. He decrees that the heaven itself is not moved by God in an "executive" or direct manner according to the opinion of Aristotle and Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle dominated Western thought for centuries.</note>, though many have thought it was so moved. Certainly Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Christian philosopher in Alexandria who wrote extensive critiques of Aristotle.</note>, the Greek author, in his commentary on the third book *On the Soul*, says that according to Aristotle, the intellect is that which turns the unerrable sphere <note>The outermost celestial sphere of the fixed stars.</note> and which he himself calls the creator. However, Philoponus asserts that to Plato, God did not seem to be merely "intellect," nor is that idea consistent with pious dogmas, since God is above the intellect. From this comes the word for providence, which is called *pronoia* in Greek [Marginal note: providence], being named, he says, "as being before the intellect" <note>original Greek: "ὡς πρὸ τοῦ νοῦ ὤν" (hos pro tou nou on). This is a folk etymology suggesting God's "forethought" exists prior to any rational process.</note>, as if He were above the intellect. 

I know, however, that others think otherwise and bring forward reasons, and I know those reasons can be answered. Nor does it escape me that in the eighth book of the *Physics*, it is noted that the name of God is said to be composed of the heaven and the intellect; and in the *Topics*, he divides "animal" into the "sensible" and the "intellectible." I shall remain silent for now on what he wrote in the first book *On the Soul* that might pertain to this matter; for in the fifth book, when definitions are disputed, and in the sixth, when metaphysical matters are treated, we shall discuss this further. It is not properly the place here to discuss this controversy or to review what others have brought for or against him. At present, we are concerned with demonstrating from Aristotle's own words, rather than the words of others, that he decreed poorly concerning religion. 

Furthermore, in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de mundo." A treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle, now usually considered "Pseudo-Aristotle."</note> addressed to Alexander, he placed God within the aetherial body, opposing Plato. For this reason, Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165) who tried to reconcile Greek philosophy with the Gospel but remained critical of Aristotle.</note> rebuked him, as did the philosopher Athenagoras in the speech he gave on behalf of the Christians to the Emperors Marcus [Aurelius] and Commodus; he showed aptly that Aristotle considered God to be a living being <note>original: "animal."</note> composed of soul and body. Galen, too, in his book *On Philosophical History*, judges that Aristotle thought this. Aristotle also made mention of God as a living being in the first book *On the Soul*, as Simplicius <note>One of the last great Neoplatonist commentators (c. 490–560).</note> also aptly testifies. 

But we shall speak more extensively on this in the final volume of this work. Let it suffice for the present to have warned that in Aristotle there was no true knowledge of God, and therefore, by the testimony of Wisdom, he is to be blamed for "vanity." His writings do not contain religion, but superstition. While this is broadly evident from what we have narrated, we shall find it even more accurately if we choose to run through the sixth and seventh books of the *Politics*, where he institutes temples and priests for the Gods, and commands that the gods themselves be honored by the citizens. He ordered that shrines be distributed through the regions not only for gods, but for heroes, and many other things which we wrote in our book *On Providence*. While we were then defending him from the charge of impiety, and teaching that he had handed down divine worship and providence to posterity through his writings, we must admit he did so not sincerely or religiously, but entirely superstitiously in the manner of the other Gentiles. He even approached the oracles of demons, and he agreed that certain causes which seemed contrary to nature should be reduced to their prophecies as if they were divine. 

Hence we find that passage in the third book *On the History of Animals*: 
☿ A certain goat in Lemnos and its male offspring produced milk while being milked in such great abundance that from it they made "pyriatidas" <note>original Greek: "πυριατίδας." This refers to colostrum, the first milk produced after birth.</note>—which Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century humanist and translator (c. 1398–1475) who translated Aristotle's works from Greek into Latin.</note> translates as *colostra*. Indeed, he [Aristotle] thought these things should be held as "symbola" [Marginal note: Justin], that is, signs—which Theodorus translates as portents—and should be accepted as referring to a prophecy. God, he says, had responded to one who consulted him that he would excel in the increase of his flock. 

Therefore, let those who worship Aristotle realize they are worshiping an idolater—a man who philosophized in such a way that, according to the martyr and philosopher Justin in that work which we translated from Greek into Latin, or according to the historian Procopius in his fourth book while speaking of the Euripus...

...even those possessing only moderate learning might rightly be held in high regard, and could be raised so high by the zeal of factions and the genius of excellent men that they might either be equaled in glory or even preferred, if their praisers strove toward that end. For nothing is so lowly that it cannot be held in high value if the consensus of those skilled in letters is added; conversely, nothing is so elevated that it cannot easily be brought low by that same consensus. This has been the case regarding the ancient estimation of Aristotle, and that which has been propagated even to our own age—although under the popes Eugenius and Nicholas <note>Popes Eugenius IV (r. 1431–1447) and Nicholas V (r. 1447–1455), both patrons of Renaissance humanism.</note>, George Gemistus and Cardinal Bessarion of Nicaea cultivated Platonic studies. Marsilio Ficino the Florentine converted that same Plato into Latin and explained him with many arguments and commentaries. Others, nonetheless, setting Plato aside, clung to Aristotle, thinking that he was less discordant with our religion. They relied perhaps on this reasoning: that Aristotle could do less harm to those who are not pulled away from the faith taken in common than Plato could. For Plato, through many suspicions, could more easily provide an entry point for a faith that is not properly and exactly driven by the faith, but taken in common, whereas Aristotle is accustomed to rely mostly and almost always on reasons, not on faith. <margin>Giovanni Pico.</margin> Giovanni Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to synthesize all schools of thought.</note>, the brother of Galeotto’s father, as I said in the first book, had undertaken to reconcile both philosophies—those of Plato and Aristotle—and had he not been prevented by death, he would easily (as I believe) have left no further longing for that matter to posterity, so great was the force and dexterity of his genius, and so great his learning. <margin>The Author.</margin> But I, to repeat what was indicated in the first volume, have attempted in the preceding books not to reconcile, but to weaken the entire doctrine of the gentiles <note>Pagan or non-Christian philosophy.</note>, and in these books which follow, specifically the Aristotelian doctrine. To this world, this most subtle reasoning would never recall souls blinded by the manifold darkness of errors and stained by the deepest filth from the body, unless the Most High God, with a certain popular mercy, had lowered and submitted the authority of the divine intellect even to the human body itself. Stirred not only by His precepts but also by His deeds, souls could return into themselves and look back toward their homeland without the strife of disputations. These are the words of Augustine. He was so far from thinking that a life should be consumed in thoroughly reading Aristotle, since he placed both the men he proposed and the whole of human philosophy in a secondary position. There are even to this day some who begin to open their eyes and think they should proceed toward better things. They do not think Aristotle should be made of such great account as he used to be; and now, through ten ways <note>Likely referring to the ten "tropes" or modes of skepticism used to demonstrate the uncertainty of knowledge.</note>, we shall show his doctrine to be uncertain in general until the end of this book, and in the following books, more particularly and effectively, through many reasons as well as authorities and examples, we shall show it to be both uncertain and false.

To be sure, for those who have drawn their knowledge of ancient matters from literature, I would not have had to traverse this first path, nor would so much labor have been expended to show it to others wandering, as if through an inhospitable region. For more stood against Aristotle than stood with him, nor did they judge his teaching to be certain. However, that it is now thought otherwise, and for that reason a **greater number defends him with phalanxes joined shield-to-shield**, <note>Original: "maior defendat numerus iunctæque umbone phalanges." Nor is something true—or should it be held as true—simply because it pleases the majority, as Aristotle himself is the authority for this: for he writes that many false things are more "probable" to some than true things—that is, they are more accepted and pleasing to the crowd. Indeed, that famous sentiment is also his: **one must speak like the many, but think like the few**, <note>Original: "loquendum ut plures sentiendum ut pauciores." A famous maxim suggesting that scholars should use common language in public while maintaining rigorous, private intellectual standards.</note> as if he were silently teaching that the judgment of literature and learning belongs to the few. Wherefore, by his own testimony, we can agree with those ancients; the few of them who stood against him ought to be considered of greater weight in rendering a sentence on matters of philosophy than the many myriads of others who live now.

<margin>An objection.</margin> But if anyone should assert that Aristotle was always held in the highest esteem by the consensus of nations, and should bring forward Alexander his disciple—who was both the conqueror of nations and (if I may say so) the terrifier of all Greece—by whose power Aristotle was made the "Prince of Philosophers," <margin>The solution.</margin> he can observe from many examples how far he is deceived. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the historical reception of Aristotle.
