**BOOK FOUR. 117**

<margin>Cavillation is removed <note>Original: "Remouetur cauillatio." A "cavillation" is a petty or unfair objection; the author is likely addressing critics who might argue over his definitions.</note></margin>

...must be considered in general. The Peripatetic philosophers, and even the Platonists who interpreted Aristotle in the Greek language, raise a question over every single one of his books: Is the very book they are taking up to explain legitimate Aristotle, or is it substituted and a "bastard" <note>Original: "nothus." In textual scholarship, this refers to a spurious work falsely attributed to an author.</note>? This was the custom of Ammonius, Magentenus, Philoponus, Simplicius, and even Olympiodorus, to say nothing of the others. Nor do I now mean a book once possessed by Aristotle, or which was formerly among his property—I am not speaking sophistically or relying on ambiguity—but a book which was ever derived from Aristotle’s own copies, composed or published by him. This doubt and uncertainty of opinion was caused by the variety of ways Aristotelian books were handled and put into order. For authors do not even agree enough for there to be one single path of discovery; it is still unknown if we possess any book composed by Aristotle, and there are other issues that will appear shortly.

<margin>Dispute over the book of *Categories*.</margin>

Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, the 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> disagrees with those who previously wrote the lives of the philosophers. Later writers vary from him and others, and as far as it pertains to the faculty of logic, we once told many stories about this, which the place itself seems to remind us to review here in some way. Thus Laertius himself writes and brings forward works of dialectic records which are not held in this century, and he is silent on many things, remembering nothing of those which are among us and constantly in our hands. For the four volumes of *Sophistical Divisions* and the books *On Contraries* are by no means held by us. Nor likewise do we know the *Methodic* volume, nor those which he composed *On Interrogation and Response*, nor the volume *On Proverbs*, nor those *On Contentious Propositions and Syllogisms*. Even less known are those he published *On Genera and Species*. Indeed, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist whose introduction to Aristotle's logic, the *Isagoge*, became a standard textbook.</note> makes it clear enough that these were unknown for many centuries before us; he provided several instructions on genera, species, and properties so that Aristotle’s book of *Categories* <note>Original: "prædicamentorum." These are the ten fundamental ways things can be described.</note> might be understood.

<margin>Dispute over the books of *Physics* and *Metaphysics*.</margin>

But regarding the very book of *Categories* which we hold to be Aristotelian, how great is the dispute over whether it is his own! Some have said it belonged to Archytas the Pythagorean; but there is another book of Categories or "Classifications" <note>Original: "Cathegoriarū ue."</note> by Archytas, written in the Doric dialect, which still exists. Others said it belonged to a certain Aristotelian named Archytas; others argued the opposite. Furthermore, Adrastus of Aphrodisias created uncertainty as to whether it should be considered a legitimate book of Aristotle, as he recorded that two books of *Categories* were usually shown as being by Aristotle. The philosopher Ammonius increased the material of the question, asserting that two books of *Categories* were found in the library of Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who greatly expanded the Library of Alexandria.</note>, even though only one is said to have been written by Aristotle. To these, Laertius cites nine books of the *Prior Analytics*; we have two.

<margin>That many Aristotelian books which are cited are not held by good authors.</margin>

So too there is a varied question concerning the philosophical books and the *Metaphysics*, as different people bring forward different titles and subjects for them. For eight books of the *Physics* <note>Original: "physcorum."</note> are circulated among us, and twelve of the *Metaphysics* among many, while among some even fourteen are claimed, although even more are said to be by Aristotle himself. There are four *On the Heavens*, two *On Generation [and Corruption]*, three *On the Soul*, and besides these, other small books on other matters are still usually circulated. But in Laertius, there is one book *On Motion*, three *On the Elements*, and thirty-eight books of *Natural Matters according to the Elements*; three *On Philosophy*, and only one *On the Soul* are listed. Furthermore, he cites one book of *Questions on the Soul*, one *On Pleasure*, and one *On Nobility*, which are unknown. Simplicius also, in a certain digression in his third commentary on *On the Soul*, before he clearly explains those words regarding the "part of the soul by which the soul knows and is wise," cites Aristotle’s dialogue *On the Soul* titled *Eudemus*, bringing it forward as a testimony—yet anyone who has seen that dialogue or...

I find no one who has read it, although Themistius also cites Aristotle’s *Eudemus* <note>original: "Eudemo"; a lost dialogue on the immortality of the soul.</note> in the third book of *On the Soul*. Fabius Quintilianus also cites Aristotle’s *Gryllus* <note>Aristotle's lost work on rhetoric.</note>, which, as far as I know, has been neither heard nor seen in our times. In Athenaeus as well, testimonies are cited from Aristotle’s book *On Drunkenness*; and often even Theophrastus’s book of that same title is brought forward in place of a testimony. To us and to our age, however, such volumes are unknown as far as I know; the fourteen books *On Separate Substances* <note>Refers to immaterial beings like angels or celestial intellects.</note> are also unknown, which Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian.</note> testifies to having seen in his book *Against Averroes on the Unity of the Intellect*. So much is the matter confused that nothing certain regarding his books can be grasped. 

But because they might say that less faith should be attributed to Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, the 3rd-century biographer of philosophers.</note> and historical books, and perhaps they would not stand by Simplicius and Thomas alone, let Aristotle himself come forward. He refers to books written by him *On Plants* in the fifth book of *On the Nature of Animals* <note>Known today as the "History of Animals."</note>; all devotees of Aristotle know that these books do not exist today; and if any that are circulated are not considered legitimate, it is because the books of Theophrastus *On Plants* are read everywhere in their place. Pliny also reported in the eighth book of *Natural History* that Aristotle wrote nearly fifty books on animals, but we have only eighteen whole ones, as it is believed, as well as a fragment on the *History of Animals* which Theodorus <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a key Renaissance translator of Aristotle.</note> did not translate into Latin, thinking that it should be numbered among the books not on history but on the *Generation of Animals*, if it should be placed anywhere. We also know of others from the Aristotelian family who wrote about animals, whose books could have the title of Aristotle prescribed for them instead of the true and legitimate one. 

<margin>Four causes in general why Aristotle's books are held to be uncertain. First cause. Second [cause].</margin>

Let his most sworn followers also come forward, to whom four causes in total are put forth as to why Aristotle’s books can be considered uncertain. The **first** is that there were many who were called Aristotle; therefore, instead of the one who was the Stagirite <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira, hence "the Stagirite."</note>, the son of Nicomachus, the title of a different Aristotle could have been substituted; indeed, eight men by that name are cited by Laertius. The **second** (as put forth by Ammonius) is the lack of a title, whence some could easily put forward one inscription and others another in place of Aristotle’s. A similar dispute was settled a few years ago among the orders of the Minorites <note>The Franciscans.</note> and the Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>. For an interpretation of the Psalms was circulating without a title; the Minorites put the name of Alexander of Hales <note>A famous 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> at the front, while the Preachers titled it under the name of Hugo <note>Hugo of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican cardinal.</note>. And the question, having been debated in Venice, reached this end: by the order of the Patriarch Prelate, it was to be printed in Venice without a title. 

<margin>Third [cause].</margin>

**Imitation** was also a cause why the books of Aristotle could not be distinguished, since it has been handed down to memory and is plainly known by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note> that the books on the *Categories* <term>prædicamentis</term> <note>The "Categories" were historically called "Predicaments" in Latin logic.</note>, *On Interpretation*, and the *Analytics* were written by Eudemus, Theophrastus, and Phanias in imitation of their teacher Aristotle. And besides these, I have observed that they also discoursed copiously on animals and on other things that are usually attributed to Aristotle. For Phanias of Eresus is often cited in Athenaeus in a work *On Plants*, especially in the fifth book. And in the same author, Theophrastus is even brought forward as testimony in the thirteenth book *On Animals*. Likewise, Alexander of Myndus is brought forward in the second book *On Animals*. I know also that there still exists 

<margin>Uncertain books of Aristotle's miscellanies.</margin>

among the learned a controversy whether some Aristotelian dogmas should be attributed to Aristotle or to Theophrastus, especially those contained in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, and the volumes *On Plants* that still exist today. I have also observed in Aristotle’s miscellanies <term>confectaneis</term> <note>From the Latin "confectanea," a collection of miscellaneous notes.</note> that the titles of the books are uncertain. For that declaration on the book of the *Categories* which is now widely held by the philosophers of our time who know Greek is attributed to Ammonius; yet I saw it inscribed to John of Alexandria in an old manuscript. Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A famous Venetian humanist (1454–1493) known for his "corrections" to ancient texts.</note> in translating the great and long [work] of Themistius on the *Physics*...

They are inscribed in such a way—as works that Aristotle sent to his son and dedicated to him—that were there not some who judged them to be the work of the son rather than the father? CXVIII &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; BOOK.

[Prob]able <note>The OCR "babilis" is the conclusion of the word "probabilis" from the previous page.</note> is that reason, too, for persuading us that the books belong not to the father but to the son: since Aristotle wrote eight books on morals to Eudemus <note>Referring to the *Eudemian Ethics*, a work often grouped with the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, and wrote two others, it is consistent with reason that he would not have written several works on exactly the same subjects, repeating the same things.

And indeed, this multifaceted cause, handed down by the ancient Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named for the *peripatos* or covered walkways of the Lyceum where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note>, renders all of Aristotle's books uncertain, so much so that they cannot even be distinguished by their style of phrasing. For it is difficult to discern by phrasing alone those books published in the same century by learned men who delight in the same style of writing; and it is more difficult still when disciples strive with great care to emulate and mold their own style after that of their masters.

Why should I speak only of the same century? Since even in books published in different centuries, a strange confusion <note>original: "allucinatio"</note> occurs. From this arose that significant labor undertaken by Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar who famously categorized which plays attributed to Plautus were authentic.</note> in distinguishing the comedies of Plautus, when, from the similarity of the name, the "Plautian" plays <note>original: "Plautianae"; works by a lesser-known playwright named Plautius.</note> were taken for "Plautine" plays <note>original: "Plautinis"; authentic works by the famous Titus Maccius Plautus.</note>, and those of various others...

**BOOK FOUR. 118.**

That even if we possess some books which are justly and lawfully attributed to Aristotle, it is nevertheless uncertain whether there is anything in those books that is purely Aristotle's, nor can it be distinguished what is his own and what belongs to others. Chapter five.

**S**uppose there are legitimate books of Aristotle; suppose no royal gifts corrupted a title to increase the majesty of that great Alexandrian library; suppose no works of Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> and Phanias <note>Phanias of Eresus, a disciple of Aristotle.</note> were mixed in with his; suppose no volume was marred by a lack of a title. If only Aristotle the Stagirite were thought to have written the *Categories* <note>original: *de prædicamentis*</note>, *On Interpretation* <note>original: *periherminias*</note>, and the *Analytics*, would any question ever have been raised about them? Would Aristotle's doctrine therefore have been certain in every detail? It certainly would have been, but only during the time he lived, when his books were kept whole; but by no means in the following age, and by no means in our own times. For Strabo relates in his thirteenth book <margin>Strabo’s history concerning the books of Aristotle.</margin> that after the death of Neleus of Scepsis—who had succeeded to the school of Theophrastus and had been appointed by Theophrastus as the sole heir of the libraries of both philosophers—all their books were buried in the earth for fear of the Attalid kings <note>The kings of Pergamon, who were aggressively collecting books for their own library, rivaling Alexandria.</note>. Later, when they were dug up in subsequent centuries, they were found torn, gnawed by moths and bookworms, and ruined by the dampness of the earth itself. From there they were brought to Athens and bought by Apellicon of Teos, yet they were even more damaged. Soon, when these same books were carried to Rome by the efforts of Sulla, they were found with such decay in their structure that a certain grammarian, Tyrannion, took up the task of filling in and correcting them, but the business ended in failure, so much so that they were further corrupted by unskillful scribes. Andronicus of Rhodes <margin>Andronicus.</margin> also worked diligently on arranging them and organized the tables, so confused were they. But even that was of no use, for the order of the books that survives is considered varied. 

Take as an example the beginning of the third book *On the Soul* <note>original: *de anima*</note>; this has the opening in Greek: "That there is no other sense besides the five," <note>original: *ὅτι δ' οὐκ ἔστι αἴσθησις ἑτέρα παρὰ τὰς πέντε*</note> for so all the ancient Greek manuscripts I have seen have it. This order and sectioning was maintained by Themistius <margin>Themistius.</margin> in his paraphrase, and not only by the expositors, among whom Simplicius also affirms it; from this, the matter usually proposed for discussion, which the Greeks call the *skopos* <note>original: *σκοπὸν*, meaning the aim or central theme of a work.</note>, is revealed. Should I call Theodorus Metochites <margin>Theodorus Metochites.</margin> an expositor or a paraphrast? Or both? I have not yet sufficiently decided. He seems to present himself in such a way as to have something in common with everyone, even if that whole work, divided into forty books, is called "Systematic" <note>original: *πραγματικὸν* (*Pragmatikon*)</note>. In this work, I say, Theodorus himself follows the division of the books *On the Soul* which other expositors and paraphrasts had followed before: so that he begins the third volume at the same place where the others began. The Latins, however, except for Saint Thomas [Aquinas], with whom Giles [of Rome] does not agree in this part—since he had approved the division of the Greeks—but certainly all the Latins, or most of them, <margin>Latin expositors.</margin> are accustomed to take the beginning of the third book from the part "Concerning that part of the soul by which the soul knows," so that they place the entire section discussing the senses in the second book and remove it from the third. I have maintained this order in the commentaries I wrote on the third book *On the Soul* <margin>Commentaries of the author on the third book *On the Soul*.</margin>. Furthermore, Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator.</note> in his first book *On the Soul* cites something of Aristotle's; and he cites that question of "whether debating about every kind of soul belongs to the physicist" <note>original: *physicum*</note> at the end of the treatise *On the Parts of Animals*, which I have never found in that place though often sought, but we know it is usually placed among the introductions of the first book of those same *Parts of Animals*. He even says that the treatise immediately precedes the books *On the Soul*, which is, however, [denied] by others...

<margin>Variation in the books of the Metaphysics.</margin>
The books of the *Metaphysics* do not agree in the Arabic and Latin translations regarding the eleventh and twelfth books; and part of the twelfth—where the Pythagorean opinion is seen exploded by the Homeric verse regarding the unity of sovereignty <note>original: "homerico carmine de unitate principatus". This refers to the famous quote "The rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler," which Aristotle uses to conclude his discussion on the First Mover.</note>—exists among the Greeks and Latins, but is not found in the codex of Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries were central to medieval Latin understanding of Aristotle.</note>. And as far as the Greeks are concerned, the fifth book behaves differently in some ancient copies than in those printed with tin type <note>An early term for moveable metal type.</note> in Venice. It should also be noted as evidence that in the Laurentian Library <note>original: "Martiana Florentina bibliotheca". Likely referring to the library of San Marco in Florence, though often associated with the Medici/Laurentian collections.</note> in Florence, there exists a sufficiently old codex in which what was said in the fifth book is repeated, unlike in others. 
<margin>Michael of Ephesus.</margin>
But even Michael of Ephesus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his commentaries on the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, cites various modes of necessity from the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, which, however, are known to be placed in the fifth book, not the fourth, among most people. And this should not seem strange to those who have read the Greek codices of Aristotle printed by Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian humanist and printer.</note> in Venice, where the entire numbering of the metaphysical books varies. For what is the second book in Averroes’ translation and most others is held as the first there, and the third is replaced by the second, and so on; much variety is seen. When there is disagreement between the Greeks and Latins, an appeal can be made to Andronicus of Rhodes <note>The 1st-century BCE scholar credited with organizing the "standard edition" of Aristotle's works.</note>. But when the disagreement is among the Greek codices themselves, there is no recourse to a "Heraclian stone" <note>A metaphor for a lodestone or magnet, used here as a definitive "touchstone" to find the truth.</note>. But even Andronicus’s judgment is not sufficiently certain, since it was led by conjecture, and it is even less legitimate and competent when it concerns the work *On Interpretation* <note>original: *periherminias*</note>. For he himself removed it from the Aristotelian family as if it were a bastard and like an "outsider" <note>original: *Asynbolum*, literally a guest who pays no share for a meal.</note>, although others consider it legitimate and home-born. In which volume there is also disagreement: 
<margin>Disagreement regarding the book *On Interpretation*.</margin>
for some divide it into two books, while some assert it is only one book; and many Greeks have dissected that work not into books, but into several *sections* <note>original: *τμήματα* (tmēmata)</note>, that is, several divisions and separations. Nor was there a small conflict over the Aristotelian text among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note> after Andronicus; while each man emended at his own discretion whatever he did not understand, or what seemed to lie incorrectly. Let this be an example in the work *On the Senses*: 
<margin>Disagreement in the book *On the Senses*.</margin>
when for so many years there has been a battle over that small phrase "natural part" <note>original: *φυσικοῦ μορίου* (physikou moriou)</note>; for some preferred to put "nutritive" <note>original: *θρεπτικοῦ* (threptikou)</note> in its place. Others, on the contrary—in which dispute Aspasius <note>A 2nd-century CE commentator.</note> judged that the word "nutritive" ought to be referred to the power of the soul—while Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, the most influential ancient commentator on Aristotle.</note>, by no means asserting that to be true, preferred it to be referred to the part by which we are nourished, and he more highly approved the former reading, but he also reported another in which both phrases were placed. So great is the variety of the whole literary context among the monuments of Aristotle, and furthermore, the order of the books is various. And to say nothing of other things, one may often notice an epilogue introduced for some matter he has disputed, and then, after other things are brought in, the previous things are repeated, inverted, and interpolated. This does not seem to correspond to the glory of a most consummate author in his writing, but rather either to the injuries of time or the ignorance of corrupters, who perhaps looked uselessly to that which suits a poet in forging a song, but not a philosopher writing in prose to explain the things of nature: "He says now what should now be said, and defers most things and omits them for the present time." <note>A quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* (lines 43–44), suggesting that poets have the license to be disorganized, whereas philosophers should be systematic.</note> It is therefore better to ascribe these things to gnawing moths and to reckless distorters rather than to Aristotle, just as Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar who translated Aristotle into Latin.</note> also, in the preface to his translation of Aristotle’s books *On Animals*, blamed Apellicon of Teos <note>The bibliophile who supposedly "restored" the damaged Scepsis manuscripts by filling in gaps with his own errors.</note> for having altered the order of the books of the *History* of those same animals.

**BOOK FOUR. 120.**

For this reason, I myself, intending to consult the Latins—among whom Theodore's translation <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a key humanist scholar whose Latin translations of Aristotle's works on animals became the standard in the Renaissance.</note> is most widespread—will use this very division in citing testimonies. Theodore did not accept, nor did he wish to translate into Latin, the fragment from the history itself which we mentioned above; he clearly rejected it, even if it should have been placed somewhere in the books *On Generation*. Indeed, Plutarch also mentions that Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general who sacked Athens in 86 BCE.</note> carried off the library of Apellicon of Teos from Athens, in which there were many volumes of Aristotle and Theophrastus previously unknown. This is a great piece of evidence that for so much time—for more than two hundred years had passed from the death of Aristotle to the rule of Sulla—such excellent monuments of writing were not known, unless because they had been entirely buried, as Strabo relates <note>The geographer Strabo famously claimed Aristotle's library was hidden in a cellar in Scepsis to protect it from book-collecting kings, leading to its decay.</note>. From this misfortune, who would not rightly conjecture that innumerable flaws have arisen? Plutarch himself mentions Apellicon, Tyrannion, and Andronicus; Athenaeus also mentions in the fifth book of the *The Learned Banqueters* <note>original: "δειπνοσοφιστῶν" (Deipnosophists); a vast Greek work detailing table-talk on various subjects.</note> that Apellicon of Teos, since he was well-moneyed, purchased Aristotle’s library for himself, just as he did others. 

Therefore, as far as the Greek manuscript of Aristotle's books is concerned, we see now that if we wish to have a certain text, we cannot achieve our desire except by a miracle. Otherwise, how shall we have a pure text? Unless perhaps the man himself is raised from the dead, and as some might say, the bookworms must be summoned back from that vast gulf of prime matter so that they might vomit up the meanings they have devoured. Likewise, one would need to hold a council with Apellicon of Teos and those grammarians and scribes—corruptors, not correctors—who, accused of extortion, should return the Aristotelian passages they took away and keep for themselves what they preferred to insert from their own stock. Then they would suggest that Andronicus the Peripatetic <note>Andronicus of Rhodes (c. 60 BCE), the scholar credited with organizing Aristotle's scattered remains into the organized "corpus" we study today.</note> be summoned, so that he might narrate in what state those mangled and torn volumes were when they came into his hands. 

<margin>Refutation of a silent response.</margin>
But if anyone should refuse to stand by Strabo—whom Plutarch also seems to follow confidently—and should deny what he affirmed, why then could I, or anyone else, not also deny that these books of Aristotle which are circulated and read in the schools are truly Aristotelian? That is, they are neither legitimate nor his own, but bastardized and forged. Shall we agree with those born only recently, when they themselves refuse to accept the history of Strabo, who either saw those things himself or certainly could have seen them? For he wrote that work of his, the *Geography* <note>original: "cosmographiæ".</note> in which he relates these things, under Augustus Caesar; and he was no youth, as one who had already nearly spent his life traversing Asia and Europe. Nor does he relate things that have not easily happened to other volumes (I except the divine books of the Old Testament, which, as Josephus and Philo <note>First-century Jewish historians/philosophers who argued for the miraculous preservation of the Hebrew Scriptures.</note> reported, were preserved with such care that neither the captivity of the people nor the desolation of the region corrupted them). 

For even the book of the nefarious law of the Arabs <note>A common Renaissance polemic referring to the Quran.</note> is distinguished differently in the East and the West by its followers, and there is varying opinion: that the book itself is not the same as it once was at the time when its author, Muhammad, was among the living <note>original: "inhumanis", likely a contraction for "in humanis".</note>, inasmuch as it has been expanded, diminished, and interpolated. Nor is there even agreement among everyone regarding the name and the author. All these things can easily be seen in the work of Nicholas of Cusa titled *The Sifting of the Quran* <note>original: "Alchorani ipsius Cribratio"; a 1461 work by the German theologian attempting a critical analysis of Islamic scripture.</note>. How much more, then, for the reasons previously narrated, could these or similar things have happened to the books of Aristotle? And many have already thought they did happen, frequently complaining that they possess corrupt Greek copies of Aristotle. Among these, Theodore Gaza was not silent, stating that he had struggled in translating the Aristotelian works because he had manuscripts that were quite full of faults, either through the fault of the scribes or by that accident which is read of in Strabo. This accident reveals itself even more clearly in the books of Theophrastus, which are scattered and almost vanished, parts of which were also translated by Theodore, if anyone...

If anyone thinks these books are not corrupted, let him consult Athenaeus; he will easily detect that they are both altered and mutilated. But if we should grant—entirely for the sake of argument and with no supporting reason—that the Greek books of Aristotle were legitimate, and that the legitimate Aristotelian meanings and his own mental concepts were preserved in them: yet when we come to the Latin Aristotle, it is a wonder that he is not Aristotle himself. I always except those books which Theodore Gaza <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475) was a Greek scholar whose translations were prized by humanists for their elegance and accuracy compared to medieval versions.</note> translated from the Greek. As for the rest, to say nothing of others, in that text which Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator," who interpreted Aristotle for the Middle Ages despite not knowing Greek.</note> explained—translated from the Arabic language into Latin—nearly as many errors are seen as there are words. See how much a true interpreter of Aristotle he can or should be considered, this Averroes who is so often celebrated by the unskilled. Consider how much value should be placed on this testimony he recorded in the preface of his exposition on natural philosophy: that for fifteen hundred years, no error of any consequence had been found in the written monuments of Aristotle. Yet he himself could offer no judgment of either truth or error, for he did not read Aristotle’s books due to his ignorance of the Greek language, but used an Arabic translation full of lies. Into this he poured his own inventions; and if by chance he did read them, he did not read the books of Aristotle, but those of Apellicon of Teos, Tyrannion the grammarian, and those who thereafter claimed the name of "Peripatetic" <note>The name given to followers of Aristotle, derived from his habit of walking (peripatos) while teaching.</note> for themselves.

**That even if the books of Aristotle are held as certain so far as his authority is concerned, and certain also regarding the context of the letter, such that they were never corrupted at any time, yet by the testimony of Theophrastus, Andronicus, Simplicius, Porphyry, and others, Aristotle's doctrine is uncertain and in some matters false. [Large initial C] Let us, however, grant to the worshippers of Aristotle that the books they call "Aristotle's" can be rightly and deservedly attributed to that very Aristotle as their author and parent. Let us also grant that they were never corrupted at any time, suffered no injury of age, and bore no wounds from scribes or printers. Will they therefore immediately judge the doctrine of Aristotle itself to be certain? If they achieve this, let them see to it that we are not given cause to appeal to his disciples, the heirs of his discipline, and his followers. <margin>Theophrastus</margin> And first to Theophrastus, who criticized his teacher Aristotle regarding the movement of the soul. <margin>Themistius</margin> Although Themistius <note>Themistius (4th century CE) was a statesman and philosopher who wrote extensive paraphrases of Aristotle to make them more accessible.</note> busies himself in protecting Aristotle, Theophrastus can nevertheless be defended against Themistius more easily, it seems to me, than Aristotle can be defended against Theophrastus. And Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a statesman and philosopher known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> reports that Aristotle wrote things which cannot be understood, and which are judged by others to have been stated and interpreted correctly, but by Aristotle least correctly of all. Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist who wrote the *Isagoge*, a standard introduction to logic.</note>—whom Boethius Severinus <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman statesman who translated Aristotle's logic into Latin.</note> says he followed when explaining the books *On Interpretation*, and who excelled in sharpness of intellect and the arrangement of ideas—wrote to the Egyptian Anebo, making it clear that there is no certain doctrine in either Aristotle or others. He testified that all philosophy consists of conjecture, and that its own principles are extremely weak. Among these things, he writes that among the Greeks there is a great battle of words, since a conjecture of the good is taken from human reasoning; he expressed this in his own language thus: "For among us there is a certain great word-battle, because the good is conjectured from human reasonings." <note>Original Greek: παρὰ μὲν γὰρ ἡμῖν λογομαχία τις ἐστὶ πολλὴ ἅτε ἐξ ἀνθρωπίνων λογισμῶν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ εἰκαζομένου.</note> And in his book *On the Soul* to Beritus: "For what account of those things in philosophy is not disputed by me?" <note>Original Greek: τίς γὰρ λόγος τῶν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ οὐκ ἀμφισβήτητός μοι.</note> which means that the things in philosophy are not certain or ambiguous. The same man, in the work he titled *On the Philosophy from Oracles* <note>Original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας</note>, writes openly that all Greek philosophers have wandered astray. In these places, Aristotle spoke universally and made no exception, even though he troubled many with his *Entelechy* <note>A term coined by Aristotle to describe the state of a thing having reached its full potential or functional realization.</note>. Alexander <margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias.</margin> of Aphrodisias, his most devoted interpreter, writes in his commentaries on the first book of the *Metaphysics* that Aristotle laid the foundations of his doctrine in the opinions of the many and the judgment of the multitude. From there he builds his demonstrations—and what could be said more effectively to weaken his doctrine and render it uncertain? Cicero <margin>Cicero</margin> does not approve of Amasanius <note>Gaius Amafanius, an early Roman writer who popularized Epicurean philosophy in a style criticized by Cicero as unrefined.</note> and those who followed the same reasoning, because they wanted to be approved by the unlearned, and they thought that was the foundation of their discipline. From this, however, Cicero draws the argument that those things are not stated with subtlety, but are merely probable. For what is "probable" except what appears true to the majority, by Aristotle's own judgment? What is more wandering than the judgment of the common folk and the multitude? But let it not be error; let it be probability that arises from the same source. Whatever is genuinely probable is clearly not certain. The same Alexander of Aphrodisias, in his commentaries on the *Meteorology*, confesses that Aristotle does not have sufficiently certain reasons concerning that branch of knowledge, as we shall show in due course. He also writes that Aristotle spoke confusingly about the potential and actual intellect, which he sometimes distinguished and sometimes confused. John Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an Alexandrian Christian philosopher who famously critiqued Aristotelian physics.</note> also noted this, and we have mentioned this matter in our own commentary on the third book of Aristotle's *On the Soul* <margin>The author's commentary on the third book of On the Soul.</margin>; and because the situation seemed to require it, we even defended Aristotle. John the Grammarian, surnamed Philoponus, does not merely rebuke and refute him as uncertain, but even as false—the very man whom he nonetheless carefully explains. For he pronounces that even the universal proposition—by whose use Aristotle had taken care to fortify his entire doctrine—always suffers an exception <note>Original Latin: *instantia*</note> in his own paraphrase of the *Sophistical Refutations* <note>Original Latin: *Elenchi*</note>. And in his commentaries on the *Physics*, he disapproves of Aristotle, refuting his views on spaces and intervals, and rejecting his reasons as weak and controversial. Then he even laughs at Themistius for that reason, because Themistius had criticized Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 210 AD), the preeminent physician of the Roman Empire whose medical theories dominated for over a millennium.</note>, by whom Aristotle had been criticized; he was so far from defending him that he would not protect him as a certain authority. Nor did he do this in a few words; for two volumes, and by no means small ones, could be compiled from those things which Philoponus poured out against Aristotle in those very extensive commentaries on the fourth book of the *Physics*. Furthermore, Philoponus eludes the reasons brought forth against the vacuum and the void, especially concerning motion, which Aristotle had thought would be eliminated thereby. We will report some, though not all, of these in the sixth book of this work, and we will touch upon them rather than explain them accurately, lest we simply redo what has already been done. I could cite countless philosophers, either Platonists or those devoted to other sects of philosophers, who would testify as witnesses—though suspect ones—that the knowledge of natural things (in which Aristotle is most highly praised) is not science but opinion, or belief, or if you prefer, "opinionative reasoning." Just as mathematical knowledge of things is "thought," and only intellectual things conceived by reason and intellect produce science, while natural things perceived by sense and reason produce conjecture. But even Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> are not lacking who do not include natural things under the category of science. Simplicius <margin>Simplicius</margin>—worthy of the title "The Great Master" among the Greek people—decides by the authority of both Aristotle and Plato in those most ample commentaries on the first book of the *Physics* that no certain knowledge can be had of natural principles, since those principles do not meet the criteria Aristotle deemed necessary for demonstration. Since Plato also decreed that "physiology" <note>In the ancient sense, "physiology" refers to the study of nature (*physis*) or natural philosophy.</note> is, as if one were to say, the faculty of conjecturing...

Just as Peter of Abano <margin>P. of Abano.</margin> <note>Petrus Aponensis (1250–1316), an Italian physician and philosopher known for his book *The Conciliator*, which attempted to reconcile Greek philosophy with Arabic medicine.</note>, when he disputes the thirty-fifth "Difference" of his book *The Conciliator* [asking] whether witnesses are necessary for procreation, preferred to oppose Aristotle rather than rely on him; yet he calls him the "first master" in that same place, and judges that the science of anatomy was not at all perfect in his [Aristotle's] time. Nor are there lacking those who frequently either attack or quibble with his very manner of speaking.

-> **That Aristotle's doctrine is uncertain, based on his way of writing. Chapter VII.** <-

Indeed, by the consensus of almost all ancient philosophers, Aristotle's way of writing was long ago condemned: as someone who would pursue things that seemed least ambiguous with many words and many arguments. But those things which required much care to be treated, and in which there was some dispute among the learned, he finished in few words. And in this kind of question, he used a series of words that was elegant indeed, but excessively concise <margin>Laconian and Chilonian brevity.</margin>, not only Attic <note>Attic: The refined and clear literary style of Athens.</note> but more than Laconian <note>Laconian: The famously brief and pithy style of the Spartans.</note>, and even more than Chilonian <note>Chilonian: Referring to Chilon of Sparta, one of the Seven Sages, known for extreme brevity.</note>, to use the word of Aristagoras of Miletus. For what could be shorter? Yet he did not wish to use riddles after the manner of the Pythagoreans, for that would have departed from his purpose. But he differed by using words either ambiguous in themselves (even if at first glance they seemed most clear), or so artfully composed and arranged that, at first sight and in the very "vestibule" of reading, they appeared clear enough; yet when you wished to be admitted, you were excluded by a hidden and overly abstruse sense, often indeed perplexed, yet always elegant. From this, I think, it happened that Cicero <margin>Cicero.</margin>, who is always accustomed to praise Aristotle's elegance of writing, writes in the preface of the *Topics* to Trebatius (in which he also extols Aristotle's incredible abundance and sweetness) that he does not wonder that this philosopher was not known to the rhetorician, since he is unknown to philosophers themselves, except for a very few. And truly so, since he was accustomed to reveal brief and involved thoughts not with clear and explained words, but to wrap them mostly in ambiguities, which were nonetheless polished and elegant. I speak of the Greek Aristotle, not of those common Latin translations, than which (if I may say so) nothing is more barbaric, nothing doubtlessly more inept. Just as those translations are foul and rough, so his own Greek elocution is adorned and polished; so much so that Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian philosopher and apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note> thinks Aristotle believed he should be trusted because of that upright and refined kind of speaking. He was, however, frustrated in his wish among most people because of the ambiguous meanings. For that reason, antiquity spread many taunts and many insults against him, to the extent that he did not even escape being nicknamed "the cuttlefish." For the philosopher Atticus <margin>Atticus.</margin> <note>A 2nd-century Platonist known for his polemics against Aristotle.</note>, whom we also mentioned above, said he was like a cuttlefish, whose nature is reported to be such that while it is sought by a fisherman...

...so that it might not be caught by fishermen, as soon as it feels their hands approaching, it scatters that ink of the blackest fluid which it has innate within itself, staining the water so that it may quickly escape from the eyes and hands of the fisherman. So too Aristotle, in those matters where there was a fear he might be "caught"—that is, refuted or proved wrong—would scatter either brevity, or ambiguity, or inconsistency of speech, so that he might elude the sharp gaze of those who wished to catch him. I believe he wrote so obscurely also to hide his own true thoughts. For Aristotle himself is the authority who states in the ninth book of *The History of Animals* <note>Original Latin: *de historia animalium*. Aristotle's pioneering work on biology.</note> that the cuttlefish does this even when it is not afraid. <margin>Aristotle, a man of preeminent genius and most cunning judgment.</margin> But in truth, as he was a man of far-reaching genius and most cunning judgment—as I have always indeed reckoned—he added two other tricks to this craftiness, with which he might first temper the discomfort of his readers. For just as he would somewhat frighten away readers with brevity and obscurity of speech, so too in matters of least controversy, [he would use] repetition...

BOOK.

<margin>Leo X</margin> [Giovanni de’ Medici] had repeated, who a little later was elected Supreme Pontiff and assumed the name of Leo X <note>Leo X (reigned 1513–1521) was a great patron of the arts and sciences, and the author likely mentions him here to ground the discussion in contemporary Renaissance scholarly circles.</note>. Aristotle also employs new ways of speaking and deciding questions, which are themselves sufficient to create questions and ambiguities. For he interjects this little word "perhaps" <note>original: *forte*</note>, and others of the same kind, with which he fortifies himself as if with a guard; he does this most of all in his books on logic, and especially in *The Categories* <note>term: *The Categories* (original: *prædicamentis*). One of Aristotle's foundational works on how we classify and talk about things.</note>. For this reason, his interpreters often say that he is speaking according to the judgment of others rather than his own. They say this especially when arguments directed at those very points cannot be easily dismissed. For this reason among others, it could happen that even his own students were uncertain about his true teaching, as will be revealed shortly. Moreover, that word "perhaps," which in Greek is called *isos* <note>original: ἴσως</note>, some of his interpreters have argued is not just a mark of doubt, but rather of affirmation and emphasis. 

<margin>Michael of Ephesus.</margin> For Michael of Ephesus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine commentator on Aristotle.</note>, in his commentary on the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, says: "*isos* [perhaps] stands for *haplos kai katholou* [simply and universally]" <note>original: 'ἴσως' δὲ 'ἴσως' ἀντὶ 'ἁπλῶς' καὶ 'καθόλου' κεῖται</note>; that is, that "perhaps" stands for that which is simple and universal. But how very clever is this sign of judgment: he does not attribute doubtful things to himself, nor to others, but reports them ambiguously. However, those things which are worthy of knowledge and beyond the risk of refutation, he ascribes to himself. Those things which are wrongly or falsely stated, he attributes to others; and even if they were commonly known, he attacks them with so many arguments that he has consumed a significant portion of his books in refuting superfluous opinions—and often ones he reported incorrectly himself. He even strives at times to excuse the very same authors he rejects, yet follows them in many things, so that it is not easy to distinguish his own views from those of others. In most cases, he condemns Homer, yet he confirms his own opinion about God with Homer’s testimony. He condemns Thales <note>Thales of Miletus, often called the first philosopher, who believed water was the primary substance of all things.</note> in the first book of *Metaphysics* <note>original: *primæ philoſophiæ* (First Philosophy).</note> because Thales, following Homer, had defined the principle of things as water. Yet in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: *de mundo*</note> addressed to Alexander—rejecting the opinion of Plato, who had placed God in a fiery substance—Aristotle placed Him in the supreme ethereal body, citing the testimony of Homer’s poems. 

<margin>Olympiodorus.</margin> Almost always, however, he speaks not consistently but obscurely. Olympiodorus <note>An important Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> is the authority for the fact that this was why many considered the first book of the *Meteorology* to be spurious and counterfeit, since he sometimes seems to stick to the point and speak clearly there. But as far as this is concerned, Olympiodorus considers those critics to be incorrect, since even there the arguments are obscure, and he speaks inconsistently and hesitatingly, having prefaced his work by saying he "doubts some things" and "touches on others in a certain way." From all these things, as far as the manner of writing is concerned, it can be gathered that Aristotle's doctrine is uncertain. It is obscure in the manner of a cuttlefish scattering ink, and even many-colored like a chameleon. 

<margin>On the variety of colors in the chameleon, how varied.</margin> Aristotle himself reveals the nature of the chameleon in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*. He argues that it changes (not because of the colors of things lying nearby—as Ovid and others claim, contending that it matches the closest color, an idea Plutarch also seems to admit, except for the color white—nor from anger or desire, as Seneca seemed to think) but rather from excessive fear. So perhaps Aristotle was "multiform" and versatile out of fear—either suggested by a desire for praise, lest he be caught and refuted, or by his bodily temperament. It is said that he grew stiff from a lack of blood, just as he relates concerning the chameleon: that of all animals, it is most destitute of blood and heat. And from this comes fear, and from fear, change. Pliny seems to have been of this opinion, writing in his twenty-eighth book that no animal is considered more fearful, and therefore it undergoes a many-colored change. The same is affirmed of the Octopus <note>original: *Polypo* (Polyp).</note> by Pliny in his ninth book, as well as by Athenaeus, Plutarch, Lucian, and others.

## That the doctrine of Aristotle is shown to be uncertain from the perpetual battle of his own followers and expositors, which is shown to be both manifold and great. Chapter Eight.

If Aristotle’s doctrine were certain—not even entirely, but even for the most part—would his followers and interpreters not be found in agreement regarding his opinions, both in understanding them and in explaining them? But since they most clearly disagree in nearly all matters, and especially in understanding those things held to be primary, and since they quarrel and fight like gladiators <note>The original Latin *digladientur* literally means to "cross swords" or "fight to the death," emphasizing the bitterness of academic rivalries.</note> in explaining them, will that doctrine itself be thought certain? 

<margin>Removal of a silent objection</margin> Nor should anyone throw back at me the disagreements of our own theologians. But concerning other matters, and especially those which depend on the teachings of the pagan <note>original: *gentium* (gentile). In this context, it refers to non-Christian, classical philosophers like Aristotle or Plato.</note> philosophers...

...can be perceived by the senses. Nor should you think, reader, that some sound the war-trumpet against others only in minute matters and things of small importance, but rather in the greatest matters, and those most pertaining to us; and not only among later ages, but among those very men who drank in the voice of Aristotle with their own ears. <margin>Theophrastus</margin> For Theophrastus, both the successor to Aristotle’s school and the heir to his library, thought that Aristotle believed the human soul to be immortal. Who could doubt that <margin>Aristoxenus</margin> Aristoxenus’s definition of the soul—which was more suited to the musical art he so intensely practiced than to the opinion of his fellow pupil Theophrastus—was any different? Nevertheless, this Aristoxenus the musician was a listener of Aristotle, according to the testimony of Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," which preserved many fragments of older philosophy.</note>. <margin>Dicaearchus</margin> Dicaearchus the Sicilian from Messina, also a listener of the same Aristotle, and as Cicero wrote of him, a primarily great and eloquent Peripatetic <note>A "Peripatetic" is a follower of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (*peripatoi*) of the Lyceum where they walked while debating.</note>, believed the soul to be mortal according to the witness of Plutarch; and according to the philosopher Sextus <note>Likely referring to the skeptic Sextus Empiricus.</note>, he believed there was no soul at all. 

<margin>Discord between Theophrastus, Dicaearchus, and others regarding the soul.</margin> Likewise, he held that there was no soul, as we said in the first book of this work on the authority of Cicero. Atticus <note>Titus Pomponius Atticus, the friend and correspondent of Cicero.</note> affirmed this very thing, asserting that Dicaearchus—who had done away with the entire substance of the soul—had decreed things consistent with Aristotle himself. <margin>Galen</margin> Galen, treating of physical history, weighed Dicaearchus's opinion just as Plutarch had done, and judged it to be consistent with Aristotle; for indeed, both elsewhere and in that same book, he determines that Aristotle thought the soul was not immortal. But concerning this matter, as well as the opinions on the soul, we said much in the first book, and we shall say many more things in the sixth book. 

But if this same Peripatetic, namely Dicaearchus, who spoke so often with Aristotle, disagreed so much from another [Theophrastus] in a matter so necessary and of such great importance <note>original: *praeiudicii* — in this context, implying a matter of great weight or a precedent-setting judgment.</note>, what then will you think of others, if you are truly wise? But perhaps this was the envy of his disciples and listeners? <margin>Plutarch</margin> What indeed was the cause that Plutarch, born nearly four hundred years later, thought Aristotle by no means believed the soul was immortal, but rather subject to corruption? And that Galen judged the same? Why did <margin>Alexander</margin> Alexander of Aphrodisias—who was certainly born after Plutarch and perhaps after Galen, though he lived in the same century—moved neither by the authority of the former nor the envy of the latter, judge while examining and explaining Aristotle’s doctrines <note>original: *placita* — literally "things that were pleasing," referring to philosophical tenets.</note> that Aristotle had decreed the soul to be mortal? 

Why, after Alexander, did many of his expositors follow his opinion? While many others, departing from it, ascribed the opposite opinion to Aristotle, such as Ammonius, Philoponus, Simplicius, Sophonias, Theodore Metochites, and others. What of the fact that from a single word in the seventeenth part of the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, Thomas [Aquinas] and others confirmed the immortality of the human intellect, Alexander its mortality, and Averroes its unity? As we wrote in our <margin>The author's commentaries on the third book of *On the Soul*.</margin> commentaries on the third book of *On the Soul* in a digression concerning its immortality. It can best be known from this very matter—as much in this business as in the other things we spoke of above, and even those we did not mention, such as the subject of the entire faculty of physics, which is still before the judge <note>original: *sub iudice* — a legal term meaning the matter is still under consideration and undecided.</note>—that Aristotle’s doctrine both is and ought to be considered utterly uncertain. For his interpreters of every kind still do not have a certainty, even though many centuries have passed since it...

...by rebuking his false doctrine, they have returned to us. **BOOK.**

[Margin: Testimony of Justin.]
...by Augustine and others of great name, who feel differently about Aristotle than the multitude now thinks. Justin, the philosopher and martyr, in his book of exhortation to the nations <note>original: "libro gentium admonitorio," referring to the *Cohortatio ad Graecos* (Exhortation to the Greeks), which was traditionally attributed to Justin Martyr.</note>—which was translated by us from Greek into Latin in previous years—writes most clearly that Aristotle held that the soul is mortal. He does not mean the soul which is considered irrational and sensory, but the soul which is called rational, and which is named by that same Aristotle "entelechy" <note>Entelecheia (entelechy) is Aristotle's term for the "actuality" or "realization" of a body that has life potentially. The author argues that defining the soul this way makes it dependent on the body and therefore mortal.</note>. Indeed, he says in Greek: <note>original: "ἀριστοτέλης δὲ ἐντελέχειαν ἀυτὴν ὀνομάζων οὐκ ἀθάνατον ἀλλά θνητὴν εἶναι βούλεται" — "Aristotle, by naming it entelechy, intends it to be not immortal but mortal."</note>. And above, he had also said that Aristotle did not wish for the soul to be triple in nature like Plato's, but that it was one and the same rational soul. Later, he writes that Aristotle did not think of it as Plato did,
[Margin: Testimony of Gregory Nazianzen.]
as something mobile, but as entirely immobile, the principle of all motion. Gregory Nazianzen—who is called "The Theologian" by excellence among the Greeks—in his disputation against Eunomius, called Aristotle’s discourses on the soul "mortal." Just as he spoke of those discourses concerning providence as "diminished," he also called Aristotle's manner of writing artificial and even crafty, and he criticized his dogmas as being too human. For while he rebuked many things of the Pythagoreans and Plato, and rejected the impiety of Epicurus, when speaking of Aristotle, he used these very words: <note>original: "ἀριστοτέλους τὴν σμικρολόγον πρόνοιαν καὶ τὸ ἄτεχνον καὶ τοὺς θνητοὺς περὶ ψυχῆς λόγους καὶ τὸ ἀνθρωπικὸν τῶν δογμάτων" — "Aristotle’s petty [or hair-splitting] providence, his lack of art, his mortal words about the soul, and the human character of his dogmas."</note>.
[Margin: Testimony of Gregory of Nyssa. Testimony of Theodoret.]
Gregory of Nyssa also, as is very well known, wrote that the soul was considered corruptible by Aristotle. Furthermore, Theodoret, the Bishop of Cyrrhus, in his book on the nature of man, when he discusses the soul, writes among other things: <note>original: "δημόκριτος δὲ καὶ ἐπίκουρος καὶ ἀριστοτέλης φθαρτὴν ἔφασαν ταύτην ἀναιδῶς ἔφησαν" — "But Democritus, Epicurus, and Aristotle said this [the soul] was perishable; they spoke shamelessly."</note>. This means: Democritus, Epicurus, and Aristotle shamelessly said that the soul itself is corruptible. And elsewhere, he also judged that the intellect was established by Aristotle as something else, distinct from the soul, and that the soul itself was
[Margin: Testimony of Origen.]
considered mortal. Origen Adamantius <note>The famous early Christian scholar from Alexandria, known for his vast output and his later-condemned views on the pre-existence of souls.</note>, while he recounts the sects of the philosophers in that work to which he gave the name *Philosophumena*, teaches that there is this great difference between Plato and Aristotle: that the former [Plato] decreed the soul to be mortal <note>The author likely means the reverse or is citing a specific Origenist argument where Plato's "irrational" soul is mortal, but the text here claims Aristotle is the one who denies immortality.</note>, while the latter [Aristotle] did so even more, and to use his words, it is "to vanish" <note>original: "ἀφανίζεσθαι" — to disappear or be annihilated.</note>. Not content to have said this once, as the work proceeds, he repeats: that "particular or individual souls vanish." Saint Thomas [Aquinas] and many others think that Aristotle believed the intellect was not separate from the soul, but was either an affection or a quality of the soul itself, flowing from its very essence. In this, Thomas varies from Theodoret, and he proceeds on a path entirely different and opposite not only to him, but also to Nazianzen and Justin, when he decides that Aristotle thought the human soul was immortal. Truly, to say nothing of Plutarch, Alexander, and Galen—whom we showed in the previous chapter to have believed that the mortality of the soul was credited to Aristotle—the authority of Nazianzen is great in the whole Church. He was not only greatly praised by Jerome as a disciple, but he was approved in the very decrees of the Popes. The authority of Nyssa is great, and so is that of Justin—who was not only adorned by the writings of Jerome and Eusebius, but crowned with martyrdom. Nor is the authority of Theodoret small; after the disputes of the third council <note>The Council of Ephesus (431 AD).</note> and the conflicts held with that most holy man Cyril, his faith was first examined and soon approved in the fourth—that is, in the Council of Chalcedon. His own illustrious and copious doctrine is distinguished by his writings, honored even by the letter of Pope Leo the Great, and held in high praise by posterity with the title of "Blessed," as I have found in his ancient manuscripts written in Greek. Nor is the authority of Origen small where he is judged not to have erred in those matters which look chiefly toward the faith. Add Augustine, who affirms that the soul was considered by Aristotle to be a "fifth element" <note>The "quintessence" or aether, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. Yet what he felt, and what he did not feel...

**BOOK [FOUR]**

[Gregory] the Pope, in the twenty-seventh book of his commentaries on Job <note>original: "commentariorum in Iob," referring to Gregory the Great’s *Moralia in Iob*.</note>, says: "In this world, therefore, while we live, we then perfectly know what things are to be known when, advancing through understanding, we recognize that we know nothing perfectly." 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
By Augustine also, in the seventh book of his work *On Genesis* <note>original: "super Genesim," likely referring to *De Genesi ad litteram*.</note>, that same fifth essence is held in contempt; and in the earlier volumes of that work, he asserts that the heaven is made of matter. Its spherical shape, in the assertion of which Aristotle labored much, Augustine himself judged as not worthy for us to be occupied in discussing, so much so that in the second volume of his work on Genesis he wrote these things: "For what does it concern me," he says, "whether the heaven, like a sphere, encloses the earth on all sides, balanced in the middle mass of the universe, or whether it [covers] it from one part from above..."

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the fallibility of Aristotle and the disagreements among his Scholastic commentators. It specifically addresses the logical contradiction between Aristotle's claim that the world is eternal and his rejection of an "actual infinite," which would necessarily occur if an eternal world produced an endless succession of immortal human souls.</meta>

**BOOK FOUR [PAGE] 126**

...narrated by the testimony of the Greek Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>. He himself [Thomas Aquinas] condemns Aristotle on the notable charge of contradiction, since he pronounces him both an upholder of the eternity of the world and a believer that human souls are both numerous and immortal. These doctrines conflict with one another for this reason: from the very eternity of the world, it follows that there are an infinite number of souls. Yet Aristotle shrinks from the infinite, especially in the third book of the *Physics* and the first book of *On the Heavens*. And although it is written in the second volume of the *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra gentes," referring to Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa contra Gentiles*.</note>, chapter eighty-one, that this [prohibition of the infinite] is not affirmed regarding immaterial substances but only in natural bodies—

<margin>A passage of Saint Thomas is explained.</margin>

—I easily believe that this was not written by Thomas himself, but added as a gloss <note>An explanatory note or comment inserted into a text by a later scribe.</note>. I am moved by the fact that shortly before, Thomas himself asserted that the opinion contending it was not absurd to think of infinite souls was repugnant to the principles established by Aristotle, since he decreed there is no <term>actual infinite</term> <note>A completed or "ready-made" infinity, as opposed to a "potential infinite" which can always be added to. Aristotle argued the universe could not contain an actual infinite.</note>. What contradiction is this, I ask, if Aristotle thought the actual infinite was absurd in natural bodies, but not absurd if found in immaterial substances? What sort of contradiction is this? For separate souls are immaterial substances. Therefore, he removes the contradiction through this distinction between natural bodies and immaterial substances, rather than asserting it. Thus we can easily guess that those words ("in natural bodies but not in immaterial substances") were added in the margin by some follower of Avicenna or Algazali <note>Two influential Islamic philosophers whose works were heavily studied and sometimes integrated into Latin Scholasticism.</note> and later crept into the book itself. Added, I say, to show that the opinion which Thomas wrote was repugnant to Aristotelian principles did not, in fact, conflict with them. 

But however the matter stands—for I do not wish to fight over this contradiction—it certainly remains that Thomas most strongly asserts in the *Summa Theologiae*, in the seventh question of the first part, that there can be no actually infinite number. Thus, if we do not wish to prove that Saint Thomas's Aristotle contradicts himself, we must certainly admit, however unwillingly, that Saint Thomas's Aristotle contradicts himself. From this, a certain most sharp interpreter of his [Thomas's], even if he reads what is written in the second volume of the *Against the Gentiles* not as we do but as others do, nevertheless affirms in the fourth article of the seventh question itself that Saint Thomas has removed every way of agreement with Aristotle's doctrine, according to his own exposition. 

<margin>Thomas Cajetan.</margin> <note>A 15th-16th century Italian philosopher and theologian, a leading commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>

For from the opinion of the eternity [of the world] narrated above, and the opinion of the multitude of immortal souls, it follows that human souls are actually infinite, which he clearly decreed in the same article could in no way be infinite. Moreover, Thomas's disciple Giles of Rome <note>original: "Egidius romanus," a medieval theologian and student of Aquinas.</note> does not deny that Aristotle contradicts himself, since from the world [being eternal], an infinite number of souls would follow, which he did not admit. 

<margin>Giles.</margin>

Nor does it escape me what many have said regarding this contradiction. Some flee to the idea that Aristotle posited the newness [beginning] of the world, but in books that are not seen by us. Others condemn Aristotle for ignorance and forgetfulness rather than contradiction, as Giles himself seemed to wish in the work called *Quodlibets*, and Durandus in his commentary on the second book of the *Sentences*. 

<margin>Durandus.</margin> <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a 14th-century philosopher known for his independent and often anti-Thomist views.</note>

And whoever else asserted that Aristotle did not look at those things which followed from his own conclusions. Others decree that infinity is not actual but potential, as something to which additions could be made; others say other things. It is enough that he was condemned by some in the name of contradiction, by others in the name of forgetfulness and ignorance, and suspected by others of slowness. Certainly, Aristotle is even criticized by Albert...

<margin>Albertus.</margin> <note>Albert the Great, the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>

...when he called the mover of the heaven an "animal," and when he discussed the number of celestial bodies and their movers with doubt. It also seemed to Henry, William, Herveus, and others that Aristotle decreed incorrectly concerning the soul; and it was proven by Henry himself with many arguments that by the way of nature no sincere truth can be held...

<margin>Henry.</margin> <margin>William.</margin> <margin>Her.</margin> <note>Referring to Henry of Ghent, William of Ockham, and Herveus Natalis, major figures in late medieval philosophy.</note>

It documents how various Scholastic thinkers, including Thomas Aquinas, Cajetan, and Giles of Rome, identified and attempted to resolve this perceived contradiction.</summary>

[...attaining] truth, and that there is a need for divine irradiation <note>A philosophical theory, notably held by Henry of Ghent, which suggests that the human mind requires a direct "beam" of light from God to grasp certain certainties.</note>. <meta>This page continues the argument that Aristotle's authority is not absolute, citing specific medieval theologians like John the Canon and Francis of Mayrone who identified fundamental errors in his work. **BOOK FOUR**                                                              **127**

I will gather everything into a brief discourse. There have not been lacking those who asserted that natural philosophy, and also that which is "beyond nature" <note>A literal translation of *metaphysica* (metaphysics).</note> or called metaphysics by the moderns, was poorly written by Aristotle. We read in the first question of John the Canon <margin>John the Canon</margin> <note>Johannes Canonicus (d. 1320), a Franciscan philosopher known for his commentary on Aristotle’s *Physics*.</note> regarding the subject of natural science, that this very natural philosophy was handed down by Aristotle both erroneously and insufficiently—to use his own words. And in Francis of Mayrone <margin>Francis of Mayrone</margin> <note>Francois de Meyronnes (c. 1288–1328), a prominent Franciscan theologian and student of Duns Scotus.</note> we read in the third question of the forty-seventh distinction of his collected works, that Aristotle was condemned not only for envy toward Plato—whose dogmas he did not report correctly or properly—but also for ignorance of abstraction, and for a very poor tradition of metaphysical matters. This same Francis, in his commentary on the fourth book of Augustine's *On Genesis*, disapproved of the theologians of his time who more willingly cited testimonies from Aristotle than from Augustine. Therefore, if there is no lack of Parisian theologians who wished to defend Aristotle as much as is permitted by our sacred rites, there have also not been lacking among those same theologians men of great name who condemned that very man. This could easily have been seen by the reader both from the first chapter of this fourth book, and from this tenth chapter itself.

**He proves his doctrine uncertain based on the many errors of Aristotle; these same points are now touched upon as a whole and will be explained in the following books. Chapter eleven.**

Moreover, since Gregory <note>Gregory of Rimini (d. 1358), a theologian who emphasized the limits of human reason compared to divine revelation.</note> and others whom we brought forward earlier write that he committed many errors, yet do not recount them one by one, we ourselves will try to find some, even setting aside for the present those which Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school, who nevertheless critiqued some of his teacher's theories.</note> and his other followers noted. But certainly, he who errs in many things takes away faith in himself in the few things. Shall we agree with a man who errs in most things? So that, just as he deceived us in those, he might also deceive us in others? Or shall we not rather suspend judgment and hold as uncertain that which remains? For in the divine books, if even one "dutiful error" <note>original: *officiosus error*—a white lie or an error intended for a good purpose.</note> or falsehood were found, the ancient theologians declare that the whole would be held as uncertain. But perhaps someone too much addicted to Aristotle will deny that he wandered from the truth, and relying on that already-refuted authority of Averroës <margin>Response</margin> <note>Averroës (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were so influential he was known simply as "The Commentator."</note>, will contend that he spoke the truth in all things.

But if my discourse is with Christians, let them answer, I ask: is his opinion on the beginning of the world true or false? <margin>A manifold refutation</margin> They will say it is false, if they are Christians. In the beginning, says Moses, *God created heaven and earth*, but Aristotle affirms it had no beginning, and strives to prove it with many arguments in the eighth book of the *Physics*. We shall show in the sixth book of this present work that those arguments are repugnant to the truth. In this matter, he also put forward a falsehood: that the world and time were made by Plato alone; for before him, Pythagoras and many others, relying on that opinion, declared that the world was established by God. Regarding the end of the world, what an unexpiable error! From which, I think, he will not escape by his own motion <note>A pun on Aristotle's theory of "motion" and the "unmoved mover."</note>: for he not only attributed it to an incorruptible substance, so that it would never be dissolved, but also granted it eternal motion. Likewise, he devised an eternal generation and an infinite cycle. Who does not see that these things are as repugnant to our Catholic truth as anything can be? And since it is repugnant to the truth, who does not notice that it is false? But let us observe how many errors sprout from here: that humans have always been, that humans will never be lacking upon the earth, and that prime matter is eternal.

...the eternal generation of mankind, infinite humans, and an infinite number of souls which, by a vain dogma, he had scattered as if never to return into bodies. He held many other views most adverse to our faith, which men of the Christian name ought to restrain lest they enslave themselves to him for so long a time. Plato is closer to the truth in this matter; he affirms both that the heaven was created by God and can be dissolved by His will, and he does not deny that humans suffer punishments for crimes in subterranean places, the judgment of souls, and the resurrection. For this reason, those greatest and inexpiable crimes of Aristotle corrupt his entire doctrine and render it uncertain in other matters. Even in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de mundo"</note> addressed to Alexander, he committed several errors in one matter, which we will show in the sixth book. 

But others are not lacking. In his *Meteorology*, he writes that it is impossible for a rainbow to be found in a shape larger than a semicircle. I reported that this error was discovered by my own eyes fifteen years ago in that book titled *On the Study of Divine and Human Philosophy*. And who will defend another error concerning the nocturnal rainbow? He denies that it can happen except at certain long intervals of time; Albert <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who integrated Aristotelian science with Christian thought, though he occasionally noted Aristotle's errors.</note> mentions this madness <note>original: "delirii"</note>, and we shall attack that very error in detail three books from now. I also pass over the related accusation concerning the Milky Way <note>original: "Gallaxia"</note>. 

In addition to these points, if faith and truth are found wanting in Aristotle while he narrates, how much more so while he disputes? For if an author is not certain when reporting the opinions and sentiments of others, by what means ought he to be trusted while he busies himself either in confirming or demolishing those views? Indeed, he commits many faults in reviewing the principles of natural things. In the fourth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, when he mentioned Anaxagoras and other ancient philosophers, he added that they all thought only sensible beings <term>sensible beings: things that can be perceived by the five senses, as opposed to abstract or spiritual realities</term> were to be found. However, he himself elsewhere, even in that very book of the same work, records that Anaxagoras made mention of Mind <note>Anaxagoras proposed *Nous* (Mind) as the primary cause of the universe.</note> or intellect. While he discusses natural principles, he speaks to such an extent that his expositors think they have discovered for certain that no philosopher existed who thought the earth alone was the principle of natural things. They even bring forward a reason for this: they think it happened because of the earth's thickness. But we have said in earlier books, and Sextus <margin>Sextus. We have stated this above, and in the same book that will be the sixth and last of this work, we shall demonstrate it most clearly.

Regarding the art of demonstration <note>Logic and formal proof.</note>, how imperfect it is, we shall speak in the following book. Concerning the fallacies he handed down to us in place of demonstrations and certain doctrine, I say nothing for the present, since the entire last book of this work will be devoted to making that very matter plain.
