**BOOK FOUR. 128**

->That all the teaching of Aristotle is founded upon sensation, which, since it is frequently fallacious and can be deceived in other ways besides those he recounted, must therefore be considered uncertain. Here also against those who say sensation, in Aristotle's opinion, is not deceived. Moreover, it is shown that the reasons with which he busied himself to prove the truth of sensation are removed. Chapter 12.<-

**V**erum, in truth, since Aristotle's teaching is founded upon sensation <note>original: "sensu"</note>, it will therefore be easily proven uncertain. This is because sensation is not only mostly uncertain, but frequently fallacious; it can both deceive and be deceived in many more ways than Aristotle supposed. For sensation is by its own nature true unless it is variable; however, it is variable in different men, and sometimes in the same man. Frequently, many people are uncertain about their own sensations, as will become clear as the work proceeds. Hence, no general rule of sensory truth—which could be applied to all men and to each individual at all times—will be found (unless I am mistaken). We shall discuss this matter more extensively in the following book. For sensation was once held to be a true state <note>original: "habitus"; referring to a stable disposition of the mind</note> unless the thing being sensed were changed or the medium of sensing were not corrupted. But very frequent variation occurs, the change of sensory objects is frequent and manifold, and the nature of the medium is fluid and unstable. Regarding these latter points, Aristotle gave some instructions, but regarding the former variation he did not discourse; on which matter we shall say a few things now, and more in the following book. It is thus everywhere possible to see in Aristotle that this foundation of sensation is usually laid with great care. And to begin with the *Posterior Analytics* of logic <note>Aristotle's primary work on formal demonstration and scientific knowledge.</note>, upon which all Aristotelian doctrine leans and by which he labors with great care to make the rest certain, we find that sensation is the unique foundation of the entire edifice and the beginning of all demonstration. For he constructs that demonstration from universal propositions, collects universal propositions from particulars through induction <term>Induction: the logical process of drawing a general rule from specific, observed instances.</term>, and perceives particulars through sensation. Furthermore, in his books on physics, he also established this principle: that the path innate to us is from those things better known to us toward those which are better known by nature; but those things which we drink in with our senses are better known to us. So it is also easy to grasp in the rest of his natural books and in the *Meteorology*. Did he not explain himself sufficiently in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*? There he asserts that those noble and deathless substances <note>Refers to the celestial bodies (stars and planets), which Aristotle believed were eternal and divine.</note> can be less known by us for the reason that they are little exposed to sensation. And in the third book of *On the Generation of Animals*, while discussing the generation of bees, he says (as was also related above) that one must believe sensation more than reason; he deems that trust should be placed in reason only afterward, if the things demonstrated agree with those things perceived by sensation. I think it unnecessary to speak of his *Ethics* now, since he himself affirmed that faculty to be uncertain and only probable, as it does not by its own nature admit of demonstrations. At in his *Metaphysics*, in which he busied himself not only to write down certain doctrine but to show that there was a faculty which was the architect and primary judge of all other faculties, does he not put sensation first? He even wanted the love of the senses to be an argument that all men by nature desire to know. Though if that beginning should rightly be ascribed to Aristotle and not to Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle’s successor; the author is questioning the authorship of the famous opening line of the *Metaphysics*.</note>. Indeed, in the fourth book of that same work—a principal and most subtle book, as it deals with the very principles of knowing which were brought into controversy by many—does he not put sensation first? Even then, when he tries to disprove the opinions of the ancients which he recounted (though falsely, as will be shown in the last book). For there he always appeals to sensation; he appeals to it repeatedly with great skill. From all of which it is clearly seen that the doctrine itself...

BOOK FOUR.                                129.

...which he himself <note>Aristotle</note> placed around the brain in his book *On the Senses* <note>original: "de sensibus"</note>. Likewise, if the flesh—through which the species <note>the "image" or "sensory form" of a thing</note> of taste and touch are perceived—is affected, the sensation is carried to the sensorium <note>the primary seat or organ of sensation</note> which he himself judged to be located around the heart. Fifth, if the sensorium is infected by disease or hindered by some external accident. <margin>Fifth.</margin> In the sixth place were those who counted proper magnitude and quality; for the former could be so small, and the latter so faint, that deception would arise from them. <margin>Sixth.</margin> Although there are those who wish to evade this, arguing that if a thing is "sensible" <note>capable of being perceived</note> it will not escape the sense. <margin>Response.</margin> But even if it does not escape entirely, a quality can nonetheless be grasped differently than it ought to be. <margin>Refutation.</margin> For a faint quality, even when attached to a smaller magnitude, will diffuse its image less than if it were in a larger mass. There are others who add further points, but all can easily be reduced to those we have already reported. Thus, those who believe that the sense is not deceived—according to the opinion of Aristotle—are far mistaken. <margin>Against those</margin> For even his most approved interpreters have enumerated so many modes of deception. <margin>who say the sense</margin> But let us see by what frivolous reasoning they have devised this claim. <margin>is not deceived</margin> They say the sense is not deceived because it judges exactly as it is affected; for if a tongue is infected with bile <note>a reference to jaundice, which was thought to make sweet things taste bitter</note>, and honey is perceived as bitter when tasted, how is the sense deceived? For it perceives a species of bitterness and judges accordingly. They apply the same logic to the deception of the intermediate medium <note>the space between the object and the eye or ear</note> and to all other cases. But why do they not decree the same for every knowing power? For what is the cause of the difference, if one judges what is not truly so based on how it appears and how it is seen? For then everyone knows what absurdities would follow: that the same thing is both false and true, and other such nonsense. It is worthwhile for them to explain: how does the sense itself deliver a verdict on ambiguous things? For in every sense there are some things that require a "discerniculum" <note>a small point of distinction or a tool for discerning</note>. Therefore, it will deliver a different and conflicting verdict, now here and now there, and never a certain one, if it does not have another faculty from within itself for discerning or judging beyond the one by which anything is first presented to it. Besides this, it will never happen that its judgment is not deceived if it does not discern the thing itself according to its own nature. For judgment is resolved toward the object, because it is primarily about the object that we inquire. For the question is not, for example, about the species <note>image</note> that is in the tongue, but about whether the honey is sweet or not. Therefore, if the sense judges it bitter because of the species of bile already impressed upon it, it brings forth a false verdict about the honey. It will never bring forth a true one if it does not judge rightly concerning the thing presented to the sense itself, which it cannot do unless it drinks in its image purely. Therefore, not only is the sense deceived, but it can also be a great occasion for error for the common sense <note>the internal faculty that combines the data from the five individual senses</note> and even for the intellect itself, since the common sense relies on the external senses as witnesses and indicators in delivering a judgment; and the intellect does the same in equal proportion. Therefore, these claims are both false and were not at all handed down by Aristotle. Aristotle does indeed think that the sense of a "proper object" <note>a quality perceived by only one sense, like color for sight or sound for hearing</note> is not deceived, but he does so for other reasons which he brought forth in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "quarto metaphysicorum"</note>: based on the "starting point" and the "end point" <note>original: "a quo et ad quem"</note> from which motion itself is grasped; from the species of a thing which remains even when its quantity is changed; and from the consistency and immovable nature of the heavens. I have dismantled these reasons in the second book, twenty-second chapter of this work, and I have opened up the greater difficulty of knowing a thing. I have also signed off, by that same author's authority, that nothing but accidents <note>outward qualities like color or shape, rather than the inner essence</note> are known by the sense. I further added that the substance of the heavens cannot be known by sense even if it were changed, for neither the heaven itself nor any immovable nature is subjected to being grasped by it. For many truths can be known through the sense, but those Aristotelian reasons did not prove it beyond controversy so that they could be known. For sensory knowledge is for the most part uncertain, and many conditions must be present lest the sense slip both in perceiving and in judging. When Aristotle and his followers—who trust the sense in a wondrous way—realized this, they brought forth many exceptions, of which we have now spoken.

BOOK [FOUR].

We have reported these things concerning the truth and the fallacy of the senses according to the opinion of Aristotle and his interpreters, briefly and sincerely. These factors, by their very nature, make the path of judging things exactly and precisely <note>original: "ad perpendiculum" — literally, "according to a plumb line," meaning with absolute vertical accuracy</note> a deceptive one. This is because the intervening air, water, or flesh can easily be tainted, and thus a sensation can escape the sense through great fading. But also the circumstance of distance <note>original: "interstitii"</note> sometimes deceives, since it has neither been decreed nor can it be decreed how great that distance ought to be that is assigned for a truthful judgment. This is because some people excel in the sharpness <margin>Seventh.</margin> of their senses, while others suffer from dullness.

But beyond these, there is one uncertainty that arises from the diverse temperament <note>The "temperament" refers to the balance of humors in the body, which was thought to determine health and perception</note> of the human body, for which various appearances and different perceptions occur to different people. From this, not just one but multiple ways of error can arise in the sense. Regarding this matter, Aristotle gave no instruction. I, however, will follow up on that very point in the following book; likewise, in my book *On Imagination*, I have taught in what way it varies and is deceived, and how it can be corrected. Aristotle, whom I followed in most things in that book, did not explain this, although he himself asserted it <note>imagination</note> to be fallacious while asserting the sense to be truthful. But if the sense is considered in itself, it is so varied that both its indication and its judgment are rendered weak and uncertain for the most part, if one and the same exact rule of sensory truth must be held by all according to Aristotle's authority. But these things are said generally about the sense; the following book will deal with it more particularly and exactly. Therefore, I wish to refer the reader who is eager for this matter to that place. For here the subject is handled in a passing narrative rather than by disputation, and without arguments that could prove such a great matter.

->**That Aristotle himself admits his own teaching is uncertain. Chapter XIII.**<-

The previous points have shown us (if you please) nothing less than how uncertain Aristotle's teaching is. If we were to question Aristotle himself, he would certainly answer—if we mention moral philosophy—that it is indeed probable, but not to be demanded according to a certain and exact standard of reason, since the nature of the matter he treats does not allow for it. Indeed, he himself warned us beforehand without hesitation that we should not seek from him what he could not provide. In his works on logic, following the opinions of others for the most part, he often repeats "they say," "it is said," and similar phrases. In his *Metaphysics*, he compares our intellect to the eye of a bat, which relates to the sun just as we relate to contemplating the first and highest things of nature; we draw from them a knowledge of things that is not exact and pure, and for this reason less certain.

And at the very beginning of the second volume of his *First Philosophy* <note>An alternative title for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>—if Aristotle is the author of that beginning—when he introduced it, he wished the contemplation of truth to be proven partly easy and partly difficult; difficult to the extent that no one can worthily attain it, and that individuals contribute either nothing or very little to it itself, the cause being (as we said) the weakness of human wit <note>original: "ingenii" — natural talent or mental capacity</note>. And in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he considers that we only lightly touch upon higher matters, even if we are more delighted by their excellence than if we held all lower things. In the second book, however, regarding man, his words declare how uncertain and inexact that knowledge is: that man is the only one of all the animals known to us to participate in divinity, or most of all. In the second book of *On the Heavens*, he also teaches us that we are often delighted by probable conjecture in these matters. In his *Meteorology*, when he introduced the things he was about to discuss, he writes these words: "concerning which things we are in doubt about some, while we touch upon others in a certain way" <note>original Greek: "εν οἷς τὰ μὲν 'αποροῦμεν τῶν δὲ 'εφαπτόμεθα τινὰ τρόπον"</note>, that is, things about which we have some doubts, but others we grasp in a certain manner...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that Aristotle, despite being the foundational authority of science, often expressed doubt and ambiguity. The previous page discussed the physical limitations of the senses; this page focuses on Aristotle’s own writings where he admits the difficulty of reaching certain knowledge, particularly regarding the soul and natural phenomena.</meta>

FOURTH [BOOK].                                                                                                130.

We only touch upon this now. In matters of nature, anyone who has noticed that a single response cannot be given in one way sometimes answers, <note>original: "ἔστι μὲν ὡς ἔστι δ᾽ ὡς οὐκ ἔ"</note> "it is in a way, and it is not in a way," or "it is so, but it is also not so." We see this at the end of the first book of the *Physics*. Likewise, elsewhere he will express his reasoning using particles that are ambiguous and render the account uncertain, such as "almost," "perhaps," and the like. Often, not content with one, he even places these ambiguous particles in pairs. For instance, in the first book of *On the Generation of Animals*, when he was about to give an account of the material, final, formal, and efficient causes—explaining how he had embraced all of them in his work on animals and satisfied everyone—he then wanted to assert that the formal and final causes were one and the same. To do this, he used these words: <note>original: "ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ σχεδὸν ὑπολαβῇ διὰ"</note> "as it were, they should be understood as nearly [one]." Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek humanist and translator of Aristotle</note> translated these words as "they are to be considered as almost one certain thing."

But indeed, even concerning other matters that had been thoroughly investigated, he did not dare to introduce universal knowledge, but rather knowledge that was probable and true for the most part, not always and entirely fixed. From this comes his statement in the sixth book of *The History of Animals*: "Truly, we set these things forth in the way that the matter happens for the greater part." Moreover, when he is about to teach *On the Soul*, he writes that it is most difficult to grasp any proof concerning it, and he prefaced it thus: <note>original: "πάντῃ δὲ καὶ πάντως ἐστὶ τῶν χαλεπωτάτων λαβεῖν τινά πίστιν περὶ αὐτῆς"</note> "it is in every way and altogether among the most difficult things to attain any certain belief about it." By these words, he rendered all the rest of his doctrine uncertain; for all teaching is grasped from the soul and its functions—sensation, intellect, and imagination. Therefore, all these things whose nature, properties, and duties he treats in that very work *On the Soul*, he left among the things most difficult to know and prove—yet these are the causes for the knowledge and proof of all other things. Truly, from a weak or obscure and most difficult knowledge of the cause, who does not see that the effects themselves are drawn from a condition equal to or even worse than that of the cause? 

It is as if he then frankly pronounced that the greater part of those things he thought he knew was the smallest part of those things he did not know. He was so uncertain even in these things that seemed clear, that from this he expressed and carried the opinion that "to doubt concerning individual things is not useless." This he would not have done if he perceived himself to be master of certain knowledge; and in this matter, he seemed to agree with the <term>Sceptics</term> <note>A school of ancient philosophy that argued absolute certainty is impossible and one should suspend judgment</note>. The same man frequently does not affirm a thing, but says "it seems so," which is proper and peculiar to the Sceptics. He even cites the opinions of others in place of testimony; indeed, he frequently strengthens his own views with the doctrines of others. He cites lyric and tragic poets, and even Homer himself, with whose poem he ended the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle concludes Metaphysics XII by quoting the Iliad: "The rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler."</note> concerning the highest matters. It is as if he, being well aware of his own human weakness—which is liable to error and falsehood—felt that if one should not assent to him, one should at least assent to those poets (whose authority in matters of philosophy is not strong but weak). 

He also frequently left a free choice to the reader, not only concerning the greatest matters, but even the smallest, in the perception of which he had been most diligently engaged. Thus, regarding the number of celestial orbs and their functions in those matters called "metaphysics," and thus concerning the mating and generation of bees in the fifth book of *The History of Animals* (to cite no more examples), he did not withhold great disputes from the judgment of posterity. 

But he not only increased this ambiguity of his through his style of writing, but also declared that he wanted his doctrine to be held as uncertain, and to be entirely unintelligible to those who had not heard him in person. There exists to this day his letter in which he responds to Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great</note>, who was annoyed that Aristotle had published his "acroamatic" <note>From the Greek 'akroasis' (hearing); refers to esoteric lectures intended only for advanced students</note> books (as he himself calls them). Aristotle affirmed that they were both "published and not published," since they would not be knowable except to those who had heard the contents of those books from his own mouth originally. Aulus Gellius mentions this letter, as do Themistius, Simplicius, and Plutarch, who relates the same in his *Life of Alexander*, insofar as it pertains to the books.

<summary>The author argues that Aristotle purposefully employed ambiguous language and cited poets to signal the limitations of human certainty, even admitting that his "acroamatic" works were incomprehensible without his direct oral instruction.</summary>

->[FOURTH] BOOK<-

metaphysical [works]. Therefore, if Aristotle himself regarded these books on first philosophy and the highest matters, as well as those on natural philosophy <note>original: "physica auscultatione," the traditional Latin title for Aristotle's *Physics*</note>, as "un-published" <note>Aristotle distinguishes between "exoteric" works for the public and "esoteric" or "acroamatic" works for his inner circle of students</note> in relation to those who had not heard him directly, shall the men of our age—and even those from much earlier times—profess to perceive his meanings against Aristotle's own opposition? If the author himself declared his own doctrine not merely uncertain but unintelligible, and proved it to those who were less inclined to believe him when he wrote in such a way that anyone might take and adapt it for themselves—much like the various colors attributed to the chameleon—what injury is it, then, to pronounce it not only unintelligible but also certain? 

But now let us approach the fifth book of the work and the second book directed against Aristotle's doctrine. In this book, we must engage in a general way and decide the matter through a kind of pitched battle <note>original: "stataria pugna," a Roman military term for a formal, stationary battle between heavy infantry</note>, where there will be a need for veteran soldiers. For the ten weapons <note>likely referring to the ten categories or ten specific arguments previously raised</note> that have already been launched can be used in common by skirmishers and even raw recruits.

->**Epilogue of the fourth book, concerning the certainty of the Sacred Scriptures. Chapter 14.**<-

We have seen that Aristotle’s doctrine ought to be considered mostly uncertain, by the general consensus of learned men of great authority—not only those who flourished most in our Church, but also those who were held in special honor among the pagans, those who actually heard Aristotle teaching, and those who composed histories of his doctrine and books. We have also seen Aristotle’s own testimonies—brought forward not in his own favor—which prevent his doctrine from being believed as certain. 

Shall we not then approach the Sacred Scriptures? To these, all who have ever read them, or considered their beginnings, or observed their course, or even perceived their most celebrated fame from afar, bear witness to the truth—a fame consecrated to immortality by the decree of men. Moths have not weakened them; the mold of damp pits has not scorched them; captivities and exiles have not corrupted them. The Hebrews themselves cherish a part; we venerate them entirely; the pagans have marveled at them. No dispute was ever undertaken regarding their certainty, because they were—and were held to be—the oracles of God. The first of the philosophers ran toward them to understand them, even if only superficially <note>original: "tenus cortice," literally "as far as the bark," meaning a surface-level understanding</note>. Human reason itself has venerated them, bowing down and almost prostrate; demons have celebrated them against their will; and the whole world has greeted them with varied agreement. 

Justin, Eusebius, and others have recorded that the teachings of Moses stand before all the doctrines of the philosophers, not only in dignity but also in time, and that many of the Hebrews and many from the most illustrious nations have confirmed this through histories. But the New Testament, by which we are ruled, is the declaration and perfection of that same Old Testament. It is so clearly established—not only by the chief and greatest foundations of all doctrine but by the most brilliant revelations of angels, the unwilling responses of demons, and the greatest miracles exceeding all created power—that anyone who does not believe the Testament is insane, while he who believes but does not draw near is both wretched and unhappy.

# BOOK FIVE. # CXXXI.

->THE SECOND BOOK OF THE EXAMINATION OF ARISTOTELIAN DOCTRINE BY GIANFRANCESCO PICO, LORD OF MIRANDOLA AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA, WHICH IS THE FIFTH BOOK ON THE VANITY OF PAGAN <note>original: "gentium," referring to the non-Christian or "gentile" philosophical traditions</note> DOCTRINE AND THE TRUTH OF THE CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE.<-

->PREFACE.<-

Among human vices, some are indeed more worthy of hatred than others: but it is not easy to find any that the uneducated and the learned alike loathe more than arrogance. For since it sprouts from the root of pride, and among the proud (as **Solomon** says) there are always quarrels <margin>Solomon</margin> <note>Referencing Proverbs 13:10: "Where there is pride, there is strife."</note>, it arms all who are infected with that same vice against one another. However, it rouses the modest and those who think humbly of themselves all the more, the more those others are polluted by the filth from which the modest keep themselves as unstained as they possibly can. And this is entirely common to both the unrefined and the learned common people, provided they are modest. 

But it is a particular trait of the learned, who are conscious of their own—that is, human—ignorance, to bear the vain displays of knowledge with gravity. For they are often sharpened (which would otherwise happen very little) and stirred to crush the arrogance of such men, sometimes so ardently that there is a danger they might unwillingly incur the very vice they condemn in others. In this class were placed the philosophers called **Sceptics**, also known as **Pyrrhonists** <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BC), who taught that one should suspend judgment to achieve mental tranquility.</note>, born to curb the reckless pride of other philosophers. For since they claimed nothing for themselves and repeatedly sought to know, they were commended on this account in the name of modesty. Yet, because they could not at all endure the haughtiness <note>original: "supercilium," literally "the eyebrow," a metaphor for a disdainful or arrogant expression</note> of those who boasted that they both knew and could teach others, they perhaps attacked them more sharply, or easily gave their enemies a handle to suspect the same of them—that they were being arrogant. 

Hence that **Greek epigram** <note>Likely referring to a poem from the *Greek Anthology* or quoted in Diogenes Laertius.</note>, the meaning of which is that it is a great thing and worthy of much admiration that **Pyrrho** should have attacked so many learned men and such a troop of wise men; for if he did it so that men might prove him wise, he would have looked out for himself poorly. But if he took up this duty from his heart and conviction, so as to show that both himself and others suffered from ignorance and lacked knowledge, he must be considered a truly excellent man.

But I fear lest I also might fall into a similar judgment, I who have attempted in three books to prove the doctrine of all the pagan nations to be uncertain—and especially that of **Aristotle** in the fourth book just preceding this one—and who in this fifth book, and the sixth that follows, will gird myself even more sharply for the refutation of Aristotle. But surely, hasty judges of things will not be fair if they deem me either arrogant or an "excellent man" in this regard. For a different cause will produce different results. For what did I bring in the first three volumes of this work? I reported the opinions of others, I refuted the pagan philosophers by the pagan philosophers themselves; and if I brought anything forward myself aided by the Sceptics, I did so entirely (with the peace of good men) so that I might admonish, as modestly as I could, the arrogant, petulant, and only half-learned crowd of philosophers, showing that there does not exist an army of philosophers which has not already, like earth-born soldiers <note>A reference to the "Sown Men" of Greek mythology who sprang from the earth and immediately killed each other.</note>, fallen by mutual wounds in a war more than civil. In the fourth book, I revealed through a historical narrative that Aristotle was a man, and not to be adored by men, but as a man, he was frequently condemned in many matters. Now we must fight with reasons, and against the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>...

### What was done in the previous book, and what is to be done here; and how uncertain is Aristotle’s art of demonstration, by which he taught that the science of things is gathered; and that this itself must be revealed in five ways, and in what manner. Chapter One. ###

In the previous book, we found the vanity of Aristotelian doctrine, when weighed in the scales and sufficiently examined (in my opinion), to be resting upon a manifold superstition. And this was primarily pleasing so that, at the same time, the handle for slandering our purpose might be snatched away from the litigious, and the reasons for the purpose itself might be opened. Then, prepared to explain other vanities, I tracked through ten "ways" <note>original: "uiis," referring to the Sceptic "modes" or tropes used to induce doubt.</note> how his doctrine is uncertain and, in many matters, false. I did this so that some—who thought Aristotle's doctrine so absolutely certain that they seemed to rely on it just as the Egyptians once did on the oracles of Vulcan or Leto—might easily restrain a headlong path to agreement. But because that was done universally, and perhaps too generally and mostly in common terms, what we have begun in this fifth volume of the work, and the sixth which will follow, must be accomplished more specifically. The matter must be handled at close quarters. 

We must not use common and borrowed arguments, nor must we insist entirely on the leaders of other sects who have refuted Aristotle. ...pleasing, but it does not even square with the art which he himself handed down; for he did not wish to demonstrate anything without applying all those conditions which he taught in the *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: "posterioribus analyticis," Aristotle's work on scientific reasoning and demonstration</note> as necessarily required in every demonstration. <margin>Five ways</margin> However, we shall be led by five ways to achieve this very goal of our proposal; soon we shall descend in our own order to demolish those specific points which are considered more famous in his work. Therefore, the entire doctrine of Aristotle concerning demonstration, written in two books, insofar as it pertains to that by which he strives to show anything—not to refute or drive into absurdity—will be rendered utterly uncertain, both from its foundation, and from its cause, middle, and end. 

From the foundation, I say, which is sensation <note>original: "sensu," the information gathered by the five senses</note> as the beginning of all knowledge, about which some things were said generally in the twelfth chapter of the previous book. For we saw there that sensation is vain, whether it be an indication <note>original: "indicium," the raw data of the senses</note> (that is, when it presents things otherwise than they are) or a judgment <note>original: "iudicium"</note> by which it thinks about those very things, which is the foundation of demonstrating. Indeed, Aristotle, in those very books on demonstration which are called the *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: "resolutorii posteriores," a literal Latin translation of the Greek title</note>, teaches that the principle of a demonstration cannot itself be a demonstration, because the matter would be tossed about in an eternal circle, since one thing would have to be proved by the other. On this account, he condemns the ancient philosophers in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, as if they thought that everything could be proved by demonstration; and in the *Posterior Analytics* itself, he affirms that it is necessary to find something prior to and more certain than the demonstrated conclusion—that is, a proposition so clear by its own nature that it is worthy of being trusted. He instructed that this proposition be prepared from the induction of particulars, and that the particulars must be gathered by sensation. 

Therefore, he set sensation as the beginning and foundation for the entire edifice of demonstration. Concerning this, he discussed in the fourth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note> in such a way that he condemned anyone who would inquire too scrupulously about it and seek a reason where reason did not exist. <margin>The first way.</margin> Likewise, in the sixth and seventh books of the same work, he both relies on sensation and teaches that one must rely on it. But if this foundation is undermined by us, shaken and moved from its place, we think that everything built upon it will collapse with a single blow. This is the first and universal way of demolishing the art of demonstration devised by Aristotle, which we shall attack more specifically in the following chapter, showing that the senses can be deceived in other ways than those set down by Aristotle. 

<margin>The second [way].</margin> The second way: even if other deceptive modes were not given, nevertheless, by both his own authority and by reasons, sensation—and the demonstration that follows—is still uncertain. 

<margin>The third [way].</margin> The third way is from the middle term <note>In a syllogism, the middle term is the link that connects the subject and the predicate in the conclusion.</note> which he uses as a cause, namely from definition. He is mistaken in this matter when he supposes the definition to be more certain than the demonstration itself, and takes this as clear and confessed; yet it contains great difficulty, not only whether it is more certain, but whether a definition is certain in itself and known to men. 

<margin>The fourth [way].</margin> The fourth way: even if a definition were held to be certain in itself, it could not for that reason be certain to us if we wish to maintain Aristotelian dogma. To this is added that it is not clearly understood what Aristotle meant, for even in this matter his followers <note>literally "they," referring to the Peripatetics or Aristotelian commentators</note> interpret him differently and in various ways, as we have taught extensively in the fourth book of our *Institutes of Logic*. For some prefer that the definition of the subject enter the demonstration, others the definition of the proper attribute <note>original: "affectionis," a property that belongs specifically to a certain subject</note>, others both; and they want one to be the subject in one proposition and the other to be the predicate in the other, so that finally the attribute is demonstrated of the subject. 

<margin>The fifth [way].</margin> The fifth way: because the progress and the end are uncertain, since no certain universal affirmative proposition is given among those who rely on Aristotle, without which he nevertheless maintained that a demonstration could in no way be fortified. Nor is the proper attribute of a subject certainly known, for when it has been shown to be in the subject, then the demonstration is said to have reached its end. From this, we shall show how far they are deceived who [believe] a universal proposition...

Certainly, it is well established that Aristotle considered both the intellect and the senses to be "judiciary powers" <note>original: "iudiciarias potestates," meaning faculties capable of making judgments or distinctions</note> without making a distinction between them in this regard. For in the fortieth section of the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>, when he is about to treat the power of motion, he assigns the duty of judging to both the intellect and the sense, decreeing that they agree in this function. Where the common translation <note>the "Vulgate" or standard Latin translation of Aristotle</note> says that "discernment is the work of the intellect and the sense," and where the Arabic version explained by Averroës <note>the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western thought</note> distinguishes "that which belongs to the action of the sense and the intellect," and where in Argyropoulos <note>John Argyropoulos, a 15th-century scholar who re-translated Aristotle into Latin</note> it stands as "the power of discerning, which is indeed the work and judgment of the mind and also of the sense," in Aristotle's own words it is: "by the judging faculty, which is the work of the mind and of sense" <note>original Greek: "τω̃ τε κριτικω̃ ὅ διανοίας ἔργον ἐστὶ καὶ αἰσθήσεως"</note>. For the sense indicates what it perceives to a higher and loftier power, having drawn it from the outside through those five little channels, as it were, of "sensible species" <note>the qualities of objects—like color or sound—as they are perceived by the soul</note>; and the sense even judges this very thing by its own power and authority. And in the book *On Dreams*, Aristotle cites the judgment of the "principal part" (that is, the mind) and of that "from which phantasms <note>images or mental apparitions</note> emerge" (that is, the sense) without distinction. He explains there how deception arises most easily in the senses of those who are held by love, or anger, or some other passion, as we mentioned in the preceding work. But because he himself properly names neither the intellect nor the sense, but rather "this is the ruling part" <note>original Greek: "τὸ κύριον"</note> and "in which images are formed" <note>original Greek: "ἐν ὡ̃ τὰ φαντάσματα γίνεται"</note>, Themistius <note>a 4th-century philosopher and commentator</note> in his paraphrase of *On Dreams* writes that there are two powers of judging within us: the mind, which holds the primacy, and the sense, from which imagination takes its origin. This evidence and judgment of the sense—which we have explained at great length so that the argument would not be cluttered by disputes over words, and which we have declared as clearly as we could—we call "uncertain"; and what follows from this is an "uncertain art of demonstration." This consequence is well known to Aristotle himself <margin>Proof of the / consequence.</margin> and to all who know what his "art of demonstration" <note>the method of proving a conclusion with absolute certainty based on true premises</note> is, what it requires, and what it necessarily admits. Finally, they appeal to the sense as to a primary indicator and judge because he teaches in the *Posterior Analytics* that universal propositions are gathered by induction from singular things, which are perceived and judged by the sense. For whether you propose something, or ask it, or suggest it, or describe it, you are using the services of the senses, or relying on the experiences of the senses, or applying something that draws its beginning and foundation from the sense itself—whether so that it may exist in itself, or so that it may be known by man. These things are held so clearly in Aristotle that they do not need proof: since he himself decreed that all human knowledge has its origin in the sense; and that "nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense"; and that he who lacks one sense must also lack the knowledge of all things pertaining to that sense. This consequence is also noted among the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle’s school</note>, of whom the most distinguished, Themistius and Simplicius <margin>Themistius. / Simplicius.</margin>, testify in their commentaries on the *Physics* that Aristotle derived the principles of demonstration from the sense. Also in the work *On Demonstration*, when Aristotle had said that all doctrine and all intellectual discipline is produced from pre-existing knowledge, there are some who take this to be said significantly without mentioning the sense, which is the foundation of all doctrine and discipline. Yet clearly Themistius <margin>Philoponus.</margin> affirms that the sense itself is preceded by no knowledge. And Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle</note> likewise confirms that the sense does not have "pre-existing knowledge" <note>original Greek: "προϋποκειμένην γνω̃σιν"</note>, that is, knowledge laid down beforehand. Alexander <margin>Alexander.</margin> says the same while explaining Aristotle's...

<margin>A multi-faceted removal of the objection.</margin>
*Theological Summa* <note>the *Summa Theologiae*</note>, in the first part of the second volume, Question 51—where he disputes whether any "habit" <note>term: habit / *habitus*; a stable disposition or quality of the mind</note> belongs to us by nature—he most clearly confesses that Aristotle showed that our knowledge of principles comes to us from the senses. But if you should say that logical demonstration is not founded on things received through the sense, but rather on "transcendentals," and that there are certain propositions among the philosophers called "dignities" <note>term: dignities / *dignitates*; self-evident axioms or fundamental principles that command immediate assent, such as "the whole is greater than the part"</note> which are not obtained by the sense, I will say, on the authority of Aristotle and the good Peripatetics <note>the traditional followers of Aristotle</note>, that demonstration is not decided in that way. Instead, it is founded in the sense, which he affirms as the guide of all human knowledge—so much so that he affirmed without a doubt that whoever is deprived of a single sense by nature will also lack knowledge of the things pertaining to that sense. 

Indeed, Aristotle himself in the third book of *On the Soul*, while repeating what he had previously disputed regarding the soul itself, writes openly that he who does not perceive can neither learn anything nor understand anything; and that it is necessary for one who contemplates to contemplate a "phantasm" <note>term: phantasm / *phantasma*; a mental image or representation derived from sensory experience, which the intellect "looks at" to find universal truths</note> at the same time. And although there are some who wish this to be found true only while the soul is considered as a "form of the body" and not as a pure intelligence (in that first state they imagine for it before it gives form to the body); others say this applies only while the soul is learning, but not after it has learned. Others say it applies only while it is occupied with apprehending natural things, as we also mentioned in the commentary on the third book of Aristotle's *On the Soul*, and in the digression...

...if you have been deceived by sensation, for the sense itself—as we have said, and as we will soon say even more broadly—can be true within itself, yet it is and is often held by experience itself to be various, ambiguous, and doubtful when it performs its duty. It is various, I say, if you wish to gather the **rule of truth** <note>original: "regula ueritatis"</note> (of which we spoke in the previous book) from the sense. I wish this to be stated now and often silently repeated elsewhere: lest I should constantly have to insist that I am speaking of this rule of sensory truth whenever mention of the matter occurs. Furthermore, I grant you for the sake of argument that one sensation may be corrected by another, and that you may gather something from many instances. But, O learned man, a **universal** <note>term: universal / *uniuerſale*; a general concept or principle that applies to all members of a class, such as "all men are mortal"</note> consists not of *many*, but of *all*. These "all" can neither be held purely, nor in the same way, as will be seen as this work proceeds; and a demonstration is not completed without a universal. He who wishes to argue from many to all falls into a fallacy condemned by Aristotle, a topic for which a place has been reserved for me later in this very book.

Therefore, whether there are many or few, if there is but one instance that is uncertain, the entire universal is rendered uncertain; for if it is to be established as certain, it must consist of all individual parts that are certain. Not to mention that what seems certain to you will seem uncertain and often false to others due to the diversity of the senses. Ultimately, it will be necessary to consult nature itself and go to its tribunal to settle the dispute: because neither your physical **temperament** <note>term: temperament / *temperatura*; in medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which was thought to determine a person's physical and mental character</note> nor that of anyone else will be held as a judgment competent for all men. For as many individuals as there are in the human species, there are as many different temperaments resulting from the differing proportions of the humors, a matter about which a dispute will be held shortly while proving what we have assumed.

<margin>First proof of the preceding proposition.</margin>
This assumption can indeed be proven in many ways: first, in general, through those things said in the twelfth chapter of the previous book, where we showed (not without the testimony of Aristotle himself) that the sense is everywhere prioritized by him and judged more certainly than reason.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, by the authority of many philosophers: Anacharsis, Xenophanes, and likewise Parmenides, Democritus, Heraclitus, and all others who held the perception and judgment of the senses to be uncertain, and who attempted to prove that very thing. We explained their opinions in the second book of this work, and on this matter, we also reviewed the arguments of the Academics and especially the **Skeptics** <note>term: Skeptics / *scepticorum*; a school of ancient philosophy that questioned the possibility of attaining certain knowledge</note>. We even assisted them as far as was permitted, especially in the twenty-second and twenty-third chapters; we do not wish to use those arguments at present, since while disputing with Aristotle, it does not please me to depart from the **Lyceum** <note>original: "lycium"; the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle in Athens</note>.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, because men frequently hesitate regarding their own sensations, doubting whether they have perceived correctly. Did they truly see, or truly hear, what seemed to them to be seen or heard? For even if that act is called "reflexive," it is nonetheless an act of the sense, either of the same person or of another. It follows that if one doubts the sensation itself, one cannot therefore be certain of it. From this, the root of the proof presents itself: that the faculty of human discourse is insufficiently firm, since every composite knowledge, or knowledge collected by a **syllogism** <note>term: syllogism / *ſyllogiſmo*; a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises</note>, depends on simple knowledge, which in turn depends on the sense.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
Fourth, because even when they perceive properly, it still remains in doubt *how* they perceive, *what* they perceive, and *how many* senses are possessed—matters which they nonetheless investigate by means of the sense itself. For when Aristotle gives instructions concerning the sense itself in the second book of *On the Soul*, he frequently hesitates and seems so inconsistent with himself that great difficulties surround all his interpreters who try to rescue him from contradiction. In this matter, it is a marvel that if they cannot explain with certainty what Aristotle intended, they nevertheless do not explain themselves when they consider their own act of sensing or weigh it, so as to decide upon the senses in a harmonious and agreeable way. Is there not a great struggle over the internal sense, whether it be one or many? Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> discussing the soul, and Themistius <note>a 4th-century statesman and philosopher known for his paraphrases of Aristotle</note> in his book *On Memory and Dreams*, claim there is only one...

<margin>Galen. Averroës.</margin>

On this matter, even the commentators do not agree. There are those who join the "common sense" <note>term: common sense / *sensus communis*; a theoretical internal power that integrates data from the five individual senses into a single perception</note> with the particular sense, and bring forward the question of *whether* a thing is and *what* it is; they assign the "whether" only to the external sense, but grant the "what" 
<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
to the internal sense and to that which is coupled with the external. <margin>Thomas.</margin>

This is not only insofar as it judges differently from how the thing actually is, but also insofar as it is a certain thing and an indicator, not a judge, of another thing. For even if it offers and presents itself to a higher power in the same way it was affected, it can nonetheless indicate and present the thing differently, and thus it is said to be false, as it sometimes exhibits a divergent estimation. 

And even in the perception of sensible objects, while they refer them in a certain order to the judgment that follows, it can offer an occasion for deception. While it both reckons and judges by differently combining and dividing, in which judgment either truth or falsehood is expressed—but not properly in the simple and bare intake and perception. Although even an external thing is often designated by the name of "false" insofar as it instills a false estimation in the senses; for even if they are said to discern their proper sensible objects <note>term: proper sensibles / *propriis sensilibus*; qualities perceived by only one sense, like color for sight or sound for hearing</note> by the guidance of nature, they are nevertheless hindered internally and externally, either by the sense organ or the medium. Indeed, if I were not writing these things for the learned and erudite, and for those well-versed in reading Aristotle and his commentators, I would certainly explain them further; let it suffice to have noted them. 

Furthermore, whence, I ask, arises such a great and frequent question regarding the sense? Is it a power that is only passive? Is it active? Or is it something in between? Those who think it is active believe they are doing something while they perceive, not just undergoing it—such as John of Jandun <note>original: *Io. candauenſis*</note> and Apollinaris. And on the opposite side, others say they are not acting at all, rejecting the idea of an active sense. Nor are there lacking those who admit both, yet neither of them, understanding a certain middle action between what is properly acting and properly being acted upon. And what of the number of acts of sensing itself? Did some not say they perceive the proper and the common sensible object <note>term: common sensibles / *commune sensibile*; qualities like shape, number, or motion that can be perceived by more than one sense</note> by two acts? Have others not recorded that they perceive those things by only one? Is there not also much discord over whether a common sensible object can be perceived without a proper one, and how? They even ascend to the "touch of the heavens" to settle the question. On this matter as well—whether there is a sense of the heavens itself or not, and in what way it might be—they openly disagree. Furthermore, concerning the sense itself, when it is said to be...

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument regarding the lack of consensus among philosophers—specifically Aristotle and his commentators—about the fundamental mechanics of human perception. BOOK FIVE.                                                                   135

Since it is said to exist in potentiality <note>The state of being able to do something but not currently doing it.</note>, how great is the dispute? In what way should it be understood—twice, or only once? That is, does it pertain to the first act and the second, or only to this final one? This dispute arises because Aristotle compared the sense to the intellect. The intellect is called a "power" in relation to the **first act**—which is knowledge or understanding—and also in relation to the **second act**, which is the actual exercise of thinking and considering. However, Aristotle had judged that the sense is led by the one who generated it toward the first act, so that in this respect it could be compared and equated to knowledge. 

But soon he also claims that the sense is a power in relation to the form or **mental image** <note>original: "speciem"</note> of the object; otherwise, if it were not aided by something external and no object were present, it would not perceive. Regarding these meanings in Aristotle, there are such diverse opinions that it is extremely difficult to distinguish which ones are more in harmony with the actual sense. On this point, some imagine a "mutation" of the object by which the sense, having absorbed the image, becomes similar to the sensible thing. Immediately, they suggest another change—one of nature, not of temporal order—which is carried to the soul when the sense is actively perceiving. Others stand in opposition, claiming that what we call "active sensing" is nothing other than the image of the sensible thing being placed in the sense. 

Others hold different views: should the duty of sensing be attributed to the body, or the soul, or to both? They seem to get stuck here. There are even those who grant the function of sensing to the soul *through* the body. Consequently, they do not agree on what "sensing" itself actually is, or to what primary thing it should be attributed. 

Even in the sense of **touch** itself, which is one of the five, how much diversity is there! Are there several senses of touch, or only one? Aristotle was so ambiguous on this matter that he does not hint at it sufficiently, nor do his interpreters clarify it; one thinks Aristotle felt one way, while another thinks he felt differently. Therefore, we have sufficiently revealed that no certain judgment can be founded upon this [un]certainty of the senses or sensations, whether they are direct or reflective. 

For in the previous book, we refuted those who said that the sense is always true because it presented what it absorbed. We taught that they are deceived because, from a poorly formed appearance of a thing, they are led to judge a mental image of the thing that is not true; their opinions are always uncertain until the judgment is resolved by the object itself. There, we remembered that Aristotle's reasons in the fourth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ," a common title for the Metaphysics</note> for asserting sensible truth were dismantled by us in the second book of this work—not indeed to deny that truth can be obtained through the sense, but because those specific reasons do not prove it.

The assumption can be proven in a **fifth** way: because even if we grant the sense and its mode of sensing to be established in a consistent and agreeable way—as far as concerns the experiments of those who judge the sense from the sensations themselves—nevertheless, an argument can be drawn from the varying nature of particular senses. These vary with the passage of time, with the diverse nature of the sensible thing, with various permutations, and with the varying encounter of both. All of these will be explained in succession: the very indication and judgment of the sense is rendered uncertain and often deceptive. 

<margin>Fifth proof.</margin>

Let us investigate this first in the sense of **sight**, which Aristotle prefers above all senses for perceiving the differences between things. Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> also taught at the beginning of his commentary on the books *On the Soul* that sight possesses such excellence that it draws the others with it. For this reason, he judges that those things which participate in sight—or as he says, **participate in sight** <note>original Greek: "μετέχει ὄψεως"</note>—also participate in hearing, and those who participate in hearing are not without smell, taste, and touch. Aristotle decrees in the second book of *On the Soul* that sight is not deceived concerning "color" insofar as it is color; and indeed, he decreed this through those very certain signs of the sense known to all. But what kind of color? For a thing that is colored in a general and universal way does not create a foundation for art or science, the kind of which he and others diligently and exactly seek. For it is necessary to descend to the **specific types** of colors, and especially those from individual things...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Aristotle’s theories on sensory perception, moving from the general definition of the "common sense" to a specific investigation of the most "excellent" sense: sight. It addresses the physical composition of the eye and the reasons why vision, though superior, is prone to deception.</meta>

**BOOK.**

<margin>Vision is often deceived in ways other than those Aristotle described.</margin>

It strives to collect the form <note>original: "speciem" — here meaning the visual image or mental representation of an object</note> to produce knowledge. In this, however, the eye is especially uncertain and is sometimes deceived, namely in the diverse appearance of colors. Yet, sight is by far the most distinguished of all the senses; as it is decreed in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, it reveals to us the many differences between things. As Aristotle himself affirms in his book *On the Senses and Sensible Objects*, it is better than the others, announcing to us "manifold" <note>original: "παντοδαπὰς"</note> (that is, of all kinds) differences "because all bodies participate in color" <note>original: "διὰ πάντα σώματα μετέχει χρώματος"</note>. 

He also added that the so-called "common sensibles"—that is, shape, magnitude, motion, and number—are most strongly perceived through this power of sight. Furthermore, toward the end of the second book of *On the Soul* (according to the Latin division we use), he called sight the most excellent sense and taught that it received its name from light.

Since, therefore, this sense is held to be chief and surpassing, I grant you an eye focused on observing color: for that is its proper object, and no foreign or common thing should be placed in its way. I grant you proximity of position and place, so that the object may be situated at whatever distance you prefer. For there are those who see better from a distance than from a common range; take whichever you prefer. I grant you the same air, affected by the same qualities. I grant that no internal disease or external accident has ever occurred by which the sensory organ was weakened, so that the eye has not corrupted the nature which it brought with it from its "mother's pouch" (as Lucilius says), and no obstacle has met the organ.

Would this sense, therefore, necessarily be true? Or would it be rather uncertain and doubtful? Certainly, it may seem certain to itself, but it is uncertain to others and often deceptive. The cause is the varying temperament <term>temperamentum: the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which was thought to determine health and personality</term> of the whole body. This is either established by its own nature or changed over time—not only by internal disease or external accident, but naturally through the progress of age. It is changed by a wondrous variety of sensitive nature so that even if it is said to be within the human "latitude" <note>The range of normal human variation</note> of the second type, and each person determines this for themselves, it will nonetheless behave differently. It varies not only in intensity but with a much greater diversity than we will show shortly.

This is true of the whole body, and certainly of the eye and the pupil itself, all the more so because its nature is not solid and compact, but thin and fluid. It consists mostly of a watery substance; hence Aristotle, speaking of it in his book *On the Senses*, says "it is of water" <note>original: "ὕδατος ἐστὶ"</note>. In the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he says the nature of water is within sight, which can most easily preserve all transparent things. In the third book of *On the Soul*, he writes that the pupil is changed by the air and, to use his words: "And he [Empedocles] made the pupil of the air" <note>original: "ὁ δὲ Ἰνὺ κο'ρην τοῦ αυδὶ ἐποίησεν"</note>. In the seventh section of his *Problems*, he testifies that the eye is the most mobile part of our body, and more than all others, it can be made similar to the object placed before it; shortly after, he affirms that the sense of sight is the most exquisite of all.

In the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he attributes sight not to fire (as Empedocles wished) but to water, remembering what he had previously decreed in the books *On the Soul* and *On the Senses*. He affirms that human eyes are not of a single color like those of other animals, but are varied and multicolored: blue-gray, yellowish, black, and goat-like. He notes that many people even have eyes of different colors, especially blue-gray. He offers a cause for such a variety of colors based on a long progression of the abundance or scarcity of humor <note>The fluid or liquid within the eye</note>. From this, he investigates the cause of sharp and dull vision, though his explanation did not fully satisfy him. Therefore, he also brought into consideration the skin that covers the pupil, which is thin, white, and smooth, so that it may be transparent and thus suitable for seeing sharply. To this, he adds that pure humor is necessary for perceiving exquisite differences in color, and that the position of the eyes—not protruding, but concave and recessed—is ideal for seeing at a distance.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the fallibility of sight, shifting from the external conditions of perception to the internal biological "temperament" of the observer. ->FIFTH BOOK.                                                                                                136<-

Truly, the variety of humors and colors, the manifold quality of the skin, and the different placement of eyes in different men all flow from the diverse temperament <note>original: "temperatione" — in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note> of the human body. Therefore, through this change of the sense—that is, the variety of the sensory power and the sensory organs—both the indication and the judgment regarding a sensible thing are altered. That is to say, not only in that the sense indicates a thing to be different or otherwise than it truly is, but also because the sense is of such a nature—namely, changeable and very frequently varying within itself—that it offers itself to the higher power <note>The "higher power" refers to the intellect or the soul's capacity for reason</note> not always in one way, but in various and diverse manners according to its varying disposition. Because of this, it perceives the object and its form <note>original: "speciem" — the mental or sensory image of the object</note> variably. Thus, what might now be truly affirmed because it appears so at this moment, could shortly after be truly denied because it appears differently than it did before. Therefore, one who relies on the senses could not deliver a certain and constant opinion, and would frequently find their judgment to be wavering.

For something similar is related by Aristotle in asserting the deception of the senses: when a motion in the sense, not caused by the object itself, is perceived just as if it had been caused by the object. For instance, when the shore one watches seems to move <note>A reference to the illusion of motion while on a boat</note>, or when the eye is pressed, and when a table seems to rise up with double lamps <note>Referring to double vision (diplopia) caused by physical pressure on the eye or intoxication</note>. 

But I suggest that the conception in the sense should be understood as being captured not by force, nor by any unnatural internal motion occurring, but as that which is suggested and brought forth by the bodily temperament by its own nature. Just as this conception is not the same as another arising from a different temperament, so it does not present or indicate the same thing to the sensory power. Therefore, different "sensings"—or as they are called by the Moderns <note>original: "Neotericis" — a term used to describe contemporary 15th or 16th-century scholars</note>, *sensations*—are produced from a different sense, not only from a different sensible object. 

Indeed, the sensible object itself varies repeatedly; that is, it takes on different qualities apparent to the senses. Thus, the nature of the sense itself becomes varied, not only from the variety of the object presented, but from the variety of the human temperament, which changes by its own nature for many reasons. This occurs not only from the surrounding air, cold, heat, and nourishment—which Aristotle admits in his book *On the Senses*—but especially because of those internal changes through which an external quality is presented differently, due to the image being rendered differently by the mixture of various humors. 

Moreover, this pertains not only to "proper sensibles" <note>Properties perceived by a single sense, like color for sight or sound for hearing</note>, but also to "common sensibles" <note>Properties perceived by multiple senses, such as number, size, or motion</note>. For an object is rendered differently in number, quantity, rest, motion, and its entire structure, so that various affections arise from them. Hence, from excessive affection, by which the internal humors are altered, many things are falsely presented. This is conspicuous in those captured by love <note>original: "capti sunt amore"</note>, to whom the ugliest women sometimes seem most beautiful, and to women, the ugliest men—even those like Thersites <note>In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War, famously described by Homer as the ugliest and most deformed of the Greeks</note>—are judged to be of the most handsome appearance. 

But why did I speak of love? When many causes of this thing are usually offered, about all of which we discourse at length when speaking of avoiding loves that oppose divine love and hinder the loving life. Why, I say, of love? Which can also proceed from an affected will and a habit of pleasure. Does not almost everyone have a different judgment regarding a sensible thing? The "property" <note>The unique individual nature or character</note> of the individual effects this: the different mixture of humors and the wondrous instability of the sensory nature, to pass over other things. For even if men are considered to be of one species, and through this their senses—insofar as they are human—do not differ in kind, yet insofar as the senses themselves are composed of different things—that is, a different temperament of humors—and spring forth from various proportions of humors, they drink in the objects presented to them differently. These things vary very frequently, both from the natural temperament and from continual change, being agitated repeatedly by both internal and external actions. Wherefore different sensations proceed from the varied temperament itself, whether those same diverse...

## BOOK FIVE. 137.

Many fallacies can arise, for some appearance of color might be so diminished that either the thickness of the air or the hour of day renders it different; this occurs to such an extent that the same sensory judgment would not exist for everyone, nor always, nor even for the same man. This is supported by the authority of Aristotle himself (as we alluded to in previous books), since he affirmed in his *Problems* <note>Aristotle, *Problems*, Book 26, 55. This work explores scientific and medical questions through a series of "problems."</note> that while the east wind <note>original: "euro flante" — referring to Eurus, the southeast or east wind</note> is blowing, the stars are seen differently than if the wind itself did not make the air thicker. Furthermore, once various diversities and various oppositions are obtained, it follows that various contrariness depends upon them, and thus contradiction remains. From this, either fallacy or uncertainty will necessarily arise from the other side.

Certainly, with Aristotle as the authority, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> I do not see how they can deny that there are as many kinds <note>original: "species"</note> of temperament as there are individuals, since he himself, in his *Problems* concerning the mixture of active humors, decreed that some differ in kind not because they have a face, but because they have *such* a face. For if that difference is said to reside in accidental qualities and matter—rather than being drawn from the human species itself—we nevertheless conclude that this diverse mixture presents different things not only internally, but also externally to the eyes of others.

Nor is this to be observed only in the whole earthy mass of the human body, but also in those most subtle little bodies called "spirits" <term>spirits<gloss>original: "spiritus" — in medieval medicine, these were subtle, vaporous substances that circulated through the body to facilitate life, movement, and thought</gloss></term>. Although some are called animal, others vital, and others natural by doctors, Avicenna nevertheless writes in his booklet *On the Powers of the Heart* <margin>Avicenna.</margin> that a "proper temperament" exists in each one, to which he gave the name "complexion" <term>complexion<gloss>original: "complexionis" — the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that defines an individual's constitution</gloss></term>. I say "proper" by reason of the proportion of quantities, the subtlety of the humors, and the form of the mixtures. But if the temperaments of the whole body differ in kind, will the sensations themselves not also differ?

For if it is manifest that the temperaments between one person's sense organ and a sensible object differ from the temperaments of another person's sensing of that same object, how could it be that the relationships between them do not openly differ? This is not only because one sensation is more intense <note>original: "intentior"</note> or more relaxed <note>original: "remissior"</note> than another, or because one is bilious, another phlegmatic, another otherwise, but because they arise from the diverse nature of the foundation and the limit <note>original: "fundamenti terminique" — logical terms for the starting point and the end result of a relationship</note>. Both of these are varied—namely the sensible object, which is composed of diverse and mutually clashing qualities—and this variation exists because of the object itself and the power of the senses.

For the object renders and presents an appearance <note>original: "speciem"</note> to the sensing power based on its quality, the quantity in which that quality is grounded, and the entire mixture of its substance from which those things flow. Therefore, it is perceived variously for almost these same reasons. If that Aristotelian maxim is true—that everything which is received is received according to the mode of the receiver <note>original: "omne quod recipiatur per modum ipsius qui recipit suscipiatur" — a fundamental principle of medieval philosophy: our internal state shapes how we experience external reality</note>—then the relationship of the appearance itself is diverse, based on the different foundation and limit.

For who would not doubt that the relationship which exists between four and eight differs in kind from that which is established between two and six? In what way, then, can one doubt that the state of temperament—which might exist between a sense organ endowed with (for example) four degrees of bile and a sensible object composed of two degrees of phlegm—does not differ in kind from that which exists between a sense organ that possesses six degrees of blood and a sensible object constituted from three degrees of black bile? 

This ought to be accepted especially by those who would establish that the temperaments of two or more bodies are diverse, even if a single humor prevailed over others in those bodies. It should be accepted by those who would not want anything to be lost from the mixture itself, and who would attribute specific forms to each individual limb. This is much more the case if we establish that the biles themselves are diverse from each other within the mixture. For instance, a bile that is placed at an intensity of four degrees might be called "caerulean" <note>original: "caerulea" — a dark, blue-black color associated with certain states of bile</note>, while that which is held at three degrees in another mixture might be noted as "vitelline" <note>yolk-colored</note> or "praxine" <note>leek-green</note>. Moreover, the proportion itself can be varied in many ways: by age, by chance, or even within the same age by nutrition, growth, or the subtraction of all or some factors...

It is likewise recorded in memory that Tiberius Caesar was accustomed to seeing in the pitch darkness of night. And so much for the uncertainty of sight, as far as what seems to have been overlooked by Aristotle <margin>Summary of examples regarding the uncertainty of sight</margin>; for if the sense were entirely certain, the same object would not appear differently to each person due to the diversity of the makeup and temperament of their humors. From this, the induction proceeding from particulars will vary, whether you refer it to the visual power or to the varying nature of the thing seen. I might add as an extra point that Averroes <margin>Averroes</margin> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher known for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> wished to state in his third commentary on *The Soul* that sight is sometimes deceived regarding its proper object. I add, therefore, "not always," and if I am not mistaken, this follows most logically.

But enough about sight, and perhaps more than was necessary. In the remaining senses as well, judgment should be rendered in equal proportion. For if you turn to taste <margin>Examples in the other senses, and especially in taste.</margin>, what a manifold and varied diversity—more than can be described—is found in men due to their humors? I speak not only of humors corrupted by fever, but of those present from birth. For what is perceived in one way by one person is not perceived so by another, especially since all flavors consist of and grow from a combination of sweet and bitter. For Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> himself writes in his book *On the Senses* that just as colors are made from a mixture of white and black, so are "all juices [flavors] from sweet and bitter" <note>original Greek: "οἱ χυμοὶ ἐκ γλυκέος καὶ πικροῦ"</note>; and he teaches that this occurs to a greater or lesser degree based on the analogy or proportion of the mixture. 

Nor should those now shout against me who decree that such a temperament of man must be weighed within a certain range, and that "Man" should be considered not by the properties of individuals but by the species. For when they discuss how many temperaments there are and how they are distinguished, they do not decree it as a settled matter, but as something ambiguous and full of difficulties, as shown before. Nor does the intensifying or relaxing of that range demand minor controversies to be shaken out. Indeed, if such a range were assigned as they say is fitting, it would necessarily have to be applied to properly and certainly perceiving sensations—and even distinguishing between them—so that it could support the preparation of a scientific demonstration. However, this does not rely on those common and most general concepts of the mind, but rather investigates and collects the species of things from singular things perceived and known by the sense itself, with Aristotle as the guide. Otherwise, I believe few—or rather, none—would be fit for demonstrating anything. And concerning Aristotle himself, it could be disputed whether he was placed within that range or not. Furthermore, individual men made of flesh are the ones who feel and judge the sensations they perceive; it is not the abstract "notions of Man" said to be placed in our minds, in which a single notion represents the entire human species with individual conditions stripped away.
