...and not entirely harmonic. The cause is certainly the varying temperament <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, 'temperament' refers to the balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which determined an individual's health and personality.</note> of the body. From this also comes the varying judgment of the ears; however, the particular and individual cause is always varying, though it is rarely discovered. For since the differences in sound are high and low <note>original: "acutum & graue"</note>, who does not see that from the varying composition of high and low, different types of sounds are forged? When these are related to the different dispositions of the perceiver, they will be perceived differently than they would be by those who are affected in another way. It would be a long task to recount the variations of human temperament concerning every sense; for each man has his own temperament so uniquely that it is impossible for another to be exactly like or equal to it—at least if Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> decreed the truth in the first book of his *Medicine*. Indeed, <margin>**Avicenna.**</margin> he teaches in his book *On the Powers of the Heart* <note>original: "de uiribus cordis"</note> that all composite things have their own temperaments and dispositions, from which their specific powers emanate. He teaches that these are unknown, both in terms of the things by which they are made and produced, and also in terms of why one thing is more disposed than another to receive such a power. He most clearly testifies that the proportion of the mixture of simple elements <note>The 'simples' are the basic components or elements in alchemy and early medicine.</note> will always be unknown to us as long as we live in this world. 

But can it be denied that every sensory organ has its own constituent principles? That it is specifically disposed toward its own power of perceiving? That it has a proportion of the mixture of simples? Add to this that they are related to the sensible objects which also have their own proportion. From all these things it happens that a variety of senses emerges, and the truth cannot be discerned purely by everyone, as many believe. Let us put aside how varied and often vain judgments are made regarding those things which are not specifically presented to the external senses, but are said to be presented commonly—such as number, quantity, rest, and motion. Are not "greater" and "lesser," or "more" and "few," often judged falsely? Even beautiful things are sometimes thought ugly, and conversely, the ugly are esteemed beautiful, as we recalled earlier. Many also believe things to be at rest when they are moving, or moving when they are at rest—not only in small and distant things, but in the greatest and most present ones. In this way, both Aristarchus the mathematician and Seleucus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE) and Seleucus of Seleucia (c. 190 BCE) were ancient astronomers who proposed heliocentric theories—the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun—long before Copernicus.</note> said that the earth alone moves, while the heavens and everything else are entirely at rest, as we have related before. 

Finally, I should not keep silent that we ourselves do not seem to have wandered very far from Saint <margin>**Thomas**</margin> Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note>, who in the first book of the *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra gentes"</note> seems to have hinted at this fallacy of the senses and even of the most exact human proof (which is called demonstration), especially in the place where he discusses the rational tradition of faith. He asserted first that falsehood is often mixed into the investigation of human reason because of the weakness of our intellect and the mixing in of "phantasms" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a 'phantasm' is a mental image or sensory impression that the intellect uses to form concepts.</note>. Then, after a few introductory words about the ignorance of demonstration among most people and the diversity of doctrine among those called "wise," he added that among the many true things that are demonstrated, falsehood is sometimes mixed in—which is not demonstrated, but asserted by some probable or sophisticated reason which is sometimes considered a demonstration. Finally, progressing to the end of the chapter, regarding what he had said about the weakness of human knowledge—and that for this reason a fixed and certain faith, beneficial to the human race, was given by divine power—he concluded and confirmed everything with the words of Paul warning the Ephesians "not to walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their senses" <note>A reference to Ephesians 4:17. In this context, the author uses the Latin "sensus" (sense) where modern translations often use "mind."</note>. For by apostolic authority, he attributed the received fallacy to the senses. And he himself had previously hinted at this by mentioning the mixture of phantasms, which are clearly drawn from the senses; hence, he thought that things called exact demonstrations in the common manner were not actually demonstrations, being mixed with error and relying on probable or sophisticated reason. Above, he had also taught that men [do not know the nature] of sensory things...

...fies that we are ignorant of not a few, nor many, nor several, but very many properties <note>original: "proprietates"; in this context, the specific qualities or inherent characteristics of a substance.</note>—to use his own word—and that a perfect explanation for even those properties we grasp through the senses cannot be found in most cases. Beyond what we have already said, I wanted to include this point here so that those who pursue us with "Vatinian hatred" <note>The phrase "Vatinian hatred" (*odium Vatinianum*) refers to an intense, proverbial animosity, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius, who was famously detested by his contemporaries.</note> and "stepmotherly" <note>original: "nouercali"; a traditional metaphor for harsh or unfair treatment, used here to describe the hostility of the author's critics.</note> malice—simply because we do not worship Aristotle in the same way they do—might either learn or be reminded that Thomas [Aquinas], a man of great judgment and a premier interpreter of Aristotle, occasionally said things that, if not exactly the same as our current arguments, were certainly not entirely different.

...that certainty is held in the light, when an object is known to be other than it actually is. <margin>Scotus’s arguments regarding the first point.</margin> He [Henry of Ghent] asserts that this happens when a changeable object is perceived as unchangeable—even though he does not think that the sensible thing being perceived is itself in a state of continuous change. Scotus argues that if this second reasoning were based on a solid foundation, it would follow that we could never grasp any truth. For humans would never rely on any truth, since whatever is placed in the soul is changeable, and the very act of understanding itself cannot be exempt from this change. Therefore, it could not be discovered how the soul might possess certain truth. Furthermore, he believes that the inherent <term>species<note>In scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental representation or "image" of an object that allows the mind to know it.</note></term> concurs uselessly with that "species" imparted by the divine ray. For when one certainty is inconsistent with another, the second cannot be certain—following the example of a syllogistic conclusion, which depends upon and is gathered from both a proposition joined to a "necessary" mode and another connected to a "contingent" mode. <note>In logic, a conclusion follows the "weaker part"; if one premise is only possibly true (contingent) and the other is necessarily true, the conclusion can only be contingent, not necessary.</note> He also argues that the species which concurs in all knowledge cannot judge distinctly, because it represents itself in both ways; nor can it happen that, by the arrival of any other factor, truth can be distinguished from what merely resembles it. Next, he gathers many points to show that this was not the opinion of Augustine, but rather that of the Academics <note>The Academic Skeptics, who argued that certain knowledge was impossible.</note>, and that it is not proven by those very reasons. Thus far, for the most part, Scotus deals with the first point.

Regarding the second point, he responds to the reasons themselves and denies the preceding <margin>Arguments regarding the second point.</margin> proposition. For he does not say that sensible things are continuously moved and changed; even if that were granted, he denies that truth is seen in a disconnected way. For if the object perceived is considered changeable, it does not follow that what is produced and gathered from it cannot represent anything under an unchangeable logic (to use his words). Mutability in the object is not the *reason* for the representation being produced, but rather the *nature* of the thing that is changeable. Furthermore, it can happen that through something that is changeable, another thing may be represented under an unchangeable logic—just as something is typically indicated under the logic of the infinite by means of the finite. Thus, the essence of God can be represented under an unchangeable logic through some changeable thing. 

To these points, he proceeds to demolish the second reason by making a distinction regarding the changeable thing in the soul. For he mentions a twofold change: one which is from affirmation to negation, and conversely from negation to affirmation—the way one goes from ignorance to knowledge, and to intellection from non-intellection (to use the words he uses). The other change is as if from one contrary to another—such as from rectitude to deception, and from deception to rectitude. He denies that this second kind of change applies to the soul, except concerning those things which are constituted by a certain complexity and are presented to the soul by their own terms, rather than by evidence. For he asserts that the soul cannot be changed regarding those things called "evident," since the terms themselves are the cause of a necessary conformity and of the mind's own composition toward such terms through which (to add what he says) it can be set right. 

He opposes the third reason for this reason: because he says it only creates an appearance against the opinion that takes away the intelligible species. But Scotus, sensing that many things stand in his way (though he seems to ignore this), raises those objections to himself and attempts to dissolve them. However, it will appear a little later that those very points were not actually dissolved by him, when we respond to him, just as we shall resist others regarding the first principles of knowledge, and those things known through experience, and the knowledge of our own acts. We shall show to the best of our ability that these arguments have less weight than they seem to display. But first, other arguments that he offers against the conclusion of the opinion must be brought forward briefly, since both those and the ones we brought up briefly above will be explained more widely during the response. First, he investigates what "sincere truth" is, <margin>Arguments regarding the third point.</margin> which he says he has proven can be had by the way of nature alone. Second, that it is not...

...any necessary knowledge of truth, beyond that itself: since that which the simple intellect understands confusedly, it can know definitively by inquiring through the method of division. Thirdly, he disputes that concurrence of light, and finally strives to conclude that either Henry's opinion is false, or it does not differ from the common opinion. This is roughly the summary of the points by which Henry is attacked: things which we have taken upon ourselves to defend in this matter, so that Scotus's arguments do not reach their intended conclusion. 

Therefore, to respond to certain points in order: That which was first brought forward by Scotus—that no certainty under an "immutable reason" can be held in any light whatsoever concerning an object that changes continuously—this seems openly false. For it can be supplemented by another light, higher and more illustrious, and all the more so because it can be shaped according to that first <term>exemplar<note>In Platonic and Scholastic thought, an "exemplar" is the perfect, divine pattern or idea of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note></term>, which is far removed from the slipping and perishing flux of things from which the sensible image was taken. For what is known as "changeable" in one more dull and weak light can be perceived as if "unchangeable" in that light which is a certain image of the entirely unchangeable exemplar: which is clearly confessed by all to be in God. For this reason, the thing will be perceived exactly as it is: since in itself it is changeable, it will be perceived as such, but in its true unchangeable exemplar, it will be perceived as stable. And thus it will also be perceived in such a way that it will be grasped one way in the first exemplar and another way in the second; and through the same heavenly light, both can be known under a different reasoning. 

It is also false that sensible things do not change continuously. This is known by experience and known by reason: because that which is composed of qualities continuously fighting among themselves must necessarily change continuously according to nature, even if that change itself is not perceived at every single moment. Moreover, it is manifest that every sensible thing, especially in the <term>sublunary<note>The "sublunary" sphere refers to the Earth and its atmosphere below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change, decay, and the four elements, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note></term> realm, is forged from contrary and ever-warring qualities. This is also known by the authority of Aristotle, both elsewhere and in his book *On Colors*, a subject about which it will be appropriate to say more as this work progresses. 

When he [Scotus] affirms that it follows from Henry's reasoning that the "act of the soul"—since it is more changeable than the soul in which it exists—could never be true, we say that this does not follow at all. Since an act, insofar as it is an act, is considered in itself as proceeding from the soul, it cannot be changed because it does not <term>subsist<note>To "subsist" in this context means to have an independent existence as a "substance." An "act" or a "thought" is a temporary state, not a permanent thing that can itself undergo change.</note></term>; however, whatever is changed is understood to have subsisted in some way. For the soul changes as much as an incorporeal thing can change, and it changes from one act into another act, but the act itself is not changed: for it arises suddenly while it is drawn out, and suddenly, when the soul's function ceases, it perishes and vanishes. 

<margin>Response to Scotus’s arguments concerning all points of recognizing the truth.</margin>

Moreover, that comparison of the concurrence of the "species"—both the gathered one and the infused one—with a contingent and necessary proposition, which Scotus seems to value so highly, seems to me to be of no importance. For I find it to be far different from what he desires. Indeed, in logic, the conclusion of a syllogism follows the "weaker part," and one proposition is opposed to the other; but knowledge follows the more powerful light, and the "infused species" is not opposed to the inherent one gathered from the thing which was presented to the power of the knower. On the contrary, that species which has flowed in from the divine, like a more powerful light, perfects the very one whose origin is the sensible thing; its role is to illuminate and perfect things that are fit to receive its brightness. Thus, the intellect perfects certainty, which is not perfected except by the intellectual light; it is so far from being repugnant to it, as Scotus falsely seems to imagine. Nor does the certain concur with the uncertain, except insofar as the latter is perfected by the former and becomes certain. Then it can also be manifest that that logical consequence and connection does not hold—specifically, the claim that certainty cannot be had from any such concurrence—since we have shown that it can be had by the brightness of that heavenly light. Nor does the truth remain disconnected from it, to be taken away from that opinion...

...by opinion, all certainty, and that the opinion of the Academics <note>The Academic Skeptics, a school of philosophy that emerged from Plato's Academy, famously arguing that nothing can be known with absolute certainty.</note> and of Augustine is introduced, which is contrary to the senses. For mention is being made of an exact, most certain, and entirely pure certainty of the truth, not of a probable or moral one. For there is a certain **probable certainty**, there is also **moral certainty**, and there is **physical certainty**. There is also a **greater certainty** which is derived from the mathematical disciplines, if their principles are admitted. There is also an **altogether greater certainty** which is perceived by the divine light. <margin>Various certainties in various things.</margin> For who would deny that there are degrees within human certainty itself, when even among the philosophers, mathematical disciplines are said to be in the first degree of certainty? And would those who say that certainty is held through a proper principle not plainly concede that principles are held both more clearly and more obscurely due to various causes, both internal and external? For they not only admit, but also celebrate that saying of Severinus <note>Boethius (Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius), a 6th-century philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval logic.</note>: that there are certain propositions known to everyone, and others known only to the wise, such as "incorporeal things are not in a place." They also affirm that a thing is more certain if it has a more certain cause, and this is held absolutely and simply. Thomas [Aquinas] constantly asserts this in the second part of the second volume of his *Summa Theologiae*, even if, as far as it concerns us, he might not wish that same thing to be more certain. However, the reason for this is that the foundation of our faith, revealed by the divine light, is placed not in the lowest things but in the sublime—that is, above human intellect. And so, who would doubt that faith is more certain than any vision? Faith, I say, "from hearing" <note>A reference to Romans 10:17, "Faith comes from hearing."</note>—namely, that which is derived from God, who neither deceives nor can be deceived at all.

But as for the opinion of the Academics, how can it be that which admits rays sent from divinity? Moreover, how manifold is the opinion of the Academics? As was declared in the second book of this work. And indeed, it is neither established nor confessed what the leaders of the Second and Third Academy felt. Were their words exactly as they seemed to suggest, or far otherwise? For Arcesilaus <note>Head of the Second Academy, known for his skepticism.</note>, in order to test whether the knots of Platonic opinions could be easily untied, turned everything into doubt, as Sextus [Empiricus] recorded; and Metrodorus affirmed that it did not please the Academics that "nothing can be comprehended," but rather that they asserted this very thing only to oppose the Stoics. And Carneades <note>Head of the Third Academy, famous for his doctrine of probability.</note> also argued against manifest and certain things so that he might rouse (if we stand with Cicero) men who were not sluggish to a desire for investigating the truth.

<margin>Many passages of Augustine are cited for this purpose.</margin> Augustine also, when explaining the counsel of the Academics while discussing them, says it was not of the kind that Scotus and most people think. Indeed, Augustine in no way attributes pure truth to the senses; and if he ever says certain things are held in a human way—such as the principles of knowing and the demonstrations of the disciplines—he is speaking of **innate knowledge**, not a knowledge investigated and discovered by the sense or imagination. For if he were speaking of all the demonstrations of the sciences which are acquired by <term>discourse<note>Discursive reasoning, or the process of moving from one premise to another to reach a conclusion.</note></term>, how would that be true in every way? Since things which are called most true by some, others have considered most false. Add that Augustine, in many places, gave it to be understood that pure truth cannot be known without a "resolution to the divine exemplar." And not only Henry [of Ghent], but others also indicated that this was Augustine's opinion; which also the excellent theologian John Gerson notes in his book *On the Eye*. But indeed, those words of Augustine from the first book of the *Retractions* seem most clearly to signify that the unskilled in the disciplines sometimes answer truly concerning those disciplines when they are well questioned, because the light of **eternal reason** is present to them when they are able to grasp it. For Augustine did not attribute this to the sense, nor to the natural light (which most people call the "light of principles"), but to the light of eternal reason: where (to use his words) these immutable truths are seen. And while he himself disputes with his own reason in the first book of the *Soliloquies*, he most clearly asserts that the truths handed down in the disciplines [are derived from] a heavenly light...

<margin>Various opinions on how the soul knows the truth.</margin>
...begins to open up. Therefore, he says, even those things handed down in the disciplines—which one concedes to be most true without any doubt—must be believed to be impossible to understand unless they are illuminated by another, as if by their own sun. And he adds: therefore, just as in this sun three things may be noticed—that which exists, that which shines, and that which illuminates—so in that most secret God whom you wish to understand, there are three things: that which exists, that which is understood, and that which makes all other things be understood.

There was indeed an ancient opinion that the soul knows true things not in itself, but above itself—namely, in another light. This has been explained in various ways. For some say that while the soul turns itself toward the higher light, it receives from that light a ray in which it may see the truth; however, this ray does not exist in the soul in the manner of a permanent form, because if the soul's "turning toward it" ceases, the knowledge that proceeded from it also ceases—much like sight, which turns itself toward a visible thing, receives its appearance, and then turns away from it, retaining nothing of what it had drawn in. 

<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
They considered this to have been the opinion of the most learned Avicenna <note>A famous Persian philosopher (Ibn Sina) whose works on metaphysics and the soul deeply influenced medieval European thought.</note>. Others prefer the idea that a ray is not received into the soul in which truth is seen, but rather that the soul looks at that light which is outside itself, as if at that by which truth is represented. They say this light is God, in whom they assert truth is seen, insofar as He is the "idea" of all things. And therefore, it is commonly said that truth is seen by the intellect in the **eternal reasons** <note>original: "aeternis rationibus"; an Augustinian concept where divine ideas are the eternal blueprints or patterns of all created things.</note>—that is, in God, not as He is God, but as He is those eternal reasons. Peter de Trabibus <note>A 13th-century Franciscan theologian who wrote on the nature of knowledge.</note>, distinguished among the Parisian theologians, considered this to have been Augustine's opinion. 

<margin>Peter de Trabibus. Francis Marone.</margin>
Francis of Mayronis <note>original: "Franciscus Maroneus"; a 14th-century philosopher known as the "Prince of Scotists."</note>, however, judged Augustine's opinion to be that the divine essence is our "reason for knowing," not in the sense of a known object, but in the sense of a medium and a universal cause concurring in our knowledge. Although he writes that this opinion is not commonly held by the doctors, he nevertheless affirms most strongly that it is Augustine's opinion, particularly while he himself narrates and explains Augustine in the "eleventh truth" upon the twelfth book of Augustine’s *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, and especially upon these words: "the light itself by which the soul is illuminated is something else, so that it may see all things truly understood either in itself or in that light; for that light is God Himself."

We have perhaps treated this opinion of Augustine at too great a length, so that we might recognize it as being discussed and declared differently than Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, the "Subtle Doctor," who critiqued the necessity of divine illumination for natural knowledge.</note> interprets it—both by others, by the readers of Scotus, and by Augustine himself. If we also add what he wrote in that same twelfth book on *Genesis* that we cited, we will not be blamed for adding it in vain. For while he was discussing the fallacy of the senses and the human spirit, and teaching that the testimony of other senses—and especially of the mind and reason itself—should be applied, he added: "so that what is true in this kind of things may be found, as much as it can be found." For he revealed enough that pure truth cannot be fully penetrated (as many think) either through any sense or through the testimony of the senses, even with the addition of the sharpness of reason and mind.

I will leave aside the manner in which the soul naturally knows various doctrines, which will be explained in their proper places as the work progresses. For what we have recounted about the soul's knowledge is sufficient regarding the point in which Scotus opposes Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a major proponent of the theory that divine illumination is necessary for certain knowledge.</note>. Furthermore, regarding the form of the **syllogism** <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note>, does it not take on a certain condition for itself? Such as: if the last term is in the whole middle term, the middle term is placed in the whole first term. To this, if Augustine ever seems to grant that the senses give knowledge—which elsewhere he had taken away from them—should it not rather be thought that he is remembering those things from the light divinely impressed upon him? This is so that he does not seem to be contrary to himself. He seems to clearly sign his name to this in the words which Scotus brings forward: "in those things," he says, "as much as He who created us and those things wished to become known to us." Therefore, as much as He wanted to be known, so much do we know. So too those things which he refers...

<margin>On intuitive knowledge and on how evidence varies.</margin>
<margin>Against Scotus.</margin>
<margin>What an "occasion" is.</margin>
<margin>Hippocrates</margin>

...he speaks of intuitive knowledge: although in the twelfth question of the following book, he brings forward a distinction regarding the "reflex act" <note>A reflex act is the mind's ability to look inward and think about its own thinking.</note>, and he asserted that nothing is properly called "reflex" except in an improper sense—specifically, that by which a "straight" or direct act is understood—and thus he prefers that one not be considered something else. But regarding intuitive knowledge itself—which ought to be the most beyond controversy if we are to hold and know anything else without dispute—there are indeed the sharpest controversies. Even William <note>Likely William of Ockham, the famous 14th-century philosopher known for "Ockham's Razor," who wrote extensively on intuitive cognition.</note> tormented himself most sharply over this: does the intellect know its own acts intuitively? In the end, the dispute seems to be reduced to the level of experience; however, we have learned that experience varies among different people, as far as can be established from their writings.

Furthermore, there is still no agreement among all thinkers as to what "intuitive knowledge" properly is. Other ideas are brought forward beyond those mentioned by Duns Scotus in the second distinction of his first book, the third of the second, the tenth of the fourth, and the thirteenth question of the work titled *Quodlibet*. For it is doubted whether this knowledge exists in the mind through an "image" of the thing, or through its "bare presence." Some have even brought forward arguments regarding intuitive cognition so skeptically that nothing in this matter can be decided as "evident."

But what "evidence" actually consists of is also not yet agreed upon. Some prefer to dissect it into that which is "simply" evident versus that which is "relatively" evident <note>original: "simpliciter et secundum quid"</note>. Pierre d’Ailly <note>The text uses "Illiacensis," referring to the Cardinal of Cambrai, a prominent philosopher-theologian.</note> strives to teach this through a long discourse in the first question of his prologue to the *Sentences*. From all of this, one can clearly recognize how much disagreement exists in identifying any given thing, and it will become even more explicitly clear throughout the course of this present book and in the twelfth chapter of the following one.

Indeed, if we are discussing an object from the outside, the matter must fall back upon the senses. If the sense is in error, the principles will be worthless, as will every discourse and conclusion that flows from them. For I am not satisfied by those arguments of Scotus: that the intellect treats the senses not as a "cause" but only as an "occasion," and that it gives assent by its own power rather than by the power of the sense. The sense itself is not an "occasion," but the cause, so that the intellect may draw out the knowledge of simple terms <note>Simple terms are the basic building blocks of a thought, like "apple" or "red," before they are combined into a sentence.</note>. It could only be called an "occasion" by the greatest abuse of the word; among Latin authors and especially among Greek doctors, an "occasion" is considered a specific part of an opportune or marked time. This is often seen when they explain that famous saying of Hippocrates: "opportunity is fleeting" <note>original: "occasio præceps." This refers to the first aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting."</note>. Therefore, it cannot be called an occasion; it is rightly and deservedly called a cause.

Even Scotus himself seems to confirm this when he says that the intellect cannot have knowledge of simple things unless it is received from the senses. What is this, I ask, other than having them as a cause? Does the sense not either deliver or provide the very material that the intellect uses? If we consider the "sensible species" <note>A "species" in this context is a mental representation or "likeness" of an object that travels from the object to the mind.</note> in the category of a "material cause," it is held as necessary to draw out knowledge. And if we consider the "intelligible species," or the vision, or the "phantasm" <note>A mental image or "ghost" of a sensory perception stored in the imagination.</note> drawn from the senses—by which the intellect itself is, as it were, "informed"—it acts as a "formal cause."

Since things are this way, if the sense is deceived, it follows that the intellect is deceived, for the intellect uses the evidence of the sense like a judge. For what else does the intellect judge (if we are speaking only of natural knowledge) except that which the sense indicates to it? He [Scotus] does not seem able to rightly deny this, even by the words he added a little later. He says: "If, from the nature of such simple things, the combination is evidently true, the intellect will assent by its own power and that of the terms." "If," he says, "it is evidently true." But how can it be evidently true if the sense, from which the terms or notions are taken, is deceived? In what way can it be true if both simple terms, or even just one of them, are falsely apprehended? For many things, stemming from the stirrings of the will or from a false appearance, can so trouble the intellect that it might even decide against a "first principle" <note>A "first principle" is a foundational truth that cannot be denied, such as "a thing cannot both be and not be at the same time."</note>. The Cardinal of Cambrai also affirms this in his first book on the *Sentences*, a matter we will discuss more broadly as this work progresses. Indeed, that example used by Scotus regarding "the whole and the part" presupposes that it has been truly discovered that there is some "whole" and some "part"...

He highlights the deep disagreements among scholars like William of Ockham and Pierre d’Ailly regarding the nature of intuitive knowledge and evidence.</summary>

...the part, which were compared in turn; for which reason that indication of the whole and the part was made necessary through sense. But if the sense was a true judge, or a witness, the intellect could rightly pass judgment on it; if false, the lawsuit was not rightly granted. For the "reason" <note>original: *ratio*; meaning the essential nature or definition</note> of the whole is not perceived by sense, as Scotus seems to—and indeed unjustly (as it appears to me)—presuppose. For sense does not reach the essential nature of a thing, as it does not go beyond the "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are external qualities like color or shape, as opposed to the internal essence.</note>; for that is the work of an altogether higher power. It was also unjustly claimed that the intellect always possesses within itself the "terms" <note>The basic components of a proposition, like "man" or "mortal."</note> which are the cause of truth, even if all or some senses were false. For how can this be? Since simple terms—as Scotus himself agrees—are received from the senses? How then are their terms true if their indication is false? If their foundation or principle is false? And how will the judge—the intellect—pronounce a true sentence while leaning on the false testimony of the senses?

<margin>Removal of an objection that was made.</margin> Nor does that example of a blind man—to whom the "species" <note>original: *species*; mental images or sensory representations</note> of whiteness and blackness were miraculously given—support him at all. For this knowledge would be neither natural, nor could it be false, because it was divinely instilled; however, that which is drawn through the sense *can* be false. 

Furthermore, in his progress, Scotus tries to deduce that from certain experiments—not all, nor always—one can know something to be thus "always" and (to use his word) "infallibly." In this matter, he is most greatly deceived. First, because by arguing from a smaller number to conclude a larger number, he falls into the "fallacy of the consequence" <note>A logical error where one assumes that because a specific result occurs, the general rule must always be true.</note> condemned by Aristotle. For a smaller number is included by a larger one, but not the other way around. Indeed, the connection would be valid if one inferred "the most" from "all," but not when one infers "all" from "many" or "the most." 

Second, because things that proceed from even natural causes do not always behave as they were once seen to behave. Many examples of this are cited in Aristotle's books *On Animals* and Theophrastus's *On Plants*. We shall mention this when we dispute the power of the "universal proposition." There we will also discover to be false what Scotus brought forward as certain and constant: that such-and-such an herb is most certainly of such-and-such a virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the medicinal power or property of a plant.</note>, and can be perceived through many experiments without any mixture of falsehood. For we shall show that the contrary is often found, whereby a "universal proposition" <note>original: *propositio de omni*; a logical statement applying to every member of a class.</note> cannot be inferred; nor can that "aptitude" of herbs to which he finally refers—that is, their disposition—be understood through experience, unless the nature of the things to which they are applied is equally explored and thoroughly known.

Other things on which Scotus relies can be easily rejected. For those things from the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*—which the Sceptics and Academics <note>Two schools of ancient philosophy that doubted the possibility of certain knowledge.</note> would laugh at—when they said things seemed differently to them than to Aristotle, yet not equally to everyone, so that a general rule could be made. Likewise, they would affirm without injury that what is called "contingent" <note>Something that can either happen or not happen; not necessary.</note> can be other than it is. They would not deny that things *appear* as he describes, but they would nonetheless doubt whether they *are* such things in reality. Thus they would say that not vision itself is prevented by illusion, but vision of such an object or in such a mode. Thus one thing would be taken for another, and in place of certainty, a fallacy would arise, which cannot be avoided even by the "concurrence of the senses" <note>The idea that if multiple senses—like sight and touch—agree, the perception must be true.</note> as the arguer [Scotus] imagines. For what appears to one of them appears different to another and of a foreign nature, a matter which was written about abundantly in the second book of this work. If they judge differently, exact certainty cannot be obtained through any proposition, since whatever it may be—if its extremes are placed externally—it will depend on the sense. Since the question arises whether the sense itself is certain or not, it cannot make other things more certain than itself. To this is added the similarity between the truth itself and that which many...

<meta>This page continues the author’s investigation into the reliability of sensory perception, moving from abstract intellectual illumination to the physical mechanics of sight and the instability of the medium through which we perceive the world.</meta>

FIFTH (BOOK).                                                                                                136.

The quality of the air, as the medium between the visible object and the eye, changes; and it changes repeatedly, according to that same author <note>Aristotle.</note> in his book *On Colors*, as we will show shortly. If anyone should call this book spurious <note>original: "nothum". Scholars in the Renaissance often debated whether "On Colors" was truly written by Aristotle or a student like Theophrastus.</note>, I wish that a distinction be granted to me so that all those things about which I discussed in the fourth book may be judged by his own works. Whenever, likewise, the disposition of the human body changes—and it changes very often, both by the testimony of experience and by the authority of Aristotle—whenever the sensible object changes, so too must the judgment of the sense change. And who, even if dull-witted, would not understand that this judgment often changes? And this is true both universally and simply. But if you were to say that the faculty of perspective or optics <term>optics</term> <note>original: "perspectiuæ seu optices". In the medieval and Renaissance periods, "perspective" referred to the mathematical study of light and sight.</note> decides on such a change, first, it ought to have been added that—if it were necessary in a demonstrative faculty—Aristotle would have mentioned it while teaching, if he were determining it correctly. <margin>Response.</margin> <margin>Refutation.</margin> Next, even if he had done so, he would have done so in vain: for the variation of the medium happens so often and so frequently that a single optical proof could not be finished before another and yet another change had occurred. Furthermore, that faculty presupposes both the sense of sight and geometric lines, and from these, it explains why something is seen in this way or that; it does not, however, prove that sight is not deceived, or that it is not uncertain—a point we have already established by so many arguments and authorities. And on this point, the authority of Seneca supports us in the first book of *Natural Questions*, where he writes: "nothing is more deceptive than our eyesight" <note>original: "nihil acie nostra fallacius"</note>; not only in those things where a diversity of colors removes the ability to see subtly, but even in those things which are seen right at hand. This is supported by examples which he and many others use, and which Aristotle himself uses elsewhere, but especially in the *Problems*, when he writes that the sun and moon seem to be circular bodies and flat and level, and that the edges of a solar shadow seem to tremble; and yet, the shadow does not tremble, but rather they are tiny fragments <note>Dust or particles in the air.</note> which are moved repeatedly, now into the light, now into the shadow. I return to the changed disposition of the body, which is most supported by reason. For who does not know that as often as the body is disposed toward illness, it does not always happen suddenly, but gradually, and sometimes imperceptibly? Indeed, even if that disposition is minimal, and even if it is not yet fully realized in action, insofar as it is different from that which the body previously possessed, to that extent—according to the different temperament <term>temperament</term> <note>The balance of the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) thought to govern health and personality.</note> of the body—it will have within itself a different principle for varying the judgment made through the senses. So much so, that if an exact opinion were then requested from it, it would be rendered differently than the one it had previously given when established in its former habit and disposition. Aristotle himself reveals that the Chameleon is changed without any disease, but by fear alone, as we taught above; and Seneca noted that it and other animals vary their color either by anger or desire, and that this also happens from the proximity of a foreign color, as Ovid and others write; and Aristotle himself writes that many animals, besides the Chameleon, change in regard to their color. However, let it be permitted to dispute Aristotle for a little while, with Aristotle himself as the guide. He himself writes in the book *On Colors* that simple colors are present in simple elements: Saffron or yellow in fire; white in water, earth, and air. Therefore, there is no simple color except white and yellow. And although this might seem contrary to the opinion he used elsewhere, and especially in the book *On the Senses*, I do not wish to vex the man much in this matter, since other conflicting and adverse views are found in him. But I ask his followers: how did he know this? By sense? But the senses, according to them, cannot perceive what is not composed of elements. Did Aristotle say this in his books *On the Soul*? Or did Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> contend this in a long dispute in his commentaries on the first book *On Sense and Sensible Objects*? <margin>Alexander [of Aphrodisias] on the book *On the Senses*.</margin> Therefore, he grasped this by conjecture. If you say that he does not mean pure elements, that is first an arbitrary explanation, and not sufficiently consistent with his words. <margin>Refutation of the response.</margin> Next, since he also attributed this same thing to the sun—not just as a pure element, but as a "fifth nature" <term>fifth nature</term> <note>original: "quintæ... naturæ". Also known as the "quintessence" or "aether," the celestial material that made up the stars and planets, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> as he judged—it was therefore grasped by conjecture. For it could not have been grasped by the intellect through itself and primarily.

BOOK [V].

[He] perceives this, since he established that nothing can be in the intellect unless it was first in the senses <note>original: "nihil statuit esse posse in intellectu quin prius fuerit in sensu". This is the famous "Peripatetic axiom," a cornerstone of Aristotle's philosophy stating that all knowledge begins with sensory experience.</note>, in whatever way that proposition is explained. For it is certainly clear enough from his own dogma that he did not properly grasp the color of the sun by sense: was it then by some likeness or conjecture? And yet he ascribed a simple color to it. Therefore, simple colors cannot be grasped by sense. 

Furthermore, since in that book <note>Aristotle’s *On Colors*.</note> he says that the color black follows the transmutation of the elements, and since the sense does not perceive the untransmuted elements, blackness alone would have been first known to him. Therefore, he could not perceive by sense that a mixture is made from white and yellow, because black was the first color known to him; and nevertheless we see that yellow and white are prior, both because he so decides in that book, and because light is the mother of all colors—and as it pleased some, light itself is properly color—and because white is prior by nature to black, since it proceeds from a purer light. 

And certainly he established, and rightly so, that infinite things cannot be traversed or perceived. But colors are not only multiple, but infinite, if we stand by his logic. For he, discussing these things, says: <note>original Greek: "δεῖ δὲ μὴ λανθάνειν τό πολυειδὲς καὶ τό ἄπειρον τῶν χρωμάτων"</note> *one must not overlook the multiform and infinite nature of colors.* And he added the cause: namely, the variety of shadow and light according to "more" and "less." And although in the book *On the Senses* <note>Aristotle's *De Sensu et Sensibili*.</note> he judged that no sensible thing is divided into infinity—and this seems to contradict what he said above—yet I do not cut the matter so close to the quick, nor do I demand the debt so strictly, as to not take "infinite" to mean "innumerable," provided that he himself or those who handle his business <note>His followers or commentators.</note> explain it to me by that reasoning. For to me, just as much will be accomplished in denying the certainty of the sense, which, whether they like it or not, we shall deny with Aristotle himself consenting. 

For he writes in the same book <note>Greek: "περὶ χρωμάτων" (*Peri Chromaton*)</note> *On Colors*, that it sometimes happens that when light falls upon something and colors it so that it takes on a purple or grass-green appearance, it is soon refracted and falls upon another color, whatever it may be, and is tempered by it and receives another mixture of color and another temperament. Nor does he say this happens once, but frequently, yet imperceptibly. For he added: <note>original Greek: "καὶ τοῦτο πάσχων συνεχῶς οὐκ αἰσθητῶς δὲ"</note> *and this indeed undergoing change continually, but not sensibly.* This seems to mean nothing other than "poorly sensible," so that the sense is frequently deceived in this matter. Otherwise, if he had understood it as entirely imperceptible, how could it have been grasped by him? Certainly either by sense, and thus he would contradict himself—for what was captured by him by sense was not imperceptible—or by the intellect, from which the same contradiction follows, because by that same author’s own word, nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the sense. 

Whether the thing itself which was in the sense, or its likeness is grasped, the same result occurs: and much more so if that very likeness is grasped, which cannot help but be dissimilar in some way in different matter or in different light. Therefore, from the mixture, the representation is varied, and this same variety is often deceptive and frequently so contingent and as if "turning its face" that no art of optics, even if it had any weight in showing the certainty of the sense, would support it. Add to this how variably it arises from various things: for we should not, as he himself teaches, think of this mixture in the likeness of druggists <term>pigmentariorum</term> <note>These "pigmentarii" were pharmacists or apothecaries who dealt in pigments and dyes as well as medicines.</note> and painters, who

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unreliability of the senses, specifically sight, by examining how physical changes in objects—like "concoction" or emotional states—alter their appearance so rapidly that the human eye can be easily deceived.</meta>

**BOOK**

...from causes, as if it were not from the usual course of nature that these very things are repeatedly agitated, slip, and flow away; as if we did not notice this so frequently that even if it were a miracle by its own nature, it would not seem like a miracle to us because of its very frequent occurrence. But indeed, this is so obvious to us that both he himself and other great men, while they were seeking higher things more strenuously, passed over these lower things as if hallucinating or blinking. As for what he added—that we cannot reasonably doubt while those conditions stand—many would not accept this. For the things we have said are not removed by that, from which others from the opposite side could also reasonably and probably doubt, moved even by those reasons which he himself opposed to his own conclusions, although he tried to dissolve them. For the arguments can seem stronger than the responses, as far as it pertains to evidence designated only by human standards and a general rule. He himself almost confesses this when he brings forth these words at the end of his response to the second reason: "It seems to me probable," he says, "on account of the aforesaid reasons, that the intellect, from the very will and a perverse affection, even with some appearance—though it be false—could naturally dissent from a first principle." If this is so, how much more could it not assent to the judgment of the sense? 

Moreover, the sense can be deceived by the varying nature of the thing seen; while not only because of "smallness" <note>original: σμικρότητα</note>, that is, a size so tiny that white and black cannot be distinguished (as Aristotle relates in his book *On the Senses*). <margin>Themistius, book on [the] philosopher.</margin> And Themistius seems to assert this even more clearly in the book titled *The Examiner* <note>original: βασανιστής (*Basanistēs*), a title referring to a critical inquiry or "tester."</note>. He is also titled "The Philosopher," writing that "concerning colors, all those who do not see sharply are deceived" <note>original: περὶ τὰ χρώματα ἀπατῶνται οἱ μὴ ὀξὺ βλέποντες</note>. For those whose sight is not very sharp and who are directed toward a small quantity to be looked at—how shall they judge colors? Not only, I say, while small things are inspected, but while the thing itself changes its colors repeatedly (as was indicated above), like a chameleon; but also according to the different concoction <note>A term in ancient science referring to the "ripening" or processing of substances by internal heat, like digestion or the maturing of fruit.</note> of humors, and according to the different changes of the thing caused from the outside. For as pertains to this very change, he himself writes in the *Problems* that not only do meats contract blackness if they are seasoned less under the sun than if they rest, but also men are flooded with paleness from exertion. But if they have sweated moderately, they take on a pleasant, cheerful color. 

But that men are changed repeatedly by fear, hope, joy, and sadness is as well-known as anything. These things happen frequently by an internal movement of the mind, and so suddenly that you might not catch how it happens; so that someone you just saw as pale, with your gaze turned away for just a moment, you soon look upon as red. <margin>Book on Animals.</margin> But in the ninth book of the *History of Animals*, does not Aristotle reveal that there are many things that draw their color from elsewhere and vary it suddenly? I do not mean only the chameleon, but the octopus, the cuttlefish, and the monkfish, in which things the sight would be deceived, not only from the proximity of the place, but from the very nature of the thing being watched, which is known to both vary and deceive greatly. 

<margin>Book on Colors.</margin> Regarding the thing itself which is "concocted," Aristotle speaks thus in the book *On Colors*: "that indeed at the same time as the concoction itself, it takes on all the differences of colors; it is manifest from many things" <note>original: ὅτι μετ' ἅμα τῇ πέψει πάσας τὰς τῶν χρωμάτων λαμβάνειν μεταβολάς. Φανερὸν ἐκ πολλῶν</note>. Therefore, if the sense now judges something, it will be deceived if the eye is turned away for a little while, because a change has indeed occurred in the thing, but not so great a change that the difference is clearly and exquisitely conveyed to just any eye. Perhaps it would be conveyed to a very sharp human eye or to the eye of a lynx <note>The lynx was historically believed to have supernatural or perfectly piercing vision.</note>; for repeatedly and in almost every single moment "digestion" <note>concoctio/pepsis</note> occurs, from which a permutation of colors arises. And we find on the authority of the same author that this happens not only in the limbs positioned on the outside, but even in the deepest and most hidden recesses of the body, in the viscera...

For indeed, the color is changed. Aristotle himself writes in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, and what he affirmed regarding colors, he taught elsewhere happens regarding odor and taste; since by the <term>concoction</term><note>The original term is *pepsis*, referring to the biological "cooking" or ripening of a substance through internal heat.</note> and digestion of fruits, both their odor and juice are thoroughly changed, inasmuch as they all proceed from the same cause. You might say <note>original: "παρὰ τὰς πέψεις ἤδη"</note> "already according to the ripenings," whence he added: <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ τῶν καρπῶν ἔνιοι καθάπερ τὰς πολλὰς διαφορὰς ἅμα περιλαμβάνουσι διὸ καὶ τὰς ὀσμὰς καὶ τοὺς χυλοὺς πολυδιαφόρους συμβαίνει τοῖς ἀνθεσι καὶ τοῖς καρποῖς συνακολουθεῖν"</note> "for indeed some fruits, just as they contain many differences at once, so it happens that many different odors and juices follow the flowers and the fruits." These are Aristotle’s words, and Theophrastus frequently puts forth many similar things in the sixth book of *The Causes of Plants*, as far as pertains to flavors and odors.

But regarding colors, Aristotle writes more in his work titled *On Colors*, from which we frequently bring forth authorities in Greek; for as far as I know, it is not available in Latin. In other cases where Latin versions are available, we sometimes do the same, lest it be turned into a fault against us that the truth of the literary context is not as we state. But indeed, in that same book *On Colors*, Aristotle intended that the temperament not only of fruits and flowers, but also of living creatures, is changed by various nourishment, and that the color is even varied by the quantity itself. For this reason, he judges that even crows, due to a defect of nourishment, are ultimately transformed into a yellow color <margin>Yellow crows.</margin> with these words: <note>original: "ἐπὶ καὶ τῶν κοράκων τὰ πτερώματα τὸ τελευταῖον ἐς τὸ ξανθὸν χρῶμα μεταλλεί τῆς τροφῆς ἐνδείας ὑπολειπούσης"</note> "also in crows, the plumage finally changes to a yellow color when a lack of food remains."

And in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, he wrote that some birds, and even some wild quadrupeds, are changed through the seasons of the year, just as humans change through age; he affirms that the season of the year has more weight than age. <margin>The crow and other white animals.</margin> He also intended that nourishment is a cause of changed color. And a little before that, he relates that an animal can be distorted at the beginning of its generation so that it takes on another color, but that this happens rarely: although a white partridge has been seen, and a white crow, and a sparrow, and a bear. I will add that I myself have seen a white hawk captured in my own domain, and I possessed it for several months.

But indeed, Aristotle writes in the third book of *On the History of Animals* that it happens because of sharper cold that the feathers—not only of other birds but even of the crow—pass from black into white. In the eighth book of *On the History of Animals*, near the end of the volume, he taught that color is varied in many fish. Likewise, in the ninth book of *On the History of Animals*, he relates that the <term>lynx</term><note>original: "lupum ceruariū", literally 'wolf-stag'.</note> among quadrupeds is changed through the seasons of the year, and many living things in the genus of birds are varied in color; even the hoopoe changes in appearance, which he confirms by the testimony of the poet Aeschylus.

From this, <margin>Against Michael of Ephesus.</margin> Michael of Ephesus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine commentator on Aristotle.</note> seems to be deceived when he writes in his commentary on the fifth book of Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals*: <note>original: "πᾶν γὰρ τὸ γένος τῶν κοράκων καὶ πᾶς κόραξ μέλας οὐ γὰρ εἰσιν ὁ μὲν τῶν κοράκων μέλανες οἱ δὲ πυρροὶ καὶ ἄλλος λευκοὶ, ἀλλὰ πάντες ὡς εἴρηται μέλανες"</note> "For the entire genus of crows and every crow is black; for it is not the case that some crows are black, others tawny, and others white, but all are black, as has been said." Thus he says that the genus of crows and every crow is black, for there are not some crows black, others tawny, and others white, but all are black as stated. In this, he might be supported by Aristotle in the tenth section of the *Problems*, who judges the crow to be always immutable. 

But so many other places by that author cited above stand in the way, and it stands in the way that he himself also found this in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*: that is, that a white crow was seen, and many birds and quadrupeds are varied by affection and by the seasons, just as men are changed by age. But experience also stands in the way. For we have seen—and we have reported this in our *Logical Institutions*—crows of both ash-gray and white color. Whence not every genus of crows, nor every crow is black, but some are white, and there is a crow of ash-gray color.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the reliability of the senses. Having discussed the specific species of flavors and colors on the previous page, the author now moves into a deeper psychological and epistemological critique of how we perceive our own sensing and the role of the "internal senses" and emotions in distorting reality.</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

Aristotle seems to have been of a doubtful mind regarding whether, when we see, we perceive that we are seeing by the sense of sight itself or by some other power. Although he seems to incline toward the view that each of the senses perceives its own sensing, the interpreters pour forth various opinions when he treats *On Sleep and Waking* <note>Aristotle’s *De Somno et Vigilia*, part of the *Parva Naturalia*.</note>. There are those who deny that the very act of sensing—which they call "sensation"—is itself perceived. There are others who affirm that no one perceives that they see, and that Aristotle meant nothing else: for this reason, he previously established that the act of the sensible object and the sense in act are one and the same <note>original: "actū sensibilis rei & sensum in actu"; a reference to *De Anima* III.2, where Aristotle argues the perceiver and the perceived object share the same "act" during the moment of perception.</note>. But however the matter stands, it is not yet clear among Aristotle and his interpreters (as was also indicated above) whether we perceive that we sense when we sense, and in what manner. Indeed, I would call this "sensing" a secondary act; even if the first act—which is judged by the sense itself—were not deceived, it cannot help but be uncertain. This is evident because so many perceptive men have not held it as certain, but have doubted it, been ambiguous, and even fought and battled over it.

Likewise, it is not clear, as was said above, if we have only one internal sense <note>The "internal senses" were thought to process data after it left the eyes, ears, etc.</note> that performs different duties. For Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher.</note> claimed there were five, Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> four, and others were content with only one, such as Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a major Aristotelian commentator of the 2nd century AD.</note> and Themistius <note>A 4th-century AD Roman statesman and philosopher.</note>. But it is certainly clear from what we have said that even if the senses could not be deceived in ways other than those handed down by Aristotle, a fallacious and very frequently uncertain judgment about the sensible object nevertheless often proceeds from them. Certainly, if the external senses go astray, then the internal sense will also wander, for it receives what is brought to it through external instruments and judges like a judge who delivers a precise sentence. 

And yet, even in this, the expositors do not agree on how that occurs: some decree that this internal sense is the first one that perceives perfectly, while others believe it is the same thing as the "phantasia" <note>original: "phantasia"; translated here as imagination or the faculty of forming mental images.</note>. But the imagination itself (or phantasia), being more varied than the sense and more erratic <note>original: "desultoria"; literally "leaping," like a circus rider jumping from horse to horse.</note>, once it has been deceived, will impose upon the intellect; the intellect’s judgment will then waver and go astray. Aristotle himself does not disagree, since in his book on the senses he sanctioned that nothing which exists externally can be understood except by the sense itself. In the second book of *On the Soul*, he decreed that the difference between sense and intellect is that the sense of "proper objects" <note>original: "propriorum"; "proper sensibles" are qualities like color for sight or sound for hearing, which Aristotle claimed the senses do not mistake.</note> is always true, but it may happen that one understands falsely. Thus, he attributed a more certain judgment to the sense—which, however, we have shown by so many and such great arguments is not actually certain.

If we add to these points what Aristotle himself writes (not the things poured out by the warring interpreters), I think nothing will remain to be done in uncovering every fallacy. He writes most openly that in every emotion <note>original: "affectione"; refers to a state of mind or passion.</note> a fallacy lies hidden, and he offers examples of those who fear, those who love, and those burning with anger. The greater the emotion, the greater the lapse, because those who are greatly affected are moved and fall into error by the slightest resemblance. He brings forward this cause especially: that the soul does not judge according to the same power that is the principal [judge] as it does by that power by which mental images <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> are made. He adds other points later: that not only does the sensible object move and bring forth a likeness, but the sense itself is moved, and a lapse occurs when it is excited in the same way it is usually moved by sensible things. For example, the earth seems to move to those who are sailing, while the sight itself is being moved by something else. These are the words of Aristotle, and Themistius says much to this effect in his paraphrase of *On Dreams*. Who is there who is not moved by some emotion? Whose senses are so steady that, when a sensible thing is presented or captured by the mind, they are not so affected that they remain devoid of anger, or desire, or hope, or fear, or any emotion whatsoever—as if they stood like "hard flint or Marpesian rock"? <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.471), describing Dido’s cold indifference in the underworld.</note> Certainly, Aristotle possessed such great and sharp genius that the uncertainty of the senses did not escape him; but because he trusted them much, he hid from revealing it openly. He did, however, indicate it obliquely, as can be seen from many places in his books which we have cited. And although he says the sense is not deceived regarding its "proper sensible," nevertheless, at the end of the second book *On the Soul*...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Aristotelian sensory theory. ->**FIFTH [BOOK]**<- ->**C.L.**<-

...though he had repeated the same opinion, he used a distinction, decreeing that the sense for prior sensibles <note>original: "sensilium"; the objects perceived by the senses.</note> is true, or has very little falsehood. However, I myself have shown that it is much, not "very little," using the same author [Aristotle] as authority; for I believe we have fulfilled our promise. For I took it upon myself to prove that the senses are easily deceived, both in other ways and in more ways than Aristotle decreed. Even if he had recounted all the modes of fallacy, we have still proven by Aristotelian doctrine that the judgment of the sense itself is uncertain. <margin>Epilogue of the previously held dispute concerning the uncertainty of sense.</margin> For who does not know that *phantasia* <note>The faculty of imagination or mental representation that mediates between sense and intellect.</note> varies according to the variety of the sense? And that from *phantasia*, the judgment of reason is frequently changed in many ways? Since, by the authority of Aristotle himself in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>*De Anima* III.7, 431a16: "The soul never thinks without a phantasm."</note>, the soul never understands without a phantasm; which phantasms are indeed drawn from the sense. Since the sense is uncertain and very often deceptive, and Aristotle's doctrine is founded upon it, we clearly gather that the doctrine itself is also uncertain and deceptive. <margin>[Michael of Ephesus]</margin> <note>Michael of Ephesus (11th-12th century) was a prolific commentator on Aristotle's works, particularly the *Parva Naturalia*.</note> Furthermore, that he himself, in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, having attempted to prove the truth of the senses, did not accomplish it, can be clear both from what we have said and from what was sufficiently shown in the second book of this work, in the twenty-second chapter above. <margin>[Theodore Metochytes]</margin> <note>Theodore Metochytes (1270–1332) was a Byzantine scholar and statesman who wrote extensively on Aristotelian philosophy.</note>

**That the judgment of the senses is confirmed to be uncertain by the authorities of Theophrastus, by which demonstration is rendered uncertain.** **Chapter Six.**

Let us confirm by the authorities of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was Aristotle's successor as the head of the Peripatetic school.</note> that the manifold judgment of the senses is uncertain: lest those who wish to oppose us say that we have poorly understood Aristotle's perceptions, let us manifest those very things, however clear they may be, by the testimony of his chief disciple. Theophrastus teaches in his book *On Flavors, Odor, and Color* that the properties of the natures of things are known in three ways, and especially regarding flavor, which he discusses most there. All these things he denies can be drawn out except through the senses, which reason supports. <margin>That the properties of things are known by three things.</margin> He affirms, however, that there are certain natural things of which knowledge can be had, but it is imperfect: he candidly confesses that there are certain things about which it is impossible for us to be rendered more certain. From this it follows that he attributes no certain and pure knowledge to the senses at all. To the sense of taste he grants much; but for hearing and touch, he denies that the natures of things can be comprehended by us, chiefly for these reasons: that only voices and sounds are drawn in by hearing alone, which, once drawn in, do not express the nature of things at all, since they are not of the nature and substance of the thing drawn in itself. For the substance does not reach the sensory organ of hearing itself. As for those things which are said to be felt by touch, although they become near to the sensory organ, they do not, however, touch the instrument of sensing in themselves. Whence it happens that touch does not comprehend those things, since it perceives them differently than their own nature is. He affirms this is seen in broken pepper and in heated water, which he says are comprehended otherwise than their own nature is; <margin>[St. Thomas]</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Thomas Aquinas's commentaries on sensation or Theophrastus.</note> and these things concern touch: although the master Aristotle previously decreed, both elsewhere and in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, that man excels in the sense of touch more than all other animals. He also warns us that we are repeatedly deceived through sight. Let the example be this: that when whiteness is seen, we think coldness is the cause, because whiteness is derived from coldness and is judged to be "its daughter" (to use his word). Nevertheless, garlic and many other things are full of much heat, even though they are suffused with much whiteness. In a like manner, most people immediately think those things which are red are hot, when many things that are reddish frequently abound in cold. He also teaches that we are very easily deceived by smell when we think fragrant things are supported by heat; nevertheless, it is clear that many things which are counted among the spices possess coldness.

...[appe]ars, which is seen clearly enough in camphor. He <note>Likely referring to Theophrastus, Aristotle's successor.</note> wished to show that fallacy arises from the fact that nothing of the thing smelled reaches the sensory organ except a certain "spiritual smoke" <note>original: *fumus spiritalis*; a fine, vaporous emission of particles thought to carry scent.</note>, by which the true nature of the thing cannot be exactly revealed. To this is often added the thinness of the smoke and the fact that the air is already occupied by other odors, by which it happens that the "species" <note>original: *species*; the sensory image or quality of the object.</note> is not carried to the sensory organ in the same state as it was emitted. In the sixth book of *The Causes of Plants*, agreeing with his master Aristotle, he also attributes the worst sense of smell to man; in that same place, he writes that vultures are killed by ointments and beetles by roses, and that those wearing perfumes are vehemently attacked by bees, and that every kind of insect flees the smell of oil. Yet in the book *On Flavors* <note>original: *De Saporibus*</note>, in which he also mentions the work *On Plants*, he places taste above the other senses, as it "drinks in" the physical substance of the thing more than the others. But we have shown above, by the authority of Aristotle, that every sense is a kind of touch. Therefore, since this sense is uncertain according to Theophrastus, and yet according to Aristotle man excels in it most, that taste cannot be entirely certain; and furthermore, we have taught that it can easily happen that the sense is deceived by the "infection" of the sensory organ itself. We have brought forward many examples above, even of those who judged honey to be bitter, or who judged it neither sweet nor bitter. In the same sixth volume of *On Plants*, he teaches that sensation occurs according to the disposition and temperament of the body, and he admits that what is unsuitable food for us is suitable for others, and conversely, what is suitable for others is unsuitable for some. But enough of these matters: for since we have dealt sufficiently with the senses, both by reason and by the authority of Aristotle, and have even gathered several points from Theophrastus out of an abundance of caution, let us make the transition to the other things we promised.

**That Aristotle’s art of demonstration is shown to be uncertain in its details because the faculty of truly defining is uncertain in his work, and there Speusippus is defended. Chapter Seven.**

<margin>**Conclusion.**</margin>
We have seen that the foundation and beginning of demonstration—that is, the sense—is not stable; we must now look at the "middle" and the "cause" <note>In an Aristotelian syllogism, the "middle term" (often a definition) is the cause that links the subject to the property being proven.</note>. For if it is not possible to find a true definition, it will be impossible in any way to demonstrate anything truly, in the manner Aristotle taught that one should demonstrate in the *Posterior Analytics*. Therefore, so that we may discuss this matter in greater detail: First, let us prove our premise by showing that no certain faculty of truly defining is given. We shall not use "Sceptic excursions" <note>Refers to the radical doubt of the Sceptic philosophers mentioned in Book 3.</note> against definition itself, which we mentioned in the third book of this work, but rather we shall stand within the Lyceum <note>The school of Aristotle in Athens.</note>, either standing still or walking about at a steady pace. <margin>**Declaration.**</margin> I said "truly defining," because I myself have handed down many modes of describing things in some fashion—though not truly and exactly defining them—in the second book of my *Logical Institutions*. <margin>**Proof of the premise.**</margin> Truly, the faculty of "truly defining" has not been handed down by Aristotle at all, even though he mentions definition in many places: as when, in the first book of the *Physics*, he said the thing defined is divided into its individual parts by the definition; <margin>**In how many places Aristotle speaks of definition, and how incorrectly and inconsistently with himself.
