# BOOK IV

## That among the ancient philosophers, and even for **Aristotle** himself, the definition of man is uncertain. Chapter Eight.

<margin>**Aristotle**</margin>
<margin>**Ambrose**</margin>
But what need is there for many words? How uncertain this definition is can finally be easily recognized once the definition of man is placed before our eyes. For if the most esteemed of the pagan philosophers, and **Aristotle** himself, disagree on this—namely, what is in us and what we ourselves are—shall we presume to grasp the natures of other living things by definition? If we do not know for certain our own **difference** <note>original: *differentia*; in logic, the specific characteristic that distinguishes a species within its genus</note>, which pertains to preserving our very essence and substance, and which ensures that we are set apart (or to speak more significantly, that we differ) from other things that are not human, how shall we know the differences of others? Or will we, in our ignorance of ourselves, truly remain ignorant of the rest?

If **Aristotle**, in the first volume of the *History of Animals*, assumes that the parts of man must be explained first because man is (as he says) necessarily the most known to us of all animals, yet **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> seems to deny this. For in the sixth book of the *Hexaemeron* <note>Ambrose’s treatise on the six days of Creation.</note> he writes: "We cannot know ourselves fully unless we have first known the nature of all living things." But however it is settled, **Aristotle** persists in his purpose and teaches by the example of numbers that one must explore things based on what is already explored and certain to oneself. 

Therefore, if according to **Aristotle’s** opinion a man is better known to himself than other animals, by what means shall the remainder of man—and those things held to be less known—be distinguished, if the principal part of man remains unknown? Add to this that in the same volume, a little later (whether he remembered what he had established or not, I am not entirely certain), he writes that the interior parts of man are uncertain and unknown; he contemplates them only by looking at the parts of other animals that are similar to the human ones. But if the bodily parts of man are not held with enough certainty or discovery, what shall we judge concerning the **incorporeal difference** <note>The soul or the rational faculty.</note>? 

If **Aristotle** himself later, in the third book of *On the Soul*, says that he knows the intellect from the knowledge of other things, and yet does not progress so far from that knowledge as to investigate and establish his own **difference**, how could the difference of others be known? Or perhaps, because we more easily know things more imperfect than man due to the weakness of our cognition, does our reasoning therefore not hold? But that intimate and, as it were, "kindred" knowledge ought not to be outweighed by the knowledge of other things; it should surely be more certain and better known. From where, then, comes such great pride in the human race—and especially in that portion of it which is devoted to discerning things? From where comes that presumption to teach properly and exactly what other things are, when one is utterly ignorant of what oneself is? 

However it may be, I will easily prove by their own doctrines and testimonies that both **Aristotle** and many of the philosophers clearly did not know what they were. **Aristotle**, speaking of the definition of man in the seventh book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Referring to the *Metaphysics*.</note>, used the example of the "two-footed [animal]"; do we think that if he had not been ignorant of the true and proper difference, he would have passed it over in silence?

How then will you establish a definition that is certain and beyond controversy? For a definition <term>definition</term> <note>original: *definitio*; in formal logic, a statement that captures the essence of a thing by identifying its general category (genus) and its unique characteristic (difference).</note> must be such that it fits the thing defined so perfectly that it applies to nothing else, and expresses the very nature of the thing. If the parts of the definition—such as the claim that man alone is "rational"—are themselves in doubt, the whole definition falls.

FIFTH [BOOK] ->CHAPTER 54<-

...that "rational animal" is said of God, and differently of man, of God, and of Pythagoras. Nor is the distinction of this difference <term>difference</term> <note>original: *differentia*; the specific quality that distinguishes one species from others within the same category.</note> called "rational" revealed—specifically, what kind it should be considered. For whether you take "rational animal" as a genus <term>genus</term> <note>The broad category under which species are grouped.</note>, the species of rational animal will be diverse, as those very words seem to portend; or whether you take it by proportion, you will derive the "rational" which is in man from that which he [Aristotle] placed in God. Therefore, in defining man, "rational" does not suffice as an exact difference, nor does "animal" suffice as the proximate genus. 

To this matter, those words of Aristotle in the seventh book of the *Politics* can apply in some way, where he wrote that gods and heroes differ from men. This can also be seen in what he disclosed in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, as we wrote in the previous book. For Aristotle was in doubt whether man was either the one who participates most in divinity among all animals, or the only one among all animals known to us to do so. By this manner of speaking, he sufficiently revealed either that there could be other rational animals of which we have no knowledge, or that, in the Platonic manner, superior and separate minds are animals. 

And indeed, it seems to me Aristotle thought the same as the Platonists regarding gods and demons. Furthermore, it also seems he thought that some particular man could so far surpass other men in the use of reason that a different "difference" of animal might be predicated of him. But this last point is perhaps by metaphor. Cicero also used this understanding in the first book of *On Duties*, but in the opposite proportion. For he wrote that some men are found to be so in name only, not in reality—that is, so inclined toward pleasures that they are counted among the number of beasts. 

In no different way, Aristotle thought a man could be raised so far above [other] men by the perspicacity of his intellect and use of reason that he would be established in a certain middle genus between other men and God. This is how Pythagoras and those like him were regarded by him. Indeed, there was also an ancient dogma said to be received from Hesiod, which Plutarch especially mentions in the book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: *peri tōn ekleloipotōn chrēstēriōn*</note>, that there are four <margin>Four genera of rational beings among the ancients.</margin> genera of rational beings. First gods, then many and good demons <note>The term "demon" (daimon) here refers to a classical spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, then heroes, then men, with demigods counted among the heroes. 

Therefore, Aristotle—perhaps mindful of the ancient opinion and an approver of it in this regard, namely that heroes, being placed between men and demons, should be judged as demigods—might have placed Pythagoras in their number; and in this part, he follows Hesiod. But in another part—namely, that he made three species of rational animal while Hesiod made four—he seems to follow Homer, who often did not distinguish demons from gods. This was also noted diligently by Cleombrotus in Plutarch’s writings. 

Beyond those things, it can also be gathered that what Plutarch himself and Maximus of Tyre call a "demon," or the "spirit" <note>original: *daimonium*</note> of Socrates, Lucius Apuleius calls a "god"; and Proclus anxiously investigates why it is called a god in his commentaries on Plato's first *Alcibiades*. Proclus affirms it was a demon, but the highest in the genus of demons, and that there are demons in gods and gods in demons; but in gods the substance is divine while the "proportion" is demonic, whereas in demons the property is demonic while that which is divine in them is declared by proportion. 

Aristotle, however, in the second book of the *Rhetoric*, said a *daimonion* is either a god or the work of a god. And after Aristotle there were Platonists who placed man so far above human nature that they gave him the name of demigod, as Labeo did for Plato, as our Augustine wrote. And those very men do not seem to shrink from Hesiod when he sang: "Holy demons upon the earth, who are called the guardians [of mortal men]." <note>original Greek: "ἁγνὸι ἐπιχθόνιοι δαίμονες ὅι καλέονται κ' μύθιοι"; Hesiod, *Works and Days* 122.</note> Furthermore, another species of rational animal is revealed among our own writers, as we also narrated in the first book: for [they say] that Satyrs both possess reason and religion... <margin>On satyrs.</margin>

...those are said to have been admitted. Finally, they do not escape the fact that the very specific attributes <note>These are "proper accidents," features like laughter that always accompany being human but do not define the essence.</note> assigned to them are also fitted to that animal to which the **constitutive difference** <term>constitutive difference: the specific characteristic—like "rationality"—that distinguishes one species from another within a broader group</term> (or whatever was taken in its place) was previously applied. For if they should assert that the quality called "rational" belongs to someone, they would immediately grant him the aptitude and faculty for laughter, provided the proportion is maintained. Therefore, let us firmly conclude that among the philosophers of the nations <note>A term for "pagan" or non-Christian philosophers.</note>, no certain definition of man is held. From this, it can be seen that they cannot know the definitions of other things, since they do not accurately know our own private and innermost nature—indeed, they do not know ourselves, or what we ourselves are. They are also unable to know this while using that worn-out rule of "genus and difference" <note>The standard Aristotelian method of defining something by its general category (genus) and its specific trait (difference).</note> and while leaning on the **Aristotelian** dogma in the eighth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note>. In that work, he maintained that a man is not the same thing as a "two-footed animal," but is something beyond these, because these components relate to one another like matter to the form of the whole. By this reasoning, it is made clear enough by Aristotle’s own opinion that man cannot be truly defined; and if the definition is taken away, the possibility of logical demonstration is also removed. This is something Aristotle himself admits, and reason itself proves.

**How man can be defined by a single Greek word expressing the ultimate difference. Chapter IX.**

**T**o ensure that we do not appear merely to attack and demolish the definition without offering something either true or at least plausible—especially concerning the definition of man—I wish to state what is probable. If I could fuse two Latin names into one so that a single word would emerge that was truly neither of them, I do not doubt I could do so; for the Greek language is most suited to the composition of names. I would dare to provide the definition of man with a single difference: **rational-intellective** <note>original Greek: *logontikē*; a fusion of *logos* (reason) and *noesis* (intellect).</note>. This word would both encompass the thing itself and exclude all others. For there are two differences in the kind of knowledge that is above the senses: one is **rational** <note>original Greek: *logikē*</note>, and the other is **intellective** <note>original Greek: *noētikē*</note>. Within each, however, there are many degrees, and they join together so that what is highest in the lower kind is the lowest in the kind that is above it.

Man is thus placed in a sort of middle ground <note>the *meditullium* or center-point</note>, which is why he has obtained the name of "the bond between the highest and lowest nature," since he connects both as a shared boundary. Below him, he has many degrees of knowledge, and above him, he also has many. For other beings of a different kind, the more they approach human knowledge, the more they are said to participate in knowledge and a certain discourse of reason. The more they recede from it, the closer they approach the dull condition of plants or shrubs and taste of that nature. This is why Aristotle gave them the name **animal-plants** <note>original: *Zoophyta*; organisms like sponges or sea anemones that seem to be between animal and plant life.</note>, as they hold the border of both natures.

Thus, regarding individual kinds that hold the bond between a higher and lower degree, a single thing could be fused and grown together out of two in equal proportion. However, the animals below man cannot truly be called "rational," as the ancients thought. That term is proper to man, who occupies the highest place among the lowest beings; to him alone, properly and exactly, does **universal reason** belong. To others, it belongs only from a distance, and less so the further they are removed from man in their way of knowing. Thus, some are almost dull, others more sensitive, and others capable of a certain "discipline" and sometimes gifted with the name of "prudence." Whether one refers this to a natural instinct, or as others preferred, to a certain "deliberation" regarding those things which are linked to an end through memory. From this, they say that an ant steals a grain from "this pile" rather than "that one," and puts it in "this burrow" rather than "that one," using a certain comparison, though it is small and imperfect. Just as they rely little on experience (in which animals have little power), it is for this reason that even some theologians have not denied that animals possess a "particular" reason or prudence in some way. But man, besides these, is also endowed with **universal reason**, insofar as he is a prince...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of "man" by examining the soul’s unique position in the hierarchy of existence. It transitions from a critique of pagan philosophers to a discussion of Christian theological definitions and a further critique of Aristotelian logic based on the unreliability of the senses.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE. # CHAPTER 157.

...[the soul is] the chief, and is placed in the highest rank of the lower nature, insofar as it lies at the lowest point of the higher, intellectual nature; its form is called the "intellectual" or "intellective" soul. For the rational or intellectual substance of the soul is, and is rightly held to be, truly and by itself the **form of the human body** <term>form of the human body: a philosophical and theological concept meaning the soul is what gives the body its life, structure, and identity</term>. This is not only proven by reason but is also sanctified by the law of our Catholic Church. <note>This refers to the Council of Vienne (1311–1312), which dogmatically defined that the rational soul is the "form" of the body.</note> Furthermore, sometimes this soul is called "rational," sometimes "intellectual," sometimes "reason," and sometimes "mind"; at other times it is designated by both names together. Hence those words of our Augustine: "the mind, by which the soul of man is rational." And those of Leo: "whether the rational soul or the mind."

To me, however, it seems that man was more appropriately called a "rational animal" rather than an "intellectual" or "mental" one in the definitions of the ancients, because the function of **reason** <term>reason (ratio): step-by-step logical thinking, also called "discursive" thought</term> suits him more properly than that of **intellect** <term>intellect (intellectus): the ability to grasp a truth immediately and as a whole, without needing to "work it out"</term> and mind. Thomas [Aquinas] explains this diligently in the second book of his commentary on the *Sentences of Theology*. Strictly speaking, the function of reason fits man better: that is, to reason and to range through arguments <note>original: "rōcinari atq; discurrere"</note> rather than to comprehend the substance of a thing in a single glance—even if he is not entirely or utterly destitute of that higher power by his own nature. Therefore, reason is proper to him, which he possesses by full right. His intellectual nature is also proper to him, but in the lowest order; for intellect is more proper to spirits separated from matter <note>i.e., Angels</note>, and among those who hold the highest place, they prevail most greatly in intellect.

Therefore, the soul of man—the very form from which his specific difference must be drawn—is both rational and intellective, and is rightly called by both names. However, he is said to excel more fully and exactly in reason. These are not two different things in the soul itself, but one thing entirely, from which flow those two properties of reasoning and understanding. For this reason, it ought to be signified by a single name that would indicate the office of both reason and intellect. But since I have not yet been able to construct such a name that is satisfactory, I have forged this Greek term from two words: **Logonoetic** <note>original: "Λογονοητικὴ" (Logonoētikē) – combining *Logos* (reason) and *Noesis* (intellect)</note>. By this "difference," all other higher qualities may be included as proper to him, and he may be set apart from all other things that are not man. For through "universal reason" he is set apart from all kinds of brute beasts, and through that same reason joined with intellect, he is set apart from the angels, who by their own nature do not need the step-by-step discourse of reason. All these things are signified by that one word expressing the "difference," which includes the higher natures and is clearly and simply interchangeable with "man"—it is neither broader nor narrower in its scope. But let us return to the common definition itself and show that it cannot be fully grasped through Aristotelian dogma.

### Chapter Ten. ###
### Even if a definition can be had, it cannot be obtained by the rules laid down by Aristotle; many points regarding the mode of understanding are placed here, which are not common but rare. ###

And even if it were granted that a definition can be had, let it be most clearly proven that it cannot be had by Aristotle's rules. This is not only because the definition is difficult to find in itself—as both Aristotle and his commentator **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for paraphrasing Aristotle's works.</note> attest in the work *On the Soul*—nor because a "definition properly so-called" belongs only to substance, while for other things it is by "addition," as he himself wished in the seventh book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. Nor is it because the definition is a statement explaining the very being of a thing (as he wrote in the *Topics*), yet while a statement has parts, a definition [in its essence] does not, if it is to be limited only to the ultimate "difference." <margin>The first reason is noted.</margin> <margin>Second.</margin> <margin>Third.</margin> <margin>Fourth.</margin> <margin>Philoponus.</margin> Nor is it because he implies—and his expositors explain, especially **Philoponus** <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle.</note> in his commentary on the last volume of the *Posterior Analytics*—that the definition of a thing can neither be demonstrated, nor gathered by induction, nor decided by the senses.

I say it is not only for those reasons, but on the same foundation we used before: namely, the weakness of the wavering and changeable senses. Because of this, we shall attempt to show that a definition—not just of this or that thing, but in general—can by no means be exactly grasped. <margin>A proof proper to the subject, depending on the previously mentioned uncertainty of the senses.</margin> For the sense itself, which Aristotle always uses like a **blind man uses a stick**, is quite useless for reaching the essence of a thing.

<meta>This page continues the critique of Aristotelian philosophy, specifically arguing that Aristotle's reliance on sensory perception prevents a truly certain definition of a "substance" like the soul.</meta>

BOOK [FIVE]

...he cannot attain [the essence], as even that author himself admits, if indeed he dwells only on **accidents** <term>accidents (accidentia): properties of a thing that can change or be absent without the thing losing its identity, such as color, height, or location</term>. Indeed, his opinion in the first book of *On the Soul* is that accidents contribute "to a great extent" to our knowing what a thing is. By using the words "to a great extent" and "contribute," he indicated that this does not happen entirely, nor can it be gathered with certainty; rather, it "contributes" to it. And what else is this but a conjecture? But where there is conjecture, there is no certainty. Therefore, he conjectures the **substance** <term>substance (substantia): the fundamental essence of a thing that exists in itself, rather than in another</term> from its accidents, all the more so because he used these words: <note>original Greek: συμβεβηκότα συμβάλλεσθαι (symbebēkota symballesthai)</note> "accidents contribute," or "assist"—evidently toward making a conjecture. Certainly, a substance can be hinted at by many accidents, but it cannot be known with certainty. Even he confirms that it is the role of the intellect and the mind to know the essence or substance of a thing.

However, it is clear to everyone—even those who have only just entered the "vestibules of Porphyry" <note>Porphyry was a philosopher whose "Isagoge" served as the standard introductory textbook to logic for over a thousand years.</note> or taken a brief stroll in the Lyceum with Aristotle—that a **difference** <term>difference (differentia): the specific quality that distinguishes one species from another within the same category</term> does not only pertain to the substance, but constitutes it in itself and separates it from others. But as is clear from his first book *On the Soul*, Aristotle teaches that we must investigate definitions starting from accidents. Since the senses do not go beyond accidents, the substantial difference of a thing cannot be known by the senses, as that is the proper duty of the intellect. Furthermore, since "nothing is in the intellect"—as he himself wills and decrees—"that was not first in the senses," it is clearly proven that anyone who relies on Aristotelian dogma and rules can have no certain and perfectly exact definition. Consequently, nothing can be perfectly demonstrated by his art.

<margin>Response</margin>
To this, someone might say that substance is known by the intellect through the "species" <term>species: here meaning a mental image or representation of the thing's essence</term> of the substance itself, not of an accident. For those who believe substance is known through the species of an accident ought rightly to surrender to these arguments and testimonies, and not resist in any way. 

<margin>Confutation</margin>
Those who do not want the substance to be known through the species of the substance itself will be very unwilling to "give up the ghost" <note>original: "porrigere herbam," an ancient idiom meaning to admit defeat</note>, because according to Aristotle, substance is prior to knowledge. 

<margin>Thomas</margin>
But whoever they may be (however learned they are in other respects), let them first see whether they speak so "Aristotelianly" that they can even be considered Aristotelians—something they hardly seem to desire. Secondly, let them see if they agree at all with Thomas [Aquinas], whose followers they profess to be? In the first book of the *Summa contra Gentiles*, he teaches that substance is said to be prior to knowledge because it is placed in the definition of an accident, not because substance is known *before* the accident. Otherwise, he himself would have blocked the path to error earlier when he wrote in that same book that "the knowledge of our intellect, according to the mode of this present life, begins from the senses." For Thomas did not agree with those who wanted there to be either innate species in the soul, or species that were merely started or sketched out as if with shadowy lines. Rather, he maintained that all natural knowledge takes its origin from the senses...

<meta>Continuing the discussion from the previous page, the author moves from the theoretical hierarchy of substance and accident to the practical difficulties humans face in attaining "exact knowledge" of any reality, citing several influential medieval and Renaissance thinkers.</meta>

**BOOK.**

<margin>The fourth and manifold difficulty of knowing a thing exactly.</margin>
...to such an extent that some have maintained that this [exact knowledge] cannot be known by humans in this life; or if it can be, others say it is not through "discourse" <note>Discourse (*discursu*) refers to the step-by-step process of reasoning from one premise to another, rather than direct, intuitive understanding.</note> and in no way perfectly. This is because something always falls between the likeness and the thing of which it is a likeness. Thus, reasoning is necessary, yet a perfect judgment of the likeness cannot be made if the thing itself has not been previously known on its own. This can easily be seen by anyone to whom something has been reported by only one sense, while a different inclination is formed through the imagination. For if something has been suggested to the mind through hearing alone, the other senses judge it in a different way. Because one who understands looks upon mental images <note>original: "phantalmata," referring to the internal sensory images the mind uses to think</note>, he immediately fashions for himself in his soul a likeness of the thing received through the ears; and when he later perceives that same thing—which he had only heard of—through sight, he often notices he was deceived by himself. He had, of course, fashioned one image for himself, which was different from the one later impressed upon him by sight. But even by sight itself, a thing is sometimes absorbed in this way and sometimes in that, through its own image; thus, some judgment through reasoning is necessary to discern whether it was truly or untruly perceived. And it follows: is that image a likeness of the thing drawn from the thing itself? Or is it wandering and inconsistent, resting on no stable foundation of the thing? If this is seen in all knowledge of the lowliest things placed beneath our senses, how much more so in the perception of those things which the senses do not properly perceive, and even those which surpass all the senses? For then the imagination is further removed from the intelligible thing <note>original: "re intellectili," a thing known by the mind rather than the senses</note> than the sense is from the imagination, or as the image is from the thing itself. On this account, neither the highest, nor the middle, nor the lowest things will be grasped in the way many suppose. The highest things are not revealed by any proper image, being incorporeal and separated from all matter and the conditions of matter. The middle things [are difficult] because when a man captures something with one sense, he makes a conjecture through another from an image fashioned within himself, not drawn properly from the thing. And as for the lowest things, even though they are captured by an image drawn from the thing, they cannot be clearly distinguished through that image unless the thing is distinguished by itself and utterly separated from its image—which we demonstrated above to be impossible.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
To this point also belongs what Augustine discusses in the second book of his *Soliloquies* regarding the knowledge of truth and falsehood, based on similarity and dissimilarity. To this also, knowledge through "species" <note>In this context, "species" are the mental "forms" or concepts we use to categorize things.</note>—both more and less universal—can be referred without difficulty. So too the difficulty of perceiving the thoughts of others, even if they are suggested to our senses or our mind. For if we captured in our soul the same things as those who teach us, we would easily fashion the same images for ourselves, or entirely similar ones. Nevertheless, it happens that these are absorbed not only more or less perfectly, but sometimes in the most remote way, and most differently from the thing itself—to the perception of which some come closer than others. From there, they often relate back to themselves in various ways: for much arises from the varying condition of the thing itself, from a varying state, from the great variety of the seasons of the year, from the varying and repeatedly changed temperament of the body, and from the different foundation of habit and the various actions of the soul.

<margin>Nicholas of Cusa</margin>
Perhaps Nicholas of Cusa <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher and theologian who wrote on the limits of human knowledge.</note> perceived this exactly; and especially if he determines correctly in his dialogue *On Genesis* that something of the "essence"—or to use his word, the "quiddity"—can be attained by man neither in whole nor in part. This is because (to use his language again) the "art of being" in all things that have been unfolded cannot be conceived except by God. And in the third book of *The Layman* <note>original: "Idiota," a work where Cusa uses a "layman" character to outwit learned scholars</note>, which is also composed as a dialogue where the Layman, the Orator, and the Philosopher dispute concerning the mind, he affirms that the "precision" (if I may use his terms) of **quiddity** <term>quiddity (quidditas): the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> is unattainable by us except in "enigma and figure" <note>original: "ænygmate & figura," meaning through riddles, symbols, or indirect shadows rather than direct sight.</note>. And this could be confirmed

<margin>Averroes, Aureolus</margin>

[Main Text]
...the thing itself. Nor is the response of those people sufficient who refer this to the mental images <note>original: "phantasmata," the internal sensory representations the mind uses to think</note> of a thing. For although a mental image is often drawn from the thing itself and represents it, it can also be drawn from the *appearance* of the thing; this can be observed in the shape of the moon and many other things about which the art of optics <note>Perspective and the science of light</note> prescribes its rules. Consequently, the appearance itself often passes into the intellect as if it were the thing itself. For various errors can creep into understanding: first, during perception by the external senses, when not the thing itself but an image, likeness, or semblance <term>simulachrum: a deceptive or superficial representation</term> is perceived. We also said just a moment ago that it happens that the appearance of a thing is taken for the thing itself. 

Next, a much greater slip can occur in perceiving it when it is captured in mental images not through its own proper image, but through a foreign one represented in the place of a mirror. Subsequently, the internal senses can be eluded in any number of ways. For instance, the things we have gathered through the external senses concerning the image of the thing itself (say, a man) or concerning the affection of the senses themselves (such as when we conceive of heat in the mind rather than fire or glowing iron)—the external sense reports these things at times to the internal senses. At other times, it does not report the things themselves but their likenesses, which do not always exactly represent the things by which they are impressed. We have either already conceived these likenesses—often in various ways depending on our age or the state of our minds, which affect the organs of the senses differently at different times—or we are forming them for ourselves for the first time in some way or another. 

<margin>How various errors can creep into understanding because of mental images.</margin>

Sometimes, too, even if we have gathered nothing from the thing itself nor from its own image, we can imagine these things in one way or another, according to the various images drawn out and the diverse perceptions of different people. It can also happen that we retain in our memory what we have gathered with our eyes, and its features and colors are presented in the power of the imagination. It can also happen that something is consigned to oblivion, especially when we have conceived the thing in the mind from its image alone. To this point, what is written in the Epistle of Saint James can easily be applied: namely, that he who has considered the face <note>The original text includes the Greek "πρόσωπον" (prosōpon), meaning face or countenance</note> of his birth in a mirror, goes away and immediately forgets what manner of man he was. 

In addition to this, we imagine in a different way the things we have seen compared to the things we have not seen but have perceived through the words of others. Whence our Augustine says in the twelfth book *On Genesis*: "In one way we think of Carthage, which we know; in another way, Alexandria, which we do not know." He attributes the former to a true image and the latter to a fictitious one. He had previously taught in the eighth book of that same work that the names of all things unexperienced are known in two ways: either from contraries, if they are names of privations <note>Defining something by what it lacks</note>, or from similarity, if they are names of species. 

<margin><unclear>illegible</unclear> <unclear>illegible</unclear></margin>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>

In the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, while he teaches that in the faith we have concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, it is not healthy for the mind to forge things for itself, but rather what we think of a man according to the species; he later mentions the same thing regarding the known and the unknown, using the same example of Carthage, which he had seen and retained in memory, and Alexandria, which he had not seen but whose image he had fixed in his mind from the narration of others. 

But truly, however you establish it, what is outside can often be easily absorbed internally in an impure way. For just as a mirror—stained by some color or placed differently—presents a thing to the eye differently than it is, so the mental image, acting in place of a mirror, can easily vary the thing in its presentation. This may be due to some predominant moisture <note>Referring to the "humors," or bodily fluids, thought to influence health and perception</note> or shape, or by the removal of something known, or by change, or by the encounter and addition of something else not previously known. This is even more the case if it presents not what it gathered from the outside, but what it fashioned while migrating from one thing to another, whether it fused it from many sources or invented it. But leaving those things aside, I ask regarding the internal reception itself—whatever it may be or contain, whether in the sense or the intellect, or in both: if they say it is this third option, the order of cognition handed down by Aristotle himself is overturned.

For he [Aristotle] first handed down the senses: and in the third book on the soul <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*, Book III</note>, intending to investigate the essence, properties, and duties of the intellect, he makes use of the functions of perceiving. And so, from the sense and the duties of perceiving, he tracks down both the intellect and its functions. But if at last, pressed by many difficulties, they should betake themselves to the sense, <margin>Response.</margin> which might supply the intellect with the knowledge of a substance, so that—as has pleased some—the form <term>species: a mental representation or "form" of an object</term> of the substance is in the sense, wrapped in the form of the accident, to be unwrapped and dug out by the intellect. <margin>First refutation.</margin> Then against them will stand those who point out that the intellect is changed by accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or smell, as opposed to the "substance" or core reality</note> even when the substance is removed, through the miracle of divine power <note>A reference to the Eucharist, where Catholic doctrine holds that the "accidents" of bread remain while the "substance" changes</note>; wherefore its absence could be naturally known, if that were true, since even the sight, affected by light and soon deprived of it, perceives the darkness by which it is not affected, as Aristotle handed down in the second book on the soul. <margin>Second [refutation]</margin> By which author I think they ought to be urged otherwise, since it is provided by his law that the sense does not step beyond the accidents, nor in any way reach the internal limits of the substance. Whence, therefore, should the image, spectrum, phantom, or form of the substance itself fall into the intellect? They will say, perhaps, <margin>Response.</margin> that it is represented to the mind by the light of the "agent intellect" <note>The part of the mind that processes raw sensory data into abstract thoughts</note>: I ask, is it together with a mental image <note>original: "phantasmate"</note>? If they deny it, an appeal to Aristotle will be granted, who has nothing in his third book on the soul more firm and constant than that the thinking soul contemplates mental images, and he decrees that it cannot happen otherwise. And so, if they grant mental images, it is immediately necessary that the sense be granted first, if they receive Aristotle’s long-celebrated definition of "phantasia" <note>the faculty of imagination or mental representation</note> as a motion made by the sense according to the act. That mental image or likeness must necessarily be drawn from the thing itself of which it is an image, if it is to be considered true. But the sense cannot know the thing itself, nor likewise is a particularly sensible thing known by the intellect without the aid of the sense. It remains, therefore, whether they wish it or not—unless they wish to desert Aristotle—that they fall back to the sense, which, as we have said, dwells upon the accidents and not the thing itself. <margin>Third [refutation]</margin> Truly, even if it were granted that the form of a substance could be known to the sense to such an extent that the intellect could take it for itself to contemplate, there still remains a knot perhaps more tangled than that Gordian one <note>The Gordian Knot: an ancient metaphor for an intractable problem</note>, and bound by this thong: that if it be so, it is also necessary that the intellect capture something different from what it presented to itself—I do not say different regarding the mode of capturing or receiving, but regarding the object itself, which is not received as he imagines it, seeing as he adds something to the known thing as if he were making another, insofar as it pertains to the "agent," and something other than what it had been is received by the "possible intellect" <note>The "intellectus potestatis," the mind's capacity to be shaped by new information</note>. If they say that the form of the accident, illustrated by the light of the agent intellect, represents in the possible intellect an intelligible form of the substance, as an effect represents a cause: <margin>First refutation.</margin> that absurdity follows, that an effect not equal to its cause refers to it in the place of an equal and proper image. For neither one accident nor many accidents swallowed together by the senses, even if many could be perceived at once in one concept, would be able to equal the substance, or the difference of its essence, or its first and proper affection. <margin>Confirmation.</margin> And much less can the followers of Thomas [Aquinas] contend this, among whom it is held as a constant that all knowledge happens by way of likeness, and that the human intellect requires an intelligible form that is proper and equalized [to the object]. Nor does he himself use any other foundation more willingly to disprove the opinion of Avempace <note>Ibn Bajja, a medieval Andalusian philosopher</note> in the third volume of his work *Against the Gentiles* <note>Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa contra Gentiles*</note>: and in the whole course of the forty-ninth chapter thereafter he observes this, when he treats the knowledge of a cause through its effect: upon the foundation, I say, of "dissimilar knowledge," and of an effect that by no means equals its cause—that is, one not expressing its whole power. But also in the fifty-sixth chapter above, he teaches most clearly that except by the notion of sensible accidents, one does not arrive at the intellect...

But if they say with Thomas [Aquinas] <margin>Response.</margin> that angelic intellects understand one thing after another, but nevertheless do not "discourse" <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to the step-by-step process of reasoning from one premise to another</note>: <margin>Refutation.</margin> let them also learn from Thomas at the end of the second volume of *Against the Gentiles* <note>Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa Contra Gentiles*, a major theological work</note>, that in that duty of understanding there is no succession or motion because act succeeds act, not potentiality. Therefore, when one perceives a cause from an effect, it arises by a certain path, so to speak (if you shrink from the name of "discourse"), just as one moves from effect to cause, so one moves from potentiality to act.

But another knot remains, still <margin>Another refutation.</margin> far more difficult, and which might seem only capable of being untied by the Macedonian's sword <note>A reference to Alexander the Great cutting the Gordian Knot, implying a problem that requires a bold, decisive solution rather than subtle untangling</note>; because if a substance were known by its own form <term>species: a mental representation or conceptual "image" of an object</term>, the "difference" <note>In logic, the "differentia" is the specific quality that distinguishes one species from another within a genus, such as "rational" for humans</note> would also be known, which is enclosed in the complete concept of the thing itself: yet all learned men concede that they are ignorant of this. Those who <margin>Removal of a silent objection.</margin> think Thomas was of that opinion should note that even the proper principles of "accidents" <note>The non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color, size, or smell</note> are frequently ignored, according to that author in his discourse *On Being and Essence* <note>original: "de ente & essentia"</note>. Therefore, he says, we take the differences of accidents from the effects of things. Much more, then, will the substance be unknown when one arrives at it through accidents. 

But since <margin>The author's opinion: how substance can be known is indicated below.</margin> knowledge occurs through a likeness of the thing known, the intellect will know the substance through no likeness of the substance or of the accident, insofar as it pertains to the perfection of the intellectual concept. Instead, it will know it by its own nature and manner: that is, by a more universal form <term>species: the mental representation</term> and one set apart from matter. And therefore, strictly speaking, it is neither by the form of the substance nor of the accident, from which it will have been drawn externally. Therefore, it will be neither this nor that, but will be represented by a certain kind of negation, as it were. Thus, the intellectual form will not be the "species" of the substance, although it represents it by a certain conjecture and by the setting aside and sequestration of other things. For just as Aristotle conjectures substance from the knowledge of accidents—because, for example, it is neither quantity, nor quality, nor relation—so he indicated that the form of substance is grasped by the mind because it is not the image or form of this or that sensible substance. Therefore, it is entirely "something else" that is consistent with being the foundation for those accidents, even if we do not comprehend exactly what that thing is. 

So also <margin>Jean Gerson</margin> Jean Gerson <note>A prominent 14th-century French scholar and Chancellor of the University of Paris</note>, in the work titled *Centilogium*, judged concerning concepts that the "quiddities" <term>quiddity: the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing</term> (as he calls them) of substances are formed through discourse and resolution. I omit making mention here of the knowledge which <margin>On intuitive and abstractive knowledge.</margin> the Parisian theologians call "intuitive" and "abstractive": whether that knowledge represents the thing in itself from the object presented, or whether it is also produced from the thing's own specific form? Or even from a more eminent representation? And also concerning "super-intuitive" knowledge (as they call it) in the most eminent light. Also, whether the first kind is intuitive in us—which draws in the accidents and can be called "experimental" in the senses regarding natural things, just as it is in the soul regarding its own habits and functions, and also in the intellect regarding the knowledge of first principles; and if the second kind is abstractive, being founded upon the first? Since we do not abstract except from things already known. And if the third kind is discursive, which is also syllogistic <note>Related to the use of formal logic and deductions</note>? When we migrate from one thing known abstractly into another of the same kind and gather it together. Likewise, whether all human knowledge either intuits or abstracts? Or whether some middle ground may rightly be placed between them? And whether one is more truly one kind of knowledge and another is another, having received a different name based on the presence or absence of the object? For as far as the present business is concerned regarding the knowledge of substance, let it be enough to have proved that it occurs neither by the form of the substance nor of the accident, strictly and exactly speaking, but by both discoursing and negating. And it also appears consistent to me that from this we may see...

FIFTH [Page Header Left]
CHAPTER 61 [Page Header Right]

[...it is understood] not simply, but through a certain negation <note>original: *per abnegationem*; the philosophical method of defining what a thing is by stating what it is not</note>, in the manner we taught above: from which a certain phantom <note>original: *spectrum*; here meaning a mental representation or shadow-image</note> of substance itself is impressed upon the power of the intellect—not of this or that [specific] substance, but of substance in itself. <margin>Proof of the same opinion.</margin> For how could it be certain whether the mental image <note>original: *phantasma*</note> of substance were true, in whatever way it might be illuminated or received? For no judgment can be made from a mental image unless the thing of which it is a likeness or image is also known. 

And how shall it be known except by the senses? Since the mental image is corporeal, and insofar as it is corporeal, it cannot represent the innermost parts—especially the form from which the constitutive difference <term>The specific quality or "essential ingredient" that defines what a thing is and distinguishes it from all other things</term> is taken. In what way, I ask, shall it be known that it is a true image and appearance <note>original: *speciem*</note> of that substance? 

For if someone shows me a likeness or image of Rome, I cannot properly and exactly pass judgment on whether it is true unless I have seen Rome before; and I am not certain so long as I am a contemplator of the image itself and do not perceive properly and exactly that of which it is an image, so that at last a sincere and exact comparison of the primary image to that of which it is an image can be made. I said "primary"—that is, the one first drawn from the thing itself. For Rome cannot be seen except through an image; for the city itself does not enter the eyes, nor does the imagination itself move according to what is in the thing itself, if <margin>Avicenna.</margin> Avicenna <note>A hugely influential Persian polymath and philosopher (c. 980–1037)</note> writes truly in his booklet *On the Powers of the Heart*, but rather moves according to what is represented in it. Nor does it seem possible to deny that the sensory power can be moved both by an image and by a likeness of an image, whether presented truly or falsely. For Rome enters the pupil by its own image; and an image of Rome manufactured from some material is also received by its appearance and image, and not by the bulky material itself. Thus, both the first image of a thing and the second—that is, the likeness <note>original: *effigies*</note> of the image—must necessarily fall into our consideration.

Therefore, I have compared the first image of Rome, conceived in the mind in some way without the thing of which it is an image, to the thing itself. And what has been brought forward regarding one sense that is eminent among others and nearly spiritual, the same will be much more evident regarding the rest—this occurs not in isolation, as was hinted at above, but by a comparison of one sense to another: as when I perceive that the image of some thing, which I drew in through my ears <note>i.e., by hearing a description</note>, is not a sincere image of the thing itself when I draw in the same through my eyes. I might find that I had shaped it in my mind far differently from hearing than I conceived it with my eyes; thus, I might fashion it differently in my mind and, once conceived, I might compose and compare it differently to the thing itself. <margin>Conclusion.</margin> I can be moved to judge by the judgment of others whom I trust, or by my own conjecture, as was partially declared above; but I cannot pass a sentence by my own proper judgment unless I have known the thing separately.

Those words of Seneca the Stoic, discussing the heavenly bow <note>The rainbow; referring to Seneca's *Naturales Quaestiones*</note>, can also support this disputation of ours: "a likeness would be a lie without the reality." <margin>On the mode of knowledge through the similar and on the various names of the similar itself.</margin> For it was a sentiment repeated from the most ancient Pythagorean philosophers that "like is known by like"—although Heraclitus the physicist preferred that "unlike is known by unlike." But Aristotle and most of the Platonists, even if they wanted that which receives to be stripped of the nature of the thing received, do not deny that knowledge is prepared through likeness. Indeed, whether you consider the name itself or the thing, different people have expressed this likeness in different ways: some have called it an appearance <note>original: *speciem*</note>, others an image or likeness <note>original: *effigiem*</note>, others an idea or form, others a notion, the "moderns" <note>Referring to the Scholastic philosophers of the late Middle Ages</note> an intention <note>original: *intentionem*; a technical term for the mind's "aiming" at or representing an object</note>, others a phantom <note>original: *simulachrum*</note>, and others a spectrum. Others preferred it expressed by the name of likeness itself. As far as the matter is concerned, some have wanted that which is received and known in "act" <note>The state of being currently perceived or real, as opposed to potential</note> to be entirely the same as that which was previously "potential" in the cognitive power itself, so that knowledge, as far as its spiritual essence is concerned, is nothing other than a form placed in the cognitive power; others have preferred to call it an action...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the human mind grasps the true essence of a "substance." Having previously discussed the mind's use of mental images, the author now addresses the limits of human reason and the senses in identifying the "ultimate difference" that defines a thing.</meta>

# **BOOK**

...[there is a debate as to whether] there is something that remains within, derived from that form; others, however, were more pleased to think that form is grasped and contained, as it were, by the cognitive power itself. But when we speak of "form," they do not want us to understand it as the form itself which is outside and sliding in, leaping into the mind; rather, they mean its likeness—a "spectrum" <note>original: *spectrum*; a mental shadow or representation</note>, an image, or if you prefer, a semblance, or the very likeness received in the soul. Even the warning of the Stoic Epictetus can be applied here: that it is the images of things that affect the minds of men, not the things themselves. 

Certainly, from everything we have said, it seems to follow that the intellect cannot, by its own nature and primarily, know a substance through its own "species" <note>original: *speciem*; here meaning the mental concept or essential form</note> so as to truly know it based on Aristotelian rules. Perhaps it cannot do so by the rules of any other philosopher of the nations either—although the Platonists, because of the "ideas" and "innate species" they place in the soul, might not be pressed by so many difficulties, even if they would not be entirely free of them. 

<margin>Diverse opinions of the Peripatetics regarding the manner of understanding substance</margin>
But the later Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> are wonderfully distressed, which is why there is such diversity among Aristotle’s newer followers, moved as they are by different sayings. For some think we know substance by the "species" of the substance; others by the "species" of the accident <term>Accidents are the non-essential, surface qualities of a thing, such as its color, smell, or size</term>; others by reasoning <note>original: *discursu*; the logical process of moving from one thought to another</note> alone; and others have judged that substance cannot properly be known perfectly in this life. 

Those indeed seem to me to have understood Aristotle better who think we must use the senses, conjecture, and the discourse of reason, since he begins from the sense and always refers back to the sense. But since the senses (as has been proven) are often deceived and conjecture fails, we cannot know with enough certainty; however, knowledge can be more perfectly known by the judgment of others who truly know. 

<margin>The excellence of Faith.</margin>
This is where the excellence of faith exerts itself over sensory knowledge—and substance can be known much more clearly through divine and supernatural illumination than by natural light. But for now, we are not speaking of theological "irradiations" <note>The idea of divine light "shining" into the human mind to grant knowledge</note>, but of natural ones and those discussed by Aristotle. 

<margin>Epilogue of the entire dispute.</margin>
From all this, we can conclude in a few words what we have pursued in a long discussion: that based on Aristotelian rules and the mode of cognition he handed down, a certain definition cannot be had that consists of the "ultimate difference" <term>The final, specific quality that distinguishes one thing from everything else in its category</term>. For if you take away this difference, you have taken away the definition itself. Furthermore, it is discovered that this difference must be removed according to Aristotelian dogma, which relies on the traces of the senses, by which that difference cannot be captured. This is because the senses linger only on the accidents and do not penetrate to the essence of the thing. 

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
If the proper definition were known, the proper difference would certainly be known, and its "affection" <note>A characteristic property or state that naturally follows from a thing's essence</note> would by no means be ignored. If that were known, the properties that flow from it would be clear. Then we would know best, as if from a proper cause: Why does a magnet pull iron? Why does a clover have three leaves instead of four? Why are the bristles of wheat jagged like a saw? Why is the shape of willow leaves different from those of a plane tree? These and all other such things would be known perfectly from their proper causes. But since it is unknown from what source these traits exactly and specifically proceed, it is manifest that the things from which they proceed—the substances themselves—are also unknown.

<margin>Further confirmations through reason and authority</margin>
For how shall we know the causes of effects as such, if we cannot know the effects of causes insofar as they flow from them by proper and exact reason? But the consensus of reputable philosophers has revealed that all such things are ignored. They teach that in things made of the elements, the "proportion of the whole mixture" is unknown. It is from this mixture that the "form" arises, the "difference" emerges, and from this, the proper power flows—like a river from its natural spring. Other powers are derived in their turn, with the life-giving light and heat of the heavens acting upon them, though received differently due to a different "imbalance of qualities" <note>original: *intemperamento*; the specific physical makeup or "complexion" of a substance</note>. ### Chapter Eleven.

**D** It will be easy to declare from this how vain that distinction of demonstrations is which he handed down: one of which proceeds from the effect, and the other from the cause. This distinction actually contradicts the author himself, even as he busies himself trying to prove many things. This is especially true because he claimed that the demonstration which proceeds from the cause—or as the moderns <note>The "neoterici" or Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages</note> say, *a priori* ("from the earlier"), to which they gave the name "on account of what" (*propter quid*)—was the true demonstration. He decreed that it was wonderfully superior to the one that proceeds from the effect—or *a posteriori* ("from the later")—which is called "because" (*quia*). 

Therefore, since Aristotle proceeds *a priori* in a simple and absolute manner, his excessive admirers could be asked: how does he grasp the effect? By what means does he determine the effect of the cause itself, whatever that effect might be? For if he first proceeds from the cause to the effect, <margin>**Argumentation**</margin> unless he brings his own rules, it is entirely necessary for him to proceed through the senses. For he could not have gathered those principles of the intellect except from the senses, once individual things were known, as we have sufficiently explained above. If he proceeds through the senses, I ask first: how did he know the cause beforehand? For if the cause is an object of the intellect, there was a primary need for the senses, since he intended for us to need the sense as a "pedagogue" <note>A guide or teacher's assistant</note>. For how will a cause be known through the intellect before the effect is known, if he intended that "nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses," and that the intellect draws its knowledge from the effect on the senses? 

If, however, the cause were a sensible thing, he could nonetheless only grasp it through conjecture—namely, through intermediate accidents—since the sense itself does not penetrate to the essence of a thing. If you say he recognized one through the other, and did so in different ways—confusedly at first and then distinctly—you will be revolving in a circle. For if you say he used the senses first and then the intellect: how could that statement of his be true, that a demonstration led through the cause is more certain than one led through the effect, when he relies on no other foundation to show this than the senses? <margin>**Response**</margin> You will say that the way of the senses is "prior," while the way of the intellect is "more certain and more worthy." <margin>**First Refutation**</margin> But you cannot deny that all certainty is owed to the senses, which perceive the effect from which the cause is known. <margin>**Confirmation from Aristotle himself**</margin> Hence, in the second book of *On the Heavens*, when Aristotle himself asked why those things which are further from the first sphere are moved by fewer motions, and had added the greatest difficulty to the question, he signaled his meager ability to grasp the truth by adding that he had little certainty from which to begin, since he had to start from effects.

...prior knowledge, implanted from our very origin, provides a recourse to that same knowledge—as it is more stable and familiar—so that we are less deceived when trying to grasp other things that are less known to our nature. For this reason, knowledge of the **effect** will be more firm and certain than knowledge of the **cause**, which is clearly not known through itself, but through something else—namely, from the effect and its operation. 

From this, it is clear that the distinction between a <term>demonstration of the fact</term> <note>original: "demonstratio quia"; a logical proof that shows that something is true based on its observed effects.</note> and a <term>demonstration of the reasoned fact</term> <note>original: "demonstratio propter quid"; a proof that explains why something is true based on its underlying causes.</note> was empty. While the former is more certain, it is not "less certain" as Aristotle wished, but rather more certain than knowledge through the senses (by which he measures everything as if the senses were the most certain judge). Indeed, knowledge is more certain when it relies on the judgment of the effect, especially in natural things where the primary demonstrations are taken through the effect, as even **Thomas Aquinas** <margin>Thomas.</margin> <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> noted in the third book of *Against the Gentiles*. 

From this we can also very clearly see the weakness of our ability to define things. This occurs when the very notions that they call <term>intentions</term> <note>In Scholastic logic, "intentions" are the mental concepts we form about things.</note>—namely, **genus** and **difference**—are said to be drawn, the former from matter and the latter from form. For a "genus" is only understood through its "difference," and a "difference" is only understood through the "operation" flowing from it (maintaining the proportion of the matter). Since the same common form is sometimes seen across many genera, one must distinguish them to see how far they diverge and how far they agree.

Consequently, one must investigate the **proper form** from which the proper species and proper difference are drawn. This form will be known through its "proper affection" (which younger physicists call a <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a property or characteristic that naturally belongs to a specific type of thing.</note>), just as the form of a species is known by its proper operation. But since the "proper operation" of any given thing cannot be perceived with certain and exact knowledge (as will be explained shortly), by the same token, the "proper affection" cannot be perceived either. For you would have had to first know the operations of *all* things if you wanted to certainly perceive the one property that is unique to a specific thing and not shared with others. By that same logic, you would need to know every single species if you desired to grasp the proper affections of one species with exact knowledge.

However, since this is in no way possible under Aristotelian doctrine, it will be impossible to know that specific "difference," and consequently, it will be impossible <margin>The difficulty regarding by what criteria forms are distinguished.</margin> to define anything properly and exactly. Furthermore, since the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> do not sufficiently agree on what criteria natural forms are most distinguished from one another, it becomes manifest that they do not agree on their species, differences, or affections—specifically, how they are separated so that one can tell which property belongs to one thing and which belongs to others. This is problematic if (as is accepted) the diversity of species—constituted by differences from which affections flow—depends on the form.

For those who said forms are distinguished by the diversity of their **active principles** (since every agent makes something similar to itself according to its species), they must explain why human offspring do not always perfectly match their parents, since they sometimes produce "monsters" or "excremental masses." <note>Early biological terms for birth defects or unformed biological matter.</note> If they attribute this to "matter," they will still need to add and subtract much for that proposition to be judged true. Likewise, they should explain how irrational animals born from **putrefaction** <note>The now-obsolete theory of "spontaneous generation," which claimed life could arise from decaying matter.</note> are similar to those born from the mating of male and female, even being of the same species, as many have asserted.

Those who said forms are distinguished by the diversity of their **operations** suffer a disadvantage from others who argue that the same form can be the principle of different operations, and that different forms cannot be the principles of those same operations—an argument that can hardly be defeated since not all operations have been fully explored. Those who distinguish not by *every* difference, but only by that which places a thing in a higher level of being (making its essence more perfect), seem to face the same problem. They appear to be saying the same thing, since every operation that differs in species is either more perfect or less perfect in essence than another.

Others have reduced themselves to different categories, such as "material" and "immaterial." In those cases, one form (as they say) is "educed" <note>From "eduction," the Scholastic theory that forms are "drawn out" from the potentiality of matter.</note> from the subject matter in which it is rooted, while those that come from the outside are not fixed in it. But one could object that in this way, one form—for example, the form of a mixed thing—could not be proven different from the form of life, and what [is said] concerning general...

### Chapter Twelve.
### That not only are the senses and the definition—which Aristotle uses as a foundation, middle term, and cause of demonstrating—uncertain, but so too are the progression and the end; nor would there be a universal proposition or a proper attribute of the subject matter.

We have proved, and clearly enough (unless I am mistaken), that the foundation, the cause, and the middle term of demonstrating and gathering sciences devised by Aristotle are uncertain. That is, the senses and definition are not of such a kind that an exact science of things can be founded upon them; and even if we could gather anything from them, the **attribute** which demonstrators wish to apply to a subject is not gathered with certainty. This is because there is a need for the senses, which are mostly uncertain, and the <term>difference</term> <note>The specific quality that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note> from which it must be drawn is unknown. Nevertheless, we must strive with further labor. For it remains for us to show that the entire progression and the end are also uncertain—that is, that the <term>proper attribute</term> <note>original: "affectionem propriam"; an essential characteristic that belongs exclusively to a particular subject.</note> of the subject which is said to be demonstrated is uncertain, as are the universal propositions which are especially required by demonstration. This is true both in the specific instance and universally, so much so that Aristotle for that reason judged that the propositions by which a demonstration is constructed must be "said of all," since such an attribute is specifically present in every subject in the conclusion itself—that is, the end or result of the demonstration. However, it cannot be gathered except from the propositions that precede the conclusion. Therefore, it is necessary that those very propositions and assumptions which perform the work are both "said of all" and universal. 

We shall prove, then, that these propositions, which Aristotle judged must be both certain and universal, are not certain at all. This is especially true of those called **affirmative**; yet without two of these (or at least one), no demonstration can be constructed, according to Aristotle, which might show us that a thing is so or is not so by its primary principle. Regarding those demonstrations which are said to lead to <term>absurdities</term> <note>original: "absurda et ad inconveniens"; the logical method of proving a point by showing that its opposite leads to a contradiction.</note>—or certain proofs, if one prefers to call them that—against vain and <margin>That we are not speaking of demonstrations that lead to an absurdity.</margin> worthless opinions, we do not speak of them here, as was said before. For it is not our purpose to deny that a certain proof can be brought against a foolish or less-certain opinion, or to infer the opposite of someone's opinion from poorly-established assumptions. Indeed, this very thing pertains more to the art and power of **argumentation** than specifically to the demonstration of the nature of a thing. If we wished to see this removed, it would even hinder us, who seek to convict the uncertain doctrine of Aristotle with a certain proof—or if we cannot do that, certainly a probable one. For it is much easier to refute what has been posited than to assert what has not been granted. A paved path is laid down for one who, from things supposed and handed down, infers something contrary and opposite to those very suppositions, provided he adds a bit of truth himself. 

But <margin>General reason [requiring] a certain universal proposition and knowledge of a proper attribute.</margin> in what way shall we have a certain universal proof, since the art of **induction** <note>The process of deriving general principles from specific observations.</note> is uncertain, without which a universal proposition is uncertain? If you say that you will prove a universal proposition *a priori* (as they say), I shall repel you with the authority of Aristotle himself—not that which we have used many times recently, but that by which he wished the primary ones to be proved with no intermediary. Nor did he admit that those common conceptions of the mind, known to all, could themselves [be subject to] demonstration...

...they would properly enter into those matters which we sufficiently hinted at the beginning of this work: that they are not known through **Aristotle's** doctrine, but by the benefit of the <term>natural light</term> <note>The innate human capacity for reason and intuition, often considered a gift from God in this period.</note>. And as we have said before, it is necessary <margin>Response to an objection.</margin> that these principles be narrowed down if they are to enter into particular subject matter. However, it would not be an obstacle if it were argued that the intellect extracts those very principles from the senses; for one must presuppose that the sense-perception has presented nothing false or uncertain to the imagination, and that the imagination has presented nothing empty—nothing that was not rightly impressed upon it by the senses—to the intellect. Nor does it help to say that some principles are recognized by their "known terms," or that principles are known (according to Aristotle) only because their terms or names are understood. He teaches that these principles are collected through a long progression at the end of the *Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle's primary work on logic and the requirements for scientific knowledge.</note>, in order to prepare the universal propositions that will serve the completion of a demonstration. Moreover, many interpreters teach that those "first things" he speaks of are the principles set down for constructing a demonstration. Therefore, those who hold the opposite view have <margin>Induction, proof, and exposition.</margin> not distinguished between <term>proximate and remote principles</term> <note>Proximate principles are immediate causes; remote principles are more general, underlying causes.</note>. They also fail to notice that induction itself is not rightly performed if it has not collected every single instance. This is true whether it is called a "proof" (as when the words "and so it is for each individual" are inferred) or whether it is named an "exposition" (as when one runs through every single item and leaves nothing untouched). However, we shall show a little later how weakly and unclearly this is actually done. Furthermore, even if you know what is signified by the name of the principles, that by itself will not suffice for you to have knowledge of the universal proposition we are discussing. Rather, it is necessary to have known what the thing itself is; to achieve this, you must have been previously imbued with a great deal of knowledge of sensible things. For it is necessary to have known whether the "subject" term agrees with or is removed from the "predicate." This is not a simple kind of knowledge, but a composite one, by which we either affirm or deny that something belongs to another. Whence, if we wish to assert this universally, it is necessary to have first run through every single instance. Nor <margin>Against Averroes.</margin> should we listen to <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university education.</note> when he teaches that there are some intellects for which two singular instances are enough to gather a universal statement. For that is utterly contrary to Aristotle, to the good <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, and most of all to reason itself. From only two instances, by what agreement do we get "all"? By what agreement, I ask, shall we have a certain universal proof? Likewise, by what agreement will a certain quality be proved regarding every possible subject? But we shall speak more widely on this matter in the course of the work; now, let us speak of induction itself. It is that which gathers universals from singulars, from which universal statements are prepared. And if any proof were to be applied to those highest propositions which are evident by the light of nature, you could produce none more true than that from induction, which, when taken and accepted, fortifies all things from which a necessary conclusion may be inferred. This entire business of demonstrating and "resolving" depends on induction, which creates universal propositions through the mediation of the senses. Aristotle himself, at the end of the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, says it is manifest that first principles are known by induction. And thus his followers teach that a "universal sense" is created. <margin>Themistius.</margin> **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> says: "The mode by which the universal is established and known is induction." I take induction to be that application by reason through which, from the knowledge of particulars (however it may be), one comes to the understanding of the universal. The assumptions of this reasoning will be the senses themselves, for the senses are also principles and causes so that singular things may be known. These are the words of **Themistius**, which signify that one does not ascend to this faculty of gathering universals with certainty, because the mediation of the senses is not always certain—because it is not exact, but only "however it may be." Nor is there any way other than induction, which <margin>Philoponus</margin> is founded on the sense. **John the Grammarian**, also surnamed **Philoponus** <note>A 6th-century Christian commentator who often critiqued Aristotelian physics and logic.</note>, at the beginning of the last [book of the] *Resolutories*...

<summary>The author critiques the Aristotelian method of induction, arguing that universal laws cannot be reliably formed from sensory observations of individual cases, especially when philosophers like Averroes claim a rule can be made from just a few examples.</summary>

...he writes thus: **analysis is an ascent from the particulars and individuals to the universal** <note>original Greek: ἀνάλυσις ἐστὶν ἀπὸ τῶν μερικῶν καὶ καθ' ἕκαστα ἐπὶ τὰ καθόλου ἄνοδος</note>; that is, a resolution from particulars and individuals toward a universal ascent.
