<meta>This page continues the author’s skeptical critique of Aristotle’s logic. Having previously argued that we cannot know all individuals within a species (like the teeth of every fish), the author now examines the structural requirement of Aristotelian syllogisms: the "universal proposition." He argues that if a universal truth must be built from individual observations, it can never be truly "universal" or "certain."</meta>

->**BOOK FIVE**<-                                                                                                **CH. LXVII**

For the exact same difficulty arises; for whatever universal proposition might be established, it will have been collected and constructed from particulars <note>original: "ex singularibus"; referring to individual cases or specific observations.</note> according to Aristotelian dogma. For no such proposition is known simply from its terms, but is instead tracked down by the senses and completed by a collection of individual instances. I will, if you please, take up this matter to be discussed within the Lyceum <note>The Lyceum was the school founded by Aristotle in Athens; the author is challenging the Aristotelians on their own ground.</note> itself, and I will add what was said by Aristotle: that propositions must be stated "of all" <note>original: "de omni"; refers to the logical requirement that a premise must apply to every single member of a category to be valid for demonstration.</note> and not merely of "some" or "most," if they are to be considered fit for preparing a demonstration. Otherwise, they may be shut out from the doors of demonstration as if they were mere tokens. 

This excludes the response of those who say that Aristotle spoke "of all" not by affirming, but by denying—because he wrote "not in some cases so and in others not, nor at some times so and at other times not." <margin>Refutation of a manifold response.</margin> For what else did he intend to be understood by those words, other than that what is predicated must belong to all and always? Would he not have known how to speak of "many" or "most"? Yet he said "of all." 

Nor do those examples satisfy me when the same thing is predicated of itself, for the condition <note>original: "affectio"; the properties or attributes of a subject.</note> of a subject is not properly and exactly what the subject itself is. Even less satisfactory is the example of the conjunctions of the planets, which do not meet always, but only at their own specific time. For there are various opinions about them, various calculations, and various experiments, as we showed in the third book of this work; and an error of a few tiny minutes in calculating and observing their locations completely subverts the entire demonstration that was being prepared. 

We also exclude the response of those who say that similar things can be conjectured from similar things. For besides the fact that it is false that all particulars are similar—since there are many parts in every thing by which the things themselves are clearly perceived to be dissimilar—certainly that would not be to bring forward propositions "of all." Nor would it harmonize with the other conditions which Aristotle insisted must necessarily belong to a demonstrative proposition: that they be primary, true, certain, and better known than the conclusion. For how can they be primary and true if they are snatched from a conjecture of similarities? How can they be anything but uncertain for that very reason? For we do not "conjecture" what we hold as certain. How can they be better known than the conclusion if the principle is only "probable"? Yet a conclusion ought to be strengthened by demonstration. For what is gathered by conjecture is not necessary, but probable—that is, it is seen as such by a multitude, or by many, or by the wise, but not by *all*. However, that which is "necessary" is so for everyone and entirely; it is decreed not just to "seem" so, but to *be* so and to stand firm.

Therefore, that first absurdity would follow: that propositions collected by conjecture—that is, brought together from a "probable" place, such as from similarity—would be held as the principle of a demonstration. It would also follow that a conclusion would be more certain than its own principle, which Aristotle, along with the whole Lyceum, cries out can in no way be possible. 

But if, pressed by these narrow straits, they turn back to the start and promise that they will collect *all* particulars, not only will this be laughed at as impossible to do, but it will be excluded from the threshold of Aristotelian doctrine by Porphyry. <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Isagoge" (Introduction to Aristotle's Categories) was a standard textbook for over a thousand years.</note> Porphyry, following Plato’s command, judged that one must stop where the process of division reaches individual things. The same applies to collecting them, for collection comes from division; all the more so because those very particulars are said by Aristotle to be infinite—especially since he devised the idea of the eternity of the world. Even if they were not infinite, they are still so great in number that they could never be possessed by any man. 

Where a universal proposition is not possessed, a universal property of the subject cannot be concluded. That a proper attribute <note>original: "affectionẽ propriam"; a characteristic that belongs uniquely and always to a species.</note> of a subject cannot be held universally and most certainly in the way Aristotle wanted has been sufficiently proven: first by the fallacy of the senses, and then by the ignorance of defining. For when the specific difference is unknown, the specific property that flows from it is also unknown, and furthermore...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Aristotelian induction, moving from the authority of Philoponus to Aristotle’s own warnings about over-generalization. The author argues that universal propositions used in logic often lack a solid foundation because the true essence of subjects remains unknown to us.</meta>

->**BOOK FIVE. CHAPTER 68.**<-

He did not want him to have proceeded in such a way because, without considering every individual case, he provided a reason for the whole. Likewise, in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he <note>Aristotle.</note> condemned those who drew conclusions about the rest of a group based only on a few discovered facts. This most clearly agrees with the points we have reported from him, and it contradicts those who did not care to ensure that every rare thing was accounted for, or that unusual occurrences were properly categorized into a genus <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category or class of things.</note>. All of these matters will be discussed more broadly as this work proceeds.

For we have sufficiently shown—both by the reasoning and the authority of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, and from the words of Aristotle himself—what we intended: that the process of proving things through universal propositions <note>A statement that claims something is true for every member of a group (e.g., "All men are mortal").</note> lacks a solid foundation. Consequently, the goal of such a demonstration—that is, the universal <term>affection</term> <note>original: "affectio"; in this context, a property or quality that necessarily belongs to a subject.</note> or property of a subject—is rendered uncertain. This is even more true because the nature of the subject is unknown, and specifically its most "proper difference" <note>The specific characteristic that defines a thing and distinguishes it from everything else in the same category.</note>. As was made clear when we discussed definitions, if the difference is unknown, the property that flows from it is also unknown.

For whether there is only one "form" for a composite thing, as St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> and many others held, or several forms, as John [Duns] Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Franciscan philosopher often contrasted with Aquinas.</note> and most others held, everyone nevertheless attempts to deduce a specific property from a specific difference. This is true whether they believe that property is a distinct thing (in the manner of Aquinas), or that it arises from the very nature of the thing (in the manner of Scotus), or however else they judge it to be separated. We have shown above that while searching for these things, one often encounters opportunities for deceptive and uncertain guesswork; it is best, therefore, if only "probability" is extracted from such efforts.

Therefore, the process will rely on probable conjecture rather than certain science, unless it is mixed with the fallacy that we will soon show follows those who believe they have gathered everything from only a few instances. Thus, from the arguments they believe to be most certain, they will slip down into "dialectical topics" <note>Arguments based on probability and accepted opinion rather than absolute, scientific certainty.</note>. These are indeed probable, but they remain uncertain precisely because other probable arguments can be brought against them from the opposite side. Aristotle prudently taught about these "topics" in eight books, so that we might know how to dispute with probable arguments on both sides of an issue.

I would also add—and not without support—that not only is no proposition truly and simply universal unless it is said "of all" (that is, when there is nothing under the subject of which the predicate is not said) or "of none" (that is, when there is nothing under the subject from which the predicate is not removed), but the very form of the <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All A is B, All C is A, therefore All C is B).</note> is entirely empty when propositions are placed in it without such conditions. For by that very rule, all good syllogisms are constructed from common terms. 

However, I believe I have done enough through my own efforts and the reasons I have brought forward to weaken the universal propositions that Aristotle and other pagan philosophers use so much. Those who wish to see these matters regarding the form of the syllogism—including what is properly called "simply universal" and what is merely universal to a certain extent, and what terms are required to construct them—should know that I do not consider everything I am writing to be sufficient for creating a perfectly universal proposition, but only one that is "in a certain respect" <note>original: "secundum quid"; a logical term meaning something is true only under certain conditions or in a specific sense, rather than absolutely.</note>. Indeed, he <note>Aristotle.</note> wanted it to be said that "everything which is" or "whatever is" must be included. If that is true, a much greater difficulty would weigh upon anyone trying to construct a universal proposition than the one we have already debated at length.

Those who desire to see these things plainly <note>original: "ingenue"</note> can look at the "Fifth Question" of Pierre d'Ailly <note>A famous 14th-century French theologian and mathematician.</note> in his first commentary on the *Sentences* of theology. For my part, I will now attempt to show that those who strive to prove these denied propositions fall into fallacies condemned by Aristotle himself.

<meta>This page concludes Book 5, focusing on the logical failures of induction—drawing universal conclusions from specific examples. The author uses Aristotle’s own biological observations to show how easily "universal" rules are broken by nature's diversity.</meta>

# **BOOK V.**

## **That those who contend that all things can be gathered from many, and who busy themselves with proving a universal proposition that has been denied by an adversary, commit both the fallacy of the consequent and the begging of the question; and that those who think they are demonstrating according to Aristotle’s doctrine are arguing only with probability, so that they may be well-situated with them. Chapter 13 and the last of the fifth book.**

Furthermore, a greater fault in the Aristotelian discipline is when someone, relying upon it, professes knowledge and teaches error, using fallacies in place of demonstrations—errors which Aristotle himself attempted to reveal and refute in two books. Among others, there is one famous fallacy called the "consequent" <note>A logical error where one assumes that if 'B' follows 'A', then 'A' must always follow 'B'. In this context, it refers to assuming that because many members of a group have a trait, the whole group must have it.</note>, into which all those fall who gather a "whole" from only "particulars," rather than from every single instance. 
<margin>It is shown how easily many fall into the fallacy of the consequent</margin> 
For they are deceived because, while particulars contained under a universal thing can be inferred and gathered from that universal, the reverse is not true. The reasoning does not flow backward; the discourse is not reciprocal. For it does not follow that if you have collected some, or many, or several, or most instances, you have therefore collected them all. Wherefore it happens that unless you know every single particular—which, according to the opinion of both Aristotle and Plato, cannot be known—you will stumble into this very fallacy as often as you attempt to establish a universal proposition (a statement made about "all"). But if you say to one who gathers a universal from singular instances that either all must be granted or an "instance" <note>In logic, an "instance" or "counter-instance" is a single exception that disproves a universal rule.</note> must be provided, you have said nothing that pertains to true science. 
<margin>Response</margin> 
<margin>A multi-layered refutation</margin> 
Indeed, as far as the duty of a dialectician <note>A practitioner of logical debate.</note> is concerned, you may have said something; for even if your adversary does not know how to bring forward a counter-instance, you will not gather "science" simply from his ignorance. Will you not rather persist in your fallacy the more you lack someone to correct you and mend the error you have committed? That is to say, you will lack a just rebuker to teach you that what you thought was universally and generally true is not, in fact, true for the whole. For there is no suitability, no necessity in your logical connection; rather, there is error, madness, and fallacy. For example, if someone were to say that "every animal moves its lower jaw," and were to generalize <note>original: "inducer," from "inductio" (induction).</note> this from a thousand or perhaps six thousand species of animals, he would appear to be a speaker of the truth. 
<margin>This is confirmed by the authority of Aristotle himself</margin> 
But when he comes to the single case of the crocodile, he will be found a liar, for among all animals, it alone moves its upper jaw. Even if you knew ten thousand species of living things possessed a mouth and affirmed by induction that it was so in the rest, when you came to the cicada, you would be pulled back by Aristotle, who teaches in the fourth book of *On the Nature of Animals* <note>Known today as *History of Animals*.</note> that this very creature lacks a mouth. From this same author, you could draw a rule that you should by no means affirm that what is found to be in many individuals is in all of the same species, or what is absent in many is absent in all. For where he wrote in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals* that the horse, the ass, the mule, the deer, and the cat lack a gallbladder <note>original: "fele" or "fel," referring to the gallbladder or bile.</note>, he added that regarding man, it is ambiguous, since some are seen to have a gallbladder in the liver while others lack it. Therefore, he says, the whole genus is in doubt. For those who find it one way attribute the same to all, as if everyone had it in the same manner as the few they observed. And regarding sheep, he added the same: that in Naxos they have a gallbladder, but in a certain part of the Chalcidian territory (as we also reported above), they do not. Who would not turn this rule against the author himself whenever he either affirms or denies anything about a whole species based on some, or even very many, of its individuals? For he could have seen a part of the individuals of that species that behave one way, but failed to see another part which nature formed in a different and diverse way. But, granted that it is not very easy to bring forward a true counter-instance, Philoponus—the most diligent interpreter of Aristotle—asserts that one can nevertheless be brought forward, and this universally and

# **BOOK V** [space] **Folio 169**

...absolutely affirms it: and Severinus Boethius also gives this to be understood, as does Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, even if he perhaps restricted himself to contingent matter. But Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> certainly makes no exception; nor is this to be taken only verbally or superficially, but in fact and thoroughly. As I say, while it might not be very easy to produce a true reason, you certainly would not deny that it is very easy to produce *some* reason. Once this reason is brought forward, even if it is not supported by all truth, if you nevertheless busy yourself with proving a universal proposition, will you not mix error with error? And from a prior fallacy, you will slip into another fallacy, which is called **begging the question** <term>petitio principii: a logical fallacy where the premise of an argument assumes the truth of the conclusion it is trying to prove</term>. One notable form of this is when those about to prove anything—either unknown or already denied by an opponent—take that very thing as if it were known or conceded. <margin>He shows by example the lapse into the fallacious proof of begging the question.</margin> Into this fallacious method, which was condemned by Aristotle himself, all those fall who, when a universal proposition is denied, try to prove that very same thing.

Take for example someone who wishes to prove that this attribute—that is, the aptitude for laughing—belongs to every human being, and someone else denies it. Will he have any other way of proving it, if he wishes to use induction, than to collect all particular instances? When he cannot bring them all together into one, having collected only some, he will say: "and so it is with each individual." If he does this, does he not "beg" what was denied, and commit a fallacy? For he who denies that "every human is capable of laughter" does not thereby affirm that "every human is *not* capable of laughter," since a universal affirmation does not follow from a universal negation; rather, it suggests that *some* individual is not capable of laughter. And if someone wants to provide a counter-example—whether that instance be true, false, or doubtful—he will nevertheless set it forth and explain it, just as it has been recorded in memory that certain people never laughed. This is perhaps where the name *Agelastus* <note>original: "agelasti"; derived from the Greek word for "one who does not laugh." Marcus Licinius Crassus was famously given this nickname.</note> came from. Yet the logician still affirms that all are capable of laughter.

->**Response.**<-
<margin>Response.</margin>
But if it is said: "I am not speaking of the *act* of laughing, but of the *aptitude* for it, which flows from wonder, which likewise stems from reason."

->**A Manifold Confutation.**<-
<margin>A manifold confutation.</margin>
If the opponent then replies that there are other things endowed with reason (as discussed above) which nevertheless do not laugh nor were made for laughing, will the first man not be stuck in his tracks, so that he can no longer contend that laughter is a property unique to humans? Especially if it is denied that those who never laughed even had the *aptitude* for laughing—which, of course, cannot be confirmed except by the effect derived from it. What if the faculty of laughter were given to every animal, even if many species of rational beings were admitted? What if it were denied that reason belongs universally to any individuals of a species? What, I ask, if it were denied? Would he be able to prove that very thing in any other way—if he relies on Aristotle—than by induction? And if he does so, does he not fall back into the same error?

->**Response.**<-
<margin>Response.</margin>
But someone will say: "Even if I or another cannot complete a perfect induction, nevertheless, over many past centuries, this or that has been observed in such a way by everyone, or by most. Therefore, I can gather a universal rule, even if I have not examined every single individual instance."

->**A Manifold Confutation.**<-
<margin>A manifold confutation.</margin>
But it is not so; for you are referring yourself back to the history of other observers, and you are being led by simple human faith. Furthermore, you could not have known all observers thoroughly. What if others observed things differently? What if they were deceived either by their own senses or by trust in history? Just as in detecting the movements of the celestial spheres, we have proved above that many did not correctly record what had been observed.

->**Another Example.**<-
<margin>Another example.</margin>
Moreover, even if the induction is done correctly and is wrongly denied, you still cannot prove it without falling into fallacies, as we have shown in the example where we now are. This will be even more evident regarding the other human attributes, which some say flow from the principles of the individual—specifically concerning sleep, and that in various ways. For someone might easily affirm that everyone sees dreams <term>insomnia: here used in the Latin sense of 'visions seen in sleep' rather than the modern medical term for sleeplessness</term>, and likewise that all people lie down when seized by sleep. But, as we also noted in the first book, Aristotle writes in the fourth volume of *The History of Animals* that there were men and women who never dreamed, and it happened to some of them as they aged that, once a dream was seen, [their health] was changed...

...by the habit of the body, whether in sickness or in death. I will pass over those whom I myself have known to do even greater and more wonderful things—so much so that you could only distinguish with great difficulty whether they were gripped by sleep or released from it, a matter which we discussed in the second book of this work. Let it suffice, as far as the present purpose is concerned, that universal propositions cannot be formed regarding human habits and affections of this kind. These do not follow the entire species, even if they seem to follow many individuals; and they themselves are subject to what more recent philosophers call **instances** <term>instantiis: specific cases that disprove a universal rule</term>, whatever those may be, which are indeed well known. Thus, we have shown above in part concerning the Ethiopians and vital organs placed backwards <note>A reference to *situs inversus*, a rare condition where the heart and other organs are mirrored from their normal positions</note>; how much more obvious, then, will the fallacy be in other things?

[Marginal note: Removal of an objection.]
If you assert that you are not speaking of accidents and those functions that follow matter, but of those that follow form and species, recall what we said in the previous chapter when we were debating the "risibility" <term>the capacity for laughter, used by logicians as the classic example of a "property" unique to humans</term> and teachability of man, and the heat of the sun and fire. Add to this that Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, in the first book *Against the Gentiles*, teaches that many properties of things—not just a few, but certainly the majority—are unknown. But in those things that are known to almost everyone, how many "instances" (exceptions) are there, I ask? Not just any kind, but the most certain.

[Marginal note: Another example.]
Let us take, if you please, an example from a very well-known matter, so that we may simultaneously detect the fallacy and confirm the opinion of Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator who critiqued Aristotle</note>: that there is no universal which does not suffer an "instance." This is how the Latin philosophers put it; the Greeks call it <note>original: ἴστασιν</note> *an objection*. Suppose, then, someone wishes to prove—from the herb aloe—the power of being able to draw out yellow bile from human bodies, whether by its juice or otherwise. Suppose another person denies it. Suppose, I say, someone has said: "Every drop of juice from the aloe herb admitted into a human stomach is capable of drawing out yellow bile." This proposition is held as true among philosophers and physicians, since from this person, and that person, and another, and from many and nearly innumerable people, the juice of aloe—whether drunk or swallowed as a pill—has drawn out yellow bile by loosening the bowels. From this, first through sense, then memory and experience, a universal is forged by induction, as Aristotle taught at the end of his *Posterior Analytics*. But let an adversary deny what was said; let him appeal to Aristotle affirming that <note>original: τὰ πρῶτα ἐπαγωγῇ γνωρίζειν ἀναγκαῖον</note> *it is necessary to know the first things—or (as Philoponus and others interpret it) the principles—by induction.* Let the adversary turn away from the Aristotelian tribunal and allege a just cause, and if you please, let him press him with this contradictory proposition: "Some aloe juice, when drunk or swallowed as a pill, does not draw out yellow bile from the human body," and let him strengthen his "instance" with an example. Certainly, he who is about to demonstrate this property of aloe must prove his universal. If he proves it by induction and collects all the particulars (for Aristotle taught no other way of constructing a universal), he will be seeking that which was denied at the beginning, which is doubtful, and frequently false. It is "denied" because it has already been answered that "not all" apply, and therefore "some do not." It is "doubtful" because it is equally doubtful regarding, for example, Peter—of whom you intend to assert this, though you do not know him—as it is of John, whom you likewise do not know. In judging these, you have used similarity and conjecture—based on, say, Martin, James, and Thomas, whom you obviously knew long ago to have experienced those things which you now wish to ascribe to others. But plainly

[Marginal note: Removal of an objection.]
you are playing the fool, because similarities that are believed to exist are often found to be dissimilar, and there is no place for conjecture where the most certain knowledge is sought. Nor does that crude reasoning stand in the way: for acting uniformly in many cases...

...in most cases, unless it is hindered. For if a thing occurs in most cases, it does not occur in all; and a thousand hindrances can occur, whether from the outside or from within. To wish to transfer the same order of universal nature to the particular natures and properties of things in every function and duty is the mark of a man poorly acquainted with natural things and unfamiliar with philosophy, who affirms doubtful things as certain. Yet that is not only doubtful, but frequently false. For although it is brought about by the juice of the aloe (not to depart from the example once accepted) that yellow bile <note>original: "flaua bilis." In the medical theory of the four humors, yellow bile was associated with heat and bitterness; aloes were used to "purge" it.</note> is conquered by the bowels, this is true in very many cases, in most cases, and in the vast majority of cases—but it is not true in all. For there exists someone who affirms that after taking aloe juice, his belly is stayed and tightened, and all those things happen which are the opposite of what others suffer when taking the same thing. We do not invent this; there lives to this day an honest and learned man, especially skilled in the medical art, who has testified this to me most firmly more than once. 

You will say, perhaps, that this happens because the juice was spoiled. But this man, a most experienced physician, does not take what has not been proven by medical arts or what is untried by others, as he was intending to make a trial of the truth in this most marvelous matter. Nor should you attribute this to some sudden change made in his body; for he says he has experienced this very often—even always—whenever he took it. Thus, as far as he is concerned, he has a certain method of healing: whenever he wanted to stay and tighten the belly, or whenever he wanted to induce a styptic <term>stypticam: a substance that shrinks or constricts body tissue to stop secretions</term> nature in the bowels, he used aloe. Thus, from that case, a path is opened to prove the opposing opinion: that not every juice of the aloe is able to lead out yellow bile. 

<margin>Multiple remedies for an objection.</margin> 

But let us not flee from a single man as if he were a monster <note>In this context, "monstrum" refers to a biological marvel or an "omen" that deviates from the natural order.</note>. Do not the records of physicians, and especially Galen, record that what is poison to some animals is healthy for a human? And conversely, that what is poison to a human is a most pleasing food for wild beasts and a most healthy fodder? But let us not depart from the human being, lest a difference in species provide a handle for caviling <note>making petty or unnecessary objections</note>. Let us stay within the same species. Let us not cite the prodigies of Pliny related in his seventh book, which he himself says were made by ingenious Nature as "playthings" for herself but "miracles" for us; instead, let us cite that poison on which a certain girl was fed and nourished (as we also said before) on the authority of Galen the physician. 

<margin>Difficulty [unclear]</margin>

And let us cite garlic, which is usually taken as food by almost everyone; that it is healthy and sought after and praised against the malice of many foods is so clear and uncontroversial that if we wished to prove it, we would be blamed for a fault. Yet that same garlic, to Jacobus of Forlì <note>Giacomo da Forlì (c. 1364–1414), a famous Italian physician and commentator on Galen.</note>—a noble physician not long before our age—acted as a poison and harmed him. He affirmed it and left it in the records of literature that it was noxious to him, and that when it was taken, he endured the same things as those who had been stricken by a deadly poison. 

Consider also my son Trimulus, to whom rhubarb is sweet and pleasant to the taste. Others say and feel that it is bitter. And unless the reasoning of medicine intervened, it would be rejected as unpleasant and hostile to the palate; but the boy takes it as a delicacy, and if ever he is troubled by worms or indigestion, he is so far from refusing it when offered that he even seeks it out when it is not offered. He is moved by no reason of a medical potion—for his age does not allow it—but solely by the delight of the taste. 

But let us not bring forward modern experiments and those of our own times more than is proper. Who will oppose Galen himself when he determines that poison did him very little harm? Who, I say, of the bolder physicians of our time will oppose not only Aristotle (as we showed a little while ago regarding the reason of digestion) but also Theophrastus, who determines on the authority of Thrasyas that the same thing is a medicine for some and not a medicine for others? And who will not agree with him when he asserts that Eudemus of Chios was not purged even after taking twenty-two doses of hellebore <note>Hellebore was a notoriously violent purgative; taking twenty-two doses without effect was considered a superhuman feat of bodily resistance.</note> in one day?

I say nothing, I repeat, of these, or of others to whom honey seems bitter, or both sweet and bitter at once, or neither.

To know this sufficiently once again, it is also necessary to understand and weigh the mutual affections—whether friendly or hostile—of the temperament and the medicine, proceeding from the nature of the thing itself, from manifest qualities, and from those which are called "occult" [hidden]. One must know their relations of proportion. For if rhubarb <note>original: "rheōbarbaricũ"</note> is to be called and held as an antidote for bad humor <term>humor: in ancient medicine, the fluids of the body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to determine health and character</term>, it is necessary to relate it to the body. For if it is considered by itself and not related to anything else, it will not be called or held to be a healthy medicine, since its power of purging is entirely ineffective unless it is received into the stomach or intestines and warmed up.

Wherefore, it is necessary to speak of man as well, regarding those things we have discussed and their mutual proportion. These matters are much more difficult to prove—not just to find—and are more uncertain than the proof itself is uncertain when taken on its own. What we have said regarding both man and the medical potion, using a very well-known example that does not shrink from Aristotelian examples (so that nothing may be granted to prove anything universally in the Aristotelian manner), the same judgment applies to other things. This is even more certain the further things are removed from the senses and common life, lest they say we merely dwell on examples from the medical faculty, which many consider an art and not a science.

For we have dealt with the instance of the universal proposition in itself, which we have sufficiently shown does not hold firm, even in those things considered most true. Nor should I be hindered by the opinion of 

<margin>Removal of an objection.</margin>

those who say that the knowledge of simple terms depends on the sense, but that which consists in a complex <note>original: "complexu." In logic, "simple terms" are individual words like "man" or "mortal," while "complex" refers to propositions or sentences like "Every man is mortal."</note> does not depend on it. For according to the authority of Aristotle: whether it be without a middle or with a middle <term>middle: the "middle term" in a syllogism that connects the premises to reach a conclusion</term>, it nonetheless acknowledges the sense as its parent; it is necessary to return to the first knowledge of the senses.

Aristotle himself teaches at the end of the second *Posterior Analytics* <note>original: "secundi analytici," a foundational work on the logic of scientific demonstration</note> that these things are known by the first induction, and he testifies with a very clear voice that the sense itself effects the universal in us. His interpreters and paraphrasts openly confirm this as well. Among them is Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for making Aristotle's dense works more accessible</note>, who teaches that the universal itself is both established and known by induction, through which one arrives at an understanding of the universal from the knowledge of particulars (as we said before). The assumptions of this reasoning will be the senses themselves, since individuals are known by sense.

Therefore, it is false to say that the mind is aided only by sensory knowledge on the grounds that the intellect can, by its own power, compose and divide terms and bring forth something by itself, either concerning the subject or its affection <term>affection: a property or quality of a subject</term>. For such people have not walked enough with Aristotle, who teaches everywhere that all our knowledge—that is, human knowledge—arises from the senses, whence the dispute falls back on experiments.

Therefore, according to Aristotle and his celebrated followers (and we speak no differently here), all human knowledge, even that which consists in a complex, depends on the sense, whether it be true or false. In his view, it is even decreed that the truth expressed in speech depends on things that are external and captured by the sense; truth, moreover, is perceived in a complex. Therefore, he denies Aristotle who denies that all human knowledge has its principle and foundation in the sense, whether that knowledge be simple or composite—the latter being formed from the knowledge of simple things.

Wherefore he undoubtedly left it recorded that **nothing is in the intellect which was not previously in the sense**, since composite knowledge arises from simple, and simple arises from the sense. From this, let them bring whatever they wish—whether by itself, or by parts, or by similarity, or by remission, or by effect—they will not be able to reject this unless they likewise reject Aristotle himself.

<margin>Epilogue of the entire process against demonstration.</margin>

We have seen, therefore, that the foundation of demonstration does not stand, because the sense is not always certain. Thus, demonstration is uncertain because it takes its principle from the senses, which vary among different men—even those who are learned and prudent. From this variation, there arises a varied imagination and opinion, and a varied judgment of the intellect, following the diversity of imagination and sense...

<summary>The author argues that all human knowledge, including complex logical propositions, is rooted in sensory experience. By citing Aristotle and Themistius, he contends that because our senses are fallible and vary between individuals, the "universal truths" used in scientific demonstration are inherently uncertain.</summary>

**BOOK.**

...[comprehended], you might very easily be able to deduce and possess for yourself other propositions of that kind, which—once you have fulfilled your words with deeds—promise and provide eternal salvation for both you and others. Once these are truly understood, no strife is born, no bitter dispute at all; for there, it is not mere opinion, but faith, and from faith comes a peace which the world cannot give <note>original: "pax quam mūdus dare non potest"; a reference to the Gospel of John 14:27</note>: a peace which, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul (Philippians 4:7)</note> says, passes all understanding. From opinion comes disagreement, lawsuits, and turmoil; because of this disadvantage, the human race—as a peculiar punishment for its own pride—wars and struggles more than all other animals. For irrational animals fight over food, shelter, or mating; but man, beyond these things, has also suffered wars due to a diversity of opinions. This happens not only within himself, but with others, since very often hatred arises from differing opinions, and from hatred come wars. Those who are led by the faith and discipline of Christ are so far removed from these things that they value nothing more highly than the love which the sacred scriptures have shown them. But since we have dealt elsewhere with these demonstrations, let us now enter upon the sixth and final book of this work.

**THE SIXTH BOOK OF GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, LORD [OF MIRANDOLA] AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA, IN THE EXAMINATION OF THE VANITY OF GENTILE DOCTRINE AND THE TRUTH OF CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE, WHICH IS THE THIRD [BOOK] AGAINST ARISTOTLE AND THE LAST.**

**PREFACE.**

It is said that Carneades <note>A Greek Skeptic philosopher known for arguing both sides of a case to show the uncertainty of human reason</note>, when he was about to write against the doctrines of the Stoics, purged the upper parts of his body with white hellebore <term>elleboro albo: a plant used in antiquity as a powerful purgative, believed to clear the mind and cure "madness" or mental cloudedness</term>. I believe no one who considers the weight of human reasoning will deny that this was done prudently. For it can easily happen that foreign or distorted visions appear present to the mind because of corrupted "humors" <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament</note>, from which those backward phantasms are both born and shaped; and from there, the true estimation of things is both corrupted and destroyed. Perhaps it is for this reason that famous writers, both among the Gentiles and among our own people, have "sung a palinode" <term>palinodiam: a Greek term for a recantation or a song in which the author retracts a view expressed in a former poem</term> after their works had been composed and published with great care. And they did this rightly and nobly when they discovered they had wandered from the truth. 

I, however, suspect that even without drinking hellebore, many will think that I am writing a "palinode" myself. They might think this because I have already published an introduction to logic, and yet soon after, in this very work, I have discussed logicians more than once [critically]. But I showed there that I had already meditated on this work, and that I would not be condemning the faculty of logic itself—which even the Sceptics could not condemn, since they used logic itself as their primary tool in order to refute it. I have sufficiently indicated that I could not patiently endure the arrogance of many people. Therefore, the art which I taught is not to be cast away, for it is useful for the "discourse of reason" given by nature itself, which human art and institutions founded upon it then perfect. 

But indeed, I also clearly testified that those very human institutions and arts could be weakened and rendered uncertain by other arts—and most of all, that "demonstration" itself (an invention of the philosophers, most cultivated and elaborated by Aristotle) could be rendered uncertain through our thought and study, even by using the foundations of Peripatetic philosophy <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching</note>. This is in addition to what we brought forward in the first volumes of this work from various philosophies to weaken human wisdom itself. It remains now to address the specific [theories] of Aristotle which are celebrated...

**That many errors in reporting and refuting the views of the ancient philosophers were committed by Aristotle in his *Physics*, in which place Parmenides and Melissus are defended in multiple ways. Chapter One.**

Hitherto we have shown that the art of demonstration established by Aristotle falters with much vanity; and we placed the end of that discussion in the fifth book of this work. It remains for us to reveal that he demonstrated poorly those things which he thought he had handled rightly, and to point out his remaining vanities so that they may be rejected. In the first place, however, his errors are many regarding the views of the ancient philosophers, whether in reporting them or refuting them. Many of his arguments are likewise based on a far from solid foundation, which many people nevertheless admire as if they were demonstrations. Let us begin, therefore, from the *Physics* <note>original: "auscultatione physica," literally "physical listening," referring to Aristotle's lectures on nature</note>, and from the first book on natural principles, and from there we shall deal with many things concerning supernatural matters. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding Aristotle’s misinterpretation of the Eleatic philosophers Parmenides and Melissus. BOOK SIX                                                                                                   PAGE 174

...is <note>The word "gis" at the start of this page is the conclusion of "magis" (more) from the previous page.</note> usually spoken of as "infinite" privatively <term>privatively: a way of defining something by what it lacks (a privation)</term>, because it is deprived of a fitting limit; in this way, many have called prime matter <term>prime matter: the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe that has the potential to take on any shape</term> infinite—that is, lacking its due form and boundary by its own nature. However, they spoke of God—whose power and might has no boundary, no limit, and no end—as infinite negatively <term>negatively: here meaning "without negation," or limitless in a positive, divine sense</term>. Moreover, they held that the name "infinite" applies to quantity, which can be divided if it is continuous or increased if it is discrete, unto infinity. Yet that infinity of quantities does not exist in actuality, nor is it perfect. For previously, this terminology of the "finite" and "infinite" was held among the Pythagoreans in the same way as "even" and "odd." Parmenides was among their number; hence, matter was not only called "infinite" (insofar as, considered in itself, it would be limited by no form, but would take on various boundaries as forms arrive and recede), but it was even called "multitude." This is because it would not be "one" if it did not have its own boundary or end. In this same way, it was called "duality" <note>original: "dualitas"</note> by Iamblichus <margin>Iamblichus</margin> in his work *On the Pythagorean Sect*. 

Therefore, by that definition of the infinite where "infinite" is taken to mean a lack of perfection—just as when something is considered in terms of quantity, it indicates that it is least perfect—by that definition, I say, Parmenides did not wish that "First Being" <note>God or the ultimate reality</note> to be considered infinite. But Melissus understood the infinite by another logic, by which the word indicates the excellence and preeminence of power and might. In this way, later theologians also speak of the infinite negatively—that is, encompassed by no end and no limit. In this manner, infinity is usually attributed not to bulk <note>original: "moli"</note> but to power and virtue. <margin>Porphyrius. / Remoter from [the physical].</margin> 

But far more could be written in their defense, from which I shall abstain, since Cardinal Bessarion <margin>Bessarion.</margin>—who was also the Patriarch of Constantinople—has written much on this matter in the second volume of his work *Against the Calumniator of Plato*. This work was written in Latin and printed twice, in Rome and in Venice. For in that work, many poems of Parmenides are translated into the Latin language, and the words of Melissus are cited, by which it is most clearly established that they intended something other than what Aristotle attributed to them. Simplicius <margin>Simplicius.</margin>—one of the Greek interpreters of Aristotle who was great in both deed and name—also wrote in defense of Parmenides and Melissus. Although Aristotle does not cite him in this matter, Bessarion seems to rely on him to some extent. For when Simplicius was explaining the first book of the *Physical Lectures*, <margin>Third defense.</margin> he wrote thus:

<note>original Greek: "δηλεῖ δὲ ὁ πλάτων θαυμάζων οὕτως τὸν παρμενίδην, ὃν διελέχθη ὑποκεῖ, καὶ βαθέως κολυμβητοῦ δεῖσθαι λέγων τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτοῦ. καὶ ἀριστοτέλης δὲ τὸ βάθος αὐτοῦ τῆς σοφίας ὑπονοεῖν φαίνεται, ὅτ’ ἀνλέγει, παρμενίδης ἔοικε ποὺ βλέπειν. καὶ οὗτοι οὐ ποτὲ μὲν τὸ παραλελειμμένον ἀναπληροῦσι, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀσαφῶς εἰρημένον, σαφηνίζοντες, ποτὲ δὲ τὸ ἐπὶ τῶν νοητῶν εἰρημένον ὡς μὴ δυνάμενα τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἐφαρμόττειν διακρίνοντες, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ ὂν καὶ ἀκίνητον λεγόντων."</note> 

That is: Plato manifests his admiration for Parmenides in this way, whom he represents as being refuted, saying that his thought requires a deep-sea diver. And Aristotle also seems to hint at the depth of his wisdom when he says, "Parmenides seems to have been looking elsewhere." And these men <note>the commentators</note> sometimes fill in what was left out, sometimes clarify what was said obscurely, and sometimes distinguish those things said about intelligible matters <term>intelligible matters: things understood by the mind/intellect rather than perceived by the senses</term> as being unable to fit physical things, as when they spoke regarding "being" and the "immobile." 

And when he [Simplicius] had proceeded a bit further, he said:

<note>original Greek: "ὁμολογεῖ δὲ ὁ ἀλέξανδρος ἐν μὲν τοῖς πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ἅπερ ἐστὶ περὶ τοῦ νοητοῦ ὄντος τὸν παρμενίδην ἕν τὸ ὄντι, καὶ ἀκίνητον λέγειν. κατὰ δὲ τὴν τῶν πολλῶν δόξαν καὶ τὰ φαινόμενα, φασί φυσιολογῶν, οὔτε ἕν λέγων εἶναι τὸ ὄν, οὔτε ἀγένητον, ἀρχὰς τῶν γινομένων ὑπέθετο, πῦρ καὶ γῆν. τὴν μὲν γῆν ὡς ὕλην ὑποθεθείς. τὸ δὲ πῦρ ὡς ποιητικὸν αἴτιον, καὶ οὐνομάζει φησὶ τὸ μὲν πῦρ, φῶς. τὸ δὲ γῆν, σκότος."</note> 

Which is to say: Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> agrees that in those matters concerning truth, which pertain to intelligible being, Parmenides says that being is one and immobile. But according to the opinion of the many and to appearances, he speaks as a natural philosopher, neither saying that being is one, nor ungenerated; he proposed the principles of things that come to be as fire and earth. He proposed earth as matter and fire as the efficient cause, and he says he names fire "light" and earth "darkness."

BOOK SIXTH [space] 176.
The definition of place handed down by Aristotle is attacked by Philoponus and others; space and its three dimensions, which Aristotle himself rejected, are openly defended. Chapter Four.

1 <margin>The definition of place</margin> Indeed, the definition of place has been much more severely attacked, and the opinion of those whom Aristotle himself had rejected has been defended. For they have said that it is not only unnecessary, but neither probable nor consistent with reason, to say that the outermost surface of a surrounding body is "place." This is because every body is located somewhere, yet the outermost body <note>This refers to the "outermost sphere" or the edge of the universe in the Aristotelian model.</note>, which encloses all other things and by which everything else is bounded, cannot be located anywhere at all. Nor do those excuses provide a sufficient explanation <margin>Refutation of the response.</margin>—namely, that such a body is "in a place" only in regards to its parts—as seemed correct to Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher known for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, Themistius, and others. For by such an abuse of language, they do not truly or properly say that bodies are set in a place, nor are they in a place in any real sense, if being "in a place" means being surrounded and enclosed by a location—that is, being contained by the surface of a surrounding body. Likewise, it is rightly decreed that a place must be equal to the thing located within it, and not smaller; and we should not establish anything against all philosophy that would suggest the same thing, in the same respect, could both locate and be located. For the commentators, <margin>Refutation of the response.</margin> says Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an Alexandrian philosopher who famously critiqued Aristotle’s physics, paving the way for later theories of momentum and vacuum.</note> in his commentary on the fourth book of the *Physics*, throw everything into confusion on this matter. And Aristotle, cloaking the weakness of his reasoning in obscurity, spoke in such a way that he allowed his arguments to be twisted however one pleased. 

To these points, some argue that if place is the limit of a containing thing that holds and situates a body within itself, it would follow that someone could be moved to a place while actually remaining at rest in their own proper place. They bring up the example of wine that is carried around inside a wine-flask <note>original: "oenophoro"</note>. Nor can it be said accurately and sincerely that the wine moves "by accident" <term>By accident: In Aristotelian logic, a movement or property that is not essential to the thing itself, like a person moving because the ship they are sitting on is moving.</term>. For it truly moves to a place, and yet it also truly seems to remain at rest, contained by the same surface that surrounded it before it was moved. <margin>Removal of the objection.</margin> Nor does the consideration of a "higher" place interfere—that place in respect to which the located object is said to move because it is positioned differently than it was before. For that is not properly the "place" which surrounds the object’s own place, but rather that which closes in and contains the body being situated. 

Furthermore, they argue that if place is a surface, it would follow that things moving toward a place are moving toward a surface, insofar as place is a surface. But insofar as it is a surface, it lacks the power to preserve the thing located within it. Yet Aristotle attributed the cause of motion to this very power: that an object might rest and be preserved in its own proper place once it has reached it. But if someone were to say that a thing is nourished <margin>Refutation of the response.</margin> and preserved by a surface—not because it is a surface, but because it is the surface of a natural body—there would easily follow a contradiction of another Aristotelian dogma. In that dogma, he holds it as certain and obvious that every body composed of elements is governed by contrary qualities; for a temperament <note>original: "temperamentum," referring to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> is constituted from them. For as John the Scholastic <note>John Philoponus is often referred to as "the Grammarian" or "the Scholastic."</note> <margin>John the Scholastic.</margin>—an interpreter of Aristotle following the school of Ammonius—discusses in his first commentary on *On Generation*, the temperament of human bodies is formed when the acting qualities of the bodies themselves pass into one another (to translate his Greek words). Furthermore, from contrary qualities comes not preservation, but destruction and corruption, both for the thing itself and for that which is located. For it is impossible that the qualities which are contrary in both should not act upon each other and, as it were, wage war; from which, sooner or later, death flows. And besides, there are those who deny that a surface is a place, but rather that "place" is the part of the body that is said to be terminated at the surface itself (when considered mathematically). And these people do not entirely agree with Aristotle. But those who say that the elements are preserved in more remote places—for example, fire in the concave of the moon’s sphere, or earth in the center—do not mean "insofar as that is a surface" or "this is a point," but insofar as they are in such a distance and position in the universe. These people call that "place" by a great abuse of the word, because it situates lower bodies not primarily and by itself, but as if by accident and through something else. And furthermore, they do a great injustice by calling a point a "place," which is more truly

It transitions from questioning if the outermost heaven has a "place" to whether any body can be said to be "in a place" if that place is merely a two-dimensional surface.</meta>

**BOOK** <note>original: "LIBER"</note>

and lacking place, and so small—or rather, non-existent—that it cannot surround even the smallest things. And we have discussed these matters largely from Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Christian philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries challenging Aristotle’s physics.</note>: to omit those who do not accept that pure fire is preserved in the concavity of the lunar sphere, nor that any entirely pure elements are held there. Thomas Garbius <note>Likely Tommaso del Garbo (d. 1370), a prominent Florentine physician and commentator.</note> affirms that they do not truly exist even in a mixture, beyond those points we noted in the book on elements.
<margin>Thomas Garbius, Hasdai.</margin>
Hasdai the Hebrew <note>Hasdai Crescas (c. 1340–1410), a Jewish philosopher whose work *The Light of the Lord* famously critiqued Aristotelianism and influenced later Renaissance thought.</note> also asserts many things against the definition of place. Among these is that many of the ancients did not agree that the definition of place handed down by Aristotle was suitable for bodies that are carried by straight-line motion. This is because the proper place of the parts that are moved toward the motion of the whole is not a surrounding surface so equal that it has a separate agreement with the parts of that place. For if (by way of example) the highest part of the air agrees with the lowest part of the fire that contains and surrounds it, the middle part of the air will not agree with it in the same way, nor will it be replaced in its own natural place. Even if it were asserted that it fits the part itself by its own nature, it would still be considered a different place from that of the whole and entire body situated there. Furthermore, it is revealed to be false that all bodies that are placed agree with their places; this is seen both from the circumference of the highest heaven and even from the earth, to which the assigned "place" is not a surface but the lowest point—to which the name of "place" does not rightly apply.

I return to Philoponus, who consistently draws out this absurdity: that a body cannot be placed in a "place" insofar as it is a body, because the boundary—that is, the surface or the extremity of the container—does not have three dimensions, which are required to surround a body insofar as it is a body. For a body is in a place precisely because it is a body, and there are three intervals <note>meaning dimensions: length, width, and depth</note> of a body; therefore, it is necessary to have a triple interval for a place so that a body may be received within it. He also deduced these absurdities: that a place would not be equal to the body placed within it, since neither a line, nor a surface, nor a point is equal to it. Likewise, place would not be immobile, since the surface of the surrounding body moves along with its body. 

<margin>Refutation of a silent response.</margin>
Nor does it hinder his argument, he says, if one says "a place is equal to the body placed within it because it is fitted to its boundaries, and it is also immobile insofar as it is a place." For it is already accepted that a place ought to be equal not to what is *around* the place, but to what is *in* the place. Indeed, a place is held to be such insofar as it has a certain relationship to the body established within it—namely, by which it touches and contains it. In this same way, a place is mobile: for while I am standing still, the air surrounding me is nonetheless repeatedly changed, along with the outermost surface by which I was enclosed. Furthermore, if this surface alone (the surface of the containing body) is "place," it will happen that no one ever completes a journey by straight-line motion. For if nothing else gives way to the one going except a surface that is repeatedly changed—and many surfaces joined together create nothing larger—how then can even two stadia <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note>, let alone myriads <note>Units of ten thousand.</note> of stadia, be traversed? 

Philoponus also thought it was vain for Aristotle to think it follows necessarily that a three-fold dimension would, as it were, pass through the whole body placed within it, and thus divide and be divided such that infinite particles of both things would jump apart at once. This seems trivial to me, says Philoponus, and supported by no persuasion. For those who say that space is a body would not earn such absurdities—much less those who establish that space is incorporeal <note>bodiless or non-physical</note>, that is, a vacuum of body. When a body enters this space and fills it, it accomplishes nothing else besides that: it does not "pass through," it does not "divide," and finally, it neither acts nor suffers anything. Thus, other qualities prepare no division for the dimensions in which they exist; and they do not fail to do this insofar as they are qualities, but insofar as they are incorporeal. Wherefore, if a thousand qualities were composed and fitted to one thing, no division would come from it, for no other reason than that they are entirely incorporeal. It is no different for that three-fold dimension, which, if it were a dimension of division...
